question_text: All of the following microbial organisms are implicated in development of ICK except?
explanation:
It is hypothesized that commensal organisms from periocular skin or the ocular surface gain access to the stroma via suture tracks or through compromised unhealthy corneal epithelium. Microorganisms that can produce this type of infection include α haemolytic Streptococcus, Peptostreptococcus, Pseudomonas and Candida, and prolonged treatment with topical vancomycin, moxifloxacin or gatifloxacin eyedrops with discontinuation or minimization of topical steroid use is generally required. Recurrence of infection and stromal scarring are common which may then require keratoplasty.

Neisseriae Gonnorhoea is a highly virulent micro-organism that can invade healthy corneal epithelium whereas ICK is caused by low grade (low virulent) commensal micro-organisms that affect damaged corneal epithelium.

question_text: Identify the marked structure:
explanation:
Explanation:

The Canal of Petit (also called Spatia Zonularia) is a sac-like canal located around the equator of the lens. It is formed by the zonular fibers (zonule of Zinn), which secure the lens to the ciliary body. This canal is situated behind the suspensory ligament of the lens and contains aqueous humor between the zonular fibers. Its presence is an important anatomical feature of the eye, contributing to lens stability and ocular function.

  • Zonular Spaces (Spatia Zonularia):
    • Zonular fibers: Also known as the zonule of Zinn, these fibers attach the lens to the ciliary body and parts of the retina.
    • Anatomy: The fibers form a ring around the equator of the lens, connecting to the ciliary body. The spaces among them create a sacculated canal called the Canal of Petit or Hannover's Canal, collectively referred to as spatia zonularia.
    • Function: These spaces provide structural support for the lens and help in accommodation. They can also be artificially inflated via a fine blowpipe inserted beneath the suspensory ligament for anatomical demonstration.

Explanation of Other Options:

Canal of Hannover (Option B): A related zonular structure, sometimes used interchangeably with the Canal of Petit, but anatomically distinct. In this context, the marked structure represents the Canal of Petit.

Hyaloid Canal (Option C): Located in the vitreous body, this canal is the remnant of the fetal hyaloid artery. It is not associated with the zonular fibers or the lens equator.

Pars Plana (Option D): A portion of the ciliary body involved in surgical access (e.g., vitrectomy). It is unrelated to the canal structures surrounding the lens.

question_text: A 35-year-old female reports recurring episodes of discomfort, pain, and a sensation of pressure behind her left eye. She exhibits intermittent reducible proptosis, and her symptoms intensify when she bends forward. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The characteristic features of intermittent, reducible proptosis that worsens with bending forward or Valsalva maneuver strongly suggest orbital varices, which are venous malformations of the orbit.

Orbital Varices

  • Definition: Dilated venous channels in the orbit, considered part of developmental venous anomalies.
  • Typical Site: Usually unilateral, most commonly in the upper nasal orbit.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Intermittent, reducible proptosis.
    • Worsens with posture change, bending forward, or straining.
    • Sensation of retro-orbital pressure or pain.
  • Pathology: Single or multiple ectatic venous channels, sometimes fibrotic. Thrombosis may lead to phleboliths.
  • Imaging:
    • CT: Serpiginous enhancing venous channels; enlarge on Valsalva.
    • MRI: T1 - iso/low intensity, T2 - signal void from blood flow, enhancement with gadolinium except in thrombosis.
  • Treatment: Observation if mild. Surgery/embolization if severe.
  • Prognosis: Generally favorable unless optic nerve compression occurs.

Explanation of Other options:

Orbital Hemangioma (Option A): Although this could also cause proptosis, orbital hemangiomas typically present as more persistent and non-reducible. They also may cause symptoms due to gradual enlargement and are more commonly seen in children or young adults.

Orbital Metastasis (Option C): This is less likely because metastases generally cause more persistent, progressive symptoms and are associated with other systemic signs of malignancy. Proptosis in metastatic disease is usually non-reducible and associated with more severe, progressive symptoms.

Orbital Dermoid Cyst (Option D): Dermoid cysts are typically present at birth and may cause a constant mass, but they usually do not lead to the fluctuating symptoms described here. They are typically non-painful unless complicated by infection or rupture.

question_text: Bergmeister papilla is the remains of primary vitreous in which part of the eye?
option_a: At the posterior surface of lens
explanation:
During the development of eye, a blood vessel runs between the optic nerve and the back of the lens, called hyaloid vessel.

  • This vessel carries nutrients and oxygen to the developing parts of anterior section of eye.
  • This hyaloid vessel along with surrounding embryonic material is called primary vitreous.
  • Hyaloid vessels and primary vitreous begin to involute in the second month of gestation giving way to the secondary vitreous (the vitreous humor).
  • Small remnants of the system are common findings in healthy adults, e.g. Bergmeister papilla (tuft of tissue at the optic disc) and Mittendorf dot (tag of tissue on the posterior capsule of lens).
  • However, extensive remnants of this "hyaloid vessel - primary vitreous" system are called persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.


OBTURATOR HERNIA

Reference: Comprehensive Ophthalmology 7th ed. – A.K.Khurana, Ch-11 Diseases of vitreous

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with a painless, slowly growing, ulcerated, pearly papule-like mass with rolled-out edges at the medial canthus of his eye. On histopathological examination, the lesion shows the presence of keratin pearls and nuclear palisading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An ulcer on the medial canthus with rolled-out margins is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma. This is confirmed by a microscopic description showing nesting cells with peripheral palisading.

Explanation of Other Options:

Sebaceous carcinoma (Option C): An aggressive tumour commonly seen in the eyelids, often presenting with yellowish nodules, loss of eyelash growth, and a tendency to mimic inflammatory conditions (chronic blepharitis).

Merkel cell carcinoma (Option D): A rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumour appearing as a rapidly growing, red or violaceous nodule on sun-exposed areas, with small round blue cells and neuroendocrine markers (CK20, synaptophysin, chromogranin A).

Key Takeaway:

A painless, ulcerated, pearly mass with rolled-out edges at the medial canthus suggests basal cell carcinoma (BCC). The presence of nuclear palisading and basaloid tumour nests on histopathology further confirms the diagnosis. Early detection and surgical excision (Mohs micrographic surgery) offer an excellent prognosis.

question_text: A 15-year-old girl experiences blurry vision OS and a frontal headache. Her acuities are 20/20 OD and 20/60 without correction OS. With -2.00 D refraction she sees 20/20 OS. In the light, pupils measure 6 mm OD and 1 mm OS and in the dark they measure 7 mm OD and 1 mm OS. The right pupil is briskly reactive; the left does not react to light or near stimuli. Her examination is otherwise unremarkable. What type of drop did she use?
explanation:
• A sympathomimetic drop would dilate the pupil, not constrict the pupil. It would not produce a myopic shift, and the pupil would remain reactive to light and near stimuli.
  • A prostaglandin inhibitor would have no effect on the pupil, and an alpha adrenergic agent would have the same effect as a sympathomimetic.
  • Only a parasympathomimetic drop would constrict the pupil and induce the myopic shift.

question_text: An object is 100 cm from a +4 D concave mirror. Where is the image located in?
option_a: 20 cm to the right of the mirror
option_b: 20 cm to the left of the mirror
option_c: 33 cm to the right of the mirror
option_d: 33 cm to the left of the mirror
explanation:
Using the vergence formula:

U + D = V

−1 + 4 = + 3

  • Because V is positive, a real image located on the same side of the mirror as the object is formed.
  • Because U and V have opposite signs, the image is inverted compared to the object.
  • The location of the image is 1/V = 1/3 m = 0.33 m to the left of the mirror.
  • Ray tracing and vergence calculations also allow determination of the answer to these questions.
  • Remember that mirrors flip object and image space.
  • Therefore, the plus vergence “leaving” the mirror actually converges toward the left.

Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e, P. 28

Distance between far (infinity) and near point (30 cm)

Refractive power of eye in fully accommodative state - power at rest = power to focus at near - power to focus at far.

Grades of Binocular Single Vision (Worth's Grades):

Binocular Single Vision (BSV) is the ability of the brain to fuse the images from both eyes into a single, three-dimensional perception. As described by Worth, it is a hierarchical function consisting of three distinct grades, which are classically tested using a synoptophore.

question_text:
A patient is suffering from gyrate atrophy of choroid which is due to the deficiency of enzyme Ornithine aminotransferase.
Which of the following is beneficial for the patient?
explanation:
Ornithine aminotransferase deficiency(also known as gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina) is an inborn error of ornithine metabolism, caused by decreased activity of the enzyme ornithine aminotransferase. Biochemically, it can be detected by elevated levels of ornithine in the blood.

Clinically, it presents initially with poor night vision, which slowly progresses to total blindness. It is believed to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Research suggests there can be some adverse effect on muscles and also the brain. The cause of this is somewhat unclear but may relate to very low levels of creatine often found in this population.

Treatment may include vitamin B6, lysine or dramatic dietary change to minimize arginine from patient's diet.

Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 473.

question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor for idiopathic central serous chorioretinopathy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Idiopathic central serous chorioretinopathy (ICSC) is caused by choroidal hyperpermeability leading to serous detachment of neurosensory retina.

It has multiple known associations, and pregnancy is a recognised risk factor, especially during the third trimester, likely due to endogenous cortisol elevation.

  • Other common risk associations can be remembered as '3 S':
    • Steroid use (systemic/topical/inhaled/nasal)
    • Stress (Type A personality)
    • Smoking
  • Additional associations include:
    • Lupus
    • Organ transplantation
    • Hemodialysis
  • Anticoagulant use (Option A):There is no established association between anticoagulant therapy and idiopathic central serous chorioretinopathy. Anticoagulants do not affect choroidal circulation or stress-cortisol pathways involved in CSC.
  • Coexisting cancer (Option B):Coexisting malignancy is not a recognized risk factor for CSC. CSC is mainly linked to factors that increase cortisol levels or sympathetic drive, not to tumor-related physiology.
  • Female gender (Option D):CSC is more common in males, typically between 20-50 years of age (male predominance = 6:1). Therefore, female gender is not a risk factor.

question_text: This chart is used to check
explanation:
This is pelli robson chart

The Pelli-Robson (PR) chart is widely used to measure clinical contrast sensitivity (CS) by finding the lowest contrast letters he/she can read correctly.

Specifically, the chart uses letters (6 per line), arranged in groups whose contrast varies from high to low. Patients read the letters, starting with the highest contrast, until they are unable to read two or three letters in a single group. Each group has three letters of the same contrast level, so there are three trials per contrast level. The subject is assigned a score based on the contrast of the last group in which two or three letters were correctly read.

A score of 2.0 indicates normal contrast sensitivity of 100%. A Pelli-Robson contrast sensitivity score of less than 1.5 is consistent with visual impairment, and a score of less than 1.0 represents visual disability

question_text: Which refractive error is seen in a patient with complaints of eye strain with an image depicting the focus of rays in different medians in the eye?
explanation:
Explanation :

The given image represents the Sturm's conoid, which is the characteristic optical phenomenon seen in regular astigmatism.

  • In a normal eye (emmetropia), light rays from a point source converge to a single focal point on the retina.
  • In astigmatism, due to unequal curvatures of the cornea or lens in different meridians, the refractive power varies between the vertical and horizontal axes.
  • As a result, instead of a single focal point, two line foci are formed at different planes:
    • One for the vertical meridian
    • One for the horizontal meridian

This separation of foci produces a three-dimensional configuration of light rays known as the conoid of Sturm.

Key Features of the Conoid of Sturm:

  • Point A: Oval image (vertical rays converge faster → horizontal oval).
  • Point B: First focal line (vertical rays focus → horizontal line image).
  • Points C-E: Images appear as ovals/ellipses as rays diverge and converge at different rates.
  • Point D: Circle of least confusion → point where blur is minimal, closest to a "clear" image.
  • Point F: Second focal line (horizontal rays focus → vertical line image).
  • Point G: Vertical oval/ellipse as rays diverge further.

Explanation of other options:

Myopia (Option A): In myopia, the eye focuses parallel rays in front of the retina due to increased axial length or increased corneal curvature. Rays still converge to a single focal point, not two line foci. Hence, Sturm's conoid is not seen.

Hypermetropia (Option B): In hypermetropia, parallel rays are focused behind the retina due to short axial length or reduced corneal curvature. Like myopia, rays converge to a single point, not two. Sturm's conoid is not a feature.

Presbyopia (Option D): This is an age-related loss of accommodation due to decreased lens elasticity. The main defect is near-vision difficulty. Presbyopia is not associated with Sturm's conoid.

question_text: Esotropia is commonly seen in which type of refractive error?
explanation:
Accommodative esotropia is most commonly associated with hypermetropia (farsightedness). When a person with hypermetropia tries to focus on near objects, they engage excessive accommodation (the process of focusing the eyes). This increased accommodation also leads to excessive convergence (eyes turning inward), causing the eyes to cross. This is particularly common in children with moderate hyperopia, and correcting their hypermetropia with glasses often improves the condition.

Incorrect Options:

A. Myopia (Nearsightedness)
Myopia usually leads to exotropia (outward deviation of the eyes) rather than esotropia. In myopia, the eyes tend to diverge rather than converge, as the focus is naturally shifted to near objects.

C. Astigmatism
Astigmatism is a refractive error where the curvature of the cornea is irregular, leading to distorted or blurred vision. It doesn’t directly cause esotropia, though it can contribute to discomfort or difficulties in focusing, which could indirectly affect eye alignment.

D. Presbyopia
Presbyopia is the age-related loss of the ability to focus on near objects. While presbyopia may require reading glasses, it doesn't lead to esotropia as it primarily affects accommodation and near vision in older adults.

Key Takeaway: Accommodative esotropia is most commonly seen in individuals with hypermetropia. The excessive accommodation required to focus on near objects leads to excessive eye convergence, causing the eyes to turn inward. Corrective lenses can help resolve this issue by reducing the need for accommodation.

    • Differences up to 2.5 D: Usually well tolerated.
    • Between 2.5 D and 4 D: May be tolerated, depending on individual sensitivity.
    • More than 4 D: Generally not tolerated and becomes a matter of concern, as it can lead to visual discomfort or amblyopia.

Explanation of other options:

Difference in visual acuity (Option A): This may result from refractive errors such as myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, or presbyopia.

Difference in axial length (Option C): Seen in axial myopia, where the eyeball is longer than normal, leading to a myopic refractive state.

Difference in size of eyeball (Option D): Occurs in structural conditions like microphthalmia (abnormally small eye) and buphthalmos (enlarged eyeball, often due to congenital glaucoma).

question_text: Pathological axial myopia is
option_c: Usually between the ages of 5 and 10 years, and increases steadily  up to 25 years or beyond
explanation:
• Pathological axial myopia is degenerative and progressive.
  • The refractive change appears in childhood, usually between the ages of 5 and 10 years, and increases steadily up to 25 years or beyond, finally amounting to -15 or -25 D or more.
  • The degenerative changes in the fundus, on the other hand, do not appear until later in life, becoming marked at about the fifth decade.
  • The condition is strongly hereditary, being commoner in women than in men. It has a racial predilection, being common, for example, among Jews and Japanese and most cases are of genetic origin.
  • Many other aetiological theories have been advanced excessive accommodation and convergence in near work, vascular congestion due to a dependent position of the head, and so on but they have little to recommend them.
  • The condition is essentially a disturbance of growth on which are imposed the degenerative phenomena; these will be considered at a later stage
  • Endocrine or nutritional disturbances, debility or illness, probably act as incidental factors which may increase the general tendency; but, despite popular belief which still lingers, environmental conditions such as excessive near work probably have little influence upon the condition which is genetically pre-determined, except in so far as they inhibit normal healthy development.

Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 75

question_text: Which drug is commonly used for refraction in a child with accommodative squint?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cycloplegic drugs temporarily paralyze the ciliary muscle, thereby inhibiting accommodation and allowing accurate measurement of refractive errors. This is particularly important in children with accommodative squint, where uncorrected hyperopia can lead to esotropia.

  • Atropine 1% is the drug of choice in children under 5 years of age because it provides strong and sustained cycloplegia, ensuring accurate refraction.
  • For older children, other cycloplegics may be considered, but atropine remains most reliable for younger children and in cases of suspected accommodative squint.

Cycloplegic drug use by age group:

  • < 5 years: Atropine (1%)
  • 5-25 years: Homatropine
  • Elderly: Phenylephrine (for dilation, not cycloplegia)

Explanation of Other Options:

Cyclopentolate (Option B): Although cyclopentolate is widely used in pediatric refraction, it is less potent and shorter acting compared to atropine. In younger children with accommodative squint, it may not provide complete cycloplegia, leading to underestimation of hyperopia.

Tropicamide (Option C): Primarily a mydriatic, tropicamide provides inadequate cycloplegia, making it unsuitable for accurate refraction in children. It is mainly used for pupil dilation in fundoscopy.

Homatropine (Option D): Homatropine is used for cycloplegia in older children (5-25 years) but is not effective enough in younger children with strong accommodation. Hence, not the drug of choice in accommodative squint in early childhood.

Reference:

  1. Objective Refraction Technique: Retinoscopy - PubMed
  2. Retinoscopes: Past and present - PMC

question_text: Facultative hypermetropes manage to see because of:
explanation:
Latent hypermetropia:

It is the amount of hypermetropia which is corrected by normal physiological tone of the ciliary muscle. It is strong in young age and slowly declines with age.

Manifest hypermetropia:

The remaining portion which is not corrected by the normal physiological tone of the ciliary muscle, is called manifest hypermetropia. It is the hypermetropia that remains uncorrected in normal circumstance. That is when accommodation is not being actively used, or, in other words it is the total hypermetropia minus the latent hypermetropia. This manifest hypermetropia is again made of two components.

  1. Facultative hypermetropia
  2. Absolute hypermetropia

Facultative hypermetropia:

It is the part of hypermetropia, which can be corrected by an additional effort of accommodation or excessive strain of the ciliary muscle.

Absolute hypermetropia:

It is the part of hypermetropia which cannot be overcome by active exertion of accommodation.

  • Distance blurred vision
  • Difficulty in doing prolonged close work

question_text: In high myopia it is always wise to prescribe
explanation:
• In high myopia it is always wise to slightly under-correct even for distance, and the same or still weaker lenses may be ordered for near work.
  • In the highest grades, patients often see best with lenses which are decidedly weaker than the full correction; they should be allowed to choose those they prefer.
  • One reason is that strong minus lenses considerably diminish the size of the retinal images and make them very bright and clear.
  • The retinal images are diminished because the lenses have to be worn further from the eye than the anterior focal plane.
  • Spectacles for high myopia should therefore be made to fit as closely to the eyes as possible.
  • The very bright, clear images are uncomfortable because the retina has become accustomed to large and indistinct images.
  • Moreover, much artificial astigmatism and therefore distortion of the image is produced by looking obliquely through strong lenses.
  • Very shortsighted people thus get into the habit of turning the head rather than the eyes to avoid looking obliquely through the lenses.
  • Indeed, some high myopes can find their way about better without any spectacles. Contact lenses may be of great value in cases of this type.

Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 76

question_text: Axial ametropia is
option_b: Abnormal curvature of the refracting surfaces of the cornea or lens
option_c: Abnormal refractive indices of the media
explanation:
AMETROPIA

  • The condition in which incident parallel rays of light do not come to a focus upon the light-sensitive layer of the retina may be due to one or more of the following conditions:
    1. Axial ametropia: Abnormal length of the globe—too long in myopia, too short in hypermetropia. A 1 mm elongation produces approximately 3 D of myopia and 1 mm shortening 3 D of hypermetropia.
    2. Curvature ametropia: Abnormal curvature of the refracting surfaces of the cornea or lens—too strong a curvature in myopia, too weak in hypermetropia. A 1 mm change in the radius of curvature of the cornea produces a 6 D refractive change. Steeper (more curved) corneas produce myopia and flatter corneas hypermetropia.
    3. Index ametropia: Abnormal refractive indices of the media. In index myopia the refractive index, either of the cornea, the aqueous or of the lens (produced by a high index in the nucleus or a low index in the cortex or both) is too high, and that of the vitreous maybe too low as in a vitrectomized eye with silicone oil in the vitreous cavity. In index hypermetropia the opposite conditions are operative, and the error is high when the lens is absent as in aphakia or absence of the lens from the pupillary plane.
    4. Abnormal position of the lens: Displacement forwards causes myopia, displacement backwards hypermetropia.

Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 73

question_text: Esotropia is most commonly associated with:
explanation:
Esotropia is most commonly associated with hyperopia (farsightedness). In hyperopic individuals, the eyes need to accommodate (focus more) to see clearly, especially for near objects. This excessive accommodation can trigger an overactive convergence reflex, leading to accommodative esotropia, a common type of esotropia in children.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(B) Myopia - Myopia (nearsightedness) causes blurred distance vision but does not require excessive accommodation. Since accommodative effort is not increased, myopia is not typically linked to esotropia. Instead, high myopia is more commonly associated with exotropia due to reduced fusional convergence.

(C) Presbyopia - Presbyopia is an age-related loss of near focusing ability due to reduced lens elasticity. It does not cause esotropia but rather leads to difficulty reading up close. Unlike hyperopia, presbyopia does not induce excessive accommodation in younger individuals.

(D) Astigmatism - Astigmatism results from an irregular corneal curvature, leading to blurred vision at all distances. It does not directly cause esotropia, although uncorrected astigmatism may contribute to visual strain.

Key Takeaways:

  • Hyperopia is the most common refractive error associated with esotropia due to excessive accommodative effort leading to increased convergence.
  • Accommodative esotropia is often seen in children with uncorrected hyperopia.
  • Myopia and astigmatism do not typically lead to esotropia and may instead be associated with other ocular misalignments, such as exotropia.

question_text: A 60-year-old patient presents with reduced clarity of distant vision but reports no longer needing glasses for near work. Based on the ocular examination image, what is the term used to describe this refractive change?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the ocular examination image and findings, the term used to describe this refractive change is Index myopia.

  • Myopia(shortsightedness) is a refractive error where parallel rays of light from distant objects focus in front of the retina when the eye's accommodation is relaxed.
  • Index myopia is a condition that often occurs in older individuals, typically associated with age-related changes in the lens. As we age, the lens of the eye becomes denser and less flexible, which can lead to myopia (nearsightedness) in some cases.
  • The patient has reduced distant vision (a hallmark of myopia) but no longer needs glasses for near vision, which suggests that the lens has become more myopic (thicker or more curved) and is compensating for the near vision loss that typically occurs with presbyopia.
  • Index myopia is usually caused by the increase in refractive index of the lens with age, making it more myopic, particularly for distance vision.

Explanation for other options:

Axial myopia (Option B): Caused by an elongated eyeball. This typically leads to myopia from birth or early in life and doesn't relate to the lens changes seen with ageing.

Curvatural myopia (Option C): Caused by a change in the curvature of the cornea, which affects the focusing power of the eye. It's not related to the age-related changes in the lens.

Positional myopia (Option D): Refers to a refractive error caused by the position of the eye or the viewing distance (e.g., looking through different parts of the lens or an unusual gaze position). It's not linked to ageing lens changes like index myopia.

Reference:

  1. Defining and Classifying Myopia

question_text: Radial keratotomy corrects myopia by causing:
explanation:
Radial keratotomy: The method involves radial incisions made in the mid-peripheral cornea to flatten a central optical zone (usually 3.0-4.5 mm in diameter)

Before the innovations afforded with laser technology, RK and AK were the popular methods of refractive surgery. The use of incisional methods has significantly declined since the advent of PRK and LASIK approaches. The main visual disadvantages of RK and AK are glare from the peripheral wounds and fluctuating vision throughout the day. For athletes in particular, the incisions may increase the potential for significant damage to the cornea in blunt eye trauma. The cornea is weakened with RK and AK, and blunt trauma forces may cause globe rupture at the site of the corneal incisions. The positive aspect of RK compared to laser ablation procedures is that the central cornea is not directly altered, thereby preserving a central optical zone.

Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

question_text: When parallel beams of light come to focus on the retina with the eye at rest, it is known as:
explanation:
• Emmetropia is the condition in which any refractive error is absent because parallel beams of light come to focus on the retina, with the eye at rest.
  • Emmetropia = normal refractive status.
  • Parallel rays focus exactly on the retina when the eye is not accommodating.
  • It contrasts with ametropia, where rays do not focus on the retina.

Explanation of other options:

Ametropia (Option B): Condition where incident parallel rays of light do not come to a focus upon the retina.

Astigmatism (Option C): Refractive error due to irregular curvature of the cornea/lens; rays focus at different points.

Myopia (Option D): Rays focus anterior to the retina with accommodation at rest; also called short-sightedness.

Key Takeaways:

  • Emmetropia = no refractive error, perfect vision at rest.
  • Ametropia includes myopia, hypermetropia, and astigmatism.
  • Clinical differentiation is important for prescribing corrective lenses.

Reference:

Parson's Diseases of the Eye, 22nd Edition, Page Number: 72

question_text: Index myopia is seen in

Nuclear cataract is an exaggeration of normal ageing change.

It is often associated with myopia due to an increase in the refractive index of the nucleus, resulting in some elderly patients being able to read without spectacles again ('second sight of the aged').

This myopic shift in refraction known as index myopia.

The main mechanism of formation of nuclear cataract is conversion of the soluble crystallins to insoluble crystalloids.

question_text: Which of the following lenses would be recommended to correct myopia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Concave lenses which are the diverging lenses are used to correct Myopia.

Myopia

  • Also known as short-sightedness, it is the condition in which parallel light rays from infinity, as they refract on cornea and lens, converge at a focus in front of the retina.

Management:

  • Concave lens in the form of spectacle or contact lenses are used to correct myopia.

Surgical management

Surgical correction is only undertaken in individuals 21 years and older who have a stable refractive error for at least 1 year.

  • Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis
    • Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis or LASIK with the excimer laser is the most popular and widely accepted treatment modality among all the choices available at present.
  • Refractive Lenticule Extraction (SMILE):
    • A minimally invasive laser procedure where a small lenticule is removed to reshape the cornea.
    • Effective for myopia up to -10 D, with or without astigmatism.
  • Phakic Intraocular Lens (IOL) Implantation:
    • Implantable lens placed without removing the natural lens.
    • Best for myopia exceeding -8 D, especially in patients unsuitable for laser surgery.

Explanation of other options:

Convex lens (Option A): Convex lenses are used in correction of refractive errors associated with presbyopia and hypermetropia.

Cylindrical lens (Option C): Cylindrical lens is used for correction of astigmatism.

Abraham lens (Option D): A 66 D lens used for peripheral iridotomy with Nd:Yag laser.

question_text: Which of the following does not represent a standard corrected refractive error?
explanation:
Explanation:

Presbyopia is a condition related to age-related decline in accommodation, rather than a primary refractive error. It typically occurs around the age of 40 in emmetropic individuals, earlier in hypermetropic patients, and later in myopic patients. Correction usually begins with a +1 D spherical lens at around age 40, increasing by approximately 0.5 D per year as accommodation declines.

Correction of other refractive errors:

  • Myopia: Corrected using a concave lens to diverge light rays onto the retina.
  • Hyperopia: Corrected using a convex lens to converge light rays onto the retina.
  • Astigmatism: Corrected using a cylindrical lens to compensate for unequal curvature of the cornea or lens.

Pathophysiology of Presbyopia:

  • Age-related changes: Reduced elasticity of the lens capsule, sclerosis of the lens, and possible decline in ciliary muscle function.
  • Premature causes: Uncorrected hypermetropia and chronic glaucoma.

Symptoms:

  • Difficulty focusing on near objects
  • Eye strain (asthenopia)
  • Intermittent diplopia

Management:

  • Optical treatment: Convex glasses based on age, correcting distance vision first; options include unifocal, bifocal, or progressive lenses.
  • Pharmacological therapy: 25% Pilocarpine (FDA-approved).
  • Surgical options: Conductive keratoplasty, monovision or multifocal LASIK, corneal inlays, or multifocal intraocular lens implantation after lens extraction.

Explanation for Other Options:

question_text: A 6-year-old child is noted to have unequal refractive errors: -2.00 diopters in the right eye and +1.00 diopter in the left. Visual acuity and fundus examination are normal bilaterally. What is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
Anisometropia is a condition where there is a significant difference in the refractive power between the two eyes. In this case:

  • Right Eye (RE): -2D (Total refractive power: 62D → 60 + 2D)
  • Left Eye (LE): +1D (Total refractive power: 59D → 60 - 1D)
  • Difference in refractive power = 62D - 59D = 3D, which is greater than 2.5D, making it clinically significant anisometropia.

Anisometropia:

is a term used when the dioptric power of both eyes is not the same, and is significant if > 2.5D difference.

Myopia (Option A): Myopia (nearsightedness) is present in the right eye (-2D), but the left eye has hyperopia (+1D). The diagnosis should reflect the difference in refractive power rather than just the presence of myopia.

Hyperopia (Option B): Hyperopia (farsightedness) is present in the left eye (+1D), but since the right eye has myopia, this case is best classified as anisometropia rather than simple hyperopia.

Amblyopia (Option D): Amblyopia (lazy eye) can develop due to anisometropia if left untreated, but the question does not indicate decreased visual acuity. Therefore, anisometropia is the more accurate primary diagnosis at this stage.

question_text: A patient has been prescribed with -1D spherical and -2D cylindrical at 180°. What type of refractive error does this represent?
explanation:
Explanation for answer:

    • The cylindrical component (-2D) at 180° suggests astigmatism, with the greatest curvature occurring along the horizontal meridian.
  • In with-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism, the steepest curvature (maximum cylinder power) is aligned vertically at 90°, while the horizontal meridian (0° or 180°) remains flatter. Since this patient's cylinder axis is placed at 180° with a higher negative cylinder value, the case is consistent with WTR astigmatism.

Explanation of Other Options:

Against-the-rule astigmatism (Option B): Characterized by steepest curvature along the horizontal axis (0° or 180°) and the flatter meridian vertically at 90°. This is not applicable here.

Simple astigmatism (Option C): Seen when one meridian has no refractive error (emmetropic), but this case includes both spherical and cylindrical errors.

Mixed astigmatism (Option D): Involves one axis being myopic and the other hypermetropic. The current prescription shows only myopic errors, so this does not apply.

Key Takeaways:

  • With-the-rule astigmatism: vertical meridian > horizontal curvature.
  • Identified by a negative cylindrical correction at 180°.
  • Differentiated from ATR and mixed astigmatism by analyzing cylinder axis and spherical combination.

question_text: What is the primary optical cause behind regular astigmatism in a patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The fundamental cause of regular astigmatism lies in the uneven curvature of the cornea, which leads to varying refractive powers across different meridians of the eye. Because of this asymmetry, incoming light rays are not focused to a single point on the retina, resulting in blurred or distorted vision.

Astigmatism is a type of refractive error where the eye has unequal refractive power in different meridians. It is classified into two types: regular and irregular.

1. Regular Astigmatism:

Occurs when the refractive power changes consistently and symmetrically between two principal meridians. These meridians are typically perpendicular to each other, and the refractive error remains uniform along each.

Regular Astigmatism Based on Focal Lines:


2. Irregular Astigmatism:

 This type involves multiple meridians with varying refractive powers, resulting in a more complex and uneven corneal shape. It is often caused by corneal scars.

Explanation for other options:

Excessive eye rubbing (Option B): It can irritate the eyes and increase the risk of infections such as keratoconjunctivitis.

Prolonged exposure to bright light (Option C): It may cause eye strain and discomfort but does not cause astigmatism.

Vitamin A deficiency (Option D): It leads to xerophthalmia, which presents with night blindness and dry eyes, but is unrelated to astigmatism.

question_text: A factory worker presented with a history of chuna (lime) exposure in both eyes a few hours ago. What is the first immediate management?
option_d: Check IOP and plan for surgery
explanation:
Explanation:

Chuna or lime is an alkali substance and can cause chemical injury upon contact with the eye. Alkali burns are ophthalmic emergencies, and immediate, copious irrigation is the first and most crucial step to reduce ocular damage.

Chemical Injuries

  • Eye injuries caused by chemicals range from mild irritation to vision loss.
  • Sources of Injury
    • Domestic: Ammonia, detergents, cosmetics
    • Agriculture: Fertilizers, insecticides
    • Laboratory: Acids, alkalis
    • Assaults & Warfare: Acid attacks, chemical weapons
    • Self-inflicted: Malingering or mental health conditions

Clinical Stages

  • Acute: Conjunctival swelling, corneal epithelial loss, iris inflammation, possible corneal sloughing and staphyloma.
  • Reparation: Epithelial regeneration, corneal vascularization, iris inflammation subsides.
  • Complications: Symblepharon, recurrent ulcers, cataracts, secondary glaucoma.

Management

Chemical injuries can cause permanent vision loss, physical disfigurement and psychological impact despite treatment.

Explanation of other options:

Take history (Option A): Taking history is important but not the priority in an emergency. Every second matters in chemical burns, and delaying irrigation can worsen corneal damage.

Check vision in both eyes (Option C): Checking vision can be done after irrigation, but delaying decontamination increases ocular morbidity.

Check IOP and plan for surgery (Option D): Checking intraocular pressure (IOP) and planning for surgery is important after initial management. Alkali burns can cause secondary glaucoma, but irrigation takes precedence over any diagnostic steps.

question_text: What is the probable cause of uniocular diplopia in a young boy who has experienced trauma to his right eye?
explanation:
Explanation:

Iridodialysis is a separation of the iris root from the ciliary body, typically caused by blunt trauma. This creates an additional aperture or distorts the pupil, leading to uniocular diplopia (double vision that persists when the unaffected eye is closed) due to light entering the eye through multiple points.

Explanation of other options:

Paresis of extraocular muscle and Displacement of one eyeball (Option A and D): These cause binocular diplopia(double vision that resolves when either eye is closed) due to ocular misalignment.

Symblepharon (Option C): An adhesion between the eyelid and globe conjunctiva that restricts eye movement but does not cause diplopia.

Key Takeaways:

  • Uniocular diplopia is caused by an optical problem within the eye itself (e.g., cataract, iris defect).
  • Binocular diplopia is caused by misalignment of the eyes.
  • Iridodialysis is a common traumatic cause of uniocular diplopia.

question_text: A patient presenting with diminishing vision in dim light with dry eyes and rougheniing of corneal surface. Which of the following deficiencies can be associated with it?
explanation:
xerophthalmia refers to the spectrum of ocular disease caused by severe Vitamin A deficiency (VAD). Vitamin A serves several essential functions in the eye, and deficiency can lead to a constellation of ocular signs and symptoms that affect the conjunctiva, cornea, and retina. Xerophthalmia continues to be a leading cause of preventable blindness in developing countries. Unfortunately, xerophthalmia signifies a severity of VAD that causes significant morbidity and mortality from malnutrition and increased susceptibility to mucosal infections.

Diagnosis

Clinical Signs

Night blindness (Grade XN): Defective vision in dim light or night blindness is one of the most common manifestations of VAD, especially in children age 2-6 or pregnant or lactating women. Although it is considered one of the earliest manifestations, children with VAD may develop one of the more severe signs, such as corneal ulcers, after infection or diarrhea without any of the classically early signs. Children may not be able to verbalize their symptoms, and parents need to be asked if they have noticed their children behaving differently in the dark, e.g. becoming less active or fearful. Night blindness is considered to be both a sensitive and specific indicator for serum retinol levels.

Conjunctival xerosis (Grade X1A): Conjunctival xerosis is characterized by a dull and dry appearance of the conjunctiva with slight wrinkling. It is caused by the loss of goblet cells and insufficient mucin secretion, and it can be subtle and difficult to detect clinically.

Bitot spots (Grade X1B): Bitot spots are collections of desquamated, keratinized epithelial cells mixed with the gas-forming bacteria Corynebacterium xerosis. They appear as triangular patches of foamy, whitish, opaque deposits, typically located on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions. They are more common temporally.

Severe corneal xerosis progressing to keratomalacia. Credit: EyeRounds.org, The University of Iowa. Reprinted without modification from an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0 Unported License.

Corneal xerosis (Grade X2): Conjunctival xerosis is characterized by a dull and hazy appearance of the cornea that is caused by drying of the cornea secondary to conjunctival gland dysfunction. It may initially present with bilateral punctate corneal epithelial erosions, and it can quickly progress to the stage of corneal ulceration. Up to this stage, high-dose Vitamin A supplementation can result in the full preservation of vision.

Corneal ulceration (Grade X3A and B): Corneal xerosis can lead corneal ulceration and melting if not treated urgently. Keratomalacia, the melting away of the cornea by liquefactive necrosis, is the most severe form of xerophthalmia. It can perforate and destroy the cornea in just a matter of days. A child who appears relatively healthy but develops keratomalacia should be questioned about a recent history of measles or diarrhea, which could rapidly deplete already deficient vitamin A stores.

Corneal scar (Grade XS): Corneal scarring due to VAD is often symmetric and bilateral. Other causes of corneal scarring must be ruled out.

Xerophthalmic fundus (Grade XF): prolonged VAD can lead to structural changes in the retina. Fundus changes appear as small, white, deep retinal lesions scattered throughout the posterior pole.

question_text: What is a common ocular finding in pterygium?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most common visual disturbance caused by a pterygium is astigmatism, due to its pulling effect on the cornea, leading to corneal distortion and irregular refraction.

Pterygium/Surfer's eye

  • Pterygium is a triangular growth of vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva, typically arising in the interpalpebral area.
  • It represents a degenerative change of the subconjunctival tissue, which proliferates as a vascularized granulation tissue, extending onto the cornea and damaging the superficial stromal layers and Bowman's membrane.
  • More common in dry, sunny climates with sandy or dusty environments.
  • Ultraviolet (UV) light exposure is a likely contributing factor.
  • It typically affects elderly individuals.
  • Pterygium has three parts:
    • Cap: An avascular, halo-like zone at the advancing edge.
    • Head: The leading portion that encroaches onto the cornea.
    • Body: The main bulk of the pterygium.

Signs and Symptoms

  • Often follows a pinguecula and may be
  • Most commonly on the nasal side of the eye.
  • Visual impairment can occur due to:
    • Induced astigmatism
    • Encroachment into the pupillary area.
  • Causes corneal flattening along the axis of the pterygium, leading to astigmatism.
  • Appearance
    • Early stages show a thick, vascularized growth
    • Later stages become thin, pale, and atrophic, at which point growth usually ceases, but the tissue never completely disappears.
  • Stocker Line: Linear epithelial iron deposition seen in the corneal epithelium just anterior to the head of the pterygium.
  • Fuchs Islets: Small, discrete whitish flecks consisting of clusters of pterygial epithelial cells, often located at the advancing edge.

Management

General Approach:

  • Observation: Small, non-progressive pterygia can be left alone.
  • Medical Management:
    • Lubricating eye drops for associated dry eye or small regressive pterygium.
    • Topical steroids to control inflammation.
    • UV protection with sunglasses to prevent progression.

Indications for Surgical Excision:

  • Lesion encroaching on the pupillary area, causing visual impairment or significant astigmatism.
  • Restricted ocular movements, cosmetic disfigurement, or diplopia.

Surgical Procedures:

  • Bare Sclera Technique: Excision of pterygium leaving bare sclera; associated with high recurrence rates.
  • Autoconjunctival or Amniotic Membrane Graft: Graft from limbal conjunctiva or amniotic membrane used to cover bare sclera, sutured at the limbus; reduces recurrence.
  • Lamellar Keratectomy/Keratoplasty: For deeply infiltrating or recurrent pterygia.

Postoperative Care:

  • Mitomycin C 0.02% drops to prevent recurrence.
  • Monitor for complications such as scleral necrosis, cataracts, and iritis.

Differential diagnosis: Pseudopterygium

A pterygium-like lesion caused by cicatrizing conjunctival overgrowth from trauma, chemical burns, or chronic conjunctivitis.

Distinguishing Features:

  • Nonprogressive in nature.
  • Can occur at any quadrant of the corneal limbus, not necessarily nasal.
  • Adherent to adjacent eyelid and scar tissue, anchoring it to the underlying surface.
  • Unlike a true pterygium, a probe cannot be passed beneath the lesion at the edges.

Explanation of other options:

Eye pain (Option A): Pterygium can cause irritation, foreign body sensation, and redness, but severe pain is not a primary feature. Pain occurs only if there is inflammation or ulceration.

Macular edema (Option B): Pterygium affects the cornea and conjunctiva, but it does not involve the retina or macula. Macular edema is seen in conditions like diabetic retinopathy or retinal vein occlusion.

Purulent discharge (Option C): Pterygium is a non-infectious degenerative condition, so it does not cause purulent discharge. Discharge may be seen in bacterial conjunctivitis or dacryocystitis.

  • Forniceal Conjunctiva: Supplied by the peripheral arcade of the eyelid.
  • Limbal (Bulbar) Conjunctiva: Supplied by both:
    1. Posterior conjunctival arteries: Branches of the peripheral arterial arcade of the eyelids.
    2. Anterior conjunctival arteries: Branches of the anterior ciliary arteries.

These two systems anastomose near the limbus (corneal margin) to form the pericorneal plexus.

question_text: Identify the lesion in the superior limbus.
explanation:
Explanation:

These are small depressions seen at the limbus, especially superiorly, representing healed limbal follicles in trachoma, known as Herbert's pit.

They are a pathognomonic sign of trachoma and persist even after the disease has resolved.

Cicatricial Trachoma

Clinical Features:

  • Seen in middle age.
  • Conjunctival scars:
    • Mild: linear or stellate.
    • Severe: broad confluent scars (Arlt's line).
  • Most marked on the upper tarsal plate.
  • Herbert's pits: shallow depressions at the superior limbus from resolved follicles.
  • Complications:
    • Trichiasis, distichiasis.
    • Cicatricial entropion.
    • Corneal vascularisation + severe corneal opacification.
    • Dry eye (loss of goblet cells & lacrimal gland ductules).

Investigations

  • Usually not required (clinical diagnosis).
  • Field tests: dipstick enzyme immunoassay.
  • Other tests are similar to adult inclusion

Management- WHO SAFE Strategy

  • S - Surgery: for trichiasis/entropion (bilamellar tarsal rotation).
  • A - Antibiotics:
    • Single-dose azithromycin (20 mg/kg, max 1 g) = drug of choice.
    • Alternatives: erythromycin 500 mg BD × 14 days, doxycycline 100 mg BD × 10 days (avoid in pregnancy, lactation, children <12).
    • Topical tetracycline 1% ointment is less effective.
  • F - Facial hygiene: a crucial preventive measure.
  • E - Environmental improvement: clean water, sanitation, and fly control.

Explanation of other options:

Pannus (Option B): Refers to superficial vascularisation of the cornea due to chronic inflammation (common in trachoma). Appears as a hazy corneal opacity with vessels, not discrete pits.

Horner Tranta dots (Option C): Collections of degenerated eosinophils and epithelial cells seen at the limbus in vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). They appear as white, chalky dots-not depressions.

Bitot's spot (Option D): Triangular, foamy keratinised spots on the bulbar conjunctiva due to Vitamin A deficiency. Seen temporally, not at the limbus.

question_text: Goblet cells are seen in
explanation:
Goblet cells are seen in the epithelium of conjunctiva and help in tear production.

The conjunctiva is a transparent mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelids and the anterior surface of the globe, terminating at the corneoscleral limbus.

  • It is richly vascular, supplied by the anterior ciliary and palpebral arteries.
  • There is a dense lymphatic network, with drainage to the preauricular and submandibular nodes corresponding to that of the eyelids.
  • It has a key protective role, mediating both passive and active immunity.

Anatomically, it is divided into the following:

  • The palpebral conjunctiva starts at the mucocutaneous junction of the lid margins and is firmly attached to the posterior tarsal plates. The tarsal blood vessels are vertically orientated.
  • The forniceal conjunctiva is loose and redundant.
  • The bulbar conjunctiva covers the anterior sclera and is continuous with the corneal epithelium at the limbus.
    • Radial ridges at the limbus form the palisades of Vogt, the likely reservoir of corneal stem cells.
    • The stroma is loosely attached to the underlying Tenon capsule, except at the limbus, where the two layers fuse.
    • The plica semilunaris (semilunar fold) is present nasally, medial to which lies a fleshy nodule (caruncle) consisting of modified cutaneous tissue.

Histology -

  • The epithelium is non-keratinizing and around five cell layers deep.
  • Mucus-secreting goblet cells are located within the epithelium, being most dense inferonasally and in the fornices.
  • The stroma (substantia propria) consists of richly vascularized loose connective tissue.
  • The accessory lacrimal glands of Krause and Wolfring are located deep within the stroma. Secretions from the accessory lacrimal glands are essential components of the tear film.

Reference: Khurana Anatomy,2/e, P. 369

question_text: Which dye and filter have been used to obtain the appearance seen in the provided image?
option_d: Fluorescein dye, with e cobalt blue filter
explanation:
Explanation:

Fluorescein dye and a cobalt blue filter have been used to obtain the appearance seen in the provided image.

Fluorescein sodium

Fluorescein penetrates poorly into the lipid layer of the corneal epithelium, and therefore, it does not stain normal cornea. Although fluorescein is a very effective stain for the diseased cornea, it is more difficult to detect fluorescein staining of the conjunctiva because of the poor scleral contrast. Fluorescein absorbs light in the blue spectrum (490 nm) and emits yellow-green light of a higher wavelength (530 nm); therefore, staining can be more readily viewed if a cobalt blue or yellow (blue-free) filter is used. This combination is particularly useful for detecting corneal defects and ulcers.

Cobalt blue filter:

Cobalt blue is a filter that is commonly used in conjunction with fluorescein stain, as it enhances the fluorescence of fluorescein, making it easier to detect corneal defects. It absorbs light in the blue spectrum (around 490 nm) and helps the fluorescein stain emit a bright yellow-green fluorescence when illuminated.

Lissamine green dye

It has a high affinity for staining dead and degenerated cells, including mucous strands. The dye appears to stain areas where there are disrupted intercellular junctions. Use of a green (red-free) filter shows the stained areas to appear black. As it is better tolerated than rose Bengal, it is the preferred dye for staining the bulbar conjunctiva.

Explanation for other options:

Lissamine green dye green filter (Option A):

  • Lissamine green stains dead or degenerated cells and mucous strands on the conjunctiva, not corneal defects.
  • A green filter is used with lissamine green because it enhances contrast, making stained areas appear black. It's not effective for fluorescein.

Lissamine green dye, cobalt blue filter (Option B):

  • Lissamine green doesn't fluoresce, so a cobalt blue filter (which works with fluorescein) won't enhance its staining.
  • Cobalt blue is useful for fluorescein fluorescence, not for lissamine green, which requires a green filter.

Fluorescein dye green filter (Option C): Fluorescein works best with a cobalt blue filter for fluorescence, not a green filter. A green filter doesn't enhance fluorescein's fluorescence, making it less effective for detecting corneal defects.

Reference:

Ocular surface staining: Current concepts and techniques - PMC

question_text: Hypersensitivity to which drugs in particular causes SJS syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is an acute, life-threatening illness often caused by type IV hypersensitivity to drugs. Sulphonamides are the most classically implicated group of drugs.

It is characterized by acute ulceration of the conjunctiva and other mucous membranes (mouth, vagina). In the eye, conjunctival ulceration is followed by cicatrizing conjunctivitis. The clinical picture at the chronic stage (symblepharon, trichiasis, severe dry eye) is indistinguishable from Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid (OCP).

Explanation of other options:

  • Fluoroquinolones (Option A): While they can cause adverse reactions, they are not the classic primary trigger for SJS compared to Sulfa drugs.
  • Aminoglycosides (Option C): Topical use is known to cause punctate epithelial keratitis and local toxicity, but systemic SJS is rare.
  • Prostaglandins (Option D): Commonly used for glaucoma (e.g., Latanoprost), side effects include iris hyperpigmentation, eyelash growth (hypertrichosis), and Cystoid Macular Edema (CME), not SJS.

Key Takeaways:

Most Common Drugs causing SJS:

  1. Sulphonamides (cotrimoxazole, sulfasalazine)
  2. Anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine)
  3. Allopurinol
  4. NSAIDs (oxicams)

question_text: Which of the following microbial organisms is not likely associated with acute blennorrhoea?

A particularly severe form of acute purulent conjunctivitis is that due to N.gonorrhoeae. It is associated with moderate to severe pain and lid swelling with copious purulent discharge and tender, sometimes suppurative, preauricular lymphadenopathy. In typical cases, the discharge reaccumulates within seconds of cleaning. This form of conjunctivitis is also termed ‘hyperacute’ conjunctivitis or acute blennorrhoea by some. Gonococcal conjunctivitis occurs in two forms, as ophthalmia neonatorum in new born babies and as severe purulent conjunctivitis in adults. question_text: Which microbial organism is associated with Swimming pool conjunctivitis?
explanation:
Chlamydia inclusion conjunctivitis is generally spread by sexual transmission from a genital reservoir of infection. The primary source of infection is a benign subclinical venereal disease producing a mild urethritis in the male and cervicitis in the female. In adults, the organism may be transferred from the genitals by the fingers, but a common mode of infection is through the water in swimming pools; thus, the disease may occur in local epidemics (swimming pool conjunctivitis). It is also commonly transmitted from the mother to the new born when follicle formation is less evident. Serotypes D–K cause acute inclusion conjunctivitis and sero varieties A, B and C cause a chronic form of conjunctivitis known as trachoma.

question_text: Which of the following infections are least likely to be associated with C.trachomatis?
explanation:
Chlamydia trachomatis:

  • Chlamydia trachomatis is a bacterium that can cause various infections.
  • It is associated with both genital and oculogenital infections.

Associations with Chlamydia trachomatis include:

  • Non-gonococcal and post-gonococcal urethritis.
  • Cervicitis.
  • Salpingitis.
  • Epididymitis.
  • Bartholinitis.
  • Reiter disease.
  • About half of the cases of reactive inflammatory arthritis occurring as a sequel to sexually acquired non-gonococcal genital tract infections are associated with C. trachomatis.

Now, let's justify each option:

A) Adult inclusion conjunctivitis - Correct

  • Chlamydia trachomatis is associated with adult inclusion conjunctivitis.

B) Urethritis - Correct

  • Chlamydia trachomatis is commonly associated with non-gonococcal urethritis.

C) Cervicitis - Correct

  • Chlamydia trachomatis is commonly associated with cervicitis.

D) Mastoiditis - Incorrect

  • Mastoiditis is not typically associated with Chlamydia trachomatis. Instead, it is caused by bacteria from the Streptococcus and Staphylococcus families of cocci.

question_text: Which of the following conditions is not associated with chronic follicular conjunctival reaction?
explanation:
A) Pediculosis (Correct): Pediculosis, which is an infestation of lice, can lead to chronic follicular conjunctival reaction. Lice infestation in the eyelashes can cause irritation and inflammation of the conjunctiva, leading to the formation of follicles.

B) Pilocarpine use (Correct): Pilocarpine is a medication used to treat conditions like glaucoma and dry mouth. Pilocarpine eye drops can cause chronic follicular conjunctival reaction as a side effect. This is a well-documented adverse reaction associated with the use of pilocarpine eye drops.

C) Trachoma (Correct): Trachoma is an eye infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and is known to cause chronic follicular conjunctival reaction. It is one of the common causes of this condition, characterized by the presence of follicles on the conjunctiva.

D) Adenoviral infection (Incorrect): Adenoviral infection is not associated with chronic follicular conjunctival reaction. Adenoviral infections typically present as acute follicular conjunctivitis, which is characterized by the sudden onset of redness, discharge, and the formation of follicles on the conjunctiva. This is different from chronic follicular conjunctival reactions, which are typically associated with the conditions mentioned in options A, B, and C.

So, the correct answer is D) Adenoviral infection because it does not typically lead to chronic follicular conjunctival reaction; instead, it causes acute follicular conjunctivitis.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

Subconjunctival haemorrhages and enlarged preauricular lymph nodes are common. The cornea is usually affected.

Ophthalmia Neonatorum:It is a preventable disease occurring in a newborn child due to maternal infection acquired at the time of birth by contamination in the birth passage.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae conjunctivitis manifests the earliest, typically within the first 48 hours of birth. In cases of virulent gonococcal infection, the discharge rapidly becomes mucopurulent and then purulent. Both eyes are nearly always affected, with one usually worse than the other. The conjunctiva becomes intensely inflamed, bright red and swollen, with a thick yellow pus discharge. Marked chemosis is a distinguishing feature from severe mucopurulent conjunctivitis.May present as membranous conjunctivitis. As gonococci have the power of invading intact epithelium, there is a risk of corneal ulceration and perforation in untreated gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding phlyctenular conjunctivitis condition is/ are incorrect?
option_a: Nodules occur with same frequency in limbal and palpebral conjunctiva
option_b: Lesion represents allergic reaction to endogenous bacterial proteins
option_c: Congestion tends to be limited to area of phlyctens
option_d: In most cases, association with Tuberculosis is seen.
explanation:
A) Nodules occur with the same frequency in limbal and palpebral conjunctiva - Incorrect

  • Nodules in phlyctenular conjunctivitis are generally seen on the bulbar conjunctiva, particularly at or near the limbus. They rarely occur on the palpebral conjunctiva, contradicting option A.

B) Lesion represents an allergic reaction to endogenous bacterial proteins - Correct

  • There is considerable evidence that phlyctenular conjunctivitis is indeed an allergic condition caused by endogenous bacterial proteins, supporting option B.

C) Congestion tends to be limited to the area of phlyctens - Correct

D) In most cases, association with Tuberculosis is seen - Correct

question_text: Which of the following statements regards to management of phlyctenular conjunctivitis is/ are incorrect?
option_b: Anti-biotics are required in cases with corneal implication
option_c: Cycloplegic is added in cases with corneal involvement.
explanation:
Option A: Response to steroids is good.

This statement is correct. Topical steroids are the first-line treatment for phlyctenular conjunctivitis. They are very effective in reducing inflammation and relieving symptoms.

Option B: Anti-biotics are required in cases with corneal implication.

This statement is also correct. If the cornea is involved in phlyctenular conjunctivitis, antibiotics are necessary to prevent infection.

Option C: Cycloplegic is added in cases with corneal involvement.

This statement is correct. A cycloplegic is a type of eye drop that paralyzes the muscles that control the pupil. It is used in cases of corneal involvement to reduce pain and spasm.

Option D: Dark glasses help with photophobia.

This statement is incorrect. Photophobia is a sensitivity to light. Dark glasses may help with photophobia in other conditions, such as dry eye or uveitis, but they are not helpful in phlyctenular conjunctivitis. In fact, dark glasses may actually delay the resolution of the inflammation in phlyctenular conjunctivitis.

Now, lets know better about Phlyctenular conjuctivitis.

Definition:

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type of inflammation of the conjunctiva (the clear tissue that covers the white part of the eye). It is characterized by the formation of small, round, grey or yellow nodules on the conjunctiva.

Causes:

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is thought to be caused by an allergic reaction to bacterial proteins, most commonly from tuberculosis or other mild, long-standing infections such as those of the tonsils or adenoids.

Symptoms:

The symptoms of phlyctenular conjunctivitis include:

  • Discomfort
  • Irritation
  • Reflex lacrimation (excessive tearing)

If the cornea is involved, there may also be:

  • Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
  • Pain
  • Blurred vision

Diagnosis:

The diagnosis of phlyctenular conjunctivitis is based on the patient's medical history and physical examination. The doctor will look for the presence of phlyctenules on the conjunctiva.

Treatment:

Treatment for phlyctenular conjunctivitis typically includes:

  • Topical steroids to reduce inflammation
  • Antibiotics to prevent infection if the cornea is involved

In some cases, other treatments such as cycloplegics (eye drops that paralyze the muscles that control the pupil) or bandage contact lenses may be necessary.

Prognosis:

Most people with phlyctenular conjunctivitis make a full recovery. However, some people may have recurrent episodes of the condition.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: A 47-year-old patient reports to OPD with redness, fleshy growth in eyes and inability to open eyes fully. History is significant for fall of acid in affected eye few years back, which was managed conservatively. Lesion is non - progressive in nature. Clinical imaging is as shown.
explanation:
Pseudopterygium, which is in fact a pterygium like lesion, is induced by cicatrizing conjunctival inflammatory overgrowth produced by trauma, thermochemical burn or chronic conjunctivitis. Distinguishing features include a nonprogressive nature, location at any quadrant of the corneal limbus and not necessarily being nasal, appearance with adhesions to the adjacent lid and scar tissue anchoring the lesion to the underlying surface unlike a true pterygium beneath which a probe can be passed at the edges.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding conjunctival lymphomas is/are incorrect?
explanation:
Conjunctival lymphoma occurs on the bulbar conjunctiva or in the fornix. They are typically described as painless, slow-growing, salmon-coloured, i.e. light pinkish, mildly elevated, homogeneous lesions which can sometimes have small, round aggregations that look like fish eggs. An excision biopsy must be done to determine the diagnosis. Systemic lymphoma may be associated; hence, a thorough systemic evaluation is mandatory. Radiotherapy is effective in treating localized conjunctival lymphomas.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the condition depicted below is/are incorrect?
option_a: Limbus is a common site for occurrence
explanation:
Naevi or congenital moles are not uncommon. They are grey, gelatinous or pigmented nodules situated by preference at the limbus or near the plica semilunaris. They have the same structure as in the skin—groups, often alveolar, of ‘naevus cells’ in close connection with the epithelium. They are congenital and tend to grow at puberty, rarely becoming malignant. In view of this, they should be excised completely before puberty, lest malignant changes follow the operative disturbance. It is to be noted that pigmentation at the limbus occurs normally in people with dark complexions, and dark patches are not uncommon in them.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which systemic condition is associated with tear deficiency?
explanation:
Tear film instability may be a result of the following:

  • Deficiency of tears, as in Sjogren syndrome.
  • Deficiency of conjunctival mucus. Mucus from the goblet cells of the conjunctiva is necessary to keep the tear film stable. Lack of mucus causes premature breakup of the tear film even in the presence of abundant tear fluid. Mucus deficiency occurs in Stevens Johnson syndrome, ocular pemphigoid, avitaminosis, old trachoma or secondary to therapy with practolol.

Reference: Parson's Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following factors pre-dispose to dry eye?
explanation:
Systemic collagen vascular disorders, especially rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren syndrome, old age, diabetes mellitus, vitamin D deficiency, chronic use of topical ophthalmic medications, chronic conjunctivitis, chemical burns, chronic cicatrizing inflammatory eye disorders such as Stevens Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, chronic use of contact lenses, smoking, LASIK, and extensive and profound use of computers or viewing television or other electronic devices all predispose to dry eye. The condition can be triggered or exacerbated by low relative humidity, dry office environment, airconditioned cars or airplane cabins, and extreme weather conditions (hot/cold/windy).

Reference: Parson's Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which deposits are seen in Argyrosis?
explanation:
This is a deep brown staining of the conjunctiva from prolonged application of silver salts (silver nitrate, proteinate, etc.) for the treatment of chronic conjunctivitis and especially trachoma. Since these drugs are seldom used, the condition is rarely seen nowadays. The staining, which is most marked in the lower fornix, is due to the impregnation of reduced metallic silver into the elastic fibres in the membrane and vessel walls.

Epinephrine: Adenochrome deposits

ConjunctivoChalasis

This is a condition that is seen in elderly people with laxity of the conjunctiva leading to folds usually visibly heaped on the lid margin. It can be asymptomatic or produce ocular discomfort due to ‘dry’ eye and a foreign body sensation with tearing. Symptomatic relief can be provided by prescribing artificial tears four to six times a day, modifying the frequency as necessary. Sometimes, surgical excision of redundant folds (conjunctivoplasty) is required.
