question_text: Which of the following is/are not a feature of Superior Limbic keratoconjunctivitis?
explanation:
Superior Limbic Kerato-Conjunctivitis-SLKC

This is characterized by inflammation of the superior tarsal and bulbar conjunctiva and oedema of the corneoscleral limbal conjunctiva; corneal filaments are frequently present.

  • Fine punctate fluorescein and Rose Bengal staining of the superior cornea, limbus and conjunctiva is commonly done.
  • Fine papillae may be seen on the superior palpebral conjunctiva and a superior corneal pannus may develop.
  • The condition is usually bilateral, occurs frequently in females and follows a chronic course with remissions and exacerbations. The prognosis is excellent as eventual resolution usually occurs.
  • There is a strong association with thyroid diseases. Hence, thyroid function tests and clinical evaluation for thyroid dysfunction should be performed.

Management of SLKC:

  • Treatment is symptomatic, with the liberal use of topical ocular lubricants.
  • Temporary punctal occlusion with collagen punctal plugs, if required.
  • Any concurrent blepharitis should be treated with antibiotic ointment such as erythromycin or chloramphenicol applied four times daily for 1 week.

If corneal filaments and mucus strands are present in excessive amounts, then acetylcysteine 10% drops are added three to five times a day.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Which type of light is responsible for photophthalmia injury?
explanation:
Photophthalmia is caused by ultraviolet rays, especially from 311 to 290 nm.

Symptoms: Extreme burning pain, lacrimation, photophobia, blepharospasm and swelling of the palpebral conjunctiva and retrotarsal folds.

Signs:

  • It is due to desquamation of the epithelium leading to multiple erosions.
  • There is a latent period of 4 or 5 hours between exposure and the onset of symptoms.
  • The condition is generally caused by the bright flash of a short circuit or exposure to a naked arc light, as in industrial welding or cinema studios.
  • It is rarely due to exposure to enclosed arc lights since the glass globe absorbs the most deleterious rays.

In snow blindness, the cause and symptoms are similar, for the ultraviolet rays are reflected from snow surfaces.

Prophylaxis consists of wearing dark glasses, when such exposure is anticipated, made particularly of materials such as Crookes glass, which cuts off nearly all the infrared and ultraviolet rays.

Management:

  • Cold compresses
  • Lubricant drops

Comfort is obtained by bandaging both eyes for 24 hours to allow the epithelium to regenerate.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Hemorrhages in the conjunctiva can be seen in
explanation:
OCULAR MANIFESTATIONS OF NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCES:

  • Deficiency of vitamin A. Ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency are referred to as xerophthalmia.
  • Deficiency of vitamin B1(thiamine). It can cause corneal anesthesia, conjunctival and corneal dystrophy and acute retrobulbar neuritis.
  • Deficiency of vitamin B2(riboflavin). It can produce photophobia and burning sensation in the eyes due to conjunctival irritation and vascularization of the cornea.
  • Deficiency of vitamin C. It may be associated with hemorrhages in the conjunctiva, lids, anterior chamber, retina and orbit. It also delays wound healing.
  • Deficiency of vitamin D. It may be associated with zonular cataract, papilledema and increased lacrimation.

Reference: A.K khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 433.

question_text: A young boy from a low socioeconomic background presents with conjunctival hyperemia and yellowish nodules at the limbus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to bacterial antigens, commonly Staphylococcus aureus in Western countries and Mycobacterium tuberculosis in regions like India. Children from poorer socioeconomic backgrounds are more susceptible due to higher exposure to infections.

Clinical Features:

  • Conjunctival hyperemia and irritation
  • Watering and itching
  • Reflex blepharospasm(involuntary blinking)
  • Phlycten: Small, round, greyish or yellowish nodules near the limbus
  • Corneal involvement: May develop fascicular or ring ulcers, potentially causing scarring

Pathophysiology:

  • Type IV hypersensitivity response to bacterial or tubercular antigens

Complications:

  • Corneal ulcers and scarring
  • Visual impairment, if untreated

Treatment:

  • Local therapy:
    • Corticosteroid drops/ointment to reduce inflammation
    • Address underlying infection (e.g., antitubercular therapy if TB-related)
    • Topical antibiotics for secondary infection
    • Cycloplegics to relieve ciliary spasm and pain
    • Dark glasses or eye shade for photophobia
  • Systemic therapy:
    • Oral tetracycline or doxycycline in recurrent cases associated with Staphylococcal blepharitis

Explanation for Other Options:

Bitot's spots (option A): Grayish-white, triangular plaques on the conjunctiva caused by Vitamin A deficiency, not associated with acute nodules or hyperemia.

Pterygium (option B): A fibrovascular growth of the conjunctiva extending onto the cornea, usually related to UV exposure, not infection.

Pinguecula (option C): A yellowish, benign conjunctival thickening near the limbus due to UV or environmental factors; it is asymptomatic and non-inflammatory.

question_text: Which of the following statements is not an accurate description of the clinical condition?
option_a: Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue
option_b: Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen
option_c: Destruction of Bowman’s layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea
option_d: Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur
explanation:
Explanation:

The statement about Bowman's layer is not accurate in the context of pterygium. Pterygium typically extends onto the cornea but does not invade Bowman's layer. Instead, it grows over the superficial corneal surface, leading to irritation and visual distortion.

Explanation for other options:

Abnormal p53 activity is observed in pterygium tissue (Option A): This is correct. Pterygium is associated with altered expression of p53, a tumor suppressor gene involved in regulating cell growth and preventing tumor development.

Reduced activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) (Option B): This is correct. Pterygium is linked to an imbalance between matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and TIMPs, resulting in excessive tissue remodeling.

Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of conjunctival connective tissue (Option D): This is correct. These are characteristic histological features of pterygium, involving the accumulation of abnormal elastic fibers and hyaline material in the conjunctiva.

question_text: Above image shows
explanation:
Clinical features of Vitamin A Deficiency

  • X N(night blindness): It is the earliest symptom of xerophthalmia in children. It has to be elicited by taking detailed history from the guardian or relative.
  • X1A(conjunctival xerosis): It consists of one or more patches of dry, lusterless, non-wettable conjunctiva, which has been well described as 'emerging like sand banks at receding tide' when the child ceases to cry. These patches almost always involve the inter-palpebral area of the temporal quadrants and often the nasal quadrants as well. In more advanced cases, the entire bulbar conjunctiva may be affected. Typical xerosis may be associated with conjunctival thickening, wrinkling and pigmentation.
  • X1B(Bitot's spots): It is an extension of the xerotic process seen in stage X1A. The Bitot's spot is a raised, silvery white, foamy, triangular patch of keratinized epithelium, situated on the bulbar conjunctiva in the inter-palpebral area. It is usually bilateral and temporal and less frequently nasal.
  • X2(corneal xerosis): The earliest change in the cornea is punctate keratopathy which begins in the lower nasal quadrant, followed by haziness and/or granular pebbly dryness. Involved cornea lacks luster.
  • X3A and X3B(corneal ulceration/keratomalacia): Stromal defects occur in the late stage due to colliquative necrosis and take several forms. Small ulcers(1-3 mm) occur peripherally; they are characteristically circular, with steep margins and are sharply demarcated. Large ulcers and areas of necrosis may extend centrally or involve the entire cornea. If appropriate therapy is instituted immediately, stromal defects involving less than one-third of corneal surface(X3A) usually heal, leaving some useful vision. However, larger stromal defects(X3B) commonly result in blindness.
  • XS(corneal scars): Healing of stromal defects results in corneal scars of different densities and sizes which may or may not cover the pupillary area. A detailed history is required to ascertain the cause of corneal opacity.
  • XFC(Xerophthalmic fundus): It is characterized by typical seed-like, raised, whitish lesions scattered uniformly over the part of the fundus at the level of optic disc.

Reference: A.K Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 433.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Trachoma infection is incorrect?
option_b: papillae gives velvety appearance on conjunctiva
option_c: Initial symptoms are non specific- foreign body sensation/ irritation/ discharge
option_d: Characterisitic follicles are mainly seen in lower fornix
explanation:
Source of infection: It spreads by the transfer of conjunctival secretions through fingers or towels and, above all, by flies, which are attracted by the presence of profuse ocular discharge. On the other hand, scrupulous cleanliness prevents extension of the disease to healthy subjects.

Clinical features

  • Symptoms: It is mainly associated with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation and discharge. When chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation and photophobia and later blurring and finally severe loss of vision.
  • Signs: These include conjunctival congestion, papillary enlargement and the development of follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva. The essential lesion is the trachomatous follicle. Their distribution is characteristic. They may commence in the lower fornix, but in most cases, they quickly appear in the upper fornix as well, where they are usually most accentuated, often forming a row along the upper margin of the tarsus as well as generally over the palpebral conjunctiva. They are rare on the bulbar conjunctiva.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

option_b: Papillae give a velvety appearance to the conjunctiva
option_c: Initial symptoms are non-specific: foreign body sensation/ irritation/ discharge
option_d: Characteristic follicles are mainly seen in the lower fornix
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Trachomatous follicles have a characteristic distribution.
  • They may commence in the lower fornix, but in most cases, they quickly appear in the upper fornix as well, where they are usually most accentuated, often forming a row along the upper margin of the tarsus as well as generally over the palpebral conjunctiva.

Trachoma infection:

  • Source: It spreads by the transfer of conjunctival secretions through fingers or towels and, above all, by flies, which are attracted by the presence of profuse ocular discharge (Option A). On the other hand, scrupulous cleanliness prevents extension of the disease to healthy subjects.

Clinical features

Symptoms:

  • It is mainly associated with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (Option B).
  • When chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation and photophobia and later blurring and finally severe loss of vision.

Signs:

  • These include conjunctival congestion, papillary enlargement, and the development of follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva.
  • The essential lesion is the trachomatous follicle.

question_text: A patient who wears contact lenses presents with eye watering, redness, and a sensation of having a foreign object in the eye for the last two months. On ocular examination, the following findings were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows large, polygonal papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, which, along with the described clinical presentation, suggest a diagnosis of Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis. 

Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis: 

Specific allergic inflammation affecting the superior tarsal conjunctiva, usually mechanically induced mediated by hypersensitivity reactions types I and IV.

Etiology

  • Soft hydrophilic contact lenses
  • Protruding suture ends
  • Ocular prostheses

Signs and symtpoms

  • Commonly presentations include excessive watering, foreign body sensation and diminished or blurred vision.
  • Signs include conjunctival congestion predominantly in the upper palpebral region with large polygonal papillae on superior tarsal conjunctiva.

Management

  • Discontinue soft contact lenses, remove offending sutures, clean and polish ocular prosthesis; replace with biocompatible material (e.g., Biocoat).
  • Ancillary therapy: Mast cell stabilizers (e.g., lodoxamide, cromolyn sodium, olopatadine) along with artificial tears, antihistaminic drops, and decongestants.

Explanation of other options:

Follicular Conjunctivitis (Option A): The most common clinical form of viral conjunctivitis. Presents as a milder form of acute conjunctivitis (less symptoms). Follicular appearance of conjunctiva is seen on examination.

Spring Catarrh (Option B): Also known as vernal keratoconjunctivitis characterized by seasonal symptoms, cobblestone-like papillae, limbal thickening with Horner-Trantas dots, and potential corneal involvement, unlike giant papillary conjunctivitis, which typically presents with large papillae associated with contact lens use.

Trachoma (Option D): Trachoma caused by chlamydia trachomatis shows the typical sago grain appearnce with other signs like arlt line and herbert pits.

question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with severe itching eyes and photophobia with sticky discharge. On examination, the findings shown in the image are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms of intense itching and sticky (ropy) discharge, along with the presence of hard, flat-topped papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with a cobblestone appearance as shown in the image are characteristic of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (Spring catarrh):

  • Recurrent bilateral conjunctivitis tends to occur with the onset of warm weather.
  • It primarily affects young children and adolescents, particularly boys.
  • Mediated by Type I hypersensitivity and Type IV hypersensitivity.
  • The condition typically starts in childhood and may resolve on its own over 5-10 years.

2 types:

  • Palpebral VKC:
    • Primarily involves the upper tarsal conjunctiva.
    • It may be associated with significant corneal disease as a result of the close apposition between the inflamed conjunctiva and the corneal epithelium.
  • Limbal Disease: Typically affects black and Asian patients.

Symptoms:

  • Burning, Itching, photophobia and lacrimation.

Signs

  • Palpebral disease:
    • Characterised by hypertrophied palpebral conjunctiva with a cobblestone appearance
    • Dense fibrous tissue with thickened epithelium.
  • Limbal disease
    • Opacification at the limbus
    • Gelatinous thickening
    • Horner-Trantas dots

Fig: Pappilae with Horner-Trantas Dots

  • Pseudogerontoxon/cupid's bow (which resembles arcus senilis) is a grayish-white ring at the limbus seen in severe limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).
  • Shield ulcers are a significant complication of VKC, particularly in severe cases. These micro erosions typically form on the upper third of the cornea.
  • Mixed form: Exhibits characteristics of both the tarsal (palpebral) and limbal subtypes, typically presenting in only one eye.
    • Maxwell Lyon's sign is a pseudomembrane formed due to excessive mucus deposition on the papilla resulting in cobblestone papillae.

Explanation of other options:

Trachoma (Option A): Trachoma typically presents with the sago-grain appearance of conjunctiva.

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option C): Type of hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous antigens like bacterial antigens, staphylococcal & tuberculosis antigens. It presents as a small, white, or yellowish nodule (phlyctenule) near the limbus and conjunctival congestion.

Xerophthalmia (Option D): Xerophthalmia is a spectrum of ocular disease caused due to vitamin A deficiency. It is characterized by night blindness (earliest feature), conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spot, corneal xerosis, ulcer, keratomalacia.

question_text: On ocular examination, the following findings were observed in the patient. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows the sago grain appearance of the follicles in conjunctiva, seen in the active stage of trachoma caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

  • Trachoma is the world's leading cause of preventable irreversible blindness.
  • Features of trachoma are divided into an 'active' inflammatory stage and a cicatricial chronic stage, with considerable overlap.

Active trachoma is most common in pre-school children and is characterized by the following:

  • Mixed follicular/papillary conjunctivitis associated with a mucopurulent discharge.
  • In children under the age of 2 years the papillary component may predominate.
  • Superior epithelial keratitis and pannus formation

Cicatricial trachoma is prevalent in middle age and manifests with

  • Linear or stellate conjunctival scars in mild cases, or broad confluent scars called the Arlt line in severe disease.

Fig: Arlt line and conjunctival follicles

  • Although the entire conjunctiva is involved, the effects are most prominent on the upper tarsal plate.
  • Superior limbal follicles may resolve to leave a row of shallow depressions - Herbert pits.

Fig: Herbert pits

  • Trichiasis, distichiasis, corneal vascularization and cicatricial entropion.
  • Severe corneal opacification.
  • Dry eye caused by destruction of goblet cells and the ductules of the lacrimal gland.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 5-year-old boy who is experiencing severe itching, and thick discharge from his eyes. Upon examination the following finding as shown in the image was observed.
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of severe itching, thick discharge, and the finding of cobblestone papillae on the tarsal conjunctiva in a young boy is pathognomonic for the palpebral form of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). VKC is a chronic, bilateral allergic condition, common in children and young adolescents, often with a seasonal pattern.

Key Features:

Signs:

  • Palpebral Form:
    • Cobblestone papillae on upper tarsal conjunctiva.
  • Limbal Form:
    • Gelatinous limbal thickening, Horner-Trantas dots (chalky deposits).
    • Pseudogerontoxon (arcus-like limbal ring in severe cases).
  • Mixed Form: Features of both palpebral and limbal forms.

Complications:

  • Shield ulcers (corneal erosions, typically superior).
  • Maxwell Lyon's sign (mucus pseudomembrane on papillae).

Treatment:

Medical:

  • Topical:
    • Mast cell stabilizers (e.g., sodium cromoglicate).
    • Antihistamines (e.g., levocabastine).
    • Mild steroids (e.g., fluorometholone, loteprednol).
    • Acetylcysteine (for mucus reduction).
  • Supportive: Cold compresses, tinted glasses.

Surgical (for severe cases):

  • Excision of giant papillae.
  • Amniotic membrane graft/bandage lens for shield ulcers.
  • Subtarsal steroid injections or cryotherapy.

Avoid: Eye rubbing.

Explanation of other options:

Trachoma (Option A): Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, it leads to conjunctival scarring (e.g., Arlt's line) and trichiasis, not cobblestone papillae or severe itching.

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option C): Presents as small, yellowish nodules (phlyctenules) near the limbus, typically associated with tuberculosis or staphylococcal hypersensitivity, not giant papillae.

Xerophthalmia (Option D): Results from Vitamin A deficiency, causing conjunctival and corneal xerosis, Bitot's spots, and night blindness, not itching or papillae.

Key Takeaways:

  • Severe itching and cobblestone papillae are hallmark signs of VKC.
  • VKC primarily affects young males and is often associated with a personal or family history of atopy.

question_text: Which of the following surgical techniques for pterygium is most likely to be complicated by recurrence?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • After excision, leaving the sclera exposed (bare) results in a very high recurrence rate.
  • This technique is no longer preferred because recurrence can be aggressive and fibrovascular.

Methods to reduce recurrence:

  • Postoperative therapy with mitomycin C drops has been tried, but complications such as scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis have been reported. (Option B)
  • Performing an auto conjunctival graft (taking a piece of limbal conjunctival tissue from the same or the other eye), or an amniotic membrane graft and suturing it at the limbus to cover the defect produced by excising the pterygium (Option C & D)

question_text: Which of the following treatment options is most frequently used for recurrent pterygium?
explanation:
Explanation:

A conjunctival autograft is the most frequent preferred management for recurrent pterygium.

Pterygium

  • Pterygium is a triangular encroachment of the vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva in the interpalpebral area.
  • It is often bilateral, usually present on the nasal side.
  • Vision becomes impaired due to induced astigmatism or progression into the pupillary area of the cornea.
  • Clinically, it appears thick and vascular in the early stages but becomes thin, pale and atrophic in later stages when it ceases to grow but never disappears.

Management of pterygium:

Reassurance/Observation: if not causing any visual problems (Option C ruled out).

Medical management:

  • Tear substitutes for small regressive pterygium with dry eye
  • Topical steroids for associated inflammation
  • Protection from UV rays with sunglasses

Surgical management

Indications

  • Progression of lesion towards the pupillary area causing excessive astigmatism and visual impairment
  • Restricted ocular movements
  • Disfiguring
  • Diplopia

Surgical Methods

  • Bare sclera technique:
    • The pterygium is excised from the cornea and conjunctiva, leaving a bare sclera
    • Associated with a high recurrence rate (Option D ruled out)
  • Auto conjunctival graft:
    • A piece of limbal conjunctival tissue from the same or the other eye or an amniotic membrane graft is used to cover the bare sclera
    • Sutured at the limbus to cover the defect
    • Less recurrence rate
  • Surgical excision with lamellar keratectomy and lamellar keratoplasty for deeply infiltrating recurrent recalcitrant pterygia

question_text: What is incorrect about this lesion?
option_a: Consist of head, neck, and body
option_b: Simple excision can reduce recurrence by 90-95%
explanation:
A pterygium of the eye (plural pterygia or pterygiums, also called surfer's eye) is a pinkish, roughly triangular tissue growth of the conjunctiva onto the cornea of the eye. It typically starts on the cornea near the nose. It may slowly grow but rarely grows so large that it covers the pupil and impairs vision. Often both eyes are involved.

The cause is unclear. It appears to be partly related to long term exposure to UV light and dust. Genetic factors also appear to be involved. It is a benign growth. Other conditions that can look similar include a pinguecula, tumor, or Terrien's marginal corneal degeneration.

Prevention may include wearing sunglasses and a hat if in an area with strong sunlight. Among those with the condition, an eye lubricant can help with symptoms. Surgical removal is typically only recommended if the ability to see is affected. Following surgery a pterygium may recur in around half of cases.

The frequency of the condition varies from 1% to 33% in various regions of the world. It occurs more commonly among males than females and in people who live closer to the equator. The condition becomes more common with age. The condition has been described since at least 1000 BC.

Signs and symptoms

Small pterygium

Large primary pterygium invading the pupil (visual axis)

Symptoms of pterygium include persistent redness, inflammation, foreign body sensation, tearing, dry and itchy eyes. In advanced cases the pterygium can affect vision as it invades the cornea with the potential of obscuring the optical center of the cornea and inducing astigmatism and corneal scarring. Many patients do complain of the cosmetic appearance of the eye either with some of the symptoms above or as their major complaint. The use of standard contact lenses can become uncomfortable or even impossible although custom shaping may improve the fit to some extent.[citation needed]

Cause

The exact cause is unknown, but it is associated with excessive exposure to wind, sunlight, or sand. Therefore, it is more likely to occur in populations that inhabit the areas near the equator, as well as windy locations. In addition, pterygia are twice as likely to occur in men than women.

Pathology

Micrograph of a conjunctiva associated with prominent blood vessels (left-bottom of image) and elastotic collagen (centre of image), as may be seen in a pterygium. H&E stain.

Pterygium in the conjunctiva is characterized by elastotic degeneration of collagen (actinic elastosis) and fibrovascular proliferation. It has an advancing portion called the head of the pterygium, which is connected to the main body of the pterygium by the neck. Sometimes a line of iron deposition can be seen adjacent to the head of the pterygium called Stocker's line. The location of the line can give an indication of the pattern of growth.

The predominance of pterygia on the nasal side is possibly a result of peripheral light focusing, where the sun's rays passing laterally through the cornea, where they undergo refraction and become focused on the limbic area. Sunlight passes unobstructed from the lateral side of the eye, focusing on the medial limbus after passing through the cornea. On the contralateral (medial) side, however, the shadow of the nose medially reduces the intensity of sunlight focused on the lateral/temporal limbus.

Some research also suggests a genetic predisposition due to an expression of vimentin, which indicates cellular migration by the keratoblasts embryological development, which are the cells that give rise to the layers of the cornea. Supporting this fact is the congenital pterygium, in which pterygium is seen in infants. These cells also exhibit an increased P53 expression likely due to a deficit in the tumor suppressor gene. These indications give the impression of a migrating limbus because the cellular origin of the pterygium is actually initiated by the limbal epithelium.

The pterygium is composed of several segments:

Fuch's Patches (minute gray blemishes that disperse near the pterygium head)

Stocker's Line (a brownish line composed of iron deposits)

Hood (fibrous nonvascular portion of the pterygium)

Head (apex of the pterygium, typically raised and highly vascular)

Body (fleshy elevated portion congested with tortuous vessels)

Superior Edge (upper edge of the triangular or wing-shaped portion of the pterygium)

Inferior Edge (lower edge of the triangular or wing-shaped portion of the pterygium).

Diagnosis

Pterygium (conjunctiva) can be diagnosed without need for a specific exam, however corneal topography is a practical test (technique) as the condition worsens.

Differential Diagnosis

Pterygium should be differentiated from pinguecula, which is histologically and etiologically similar to pterygium. Unlike pterygium, pinguecula is seen only on the conjunctiva, it will not progress to limbus or cornea.

Another condition which is similar to pterygium is inflammatory adhesion of conjunctiva to cornea known as pseudopterygium. Unlike pterygium, it may occur anywhere around cornea and the adhesion is usually limited to its apex.

Prevention

As it is associated with excessive sun or wind exposure, wearing protective sunglasses with side shields and/or wide brimmed hats and using artificial tears throughout the day may help prevent their formation or stop further growth. Surfers and other water-sport athletes should wear eye protection that blocks 100% of the UV rays from the water, as is often used by snow-sport athletes. Many of those who are at greatest risk of pterygium from work or play sun exposure do not understand the importance of protection.

Treatment

A pterygium typically does not require surgery unless it grows to such an extent that it causes visual problems. Some of the symptoms such as irritation can be addressed with artificial tears. Surgery may also be considered for unmanageable symptoms.

Surgery

Pterygium removal surgery

A Cochrane review found conjunctival autograft surgery was less likely to have reoccurrence of the pterygium at 6 months compared to amniotic membrane transplant. More research is needed to determine which type of surgery resulted in better vision or quality of life.The additional use of mitomycin C is of unclear effect. Radiotherapy has also been used in an attempt to reduce the risk of recurrence.

Auto-grafting

Conjunctival auto-grafting is a surgical technique that is an effective and safe procedure for pterygium removal. When the pterygium is removed, the tissue that covers the sclera known as the Tenons layer is also removed. Auto-grafting covers the bare sclera with conjunctival tissue that is surgically removed from an area of healthy conjunctiva. That "self-tissue" is then transplanted to the bare sclera and is attached using sutures or tissue adhesive.

Amniotic membrane transplantation

Amniotic membrane transplantation is an effective and safe procedure for pterygium removal. Amniotic membrane transplantation offers practical alternative to conjunctival auto graft transplantation for extensive pterygium removal. Amniotic membrane transplantation is tissue that is acquired from the innermost layer of the human placenta and has been used to replace and heal damaged mucosal surfaces including successful reconstruction of the ocular surface. It has been used as a surgical material since the 1940s, and has been shown to have a strong anti-adhesive effect.

Using an amniotic graft facilitates epithelialization, and has anti-inflammatory as well as surface rejuvenation properties. Amniotic membrane transplantation can also be attached to the sclera using sutures, or glue adhesive. Amniotic membrane by itself does not provide an acceptable recurrence rate.

Incorrect Option Explanations:

Option A : Consist of head, neck, and body - Pterygium consists of distinct anatomical parts, including the head, neck, and body.

Option C : Progressive and regressive type - Pterygium can be classified as either progressive, where it actively grows towards the cornea, or regressive, where growth remains static or decreases.

Option D : Elastoid degeneration of collagen - Pterygium is characterized by elastoid degeneration of collagen (actinic elastosis), which contributes to its fibrovascular growth.

Key Takeaway:

Pterygium is a fibrovascular growth of the conjunctiva that can be progressive or regressive and involves elastoid degeneration of collagen. Simple excision alone does not effectively prevent recurrence, making adjunctive measures necessary for long-term success.

Explanation:

The ocular condition illustrated in the image is active trachoma, an infectious disease caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. It is the leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide, most prevalent in areas with inadequate sanitation and limited healthcare access.

  • Signs of Active Trachoma
    • Conjunctival signs:
      • Conjunctival congestion
      • Follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva (resembling sago-grains)
      • Papillary hypertrophy giving a red, velvety appearance
    • Corneal signs:
      • Superficial keratitis (detected on slit-lamp with fluorescein)
      • Herbert's follicles
      • Progressive pannus involving the upper cornea, resulting in cloudiness
      • Corneal ulcers at the pannus edge → shallow, infiltrated, causing photophobia & lacrimation


  • Signs of Cicatricial Trachoma
    • Conjunctival signs:
      • Conjunctival scarring (irregular, linear, or star-shaped)
      • Arlt's line: linear scar in the sulcus subtarsalis
      • Dead epithelial cell/mucus accumulation in Henle’s glands
      • Pseudocysts, xerosis, symblepharon
    • Corneal signs:
      • Regressive pannus or pannus siccus with receding vessels
      • Herbert's pits: oval/circular scars following follicle healing
      • Opaque and vascularized cornea, xerosis, ectasia, or total pannus → blindness
    • Lid signs:
      • Lid distortion, tylosis, trichiasis, entropion, madarosis, ankyloblepharon
    • Lacrimal sequelae:
      • Chronic dacryocystitis
      • Chronic dacryoadenitis





WHO Classification of Trachoma (FISTO):


Explanation of Other Options:

Mycoplasma (Option B): Although it can cause ocular infections, it is not the causative organism of trachoma.

Pseudomonas (Option C): Known for corneal ulcers and keratitis, but unrelated to trachoma.

Staphylococcus (Option D): Can produce conjunctivitis and other eye infections but is not linked to trachoma.

Key Takeaways:

  • Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.
  • Active stage shows follicles, papillary hypertrophy, pannus, and keratitis.
  • Cicatricial stage presents with Arlt's line, Herbert's pits, pannus siccus, lid deformities, and corneal opacities.
  • WHO FISTO classification is essential for grading and management.

question_text: 14 DAY NEONATE WITH BILATERAL CONJUNCTIVITIS X-ray showing infiltrates. which of the following is the most probable infection?
explanation:
Neonatal conjunctivitis is a form of conjunctivitis (inflammation of the outer eye) which affects newborn babies following birth. It is typically due to neonatal bacterial infection, although can also be non-infectious (e.g. chemical exposure). Infectious neonatal conjunctivitis is typically contracted during vaginal delivery from exposure to bacteria from the birth canal, most commonly Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis.

Antibiotic ointment is typically applied to the newborn's eyes within 1 hour of birth as prevention for gonococcal ophthalmia. This practice is recommended for all newborns and most hospitals in the United States are required by state law to apply eye drops or ointment soon after birth to prevent the disease.

If left untreated, neonatal conjunctivitis can cause blindness.

Signs and symptoms

Neonatal conjunctivitis by definition presents during the first month of life. Signs and symptoms include:[citation needed]

Pain and tenderness in the eyeball

Conjunctival discharge: purulent, mucoid or mucopurulent (depending on the cause)

Conjunctival hyperaemia and chemosis, usually also with swelling of the eyelids

Corneal involvement (rare) may occur in herpes simplex ophthalmia neonatorum

Time of onset

Chemical causes: Right after delivery

Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Delivery of the baby until 5 days after birth (early onset)

Chlamydia trachomatis: 5 days after birth to 2 weeks (late onset - C. trachomatis has a longer incubation period)

Complications

Untreated cases may develop corneal ulceration, which may perforate, resulting in corneal opacification and staphyloma formation.[citation needed]

Cause

Non-infectious

Chemical irritants such as silver nitrate can cause chemical conjunctivitis, usually lasting 2-4 days. Thus, prophylaxis with a 1% silver nitrate solution is no longer in common use. In most countries, neomycin and chloramphenicol eye drops are used, instead. However, newborns can develop neonatal conjunctivitis due to reactions with chemicals in these common eye drops. Additionally, a blocked tear duct may be another noninfectious cause of neonatal conjunctivitis.[citation needed]

Infectious

The two most common infectious causes of neonatal conjunctivitis are N. gonorrheae and Chlamydia, typically acquired from the birth canal during delivery. However, other different bacteria and viruses can be the cause, including herpes simplex virus (HSV 2), Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.[citation needed]

Ophthalmia neonatorum due to gonococci (N. gonorrhoeae) typically manifests in the first 5 days after birth and is associated with marked bilateral purulent discharge and local inflammation. In contrast, conjunctivitis secondary to infection with C. trachomatis produces conjunctivitis 3 days to 2 weeks after delivery. The discharge is usually more watery in nature (mucopurulent) and less inflamed. Babies infected with chlamydia may develop pneumonitis (chest infection) at a later stage (range 2-19 weeks after delivery). Infants with chlamydia pneumonitis should be treated with oral erythromycin for 10-14 days.

Diagnosis is performed after taking swab from the infected conjunctivae

Prophylaxis needs antenatal, natal, and postnatal care.

Antenatal measures include thorough care of mother and treatment of genital infections when suspected.

Natal measures are of utmost importance, as most infection occurs during childbirth. Deliveries should be conducted under hygienic conditions taking all aseptic measures. The newborn baby's closed lids should be thoroughly cleansed and dried.

If the cause is determined to be due to a blocked tear duct, gentle palpation between the eye and the nasal cavity may be used to clear the tear duct. If the tear duct is not cleared by the time the newborn is 1 year old, surgery may be required.

Postnatal measures include:

Use of 1% tetracycline ointment, 0.5% erythromycin ointment, or 1% silver nitrate solution (Crede's method) into the eyes of babies immediately after birth

Single injection of ceftriaxone IM or IV should be given to infants born to mothers with untreated gonococcal infection.

Curative treatment as a rule, conjunctival cytology samples and culture sensitivity swabs should be taken before starting treatment.

Chemical ophthalmia neonatorum is a self-limiting condition and does not require any treatment.

Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum needs prompt treatment to prevent complications. Topical therapy should include:

Saline lavage hourly until the discharge is eliminated

Bacitracin eye ointment four times per day (because of resistant strains, topical penicillin therapy is not reliable, but in cases with proven penicillin susceptibility, penicillin drops 5000 to 10000 units per ml should be instilled every minute for half an hour, every five minutes for next half an hour, and then half-hourly until the infection is controlled.)

If the cornea is involved, then atropine sulfate ointment should be applied.

The advice of both the pediatrician and ophthalmologist should be sought for proper management.

Systemic therapy: Newborns with gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum should be treated for 7 days with ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ciprofloxacin, or crystalline benzyl penicillin.

Other bacterial ophthalmia neonatorum should be treated by broad-spectrum antibiotics drops and ointment for 2 weeks.

Neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis caused by C. trachomatis should be treated with oral erythromycin. Topical therapy is not effective and also does not treat the infection of the nasopharynx.

Herpes simplex conjunctivitis should be treated with intravenous acyclovir for a minimum of 14 days to prevent systemic infection.

Incorrect Options Explanation

Option B: Haemophilus influenzae - While H. influenzae can cause conjunctivitis and respiratory infections, it is not a common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis. It is more frequently associated with childhood conjunctivitis rather than infections in neonates.

Option C: Streptococcus - Group B Streptococcus (GBS) can cause neonatal pneumonia and sepsis, but it is a rare cause of neonatal conjunctivitis. It usually presents with severe systemic infections rather than isolated conjunctivitis.

Option D: Mycoplasma - Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not a typical cause of neonatal conjunctivitis. It is more commonly associated with atypical pneumonia in older children and adults rather than neonates.

Key Takeaway

Chlamydia trachomatis is a leading cause of neonatal conjunctivitis, especially when symptoms appear after 5 days of birth. It can be associated with pneumonitis, leading to X-ray infiltrates, making it the most probable infection in this case. Oral erythromycin is the treatment of choice.

Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neonatal_conjunctivitis

question_text: Which of the following ocular findings is commonly associated with Vitamin A deficiency?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bitot's spots are the most common ocular findings associated with Vitamin A deficiency.

Causes of Vitamin A Deficiency:

  • Inadequate dietary intake
  • Obstructive jaundice: Impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
  • Liver disease (cirrhosis): Reduced synthesis of retinol-binding protein (RBP)
  • Severe malnutrition: Lack of amino acids needed for RBP synthesis
  • Chronic kidney disease: Excessive urinary loss of RBP

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Ocular Changes:
    Vitamin A deficiency is a major preventable cause of blindness, especially in children under 5 in developing countries.
    • Early signs:
      • Night blindness
      • Difficulty adjusting to dim light
      • Decreased sensitivity to green light
    • Prolonged deficiency: Xerophthalmia - dry, thickened, keratinised conjunctiva and cornea, which can progress to corneal ulcers and blindness.

WHO Grading of Xerophthalmia:

  • XN: Night blindness
  • X1: Conjunctival xerosis
    • X1A: Simple dryness of the conjunctiva
    • X1B: Bitot's spots (gray-white, triangular plaques adherent to conjunctiva)
  • X2: Corneal xerosis
  • X3: Corneal ulceration
    • X3A: Less than one-third of the cornea
    • X3B: More than one-third of the cornea
  • XS: Corneal scarring
  • XF: Xerophthalmic fundus
  • Advanced changes: Keratomalacia (softening of the cornea) if deficiency persists.
  • Immune Function:
    Vitamin A deficiency impairs immunity, increasing susceptibility to infections. Infections can further reduce RBP synthesis, lowering retinol levels.
  • Skin and Mucous Membrane Changes:
    • Follicular hyperkeratosis (Phrynoderma): Rough, bumpy skin due to keratin accumulation in hair follicles
    • Keratinising metaplasia: Atrophy of epithelial lining in respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts
  • Other Effects:
    • Growth retardation from impaired chondroitin sulfate synthesis
    • Reduced overall protein synthesis

Explanation for Other Options:

Pinguecula (option A): Degenerative conjunctival change, often due to UV exposure, unrelated to Vitamin A deficiency.

Pterygium (option C): Fibrovascular growth extending from the conjunctiva onto the cornea, usually caused by chronic UV exposure rather than nutritional deficiency.

Stocker's line (option D): Iron deposition seen at the edge of a pterygium, not associated with Vitamin A deficiency.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Pinguencula is/are incorrect?
option_a: Caused due to hyaline infiltration of submucosa
option_b: Triangular lesion with apex of triangle facing cornea
explanation:
Pinguecula:

It is due to hyaline infiltration and elastotic degeneration of the submucous tissue.

Features:

  • It is usually found in elderly people, especially those who are exposed to strong sunlight, dust and wind.
  • It occurs near the limbus in the palpebral aperture, the apex of the triangle being away from the cornea, and affects the nasal side first and then the temporal.
  • It is yellow and looks like fat, hence the name (pinguis, fat) Since the pinguecula remains relatively free from congestion, it is particularly conspicuous when the eye is inflamed; mistakes in diagnosis may then occur. It requires no treatment.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which type of corneal vascularisation is seen in Cogan's Syndrome?
explanation:
Deep vascularization occurs, consisting of radial bundles of brush-like vessels, and since they are covered with a layer of hazy cornea, their bright scarlet is toned down to a dull reddish pink (‘salmon patches’), wherein separate vessels can be seen only with difficulty. The opacity extends a little beyond the vessels, which seem to push the opacity in front of them and at the height of the condition the vessels run in radial bundles almost, but seldom quite, to the centre of the cornea. There is often a moderate degree of superficial vascularization, but it never extends far over the cornea and at the limbus the conjunctiva may be heaped up.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text:
A 56-year-old farmer presents to OPD with complaints of redness, irritation and growth over the eye. Clinical imaging is as below.

Identify the lesion depicted in the image.
explanation:
Phlycten: nodular lesions situated near limbus

Pinguencula: degenerative nodular lesions in palpebral conjunctiva

Pannus: lymphocytic and vascular ingrowth into cornea

Pterygium Overview:

  • Definition: Pterygium, meaning 'a wing,' is a triangular growth of vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva that encroaches into the interpalpebral area of the eye.
  • Aetiopathogenesis: It is a degenerative condition of the subconjunctival tissue, characterized by avascularized granulation tissue that invades the cornea, destroying superficial stromal layers and Bowman's membrane. This condition is common in dry, sunny climates with sandy soils, possibly due to exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light. Localised stem cell deficiency is also a risk factor
  • Clinical Features:
    • Pterygium often follows a pinguecula.
    • Typically bilateral, commonly found on the nasal side of the eye.
    • Can impair vision due to induced astigmatism or progression into the pupillary area.
    • Induces astigmatism (with the rule) with corneal flattening along the axis of the pterygium.
    • Initially appears thick and vascular, but becomes thin, pale, and atrophic in later stages.
  • Differential Diagnosis: Pseudopterygium is similar but nonprogressive, can occur at any corneal limbus quadrant, and has adhesions to the adjacent lid and scar tissue anchoring it to the underlying surface.

Treatment:

  • Pterygium should be left alone unless it progresses toward the pupillary area, causes excessive astigmatism, restricts ocular motility, or is disfiguring.
  • Surgical removal involves:
    • Seizing the neck near the corneal margin with fixation forceps.
    • Raising and dissecting the pterygium from the cornea, starting from the apex.
    • Careful dissection to avoid going too deep.
    • Excising as much of the pterygium as possible.
    • Leaving a bare area of sclera at the edge of the cornea.
  • Recurrence can occur, and prevention methods include:
    • Postoperative therapy with mitomycin C drops (with associated complications).
    • Using an autoconjunctival graft or an amniotic membrane graft, suturing it at the limbus to cover the excision site.
    • For recurring pterygium extending towards the pupillary area, freeing the apex, excising the lesion, and inserting a lamellar graft over the affected area. MMC can be tried during surgery and post operative to reduce recurrence

This systematic summary provides concise information about pterygium, its clinical features, differential diagnosis, and treatment options.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding pterygium is/are incorrect?
option_a: Caused by elastotic degeneration of subconjunctival tissue
option_b: Encroaches into superficial stromal layers of the cornea with destruction of Bowman's membrane
option_c: Is firmly adherent to underlying sclera
explanation:
Pterygium (meaning 'a wing') is a triangular encroachment of the vascularized granulation tissue covered by conjunctiva in the interpalpebral area.

Aetiopathogenesis of Pterygium:

  • Condition: It is a degenerative condition of the subconjunctival tissue.
  • Characteristics: This condition proliferates as avascularized granulation tissue that encroaches upon the cornea.
  • Effect: It destroys the superficial layers of the corneal stroma and Bowman's membrane.
  • Appearance:
  • Location: The opacity lies deeply in the neighboring part of the cornea.
  • Position: It is located in front of the cornea's blunt apex.
  • Visual Impression: The lesion appears as thick vascularized conjunctiva growing onto the cornea.
  • Adherence: It is loosely adherent to the sclera along its entire length.
  • Folds: Folds are present at the upper and lower borders of the lesion.
  • Impact on Vision:
  • Corneal Astigmatism: The formation of dense fibrous tissue leads to the development of considerable corneal astigmatism.
  • In summary, this condition involves the proliferation of avascularized granulation tissue from the subconjunctival area onto the cornea. It creates an opacity in front of the cornea's apex, and the tissue is loosely adherent to the sclera, leading to folds. Additionally, it can result in significant corneal astigmatism.

Reference: Parson's Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

explanation:
Follicular reaction: aggregation of lymphocytes in adenoid layer of conjunctiva

Papillary reaction: vascular hyperplasia within the conjunctiva

Herbert pits: follicular reaction specific to Trachoma, occurring at limbus

Trachomatous pannus: lymphoid infiltration with vascularization of the margin of the cornea, usually limited to the upper half but tending to spread towards the centre and to involve the whole cornea. The upper part of the margin of the cornea becomes cloudy, and minute superficial vessels, springing from the corneal loops, grow inwards towards the centre. The haziness and vascularization increase until the upper half of the cornea is affected.

question_text: On ophthalmologic examination, the presence of Koeppe's nodules is observed in a patient diagnosed with sarcoidosis. In which area of the eye are these nodules typically observed?
explanation:
Explanation:

Koeppe's nodules are small, granulomatous nodules that are a hallmark of granulomatous anterior uveitis, commonly seen in sarcoidosis. They are characteristically located at the pupillary border on the iris.

Explanation of other options:

Conjunctiva (Option B): Sarcoidosis can cause conjunctival granulomas, but these are distinct from the iris-based Koeppe's nodules.

Retina (Option D): Retinal findings in sarcoidosis include periphlebitis ("candle wax drippings") or choroidal granulomas, not Koeppe's nodules.

Key Takeaways:

  • Koeppe's nodules are located on the iris at the pupillary margin.
  • They are a sign of granulomatous inflammation (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis).

question_text: Most common cause of conjunctivitis in COVID-19?
explanation:
COVID-19 is a disease caused by a SARS-CoV-2 viral infection, a disease that was first detected in December 2019 in Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. COVID-19, formerly known as 2019 Novel Coronavirus (2019-nCoV) respiratory disease, was officially named COVID-19 by the World Health Organization (WHO) in February 2020. By 25 May 2021, there were 33,579,116 confirmed cases with 599,109 COVID-19 deaths worldwide. The purpose of this review article is to provide an update on what is currently known about COVID-19 ocular symptoms in adults, the elderly, and children in the literature. question_text: Which of the following would not cause discharge in patients with an anophthalmic socket and ocular prosthesis?

• Patients with ocular prostheses frequently complain of chronic production of a mucoid discharge emanating from the eyelids.

question_text: Safe strategy includes all except:
explanation:
Management

Antibiotics

Azithromycin (single oral dose of 20 mg/kg) or topical tetracycline (1% eye ointment twice a day for six weeks). Azithromycin is preferred because it is used as a single oral dose. Although it is expensive, it is generally used as part of the international donation program organized by Pfizer. Azithromycin can be used in children from the age of six months and in pregnancy. As a community-based antibiotic treatment, some evidence suggests that oral azithromycin was more effective than topical tetracycline, but no consistent evidence supported either oral or topical antibiotics as being more effective. Antibiotic treatment reduces the risk of active trachoma in individuals infected with chlamydial trachomatis.

Surgery

For individuals with trichiasis, a bilamellar tarsal rotation procedure is warranted to direct the lashes away from the globe. Evidence suggests that use of a lid clamp and absorbable sutures would result in reduced lid contour abnormalities and granuloma formulation after surgery. Early intervention is beneficial as the rate of recurrence is higher in more advanced disease.

Lifestyle measures

The WHO-recommended SAFE strategy includes:

Surgery to correct advanced stages of the disease

Antibiotics to treat active infection, using azithromycin

Facial cleanliness to reduce disease transmission

Environmental change to increase access to clean water and improved sanitation

Children with visible nasal discharge, discharge from the eyes, or flies on their faces are at least twice as likely to have active trachoma as children with clean faces. Intensive community-based health education programs to promote face-washing can reduce the rates of active trachoma, especially intense trachoma. If an individual is already infected, washing one's face is encouraged, especially a child, to prevent reinfection. Some evidence shows that washing the face combined with topical tetracycline might be more effective in reducing severe trachoma compared to topical tetracycline alone. The same trial found no statistical benefit of eye washing alone or in combination with tetracycline eye drops in reducing follicular trachoma amongst children

question_text: All of the following are treatment options for Trachoma as per WHO except?
explanation:
The WHO has recommended a combination of interventions to treat trachoma and limit its blinding consequences.

Known by the acronym SAFE,

  • Surgery for cicatricial entropion and trichiasis
  • Antibiotics to eliminate the organism
  • Facial cleanliness to avoid infection and
  • Environmental improvement with better hygiene and sanitation.

Antibiotics used to eradicate the organism are administered as topical medication, tetracycline 1% eye ointment three times a day for a month OR azithromycin 1% eyedrops four times a day for 2 weeks and systemic medication: a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g is effective.

So, Choice B (Antibiotics- Floxacins) is the correct answer because, while fluoroquinolones can be effective, they are not the primary antibiotics recommended by the WHO for trachoma treatment. Azithromycin and tetracycline are the preferred choices.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding management of acute cases of VKC is incorrect?
option_a: Topical anti-histaminics/ mast cell stabilizers help control inflammation
option_b: Acetyl cysteine drops help control mucus secretion
option_c: Triamcinolone injections sub-tarsally are indicated in all cases
option_d: Oral anti-allergic medications can be considered in severe bilateral cases
explanation:
The statement in Option C is incorrect. Triamcinolone injections sub-tarsally (under the tarsal conjunctiva) are not indicated in all cases of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). They are typically reserved for severe, refractory cases of VKC that do not respond to other treatment modalities.

In the management of acute cases of VKC:

A) Topical anti-histaminics/mast cell stabilizers (Choice A) are indeed used to help control inflammation and itching.

B) Acetyl cysteine drops (Choice B) can help control excessive mucus secretion, which is a symptom of VKC. Acetyl cysteine as 10% or 20% drops three to four times a day for 1–2 weeks is useful in controlling excess mucus.

D) Oral anti-allergic medications (Choice D) can be considered in severe bilateral cases to provide relief from symptoms, especially itching, when topical treatment alone is not sufficient.

Subtarsal injections of long-acting steroids like triamcinolone are more aggressive interventions and are not used as a first-line treatment. They are reserved for cases that do not respond adequately to other treatments. Cryotherapy to the tarsal conjunctiva may also be considered in severe cases.

Topical steroids can be given for control of initial acute itching phase

Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)

  • Brief description, course and prognosis:
    • Recurrent, seasonal allergic conjunctivitis that affects both eyes
    • Most common in children and adolescents
    • Thought to be caused by an allergic reaction to pollen, dust mites, or other allergens
    • Chronic condition, but typically improves with age
    • Most children will outgrow VKC by their early teen years
  • Symptoms:
    • Itching
    • Burning
    • Redness
    • Tearing
    • Light sensitivity
  • Signs:
    • Palpebral VKC: Cobblestone-like papillae on the upper eyelids
    • Limbal VKC: White, gelatinous thickening of the limbus
  • Treatment:
    • Topical therapy: Eyedrops containing antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and/or steroids
    • Systemic therapy: Oral antihistamines
    • Supportive therapy: Cool compresses and tinted glasses
    • Surgery: In some cases to remove giant papillae or to treat corneal ulcers

Additional notes:

  • Chronic steroid usage in the treatment of VKC puts the patient at risk of developing serious complications, such as steroid-induced glaucoma, bacterial or fungal corneal superinfections, and keratoconus. Therefore, steroids should be used only for short periods under the careful supervision of an ophthalmologist.
  • Patients with VKC should be discouraged from rubbing their eyes, as this can worsen symptoms and increase the risk of complications.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text:
A 24-year-old student presents to OPD with watering, redness, pain, photophobia in both eyes since last 2/3 days. Multiple family members are having similar complaints. On examination, follicular conjunctival reaction and corneal sub-epithelial opacities are noted. Clinical imaging is as depicted below.

Which of the following statements regarding this case is/ are incorrect?
option_c: Treatment is non-specific: Lubricants plus anti-microbials to prevent secondary infection
option_d: Topical anti-viral Acyclovir is drug of choice
explanation:
Epidemic Kerato-conjunctivitis

  • Causative organism: This disease is usually caused by adenovirus of serotypes 8 and 19 but also of serotypes 3 and 7.
  • Clinical features: Characterized by a rapidly developing follicular conjunctivitis with marked inflammatory symptoms and scanty exudate, associated with a preauricular lymphadenopathy. Occasionally, it takes on a membranous form 7–10 days after the infection. question_text: What is the recommended approach for managing a middle-aged woman with a progressive pterygium that is extending towards the pupillary area?
explanation:
Explanation:

For a progressive pterygium threatening the visual axis, surgical excision is indicated. The conjunctival autograft technique is the current gold standard. It involves removing the pterygium and covering the defect with a graft of healthy conjunctiva from the same eye, which significantly reduces the risk of recurrence compared to simple excision (bare sclera technique).

Explanation of other options:

Keratoplasty (Option A): A corneal transplant is reserved for cases where the pterygium has caused significant corneal scarring that affects vision, not for the primary excision.

Observation (Option C): Observation is for small, asymptomatic, non-progressive pterygia. A lesion progressing towards the pupil requires intervention.

Beta-radiation (Option D): This is an adjunctive therapy used in the past to prevent recurrence but has fallen out of favor due to sight-threatening complications like scleral necrosis and cataract formation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Surgical indication: Progression, visual impairment, chronic inflammation.
  • Excision with conjunctival autograft is the preferred surgical method to minimize recurrence.

question_text: The following CT image is provided. Based on the findings, identify the most likely diagnosis.
explanation:
Explanation :

The CT image reveals orbital floor discontinuity with soft tissue herniation (orbital fat/inferior rectus muscle) into the maxillary sinus, also known as the teardrop sign. These findings are pathognomonic for a blowout fracture of the orbit.

  • Mechanism: Occurs after blunt trauma (e.g., punch, ball injury) → sudden rise in intraorbital pressure → the thin orbital floor (posteromedial maxillary bone) gives way.
  • Structures commonly involved: Orbital fat, inferior rectus muscle → herniate through defect.
  • Clinical features:
    • Diplopia (especially on upward gaze, due to inferior rectus entrapment)
    • Enophthalmos (posterior displacement of globe from loss of orbital volume)
    • Infraorbital anesthesia (damage to infraorbital nerve)
    • Periorbital ecchymosis, subconjunctival hemorrhage
  • Imaging hallmark: CT "teardrop sign' or 'hanging drop sign."

Explanation of other options:

Le Fort fracture (Option A):

  • A horizontal fracture involving the alveolar ridge, hard palate, and inferior maxilla, creating a "floating palate."
  • Seen in severe midfacial trauma.
  • No herniation into the maxillary sinus and no teardrop sign on CT.

Types of Le Fort fracture:

Zygomatic fracture (Option B):

  • Involves zygomatic arch or zygomaticomaxillary complex.
  • Features: flattened malar eminence, infraorbital rim step deformity, trismus due to coronoid impingement.
  • Although zygomatic fractures can extend into the orbital rim, they do not classically produce orbital floor herniation with teardrop sign.

Nasal bone fracture (Option D):

  • Most common facial fracture due to direct trauma.
  • Presents with nasal deformity, tenderness, crepitus, epistaxis.
  • Involves nasal bridge, not the orbital floor. CT would not show herniation into maxillary sinus.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis when blanching of vascularity is observed after instillation of 10% phenylephrine, as shown in the provided image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient presents with painless ocular redness which blanches upon administration of 10% phenylephrine, consistent with episcleritis-specifically nodular episcleritis.

  • Episcleritis
    • Definition: Inflammation of the loose connective tissue between conjunctiva and sclera.
    • Aetiology:
      • Idiopathic
      • Systemic diseases: gout, rosacea, psoriasis, connective tissue disorders
      • Hypersensitivity reactions to tubercular or streptococcal toxins
      • Infectious: herpes zoster virus, syphilis, Lyme disease, tuberculosis
    • Clinical Features:
      • Common in young females
      • Acute onset redness
      • Discomfort with gritty/foreign body sensation
      • Mild or no pain
      • Resolves spontaneously but often recurs
    • Clinical Types:
      • Simple episcleritis: Sectoral/diffuse inflammation; vessels run radially under conjunctiva.
      • Nodular episcleritis: Firm, tender nodule 2-3 mm from limbus, pink/purple in color; can be moved separately from sclera, with freely mobile conjunctiva.
    • Diagnosis:
      • 10% phenylephrine blanches conjunctival and episcleral vessels.
    • Differential Diagnosis:
      • Conjunctivitis → blanching with 2.5% phenylephrine
      • Phlyctenulosis (Option C ruled out)
      • Inflamed pinguecula
      • Scleritis (deep, painful, does not blanch with phenylephrine; Option B ruled out)
    • Treatment:
      • Topical NSAIDs
      • Mild corticosteroid eye drops
      • Artificial tears
      • Cold compresses for symptomatic relief
      • Systemic NSAIDs if needed

Explanation of Other Options:

Nodular scleritis (Option B): A painful, deeper inflammation involving the sclera; vessels do not blanch with phenylephrine, unlike episcleritis.

Nodular phlycten (Option C): Represents a hypersensitivity reaction, often at the limbus; does not blanch with phenylephrine.

Scleral ectasia (Option D): A degenerative thinning and bulging of the sclera (e.g., keratoconus); not inflammatory and does not cause blanching with phenylephrine. It typically shows corneal changes rather than episcleral involvement.

Key Takeaways:

Vascular Plexuses over the Sclera

question_text: Subtenon space is between
explanation:
Spaces in orbit

Subperiosteal space

This is a potential space between orbital bones and the periorbita. Dermoid cyst, epidermoid cyst, mucocele, subperiosteal abscess, myeloma, osteomatous tumor, hematoma and fibrous dysplasia are commonly seen in this space.

Peripheral Orbital space (Anterior space)

This space is bounded peripherally by periorbita, internally by the four extra ocular muscles, anteriorly by the septum orbitable. Posteriorly, it merges with the central soace. Tumors present in this space produce eccentric proptosis and can usually be palpated. Common tumors present in this space are malignant lymphoma, capillary hemangioma, neoplasms of the lacrimal gland and pseudotumors.

Central space

It is also called muscular cone or posterior or retrobulbar space. Contents of this space include optic nerve and its meninges, superior and inferior divisions of oculomotor nerve, abducent nerve, nasociliary nerve, ciliary ganglion, ophthalmic artery, superior ophthalmic vein and central orbital fat. Many of the circumscribed orbital tumors such as cavernous hemangioma, solitary neurofibroma, meningioma, optic nerve glioma occur in this space and usually produce axial proptosis.

Sub- Tenon’s space

It is a potential space around the eyeball between the sclera and tenon’s space. Pus collected in this space is drained by incision of tenon’s capsule through the conjunctiva.

Apical space

It is bounded peripherally by periorbita; anteriorly becoming continuous with the anterior and central spaces.

Reference: parson 21st edition pg 471

question_text: True about episcleritis
explanation:
Episcleritis

  • This is a benign inflammatory affectation of the deep sub-conjunctival connective tissues, including the superficial scleral lamellae and frequently affects both eyes, though their involvement may not be simultaneous.
  • Anatomically, dense lymphocytic infiltration of the subconjunctival and episcleral tissues is found.
  • Aetiology: Idiopathic in origin, it is often regarded as an allergic reaction to an endogenous toxin. The condition falls within the vague category of collagenous diseases. A history of rheumatoid arthritis is commonly obtained.
  • Symptoms: Patients-usually young adults and commonly females present with an acute onset of redness, mild or no pain in one or both eyes, with no discharge.
  • A history of recurrent episodes is common
  • It is often self-resolving. If mild, the disease can be treated with lubricants alone. If moderate to severe, a mild topical steroid(e.g., fluorometholone) prescribed four times a day relieves the discomfort and inflammation. Rarely, more frequent and potent steroids are required.

Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 59.

question_text: A patient presented with complain of pain, photophobia, itching and have history of eye trauma with fish tail. What would be the diagnosis?
explanation:
Fungal keratitis is a serious ocular infection with potentially catastrophic visual results. Caused by any of the many species of fungi capable of colonizing human tissue, its occurs worldwide and its incidence is increasing in frequency.

Etiology

The list covers many fungi including but not limited to yeasts of Candida spp., filamentous with septae such as Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp., Cladosporium,spp., Curvularia, and non septated such as Rhizopus. Bare in mind that any agent capable of infecting humans is a potential infectious agent, especially if the host has a debilitating disease.

Diagnosis

A high degree of suspicion from the physician accounts for early diagnosis and treatment, which are paramount for a successful resolution of the fungal keratitis. Corneal ulcers unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics, the presence of satellite lesions, and scanty secretions in a large ulcer are some signs that should raise flags to the attending professional about the possibility of a mycotic agent.

History

Blurred vision, redness, tearing, photophobia, pain, foreign body sensations, secretions related to trauma, ocular surface disease and topical steroid use are all important characteristics to ascertain in the history.

Physical examination

After establishing the patient's general condition, the examiner should look for evidence of ocular surface disease and determine the amount and type of secretions and lid swelling. The upper eyelid should be everted to exclude a retained foreign body. The examiner should measure the size and depth of the lesion as well as the presence of satellite lesions. The intraocular pressure should also be ascertained. Anterior chamber reaction and evidence of hypopyon should also be recorded. Vitreous reaction if present may suggest intraocular spread of the disease.

Signs

With filamentary fungi, the corneal lesions have a white/gray infiltrate with feathery borders. There might be satellite lesions with a hypopyon and conjunctival injection as well as purulent secretions. Ulcers caused by yeast are plaque-like and slightly more defined, similar to bacterial keratitis.

Symptoms

Symptoms are similar to any corneal infection including blurred vision, redness, tearing, photophobia, pain, foreign body sensation and secretions. In some cases the lesion are rather indolent which help to delay the diagnosis and hence delay the treatment. Suspicion should be high in cases of trauma with vegetable matter.

Clinical diagnosis

Under the slit lamp, early on the lesion might look like an unhealed corneal abrasion with scanty infiltrates and no secretions. With time however, the ulcer develops thicker infiltrates and fuzzy margins. The presence of satellite lesions strongly suggests a fungal infection. Redness and periocular edema are also common. This combined with a history of trauma, especially with vegetable matter, ocular surface disease or chronic use of topical steroids should alert the practitioner to the possibility of a mycotic etiology.

Diagnostic procedures

Corneal scrapings are taken from deep within the lesion with a surgical blade or sterile spatula. To perform a corneal biopsy, a dermatological 2mm punch can be used.

Laboratory test

For a definitive diagnosis, scrapings taken from deep within the lesion should be made and inoculated in Sabouraud agar. The shortcoming is that it can take up to 3 weeks to grow and identify the organism. For a faster result, smears with special stains such as Gomori, PAS, acridine orange, calcofluor white or KOH should be performed. The drawback is that not all laboratories have these stains available, so, again we might need to rely on the patient's evolution and the physician's clinical acumen. If all labs and cultures are negative, corneal biopsy should be considered to obtain a specimen.

Risk Factors

Risk factors include trauma, ocular surface disease, and topical steroid use. Risks and type of fungi also might vary by geographic location and climate. In warmer climates the rule is that the most common organisms are filamentous fungi, like Fusarium spp and Aspergillus spp. with a strong relationship to trauma. Reports from Brazil show the most common isolates in descending order were Fusarium spp in 67%, Aspergillus spp in 10.5%, and Candida spp in 10%. About 40% of the infections were related to trauma.

In the northern USA, corneal infection by fungus was, until recently, more common in debilitated or immunocompromised patients and the causative organism being a yeast, such as Candida albicans. Filamentous fungi in these latitudes were then rarely reported. A few years ago a breakout of Fusarium keratitis associated with a type of contact lens solution displaced yeasts as the most common fungal corneal infection in some areas. This trend persists in the most recent epidemiological reports. Still they are, in most cases, related to contact lens use. It should be noted that the incidence of contact lens-related fungal keratitis was increasing before the Fusarium outbreak.

This new distribution means that we no longer can rely on the geographical distribution only to initiate empirical treatment. Broad-spectrum treatment should be administered once there is a strong probability of a mycotic infection.

Incorrect options:

Option A: Hyphema (Incorrect)

  • Hyphema is blood in the anterior chamber, not pus.
  • It is usually due to blunt trauma, not trauma involving organic matter (fish tail).

Option B: Aqueous Flare (Incorrect)

  • Aqueous flare is protein leakage into the aqueous humor due to uveitis or inflammation.
  • It does not present with hypopyon or fungal infiltrates.

Option D: Conjunctivitis (Incorrect)

  • Conjunctivitis causes redness, discharge, and itching, but does not cause hypopyon.
  • It is not linked to deep corneal infection or trauma with organic material.

Key Takeaway:

  • Fungal keratitis should be suspected in cases of trauma with organic matter (e.g., fish tail, vegetable matter).
  • Hallmark signs: Feathery margins, satellite lesions, hypopyon, and delayed healing.
  • Diagnosis: Corneal scrapings, Sabouraud agar culture, and special stains (KOH, PAS, Calcofluor white).
  • Prompt antifungal treatment (Natamycin or Voriconazole) is essential to prevent vision loss.

question_text: A farmer presented with pain, photophobia & watering from the eye for last 36 hours. On examination, following findings were seen. Identify the lesion marked.
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation, along with ocular findings such as hypopyon, satellite lesions, and conjunctival congestion, strongly suggests a diagnosis of Fungal Keratitis. The marked lesion in the image represents a satellite lesion, which is typical of a fungal corneal ulcer.

Fungal Keratitis

  • Mycotic or fungal keratitis is frequently seen in tropical countries, rural areas and in immunocompromised individuals.
  • Causative organisms:
    • Aspergillus, Fusarium or Candida albicans.
  • Predisposing factor:
    • Injury with vegetable matter such as a thorn or wooden stick

Clinical features

  • Relatively indolent course.
  • Compared to bacterial ulcers, symptoms are much milder than the clinical signs would suggest.
  • Symptoms: Marked ciliary and conjunctival congestion with pain, watering and photophobia
  • Signs
    • Ulcers appears greyish-white and dry with feathery borders.
    • Hypophyon:
      • If present is thick and immobile and is due to direct i into anterior chamber.
    • Wessely immune ring:
      • Yellow line of demarcation which gradually deepens into a gutter.
      • Due to deposition of immune complexes and inflammatory cells around the ulcer.
    • Satellite lesions may also be seen.

Fig: (A) Fungal corneal ulcer showing a dry looking ulcer with feathery margins and thick hypopyon. (B) Fungal corneal ulcer with satellite lesions.

Treatment

Medical management:

  • Topical Antifungal Agents
    • Treatment is by means of local natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium.
    • Nystatin is effective against Candida.
  • Oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole may be needed if the ulcers are severe with hypopyon, perforated, or there is a suspicion of endophthalmitis. 

Surgical Management: If the ulcer progresses despite therapeutic measures,

  • Repeated Scraping of the floor of ulcer with a spatula for removal of necrotic material
  • Cauterization: Performed with Carbolic acid (100%), Trichloroacetic acid (10%-20%), Povidone-iodine (5%)
  • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Corneal transplantation

Explanation of other options:

Reverse hypopyon (Option A): Reverse hypophyon is a collection of silicon oil in the anterior chamber, usually seen as a complication of Vitreoretinal surgeries.

Dendritic ulcer (Option B): This is not dendritic ulcer as dendritic ulcer is a feature of epithelial keratitis and not fungal corneal ulcer.

Ring abscess (Option C): Ring abscess is usualy seen in helminthic keratitis.
