question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Ocular Pemphigoid are true?
option_b: Pathology is loss of hemidesmosomal attachment of epithelium to basement membrane
option_c: Multiple remissions and exacerbations are common
explanation:
Ocular Cicatricial Pemphigoid (OCP)

Previously sometimes referred to as benign mucous membrane pemphigoid, this is a rare but very serious disease of unknown origin affecting both eyes. It generally affects those older than 50 years and is of insidious onset with remissions and exacerbations. There is a loss of hemidesmosomal attachment of the epithelium to the basement membrane.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following drugs is not implicated in Stevens-Johnson's syndrome?
explanation:
Stevens–johnson syndrome (erythema multiforme major) 

  • This condition is characterized as a type II hypersensitivity reaction.
  • Causes: It is typically triggered by an immunological response to drugs (e.g., sulphonamides, NSAIDs, antibiotics, antimalarials, antiepileptics like barbiturates and phenytoin) or systemic infections (caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, herpes simplex virus, and certain fungi).
  • Severity: It is a serious disease that can be fatal in some patients.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Skin Rash: It is characterized by a skin rash with erythematous lesions, which may progress to bullae formation.
  • Systemic Symptoms: Patients often experience fever and malaise.
  • Mucous Membrane Involvement: Ulcerative lesions of the mucous membranes, particularly in the mouth and eyes, are common.

Ocular Effects:

  • Late Ocular Sequelae: Ocular complications can occur, including severe dry eye, symblepharon (adhesions between the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva), lid deformities (like cicatricial entropion), corneal vascularization, and scarring.

Ocular Treatment:

  • Acute Stage: Treatment in the acute stage includes supportive therapy with topical lubricants, antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infections, and lysis of adhesions formed between the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva. This is achieved by passing a glass rod coated with antibiotic or plain paraffin ointment in the fornices.
  • Late Cicatricial Stage: In the late cicatricial stage, medical treatment can be used to manage dry eye symptoms, and lid deformities can be surgically corrected.
  • Additional Measures: Additional measures may include punctal occlusion, transplantation of conjunctival or buccal mucous membrane, and transplantation of limbal stem cells with amniotic membrane to promote healing. These procedures aim to restore the integrity of the damaged ocular surface.

In summary, this condition is a type II hypersensitivity reaction triggered by drugs or systemic infections. It can lead to severe skin and mucous membrane manifestations, with late ocular complications that require both medical and surgical interventions for management and restoration of ocular health.

As per the references, there is no evidence of Tetracyclines being causative of Stevens–johnson syndrome.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: A patient presents with symptoms of fever, severe pain, and swelling in the left eye, along with findings as shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation with occular findings of proptosis, chemosis and orbital swellings evident from the image suggests orbital swelling.

Orbital cellulitis:

Orbital cellulitis is an acute infection of the soft tissues of the orbit located behind the orbital septum.

Etiology

  • Sinusitis: Ethmoid sinusitis (most common) carries a high risk of causing orbital cellulitis.
  • Underlying dental problem.
  • Dacryocystitis (inflammation of the lacrimal sac).
  • Endogenous cause: Septicemia
  • Exogenous cause: Fracture or surgery of the orbit.

Causative Organisms

  • Staphylococcus aureus (most common)
  • Hemophilus influenzae (most common in children)
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Streptococcus pyogenes

There are two recognized types of cellulitis with differing presentations, therapy and prognosis.

Preseptal cellulitis

  • Involves structures anterior to the orbital septum that is largely the lids. (Option D ruled out)
  • Presents as a swelling of the lids, with erythema and chemosis.
  • There is often a conjunctival discharge associated, but no proptosis or restriction of ocular movements or visual function is present.
  • Preseptal cellulitis is treated with appropriate oral antibiotics, depending on the source of the infection, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Orbital cellulitis

  • Orbital cellulitis is a term reserved for infections behind the orbital septum, which may or may not spill over to the lids. Clinical features include:
  • Extensive swelling of the lids with chemosis
  • Proptosis
  • Pain is severe, increased by movement of the eye or pressure.
  • Fever is present and cerebral symptoms may arise.
  • Decreased visual acuity

The modified Chandler staging system describes the following stages of disease:

  • Stage I: Preseptal cellulitis
  • Stage II: Inflammatory orbital oedema
  • Stage III: Subperiosteal abscess
  • Stage IV: Orbital abscess
  • Stage V: Cavernous sinus thrombosis

Treatment

  • Antibiotics (IV): Empirical therapy treats orbital cellulitis by giving Ceftazidime, Vancomycin, and Metronidazole.
  • Monitoring of optic nerve function
  • Surgery: Drainage of an orbital abscess or infected sinuses should be considered if there is a lack of response to antibiotics.

Explanation of other options:Endophthalmitis (Option B): Endophthalmitis is defined as the intraocular inflammation which predominantly affects the inner spaces of the eye and its contents, like the vitreous and/or the anterior chamber.

Panophthalmitis (Option C): Panophthalmitis refers to the infection that spreas beyond the sclera.

question_text: Systemic association with limbal dermoid involves all except
explanation:
• A limbal dermoid is a choristoma(a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location) consisting of a mass of collagenous tissue containing dermal elements; it is covered by stratified squamous epithelium.
  • Presentation is in early childhood, with a smooth, yellowish, soft subconjunctival mass commonly located at the inferotemporal limbus, often with protruding hair.
  • Lesions are occasionally very large and may virtually encircle the limbus.
  • Treatment is indicated for cosmesis, chronic irritation, dellen formation and amblyopia from astigmatism or involvement of the visual axis.
  • Small dermoids can undergo simple excision, but lamellar keratosclerectomy may be required for large lesions.

Systemic associations

  • Goldenhar syndrome(oculoauriculovertebral spectrum) is usually sporadic.
    • Systemic features include hypoplasia of the malar, maxillary and mandibular regions, macrostomia and microtia, preauricular and facial skin tags, hemivertebrae(usually cervical), mental handicap, cardiac, renal and central nervous system(CNS) anomalies.
    • Ocular features, apart from dermoids, include upper lid notching or coloboma, microphthalmos and disc coloboma.
  • Treacher Collins syndrome.
    • Treacher Collins syndrome(mandibulofacial dysostosis) is a genetically heterogeneous condition characterized by malformation of derivatives of the first and second branchial arches, principally mandibular and ear anomalies. Lower eyelid coloboma is a feature; ocular anomalies also described include slanted palpebral apertures, cataract, microphthalmos and lacrimal atresia.
  • Linear naevus sebaceous of Jadassohn.
    • Systemic features include warty or scaly cutaneous lesions, infantile spasms, CNS anomalies and developmental delay.
    • Ocular features, apart from dermoids, include ptosis, cloudy cornea, lid colobomas, fundus colobomas and microphthalmos.

Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema(UGH) Syndrome or Ellingson syndrome is a complication of intraocular chafing from intraocular lens(IOL) implants leading to a spectrum of iris transillumination defects and pigmentary dispersion to microhyphemas and hyphemas with elevated intraocular pressure(IOP).

Reference: Kanski, 8th Edition, Page no. 468.

question_text: Ocular manifestation of AIDS commonly includes all of the following except:
explanation:
Meningioma is generally not seen in AIDS patient.

Ocular manifestations.

These occur in about 75 percent of patients and sometimes may be the presenting features of AIDS in an otherwise healthy person or the patient may be a known case of AIDS when his eye problems occur. Ocular lesions of AIDS may be classified as follows:

  • Retinal micro vasculopathy: It develops from Vaso-occlusive process which may be either due to direct toxic effects of virus on the vascular endothelium or immune complex deposits in the precapillary arterioles. It is characterized by non-specific lesions: Multiple 'cotton-wool spots' occur in 50 percent cases; Superficial and deep retinal hemorrhages occur in 15-40 percent cases. Microaneurysms and telangiectasia may also be seen rarely.
  • Usual ocular infections: These are also seen in healthy people, but occur with greater frequency and produce more severe infections in patients with AIDS. These include: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Herpes simplex infections, Toxoplasmosis(chorioretinitis), Ocular tuberculosis, syphilis and fungal corneal ulcers.
  • Opportunistic infections of the eye: These are caused by microorganisms which do not affect normal patients. They can infect someone whose cellular immunity is suppressed by HIV infection or by other causes such as leukemia. These include: cytomegalovirus(CMV) retinitis, candida endophthalmitis, cryptococcal infections and pneumocystis carini, choroiditis.
  • Unusual neoplasms: Kaposi's sarcoma is a malignant vascular tumour which may appear on the eyelid or conjunctiva as multiple nodules. It is seen in about 3 percent cases of AIDS. Burkitt's lymphoma of the orbit is also seen in a few patients.
  • Neuro-ophthalmic lesions: These are thought to be due to CMV or other infections of the brain. These include isolated or multiple cranial nerve palsies resulting in paralysis of eyelids, extraocular muscles, loss of sensory supply to the eye and optic nerve involvement causing loss of vision.
  • Management: It consists of the measures directed against the associated infection/lesions. For example: CMV infections can be treated by zidovudine, ganciclovir and foscarnet. Kaposi's sarcoma responds to radiotherapy. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, is treated by acyclovir.

Reference: A.K. Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 437.

question_text: What would be the investigation for bilateral proptosis and chloroma in a child?
explanation:
Blood film in leukaemias. (A) Bone marrow aspirate in acute myeloid leukaemia showing immature blast cells; (B) peripheral blood smear in chronic lymphatic leukaemia showing many mature lymphocytes

Leukaemia Introduction

The leukaemias are malignancies of haematopoietic stem cells involving abnormal proliferation of white blood cells. Acute leukaemia is characterized by the replacement of bone marrow with immature (blast) cells. Chronic leukaemia is associated, at least initially, with well-differentiated (mature) leukocytes and occurs almost exclusively in adults. The four major variants of leukaemia are:

  • Acute lymphocytic (lymphoblastic) predominantly affects children, in whom there is around a 90% 5-year survival rate.
  • Acute myeloid (myeloblastic) is most frequently seen in older adults.
  • Chronic lymphocytic has a very chronic course and many patients die from unrelated disease.
  • Chronic myelocytic has a progressive clinical course and often a less favourable prognosis.

Ocular features

Ocular involvement is more commonly seen in the acute than the chronic forms and virtually any ocular structure may be involved.

Primary leukaemic infiltration is fairly rare. Secondary changes such as those associated with anaemia, thrombocytopenia, hyperviscosity and opportunistic infections are more common and include intraocular bleeding, infection and vascular occlusion.

  • Fundus
    • Retinal haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are common.
    • Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with white centres, the whitish element is thought to be composed of coagulated fibrin in most cases. They occur in acute leukaemia and in a range of other conditions such as bacteraemia (classically subacute bacterial endocarditis), diabetes, hypertension and anaemia.
    • Peripheral retinal neovascularization is an occasional feature of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
    • Retinal and choroidal infiltrates may occur, most commonly posterior to the equator and may masquerade as posterior uveitis. In chronic leukaemia they may give rise to a 'leopard skin' appearance.
    • Scattered haemorrhages may occur in patients with thrombocytopenia.
    • Optic nerve infiltration may cause swelling and visual loss.
  • Other features
    • Orbital involvement, particularly in children
    • Iris thickening, iritis and pseudohypopyon Spontaneous subconjunctival haemorrhage and hyphaema.
    • Cranial nerve palsies.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

Option B: HB Estimation - While anemia is common in leukemia, HB estimation alone cannot diagnose leukemia or chloroma. A low HB might be present, but it does not provide specific information about leukemic cell infiltration.

Option C: Total Leucocyte Count - While leukocytosis or leukopenia can be seen in leukemia, TLC alone is not diagnostic. It does not differentiate between leukemia and other infections or hematological disorders.

Option D: Platelet Count - Leukemia often leads to thrombocytopenia, but a low platelet count does not confirm leukemia or chloroma. It is a secondary finding rather than a primary diagnostic tool.

Key Takeaway:

  • Peripheral blood smear is the first-line investigation in suspected leukemia cases.
  • Chloroma (myeloid sarcoma) is a rare extramedullary tumor seen in AML.
  • Bilateral proptosis in a child is a red flag for hematological malignancies.
  • Further bone marrow aspiration and biopsy confirm leukemia.

question_text: The most common cause of proptosis in adults is:
explanation:
Preseptal cellulitis is an inflammation of the tissues localized anterior to the orbital septum. The orbital septum is a fibrous tissue that divides the orbit contents in two compartments: preseptal (anterior to the septum) and postseptal (posterior to the septum). The inflammation that develops posterior to the septum is known as “orbital cellulitis”. Both entities are caused by an infectious process.

Etiology

The majority of these infections are caused by bacteria. Adenovirus, herpes simplex and varicella zoster are also associated to cellulitis. In the immunocompromised patient we must suspect fungi as a possible etiology. Gram positive cocci are the most prevalent microorganisms identified in preseptal cellulitis - typically Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species (pyogenes and pneumonia). Staphylococcus aureus and epidermidis are commonly found after a penetrating eyelid trauma. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common etiology in preseptal cellulitis secondary to sinusitis. In the era before the establishment of the universal vaccination against Haemophilus influenza type b, this was a frequent etiology especially in children under 5 years of age. It is still common in unvaccinated patients. In preseptal cellulitis secondary to a human bite it is frequent to isolate anaerobic bacteria such as Clostridium.

Diagnosis

Patients complain of eyelid swelling and redness. But also general malaise and low grade fever are commonly reported. Among the classic signs of preseptal cellulitis are eyelid edema/erythema/warmth and fever. There are clinical keys that help us distinguish between preseptal and orbital cellulitis.

Incorrect options:

Preseptal cellulitis; eyelid edema and erythema, normal visual acuity, absence of proptosis, pupil with normal reaction to light, normal color saturarion, normal conjunctiva and normal ocular movements.

Orbital cellulitis: eyelid edema and erythema, diminished visual acuity, proptosis is present, relative afferent pupillary defect may be present, reduced color saturation, chemotic conjunctiva and reduced extraocular movements with pain elicited by these movements.

Cellulitis may extend to the cheek and forehead. Also, it is common to see an eyelid abscess associated with preseptal cellulitis, which may require incision and drainage.

Capillary hemangioma : A capillary hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor that can cause proptosis, but it is rare and less common than thyroid eye disease in adults. It is more often seen in infants and typically resolves on its own over time.

Key Takeaway: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of proptosis in adults, particularly those with thyroid dysfunction. It leads to inflammation and swelling of the orbital tissues, causing the eyes to bulge.

question_text: Middle aged women with b/l proptosis with restricted ocular movement and chemosis is euthyroid. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Nonspecific orbital inflammation (NSOI), also known as orbital inflammatory pseudotumor, idiopathic orbital inflammation ( IOI)and orbital inflammatory syndrome is the most common cause of painful orbital mass in adults. NSOI can be localized or diffuse. When localized, inflammation can affect the extraocular muscles (orbital myositis), lacrimal gland (dacryoadenitis), sclera (scleritis), uvea (uveitis), and the superior orbital fissure and cavernous sinus (Tolosa-Hunt syndrome). Others include periscleritis, perineuritis, and mass. When diffuse, NSOI may diffusely involve the orbital fatty tissues. NSOI is the third most common orbital disease after thyroid eye disease and orbital lymphoma. NSOI can both radiologically and clinically mimic a malignant process. Therefore, it is a diagnosis of exclusion, only after all other causes of inflammation have been eliminated. Treatment options are varied and can include surgery, steroids, chemotherapeutic agents and irradiation.

All patients with suspected NSOI require a full ophthalmic assessment/workup. NSOI is typically characterized by the abrupt onset of pain, proptosis and other inflammatory signs such as swelling and erythema. Unilateral presentation is more typical but bilateral presentations are not uncommon. Pediatric NSOI differs from the adult presentation and is more commonly characterized by bilateral manifestation, uveitis, disc edema and eosinophilia. Pain is the most common symptom in adult NSOI and occurs 58-69% of the time followed by diplopia (31-38%). Periorbital edema/swelling is the most common sign and occurs 75-79.2% of the time (figure) followed by proptosis (32-62.5%), EOM restriction (54.2%) red eye (48%), chemosis (29%), decreased vision (20.8%), and ptosis (16.7%).34-35 Therefore, physical examination of patients with suspected NSOI involves lid assessment (retraction/lid lag/lagophthalmos), orbital assessment (proptosis), extraocular muscles (restriction), globe (injection/chemosis), and optic nerve function (visual acuity/color plates/relative afferent pupillary defect). Because of the association between rheumatologic disease and NSOI the typical laboratory work-up for suspected NSOI should include a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, thyroid function studies, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, rapid plasma reagin test, and rheumatoid factor.

Key features in the question:

  • Middle-aged woman
  • Bilateral proptosis
  • Restricted ocular movements
  • Chemosis (conjunctival edema/swelling)

These symptoms are highly suggestive of Idiopathic Orbital Inflammation (IOI), also known as Orbital Inflammatory Pseudotumor, which is the correct answer.

Why Not the Other Options?

  • (A) Orbital Cellulitis: Usually unilateral, associated with fever, pain, and systemic infection signs.
  • (B) Thyroid Ophthalmopathy: Commonly presents with bilateral proptosis but typically has lid retraction and occurs in hyperthyroid patients. This patient is euthyroid.
  • (D) Orbital Lymphoma: Usually painless, slowly progressive proptosis without significant inflammation or restricted eye movements.

Key Features of Orbital Inflammatory Pseudotumor (IOI)

  • Sudden onset of painful proptosis
  • Bilateral (though unilateral can also occur)
  • Extraocular muscle restriction
  • Chemosis, conjunctival injection
  • Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out infections, thyroid disease, and malignancy
  • Responds well to corticosteroids

question_text: A 74 year old patient reports to OPD with pigmented mass in the eye with clinical imaging as depicted below. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are incorrect?
option_a: Common site of occurrence is fornices
option_b: Melanosis is a precancerous predisposing lesion
option_d: Spreads over surface of the globe
explanation:
Malignant melanoma

It occurs typically at the limbus, is usually pigmented and occurs mostly in the elderly. It spreads over the surface of the globe but rarely penetrates it; recurrences and metastases occur as elsewhere in the body. The neoplasm may be alveolar (derived from naevi) or round- or spindle-celled. The treatment is by excision of the globe or exenteration of the orbit.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following management options for OCP yields poor result?
explanation:
• Artificial tears: Artificial tears are a safe and effective treatment for dry eye. They can help to relieve the symptoms of dryness, irritation, and discomfort.
  • Immunosuppressive therapy: Immunosuppressive therapy can be effective in reducing inflammation and slowing the progression of OCP. However, it is important to weigh the risks and benefits of immunosuppressive therapy before starting treatment.
  • Mucous membrane grafting: Mucous membrane grafting is a surgery to replace damaged conjunctiva with healthy tissue from another part of the body. It can be a helpful treatment for patients with OCP, but it is a challenging surgery with a high rate of complications.
  • Keratoprosthesis: A keratoprosthesis is an artificial cornea that can be implanted in patients with severe corneal opacification. It can be a life-changing surgery for patients with OCP, but it is also a complex surgery with a number of risks.

Why mucous membrane grafting yields poor result:

Mucous membrane grafting is a challenging surgery with a high rate of complications. The graft may not survive, or it may become scarred and contracted. In addition, mucous membrane grafting does not always prevent the progression of OCP.

Overall, mucous membrane grafting is a high-risk surgery with a limited chance of success. It is only recommended for patients with severe OCP who have failed other treatments

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: What is treatment of choice for conjunctival melanomas?
explanation:
β-Irradiation, either primary or after tumour excision, is the treatment of choice for conjunctival melanomas.

Malignant lesions may become radioresistant, in which case the only effective treatment is wide excision with exenteration of the orbit and extensive reconstitution by skin grafting.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding dry eye treatment is/are correct?
option_a: Collagen plugs cause temporary occlusion of puncta and help to preserve natural tears
option_b: Lateral tarsorrhaphy helps evaporation of tears
option_c: Trans-retinoic acid can correct squamous metaplasia of surface
explanation:
Treatment of DRY EYE

  • Tear supplements: Several varieties of effective artificial tears are commercially available. The slow-release variety is a pellet of a cellulose compound without preservative that is inserted below the tarsus of the lower lid where it dissolves slowly, providing a continuous source of tears.
  • Preservation of the natural tears: Temporary occlusion of the puncta by inserting dissolvable collagen plugs, or permanent occlusion by inserting silicone plugs or by thermal cautery. Lateral tarsorrhaphy can also be performed to reduce evaporation of tears.
  • Excess mucus may be treated by acetyl cysteine 5% drops buffered to pH 8.4 with sodium bicarbonate.
  • Squamous metaplasia of the ocular surface epithelium may play a part in the production of symptoms. This abnormality can be reversed by the application of topical trans-retinoic acid ointment with alleviation of discomfort.

Reference: Parson’s Diseases of the Eye-Edition 23-Chap 11-Diseases of the Conjunctiva

question_text: Which of the following is false about corneal epithelium?
explanation:
The cornea has unmyelinated nerve endings sensitive to touch, temperature and chemicals; a touch of the cornea causes an involuntary reflex to close the eyelid. Because transparency is of prime importance, the healthy cornea does not have or need blood vessels within it. Instead, oxygen dissolves in tears and then diffuses throughout the cornea to keep it healthy. Similarly, nutrients are transported via diffusion from the tear fluid through the outside surface and the aqueous humour through the inside surface. Nutrients also come via neurotrophins supplied by the nerves of the cornea. In humans, the cornea has a diameter of about 11.5 mm and a thickness of 0.5-0.6 mm in the center and 0.6-0.8 mm at the periphery. Transparency, avascularity, the presence of immature resident immune cells, and immunologic privilege makes the cornea a very special tissue.

The most abundant soluble protein in mammalian cornea is albumin.

The human cornea borders with the sclera at the corneal limbus. In lampreys, the cornea is solely an extension of the sclera, and is separate from the skin above it, but in more advanced vertebrates it is always fused with the skin to form a single structure, albeit one composed of multiple layers. In fish, and aquatic vertebrates in general, the cornea plays no role in focusing light, since it has virtually the same refractive index as water.

Microanatomy

Vertical section of human cornea from near the margin. (Waldeyer.) Magnified. 1: Epithelium. 2: Anterior elastic lamina. 3: substantia propria. 4: Posterior elastic lamina (Descemet's membrane). 5: Endothelium of the anterior chamber. a: Oblique fibers in the anterior layer of the substantia propria. b: Lamellae, the fibers of which are cut across, producing a dotted appearance. c: Corneal corpuscles appearing fusiform in section. d: Lamellae, the fibers of which are cut longitudinally. e: Transition to the sclera, with more distinct fibrillation, and surmounted by a thicker epithelium. f: Small blood vessels cut across near the margin of the cornea.

Corneal cross-section imaged by an SD-OCT

The human cornea has five layers (possibly six, if the Dua's layer is included). Corneas of other primates have five known layers. The corneas of cats, dogs, wolves, and other carnivores only have four. From the anterior to posterior the layers of the human cornea are:

Corneal epithelium: an exceedingly thin multicellular epithelial tissue layer (non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium) of fast-growing and easily regenerated cells, kept moist with tears. Irregularity or edema of the corneal epithelium disrupts the smoothness of the air/tear-film interface, the most significant component of the total refractive power of the eye, thereby reducing visual acuity. Corneal epithelium is continuous with the conjunctival epithelium, and is composed of about 6 layers of cells which are shed constantly on the exposed layer and are regenerated by multiplication in the basal layer.

Bowman's layer (also known as the anterior limiting membrane): when discussed in lieu of a subepithelial basement membrane, Bowman's Layer is a tough layer composed of collagen (mainly type I collagen fibrils), laminin, nidogen, perlecan and other HSPGs that protects the corneal stroma. When discussed as a separate entity from the subepithelial basement membrane, Bowman's Layer can be described as an acellular, condensed region of the apical stroma, composed primarily of randomly organized yet tightly woven collagen fibrils. These fibrils interact with and attach onto each other. This layer is eight to 14 micrometres (μm) thick and is absent or very thin in non-primates.

Corneal stroma (also substantia propria): a thick, transparent middle layer, consisting of regularly arranged collagen fibers along with sparsely distributed interconnected keratocytes, which are the cells for general repair and maintenance. They are parallel and are superimposed like book pages. The corneal stroma consists of approximately 200 layers of mainly type I collagen fibrils. Each layer is 1.5-2.5 μm. Up to 90% of the corneal thickness is composed of stroma. There are 2 theories of how transparency in the cornea comes about:

The lattice arrangements of the collagen fibrils in the stroma. The light scatter by individual fibrils is cancelled by destructive interference from the scattered light from other individual fibrils.

The spacing of the neighboring collagen fibrils in the stroma must be < 200 nm for there to be transparency. (Goldman and Benedek)

Descemet's membrane (also posterior limiting membrane): a thin acellular layer that serves as the modified basement membrane of the corneal endothelium, from which the cells are derived. This layer is composed mainly of collagen type IV fibrils, less rigid than collagen type I fibrils, and is around 5-20 μm thick, depending on the subject's age. Just anterior to Descemet's membrane, a very thin and strong layer, Dua's layer, 15 microns thick and able to withstand 1.5 to 2 bars of pressure.

Corneal endothelium: a simple squamous or low cuboidal monolayer, approx 5 μm thick, of mitochondria-rich cells. These cells are responsible for regulating fluid and solute transport between the aqueous and corneal stromal compartments. (The term endothelium is a misnomer here. The corneal endothelium is bathed by aqueous humor, not by blood or lymph, and has a very different origin, function, and appearance from vascular endothelia). Unlike the corneal epithelium, the cells of the endothelium do not regenerate. Instead, they stretch to compensate for dead cells which reduces the overall cell density of the endothelium, which affects fluid regulation. If the endothelium can no longer maintain a proper fluid balance, stromal swelling due to excess fluids and subsequent loss of transparency will occur and this may cause corneal edema and interference with the transparency of the cornea and thus impairing the image formed. Iris pigment cells deposited on the corneal endothelium can sometimes be washed into a distinct vertical pattern by the aqueous currents - this is known as Krukenberg's Spindle.

Nerve supply

The cornea is one of the most sensitive tissues of the body, as it is densely innervated with sensory nerve fibres via the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve by way of 70-80 long ciliary nerves. Research suggests the density of pain receptors in the cornea is 300-600 times greater than skin and 20-40 times greater than dental pulp, making any injury to the structure excruciatingly painful.

The ciliary nerves run under the endothelium and exit the eye through holes in the sclera apart from the optic nerve (which transmits only optic signals). The nerves enter the cornea via three levels; scleral, episcleral and conjunctival. Most of the bundles give rise by subdivision to a network in the stroma, from which fibres supply the different regions. The three networks are, midstromal, subepithelial/sub-basal, and epithelial. The receptive fields of each nerve ending are very large, and may overlap.

Corneal nerves of the subepithelial layer terminate near the superficial epithelial layer of the cornea in a logarithmic spiral pattern. The density of epithelial nerves decreases with age, especially after the seventh decade

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Option B. Limbus has stem cells - True. The limbus contains limbal stem cells, which play a crucial role in regenerating the corneal epithelium. Damage to these stem cells can lead to corneal opacity and vision loss.

Option C. Lined by stratified epithelium - True. The corneal epithelium is a non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium composed of about 5-7 cell layers. It serves as a protective barrier and is capable of rapid regeneration.

Option D. Apical cells have microvilli - True. The apical epithelial cells of the cornea have microvilli and microplicae, which help stabilize the tear film and enhance corneal transparency.

Key Takeaway:

The corneal epithelium has a high capacity for regeneration due to limbal stem cells, but Bowman's membrane does not regenerate if damaged.

question_text: Congenital Microphthalmos can be seen in which of the following:
explanation:
A picture of Left eye microphthalmia

  • Measles: Ocular lesions are: catarrhal conjunctivitis, Kolpik's spots on conjunctiva, corneal ulceration, optic neuritis and retinitis.
  • Mumps: Ocular involvement may occur as conjunctivitis, keratitis, acute dacryoadenitis and uveitis.
  • Rubella: Ocular lesions seen in rubella(German measles) are congenital microphthalmos, cataract, glaucoma, chorioretinitis and optic atrophy.
  • Whooping cough: There may occur subconjunctival hemorrhages and rarely orbital hemorrhage leading to proptosis.

Reference: A.K. Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 436.

question_text: Structures originating from surface ectoderm are all except

Optic nerve originates from neuroectoderm.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding disease involvement in this patient are correct? Clinical imaging is as depicted below.
option_a: Skin involvement is in dermatome supplied by first branch of Trigeminal nerve
option_b: Skin involvement is in dermatome supplied by second branch of Trigeminal nerve
option_c: Involvement of tip of nose indicates Nasociliary branch involvement
explanation:
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus. question_text: A 70-year-old man presents with worsening vision in his right eye. He describes it as a curtain falling over the visual field. He has no pain, but sees flashes of light and floaters. Examination shows a loss of the red reflex in the right eye and on fundoscopy diagnosis is confirmed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Retinal detachment is characterized by symptoms of flashes of light, floaters, and a sudden curtain-like shadow over the visual field, indicating separation from the underlying retinal layers.
  • The loss of the red reflex and findings of a detached retina on fundoscopy further confirm this diagnosis.
  • Other conditions, such as cataracts, central retinal vein occlusion, and glaucoma, exhibit different symptom patterns.

Why not others:

  • B) Cataract: Presents with gradual, painless vision loss described as blurriness or clouding. Symptoms do not include flashes, floaters, or the curtain effect, making it less likely in this scenario.
  • C) Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO): Typically shows sudden, painless vision loss without the classic curtain effect or flashes. Fundoscopy would reveal a "blood and thunder" appearance with hemorrhages and edema, not detachment.
  • D) Glaucoma: Acute angle-closure glaucoma involves sudden, painful vision loss with symptoms like a red eye and corneal edema. Chronic glaucoma causes gradual peripheral vision loss and does not align with the acute symptoms presented here.

Key Takeaways:

  • The presentation of flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like shadow over vision is classic for retinal detachment.
  • Other diagnoses show distinct symptomatology that does not match the patient's experience, reinforcing the likelihood of retinal detachment.

Tags: Fmge aug 2020

Tag: Special senses

Level: Good to know

Reference: Guyton & Hall, text book of medical physiology, 14th ed, pg. 641

Staphyloma is an abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through a weak point of the eye.

Acquired anterior staphyloma occurs subsequent to corneal perforation, usually following untreated or non-responding infective keratitis. Anterior staphylomas are rarely observed in patients with Peters anomaly.

When the cornea perforates, the iris plugs the wound and a pseudocornea forms over the iris. It is unable to withstand the intraocular pressure and thus, progressively protrudes.

The treatment of anterior staphyloma usually involves evisceration of the affected eye and sclerokeratoplasty.

question_text: A 5-year-old boy is brought in with a small nodule on the sclera, as seen in the provided image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Dermoid cyst appears as a lenticular yellow tumour near the corneal margin and consists of epidermoid epithelium with sebaceous glands and hair.

  • Dermoid cyst is a congenital, often benign growth that contains skin-like structures, such as hair follicles, sweat glands, and sebaceous glands.
  • It can present as a small, firm, yellowish nodule on the sclera or conjunctiva.
  • These cysts are often located near the limbus (the junction between the cornea and sclera) and may be noticed in childhood, especially if they grow or become more noticeable over time.

A dermoid cyst may be diagnosed based on its characteristic appearance and location, and sometimes imaging or excision is needed for confirmation.

Explanation for other options:

Pterygium (Option A): A pterygium is a fibrovascular growth that extends from the conjunctiva onto the cornea, typically seen on the nasal side of the eye. It is usually triangular and may cause visual disturbance. It is not typically a nodule confined to the sclera.

Pinguecula (Option B): A yellowish, triangular patch on the conjunctiva near the limbus, typically in the elderly, associated with sun exposure and not extending onto the cornea.

Dermolipoma (Option C): A dermolipoma is a benign tumour consisting of fat and skin-like tissue. While they may be located in the eye area, they typically present as larger, softer masses, and this does not match the presentation of a small nodule on the sclera.

question_text: In thin sclera, blue color appearance comes from
explanation:
Several things can cause the entire sclera to change color or spots of color to appear:

Blue sclera:

  • If the sclera is thinner than normal, blood vessels may show through, giving your eyeballs a blue or gray hue due to visualization of underlying uvea.
  • This may occur in people with certain health conditions. Examples include osteogenesis imperfecta(a genetic bone disease) and Marfan syndrome(a disorder in connective tissue throughout the body). Other examples include iron deficiency and anemia.

Icteric sclera and jaundice: If the entire sclerae turn yellow, that could mean you have jaundice. Jaundice indicates liver disease, which means the liver isn't filtering blood properly.

Injury: If your eyeball is injured, it may have a bright red spot. This indicates a broken blood vessel that has leaked some blood. These red spots are usually harmless and go away in a few days or weeks.

Irritation: If your eyes are "bloodshot", you can see redness throughout the sclerae. Eyes may be irritated due to smoke, allergies, exhaustion or infection.

Medication: Some medications can tint the sclerae blue or gray(for example, an antibiotic called minocycline).

Melanosis: Your sclera may contain a flat, brown spot, almost like a freckle. This is more common in Black people. The spots are caused by high levels of pigment called melanin and they're harmless.

Pinguecula: A small patch of yellow may bulge out from your sclera after damage from the sun, wind or dust. The patch may become inflamed and turn pink or red.

Pterygium: If a pinguecula goes untreated, it can get larger, expand into the cornea and block vision.

Primary acquired melanosis(PAM): If you have a flat brown spot on the eye that changes over time, this may indicate PAM. This condition can become cancerous, so report any new or changing spots on the sclera.

The sclera is made of tough collagen fibers, which crisscross in random directions. That random pattern gives your eyeball its white color and gives the sclera strength. This contrasts with the collagen fibers in your cornea, which are very organized and allow the cornea to be clear.

Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 52.

question_text: Which of the following is the function of sclera
explanation:
• The sclera forms the posterior five-sixths of the connective tissue coat of the globe.
  • It is continuous with the dura mater and the cornea and maintains the shape of the globe, offering resistance to internal and external forces and provides an attachment for the extraocular muscle insertions.
  • The sclera is perforated by many nerves and vessels passing through the posterior scleral foramen, the hole that is formed by the optic nerve.
  • At the optic disc the outer two-thirds of the sclera continues with the dura mater(outer coat of the brain) via the dural sheath of the optic nerve.
  • The inner third joins with some choroidal tissue to form a plate(lamina cribrosa) across the optic nerve with perforations through which the optic fibers(fasciculi) pass.
  • The thickness of the sclera varies from 1 mm at the posterior pole to 0.3 mm just behind the rectus muscle [disambiguation needed] insertions.
  • The sclera's blood vessels are mainly on the surface. Along with the vessels of the conjunctiva(which is a thin layer covering the sclera), those in the episclera render the inflamed eye bright red.
  • In many vertebrates, the sclera is reinforced with plates of cartilage or bone, together forming a circular structure called the sclerotic ring.

Reference: Parson 22/e, Pg: 50.

question_text: The innermost layer of sclera is
explanation:
The collagen of the sclera is continuous with the cornea. From outer to innermost, the four layers of the sclera are:

  • Episclera
  • Stroma
  • Lamina fusca
  • Endothelium

The sclera is opaque due to the irregularity of the Type I collagen fibers, as opposed to the near-uniform thickness and parallel arrangement of the corneal collagen.

Moreover, the cornea bears more mucopolysaccharide(a carbohydrate that has among its repeating units a nitrogenous sugar, hexosamine) to embed the fibrils.

The cornea, unlike the sclera, has six layers. The middle, thickest layer is also called the stroma. The sclera, like the cornea, contains a basal endothelium, above which there is the lamina fusca, containing a high count of pigment cells.

Sclera has mainly three layers. Episcleral, sclera proper and lamina fusca.

But some books mention 4th layer as endothelium.

So if in a question endothelium is also given as option one can mark endothelium, else lamina fusca.

Sometimes, very small gray-blue spots can appear on the sclera, a harmless condition called scleral melanocytosis.

question_text: Sclera is not transparent due to
option_a: Collagen bundles in sclera are of varying sizes and are irregularly arranged
explanation:
The sclera proper, also known as the scleral stroma, is also called the substantia propria.

Ultrasructurally, sclera is composed of:

  • Collagen bundles
  • Elastic fibers
  • Fibroblasts
  • Ground substances

These components are responsible for its non-transparent nature. The ground substances consist of proteoglycans and glycoproteins.

The collagen bundles in the sclera vary in size and are irregularly arranged, which is why the sclera is not transparent like the cornea.

These variations in scleral collagen fibers are more pronounced in the mid-sclera, where the diameter of the fibers ranges from 50 to 400 nm.

question_text:
What is the order of insertion of the recti muscles on the Annulus of Zinn?
A. Medial rectus
B. Inferior rectus
C. Lateral rectus
D. Superior rectus
explanation:
Explanation:

The recti muscles originate from the common tendinous ring (Annulus of Zinn) at the orbital apex. Their insertions on the sclera follow a specific sequence:

Order of insertion:

  • Medial rectus (A)- closest to the limbus (~5.5 mm)
  • Inferior rectus (B)- ~6.5 mm from the limbus
  • Lateral rectus (C)- ~6.9 mm from the limbus
  • Superior rectus (D)- farthest from the limbus (~7.7 mm)

This sequence is sometimes referred to in relation to the Spiral of Tillaux, which describes the increasing distances of rectus insertions from the limbus.

Key takeaway:

The sequence medial → inferior → lateral → superior is clinically relevant for surgeries involving rectus muscles, such as strabismus correction.

question_text: In an eye with increased episcleral venous pressure, which of the following medical agents would be expected to have the least intraocular pressure-lowering effect?
option_a: Topical miotic (cholinergic) therapy (pilocarpine, carbachol, echothiophate iodide)
option_b: Betaadrenergic antagonist (betaxolol, carteolol, levobunolol, metipranolol, timolol)

explanation:
Explanation:

  • Increased episcleral venous pressure (EVP) reduces aqueous outflow via the trabecular meshwork. Topical Miotics (pilocarpine, carbachol, echothiophate) work by increasing trabecular outflow, so they are least effective when EVP is elevated.
  • Agents that reduce aqueous production (beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) or increase uveoscleral outflow (prostaglandin analogs) are more effective in this setting.
  • Laser trabeculoplasty is also less effective when EVP is high.

Key Takeaways:

  • LPI prevents progression from narrow/occludable angles to chronic angle-closure glaucoma.
  • Gonioscopy remains the gold standard to evaluate angle anatomy

question_text: What is regarded as the most accurate tonometer used in clinical practice?
explanation:
Explanation:

Types of Tonometry:

Indentation Tonometry:

  • Principle: Determines intraocular pressure (IOP) by assessing how much a plunger indents the eye - softer eyes indent more
  • Schiotz Tonometer (Option A ruled out):
    • Among the most widely used tonometers globally.
    • Advantages: Affordable, easy to handle, and dependable.
    • Limitations: May provide inaccurate IOP readings in eyes with abnormal scleral rigidity (e.g., high myopia, post-operative eyes).

Applanation Tonometry:

  • Principle: Based on the Imbert-Fick law (P = W/A), it calculates IOP by measuring the force required to flatten a set area of the cornea.
  • Goldmann Applanation Tonometer:
    • The gold standard for measuring IOP.
    • Method:
      • The cornea is numbed and stained with fluorescein dye.
      • A biprism is placed against the cornea and illuminated using cobalt blue light.
      • The examiner aligns the inner edges of the fluorescein semicircles.
      • The reading on the dial is multiplied by 10 to obtain the IOP.

Variable Force Tonometers:

  • Measure pressure based on adjustable or electronically applied force.
  • Examples include:
    • Goldmann Applanation Tonometer - standard for accuracy.
    • Perkins Tonometer - portable, handheld version of the Goldmann.
    • Draeger Tonometer - measures a broad IOP range, uses a motor and unique prism design.
    • Non-contact Tonometers (e.g., Pulsair, Air Puff, Grolman) - use air jets to flatten the cornea without physical contact.
    • Tono-Pen - handheld, combines applanation and indentation; useful for children and irregular corneas.
    • MacKay-Marg Tonometer - combines both indentation and applanation.
    • Rebound Tonometer - bounces a probe off the cornea to measure IOP.
    • Transpalpebral Tonometer - measures IOP through the eyelid (avoids corneal contact).

Fixed Force Tonometers:

  • Apply a constant pressure to the eye and infer IOP based on corneal flattening or indentation.
  • Examples:
    • Maklakov Tonometer
    • Barraquer Tonometer

Explanation for other options:

Tonopen (Option C): It is a portable, electronic tonometer that assesses intraocular pressure (IOP) using a combination of applanation and indentation techniques. It is especially useful in situations where conventional tonometers are less practical, such as with pediatric patients or those with irregular corneas.

Pascal Dynamic Contour Tonometer (Option D): It is a modern, non-applanation-based device that measures IOP by conforming to the natural contour of the cornea. It provides continuous pressure readings during gentle corneal contact, aiming for more accurate measurements that are less influenced by corneal thickness or rigidity.

question_text: Tonometry in irregular corneas can be done by
explanation:
Types of Tonometers

  • Indentation tonometer
    • Schiotz tonometer. It is widely used because it is portable and the technique is simple to learn. But the main disadvantage is that the reading is affected by scleral rigidity.
  • Applanation tonometer: It is based on Imbert-Fick law. The law states P = F/A where P = Pressure inside a sphere, F = Force and A = Area. In most applanation scleral tonometers, the area (A) is fixed and the force (F) is variable.

Types of applanation tonometer

  • Goldmann Applanation tonometer: It is the gold standard tonometer. It gives accurate and reproducible readings. The main disadvantage is that the reading is dependent on the corneal thickness. Also its accuracy is decreased in irregular corneas.
  • Perkin's handheld tonometer: It is a portable tonometer and used mainly in children.

question_text: Drug used in patient with increased IOP& optic disc changes, ciliary congestion for Decrease IOP BY increases uveo scleral outflow:
explanation:
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog used in the treatment of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), particularly in conditions like glaucoma. It works by selectively stimulating the prostaglandin F2 alpha receptor, which increases the outflow of aqueous humor through the uveoscleral pathway. This increased outflow helps lower IOP, making latanoprost an effective treatment for conditions like primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

Incorrect Options:

B. Dorzolamide
Dorzolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that decreases IOP by reducing the production of aqueous humor. It does not increase the outflow of aqueous humor but rather reduces its production, leading to a decrease in IOP.

C. Pilocarpine
Pilocarpine is a cholinergic agent that works by constricting the pupil, which opens the trabecular meshwork and increases aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular pathway. However, it is not primarily known for increasing uveoscleral outflow, which is the mechanism targeted by latanoprost.

D. Timolol
Timolol is a beta-blocker that decreases the production of aqueous humor, thus lowering IOP. It does not affect the outflow pathways directly, especially not the uveoscleral outflow, as latanoprost does.

Key Takeaway: Latanoprost works by increasing uveoscleral outflow, thereby lowering intraocular pressure. It is particularly useful in managing conditions like glaucoma where increased IOP is a concern.

question_text: Which of the following instruments are considered the gold standard for measuring intraocular pressure?
explanation:
Explanation:

The gold standard instrument for measuring intraocular pressure is Goldmann applanation tonometer.

Goldmann Applanation Tonometer:

  • Most popular and accurate; uses a double prism on a slit lamp.
  • Considered the reference standard
  • Gold standard for assessing IOP in the clinic.
  • Based on Imbert-Fick principle; the amount of force necessary to applanate a perfectly elastic, infinitely thin, dry sphere divided by the area flattened equals the pressure inside the sphere.
  • The area is set at 7.35 mm2 (3.06 mm diameter) to account for corneal thickness, scleral rigidity, and tear film surface tension

Explanation of other options:

Gonioscope (Option A): Gonioscope is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber.

Hertel's exophthalmometer (Option C): Hertel's exophthalmometer is used to measure the protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin.

Tonopen (Option D): A portable, handheld electronic tonometer used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). Cost of disposable covers and battery. In some cases, readings can vary significantly from Goldmann.

question_text: In which of the following quadrants are retinal dialyses most often found following blunt trauma?
explanation:
Blunt trauma may result in a variety of retinal breaks including retinal dialyses, macular holes, giant retinal tears, horseshoe retinal tears, operculated retinal tears, and large, necrotic, sometimes posterior retinal breaks often associated with chorioretinitis sclopetaria. Retinal dialyses, however, are the most common retinal breaks found following blunt ocular trauma. Retinal dialyses resulting from blunt trauma are most often found in the inferotemporal and superonasal quadrants. All patients with a history of blunt trauma need to be given a careful retinal examination with scleral depression to look for retinal breaks after their pain, iritis, or hyphema, if any, has resolved.

Blunt trauma can cause an acute rise in intraocular pressure and cause a rupture in the location where the eye is the weakest.

The site of rupture commonly occurs where the sclera is thinnest and weakest near the equator directly behind the insertion of the rectus muscles. Other regions prone to rupture include the limbus, insertion of the optic nerve, and sites of prior eye surgery.

In indirect trauma, the most common location of rupture is at the superior-nasal quadrant close to the limbus

explanation:

Spoke-like iris transillumination defects in the iris midperiphery develop from the irido zonular friction and are characteristic of this syndrome. Liberated pigment deposits on the corneal endothelium in a vertical spindle pattern (Krukenberg spindle), in the trabecular meshwork, and on the lens periphery (Scheie stripe). Peripupillary atrophy is commonly observed in exfoliation syndrome. Blood in Schlemm's canal may be seen with elevated episcleral venous pressure. Iris bombe develops in the presence of a pupillary block.

question_text: What is the best way to distinguish a restrictive motility disorder from a paretic disorder after a blowout fracture?
option_c: Motility examination of the cardinal positions of gaze
explanation:
• Alternate prism cover tests, Goldmann single binocular fields, and a careful motility examination are all good ways to identify or quantify ocular misalignment, but will not distinguish paralytic from restrictive cases.
  • Forced-duction testing is the best clinical tool to distinguish these two entities and should be done several days after the injury.
  • Edema and/or a hematoma may cause initial forced ductions to appear positive and give a false impression that entrapment exists.
  • After topical anesthesia is obtained with tetracaine or cocaine, the episcleral tissues at the inferior limbus are grasped with toothed forceps.
  • The eye is then rotated in the desired direction, and comparisons can be made with the uninjured side.
  • In cases of paralytic strabismus, the forced ductions are free, unlike cases of restrictive strabismus.

question_text: Following substance has more concentration in aqueous than plasma
explanation:
AQUEOUS HUMOUR DYNAMICS

  • Aqueous humour is basically an ultrafiltrate of the plasma.
  • The site of production is the ciliary processes of the pars plicata. Each ciliary process is lined by two layers of epithelium namely pigmented and non-pigmented.
  • At the centre of the ciliary process is a rich capillary network within the surrounding stroma.

Aqueous humour production involves the following steps:

  • A Formation of a plasma filtrate from the capillary network within the stroma by the process of ultrafiltration
  • Transfer of this plasma filtrate from the ciliary stroma into the aqueous compartment across the epithelium. This involves two processes namely diffusion and active secretion
  • Rate of aqueous production is 2-3 μL/min
  • Substances whose concentration in aqueous is less than plasma: Protein, glucose, urea.
  • A Substances whose concentration in aqueous is more than plasma: Ascorbate, lactate, pyruvate
Pneumonic: ATE more in aqueous
  • Aqueous humour flows from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber through the pupil. From the anterior chamber it has two outflow pathways

Conventional or Trabecular pathway: It operates through the angle of anterior chamber and accounts for 90% of aqueous outflow. The structures in the pathway are Trabecular meshwork → Schlemm's canal→ Collector vessels→→ Episcleral veins. The site of maximum resistance in this pathway is the juxtacanalicular part of the trabecular meshwork

Unconventional or Uveoscleral pathway: Accounts for remaining 10% aqueous outflow: Ciliary body→ Suprachoroidal space →→ Episcleral veins
Ciliary body→ Suprachoroidal space →→ Vortex veins.

question_text: Nerve supply of the cornea is derived from which cranial nerve/ sub-branch?
explanation:
• The cornea is supplied by nerves which originate from the small ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, mainly by the long ciliary nerves which run in the peri choroidal space and pierce the sclera a short distance posterior to the limbus.
  • Here, they form an annular plexus from which branches travel radially to enter the corneal stroma.
  • The nerve fibres lose their myelin sheaths and unite to form a subepithelial corneal
  • Fine terminal branches then pierce the Bowman’s membrane and pass between the epithelial cells to form the intraepithelial plexus.
  • There are no specialized nerve endings or sensory organelles.
  • The axons do not have a Schwann cell sheath.
  • These naked axons are responsive to pain and temperature.
  • Due to its dense nerve supply, the cornea is an extremely sensitive structure.
  • The Maxillary and Mandibular branches of the Trigeminal Nerve supply other aspects of the face whereas the Facial nerve provides motor innervation to Orbicularis Oculi muscle.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Edition 23rd- Chap 12- Diseases of the cornea

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the below depicted condition is/are incorrect?
option_a: Occurs due to incomplete closure of lens vesicle
option_b: Commonly situated at inferior pole of disc
option_d: Can be associated with optic disc pits
explanation:
Optic Disc Coloboma

  • This occurs in two forms, one of which is common and the other rare. The common form is due to incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure, and manifests itself as an inferior crescent, resembling the myopic crescent but situated at the lower edge of the disc.
  • It occurs most commonly in hypermetropic and astigmatic eyes, which often have slightly defective vision in spite of the correction of any error of refraction. It is often slightly ectatic (conus).
  • In coloboma of the disc (or nerve sheath), there is greater failure of the embryonic fissure to close.
  • The disc looks large and the vessels have an abnormal distribution, appearing only above or irregularly around the edges.
  • Apparent disc is really the sclera and the inner surface of the sheath of the nerve, the nerve itself being usually spread out as a pink, horizontal, linear band at the upper part.
  • The floor of the coloboma is white and measurably depressed, and often ectatic. The eye usually has defective vision.
  • Rare anomalies related to coloboma are round cavities (holes) on the disc known as optic disc pits, generally situated in the temporal portion.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

Contraindications for evisceration include:

  • Known or suspected intraocular malignancy. A preoperative ocular ultrasound is mandatory to rule out occult malignancy.
  • Phthisis bulbi, microphthalmia, scleral contracture(relative) - evisceration may be more difficult due to a lack of sufficient scleral shell volume to adequately encase the implant.
  • Evisceration surgery in a recently injured eye carries a definite small risk of sympathetic ophthalmia in the apposing eye, because some uveal tissue is always left behind in scleral canals.
  • Picture of eviscerationn

Except in these situations, evisceration is considered as an alternative to enucleation.

question_text: MC method of spread of retinoblastoma is
explanation:
Retinoblastoma can demonstrate local spread along the optic nerve directly into the orbit ( MC method of spread of this tumour). It can also metastasize hematogenously to bone, liver, brain and other organs. Retinoblastoma can spread through the optic nerve with relative ease especially once the lamina cribrosa is breached. Orbital extension may present with proptosis and is most likely to occur at the site of the scleral emissary veins. Systemic metastasis occurs to the brain, skull, distant bones and the lymph nodes

When an eye is enucleated for retinoblastoma, the goal is to remove as much optic nerve as possible to try ensure that the cut end of the nerve is free of tumor. Enucleation may best be performed by oculoplastic surgeons who may consider lateral canthotomy and other techniques to optimize the length of optic nerve obtained on the enucleated specimen

question_text: Where are the corneal stem cells situated?
explanation:
• The corneal physiology is designed in such a way to maintain transparency and take care of healing and/or regeneration capacity of the cornea.
  • In case the cornea sustains injury due to any cause such as trauma, infection or surgery, and if the injury is superficial involving only the epithelium, the stratified squamous epithelium covering the anterior surface of the cornea rapidly regenerates.
  • This regeneration of corneal epithelial cells is mainly from stem cells, which are epithelial cells present as palisades of Vogt at the limbus.
  • These mitotically active cells with an increased surface area of basal cells present in folds, and palisades are ideally suited for this purpose.
  • There is very little mitotic activity in the basal cells at the centre of the cornea.

question_text: Corneal transparency is decided by
explanation:
GAGs (Glycosaminoglycans) or so called acidmucopolysaccharides represent 4-4.5% of the dry weight of the cornea.

Cornea contains three major GAG fractions namely: Keratan sulfate (50%), chondroitin sulfate (25%) and chondroitin (25%)-present exclusively in cornea.

The GAG are present in the interfibrillar space of the corneal stroma and account for the `stromal swelling pressure'(normal-60 mmHg) ie. Its tendency to imbibe water and thus plays an important role in the maintenance of corneal hydration level and transparency. An abnormal accumulation of GAG occurs in the corneal stroma of the patients affected by the inborn errors of GAG metabolism known as mucopolysaccharidosis

  • Keratan sulfate is the most abundant glycosaminoglycan (GAG) in the cornea, making up 50% of corneal GAGs.
  • It is located in the interfibrillar space of the corneal stroma and helps regulate stromal hydration and maintain corneal transparency by preventing excessive water accumulation.
  • It plays a crucial role in maintaining stromal swelling pressure (~60 mmHg), which is essential for clarity and light transmission.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(A) Chondroitin sulfate: Present in the cornea (~25%) but mainly contributes to structural integrity rather than transparency.

(B) Heparan sulfate: Found in the basement membranes of various tissues but does not significantly influence corneal transparency.

(C) Hyaluronic acid: Present in the vitreous humor and synovial fluid, but not a major component of the cornea. It is more involved in hydration and lubrication than in corneal clarity.

Key Takeaway:

Keratan sulfate is the primary glycosaminoglycan responsible for corneal transparency by regulating stromal hydration and maintaining optimal swelling pressure.

question_text: Which of the following factors contribute to corneal transparency?
option_a: Hydrophobic epithelium/ endothelium and dehydrated stroma
option_c: Lack of pigment and blood vessels
explanation:
Explanation:

The following factors contribute to corneal transparency:

  • Its relatively dehydrated state.
    • This relative state of dehydration is maintained by the integrity of the hydrophobic epithelium and endothelium, the endothelial pump and the osmotic gradient, because the aqueous and tears are relatively hypertonic.
    • The main role of the endothelial cells is to limit the fluid intake of the cornea from the aqueous.
  • Absence of blood vessels and pigment.
  • Uniform refractive index of all the layers.
  • Uniform spacing of the collagen fibrils in the stroma.
    • The collagen fibrils are separated by a distance which is less than the wavelength of light so that any irregularly refracted rays of light are eliminated by destructive interference.
    • If there is an increase in separation of the stromal collagen or a disruption in their regular arrangement, for example, with an increase in tissue fluid, the cornea becomes opaque.

question_text: Most dangerous intraocular foreign body is
explanation:
Chalcosis, also called chalcosis bulbi, is a chronic reaction to a copper-containing intraocular foreign body (IOFB)

When copper enters the eye, it is oxidized from its uncharged elemental form, Cu, to Cu2+ ions. Though the ions are free to diffuse throughout the vitreous, they have a propensity to deposit in intraocular basement membranes including Descemet's membrane of the cornea (KF ring) and the internal limiting membrane (ILM)

Foreign bodies containing less copper (<85%), such as brass and bronze, may lead to a localized inflammatory response and are typically the cause of chalcosis. Materials containing less than 70% copper are relatively inert, leading to low-grade chronic inflammation or no discernible symptoms. However, foreign bodies with higher concentrations of copper (>85%) show a generalized pattern of intraocular copper deposition and are associated with more devastating outcomes such as suppurative endophthalmitis and phthisis bulbi.

Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 911 IOFB

question_text: 25-year-old patient presents with redness, pain and foreign body sensation in the right eye. On the slit lamp, a linear branching corneal lesion with terminal bulbs was seen. Also has reduced corneal sensation. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A linear branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs and reduced corneal sensation is pathognomonic of HSV keratitis (viral corneal ulcer).

General Features

  • HSV: Enveloped, linear dsDNA virus; two types:
    • HSV-1 → above waist (face, lips, eyes).
    • HSV-2 → genital; may infect the eye at birth.
  • Transmission: Droplet, direct inoculation; ↑ risk with crowding/poor hygiene.
  • The commonest infectious cause of corneal disease in developed countries.

Primary Infection

  • Usually, in childhood, maternal antibodies protect first 6 months.
  • Mostly subclinical; may cause mild fever, URTI, blepharitis, follicular conjunctivitis.
  • Rare severe neonatal systemic disease.
  • Treatment: topical/oral antivirals if needed; doesn’t prevent recurrence.

Recurrent Infection

  • Virus lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion; reactivation due to stress, fever, UV, trauma.
  • Recurrence risk: 10% at 1 year, 50% at 10 years.
  • Risk ↑ with atopy, immunosuppression, malnutrition, measles, malaria, or steroid misuse.
  • Reactivation pattern depends on ganglion site → may differ from primary disease.

Epithelial Keratitis (Dendritic/Geographic ulcer)

  • Symptoms: Pain, redness, watering, photophobia, blurred vision.
  • Signs:
    • ↓ vision, reduced corneal sensation.
    • Coarse punctate lesions → linear dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs.
    • Ulcer stains: bed = fluorescein, margins = rose Bengal.
    • Risk of geographic ulcer with topical steroids.
    • Mild subepithelial haze; sometimes ↑ IOP.
  • Differential diagnosis: HZV keratitis, corneal abrasion, Acanthamoeba keratitis, graft rejection, contact lens toxicity, drug-induced keratopathy.

Treatment

  • Topical antivirals:
    • Aciclovir 3% ointment, ganciclovir 0.15% gel (5× daily).
    • Trifluridine (more frequent dosing).
    • Heal ~99% within 2 weeks.
  • Oral antivirals: aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir (for immunocompromised, children, refractory cases).
  • Debridement: for resistant ulcers (remove infected epithelium).
  • Supportive: cycloplegia, topical antibiotics (prophylaxis), IOP control (avoid prostaglandins).
  • Steroids: contraindicated in epithelial keratitis (unless disciform keratitis coexists).
  • Resistant/refractory cases may require dual therapy ± oral antivirals.

Explanation of other options:

Protozoan corneal ulcer (Option A): Presents with Severe pain out of proportion to signs, with a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate; no terminal bulbs, corneal sensation normal.

Fungal corneal ulcer (Option B): Presents with feathery-edged, dry ulcer with satellite lesions, usually after trauma with vegetative matter; slow progression.

Traumatic corneal abrasion (Option D): Presents with a linear epithelial defect following trauma (e.g., fingernail, vegetative matter); heals quickly, no terminal bulbs, normal corneal sensation.

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for a 27-year-old male patient who experiences eye trauma from vegetative matter, and currently exhibits symptoms including a corneal ulcer, hypopyon, satellite lesions, mild pain, photophobia, and redness?
explanation:
Explanation:

The history of trauma with vegetative matter (e.g., a tree branch, thorn) is a classic risk factor for fungal keratitis.

Key Symptoms:

  • Pain & foreign body sensation
  • Watering, photophobia, blurred vision
  • Redness
  • Mild pain (often less severe than clinical signs suggest)

Pathognomonic Signs:

  • Corneal ulcer with a dry, greyish-white, "punched-out" appearance and rolled, elevated margins
  • Feathery extensions infiltrating the surrounding stroma
  • Satellite lesions (smaller infiltrates around the primary ulcer)
  • Sterile immune ring (a yellow line of immune precipitation)
  • Large hypopyon (even with a relatively small ulcer)
  • Endothelial plaque (fibrin and leukocytes)
  • Notable absence of corneal vascularization in pure fungal ulcers

Investigations:

  1. Corneal scraping under topical anesthesia for:
    1. Microscopy: KOH wet mount (reveals branched, septate hyphae or yeast cells), Gram stain, Giemsa stain.
    2. Culture: On Sabouraud's dextrose agar.
  2. Advanced Diagnostics: PCR for rapid identification, in vivo confocal microscopy to identify fungi in cornea, anterior chamber paracentesis if intraocular extension suspected, corneal biopsy if scraping is negative or lesion is deep.

Treatment:

  • Primary Topical Antifungals:
    • Natamycin (first-line for filamentous fungi)
    • Voriconazole
    • Amphotericin B (for Aspergillus and Fusarium)
    • Nystatin (for Candida)
  • Systemic Oral Antifungals (e.g., Voriconazole, Ketoconazole): Indicated for severe cases with hypopyon, perforation, or suspicion of endophthalmitis.
  • Adjunctive Procedures:
    • Repeated corneal scraping/debridement
    • Cauterization with iodine or trichloroacetic acid
  • Surgical Intervention: Therapeutic keratoplasty (corneal transplant) for perforation or cases unresponsive to medical therapy.

Explanation of other options:

Acanthamoeba keratitis (Option B): Associated with contact lens use and water exposure, presenting with severe pain and radial keratoneuritis.

Viral keratitis (Option C): Presents with dendritic ulcers (HSV) or disciform keratitis, not satellite lesions.

Bacterial keratitis (Option D): Presents with a rapidly progressive, purulent ulcer with significant pain and a dense stromal infiltrate.

Key Takeaways:

  • Trauma with organic material is a key risk factor for fungal keratitis.
  • Satellite lesions and a relatively quiet eye despite a severe-looking ulcer are characteristic.

question_text: Characteristic finding of fungal ulcer
explanation:
Satellite lesions are a characteristic finding of fungal keratitis. These multifocal stromal infiltrates appear as small, round, white lesions surrounding a central ulcer. They are often considered a hallmark feature of fungal infections of the cornea. The presence of these satellite lesions is a key indicator for diagnosing fungal keratitis, particularly when the integrity of the epithelial surface is compromised, allowing the fungus to invade the tissue.

Incorrect Options:

B. Dendritic ulcer
Dendritic ulcers are typically associated with herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis, not fungal infections. They appear as branching, tree-like patterns on the corneal surface and are not characteristic of fungal keratitis.

C. Ring abscess
Ring abscesses are more commonly seen in bacterial keratitis, particularly with pseudomonas infections. They can appear as a ring-shaped infiltrate with an abscess, but they are not a typical finding in fungal keratitis.

D. White Hypopyon
A white hypopyon refers to the accumulation of white blood cells (WBCs) in the anterior chamber, which is usually associated with inflammatory conditions like infectious keratitis or uveitis, but it is not a specific finding for fungal keratitis. While hypopyon can be present in fungal keratitis, a white hypopyon is more characteristic of bacterial infections.

Key Takeaway: The presence of satellite lesions is a characteristic finding of fungal keratitis, which involves multifocal stromal infiltrates surrounding a central ulcer. This feature helps differentiate fungal infections from other types of keratitis.

Reference: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Fungal_Keratitis

question_text: Which layer of cornea helps in maintaining hydration of stroma of cornea.
explanation:
• The corneal endothelium is responsible for maintaining the hydration of the cornea.
  • This is through a "Pump-Leak" mechanism where the active transport properties of the endothelium represent the "Pump" and the stromal swelling pressure represents the "Leak"

Incorrect Options:

A. Descemet's membrane
Descemet's membrane is the basement membrane of the corneal endothelium, but it does not directly regulate the hydration of the cornea. It acts as a protective barrier.

C. Epithelium
The epithelium is the outermost layer of the cornea and serves as a protective barrier against environmental damage. It does not play a major role in maintaining hydration of the stroma.

D. Stroma
The stroma is the middle layer of the cornea, composed mostly of collagen fibers and ground substance. While it is important for the structural integrity of the cornea, it does not actively regulate hydration.

Key Takeaway: The corneal endothelium is responsible for maintaining the hydration of the cornea through the "Pump-Leak" mechanism, ensuring proper hydration levels to maintain corneal clarity and function.

Infectious crystalline keratopathy (ICK) is a special variety of stromal keratitis distinguishable by the appearance of crystalline arboriform white opacities or deposits in the corneal stroma with minimal or no associated inflammatory reaction. It is typically seen in immunocompromised corneas such as following corneal grafts, long-term topical corticosteroid use or contact lens wear. It is hypothesized that commensal organisms from periocular skin or the ocular surface gain access to the stroma via suture tracks or through compromised unhealthy corneal epithelium. Alcohol abuse is not a cause of local corneal immunosuppression.

question_text: All of the following statements regarding Herpes Simplex virus (HSV) Epithelial keratitis are true except?
option_a: Superficial Punctate Keratitis and erosions heal without sequelae
option_b: Dendritic ulcers end with typical knobbed shape
option_c: Dendritic ulcers rapidly proceed to involve deeper layers of stroma
option_d: Dendritic ulcers show double staining: base with Sodium fluorescein and margins with Rose Bengal
explanation:
Features of Epithelial keratitis caused by HSV:

Manifestations include an SPK (Superficial Punctate Keratitis) followed by erosions which are accompanied by acute irritation, lacrimation and blepharospasm but heal rapidly, leaving no opacity. Usually, however, fresh crops appear and the condition may prove very obstinate.

In all cases, the cornea is relatively insensitive. In severe forms, dendritic ulcers develop. Initially superficial, the infiltrates develop and spread in all directions as grey striae which extend and increase in length and send out lateral branches which are generally knobbed at the ends so that a dendritic figure is formed. This resembles no other condition and is pathognomonic. The surface over the infiltrates breaks down and an extremely irritating ulcer is produced, persisting with exacerbations for weeks or months, sending out fresh branches but never extending in depth. The ulcer base stains with fluorescein and the margins with Rose bengal. Fresh spots are continually being formed and the disease frequently recurs; alternatively, a large confluent ulcer may be formed.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

question_text: Which of the following drugs is not useful for treatment of Epithelial HSV keratitis?

  • Epithelial keratitis responds well to topical antivirals - 3 % acyclovir ointment 5 times a day which are prescribed along with topical antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection, lubricants to relieve discomfort and cycloplegics.
  • Debridement of the edges of the dendritic ulcer with a moistened, fine, cotton-tipped applicator is also useful in reducing the load of active virusinfected cells.
  • It is uniformly accepted that topical steroids are contraindicated in the presence of active viral replication as that occurs in herpes simplex epithelial keratitis leading to a huge geographical ulcer.
