question_text: Which of the following statements regarding treatment of HSV keratitis is false according to HEDS?
option_a: Stromal keratitis should be treated with combination of topical anti-viral plus topical steroid eye drops
option_b: Oral anti-viral Acyclovir may be added to topical anti-viral + steroid eye drops in patients with irido-cyclitis
option_c: Low dose oral acyclovir over prolonged periods helps reduce chances of recurrence in prone individuals
option_d: Herpetic scarring cannot be treated by penetrating keratoplasty
explanation:
Treatment guidelines for HSV Keratitis as described by Herpetic Eye Disease Study (HEDS):

  • In the absence of accompanying HSV epithelial keratitis, stromal keratitis improves more rapidly when corticosteroid eyedrops are used along with a topical antiviral agent.
  • Oral acyclovir (400 mg five times a day) does not seem to prevent the occurrence of iridocyclitis or stromal keratitis following epithelial keratitis treated with trifluridine and appears to provide no extra benefit over topical steroids and trifluridine in the treatment of stromal keratitis. However, oral acyclovir may be added to a regimen of a topical antiviral agent and corticosteroids in treating patients with HSV iridocyclitis.
  • Low-dose oral acyclovir (400 mg 12 hourly) prescribed for long periods (6 months to a year or longer) does reduce the rate of recurrent herpetic eye disease and hence is indicated in those patients who are prone to frequent recurrences.
  • Penetrating keratoplasty is useful in cases with herpetic scarring where the eye has been free of activity for a year. Eyes with extensive vascularization invite rejection of a graft, and recurrence of active herpetic infection in the transplant is often a problem.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

question_text: A 37 year old patient with no significant systemic history reports to OPD with severe pain and lacrimation in both eyes with clinical imaging as depicted below: corneal ulcers with over hanging edge noted at periphery in cresenteric manner.Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
option_a: Cause of ulcer is autoimmune destruction of epithelium.
explanation:
Young patient, no systemic history, severe pain and characteristic marginal ulceration with over hanging edge: Pathgonomonic of Mooren’s Ulcer.

Etiology:

The exact underlying cause is unknown. Erosion is initiated by autoimmune lysis of the epithelium with consequent release of collagenolytic enzymes.

Symptoms: It is accompanied by severe and persistent neuralgic pain and lacrimation.

Signs:

  • It commences as one or more grey infiltrates, which break down forming small ulcers that spread and sooner or later coalesce.
  • The ulcer undermines the epithelium and superficial stromal lamellae at the advancing border, forming a whitish overhanging edge which is characteristic, while the base quickly becomes vascularized.
  • It rarely perforates but progresses with intermissions for months until eventually a thin nebula is formed over the whole cornea and sight is greatly diminished.
  • Bilateral involvement with severe pain and relentless progression (‘malignant’) is more common in young adults, while a milder, usually unilateral, less painful form is seen in elderly patients.

Mooren ulcer is a diagnosis of exclusion after all other systemic disorders predisposing to marginal ulceration are ruled out.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Syphilitic Interstitial Keratitis is/are incorrect?
option_b: Corneal lesions heal rapidly with penicillin treatment
explanation:
Syphilitic (luetic) interstitial keratitis:

  • Interstitial keratitis due to inherited syphilis, most commonly affects children between the ages of 5 and 15 years.
  • Delayed interstitial keratitis occasionally occurs in patients older than 30 years.

Syphilitic interstitial keratitis is almost invariably bilateral, although an interval of 3 or more weeks usually intervenes before the onset in the second eye; rarely, the interval is several months. The acute stage lasts at least 6 weeks and may extend to several months. The cornea takes weeks or months to clear, but little improvement can be expected after 18 months. Diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on other evidence of congenital syphilis and positive serological reactions.

Treatment: It is doubtful if anti-syphilitic remedies have any influence over the course of the keratitis, partly because the cornea is nonvascular and partly because the reaction is probably largely allergic. It is possible, however, that intensive systemic treatment with penicillin may shorten the course of the disease.

Local treatment in the form of lubricants, topical steroids and cycloplegics to control the uveitis is helpful in the acute stage. In the later stages, the best results are obtained by corneal grafting of the penetrating type, which generally has a good prognosis.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Which of the following is/are features of Disciform keratits?
option_c: Caused by tissue reaction to viral antigens
explanation:
Disciform keratitis occurs generally in adults and is unilateral.

Aetiology:

  • It is probably associated with a viral infection and has long been known to result from vaccinia affecting the lid margins, or from herpes, and not infrequently develops from an SPK.
  • The condition is probably not due to a direct infection of the corneal stroma by the virus from the epithelium but seems to be the expression of a tissue response, sometimes involving necrosis, due to the reaction between antigens liberated by the virus in the epithelium and antibodies produced in the stroma or carried there by the bloodstream.
  • The pathology may thus be analogous to that of syphilitic interstitial keratitis.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Disciform keratitis is/are incorrect?
option_a: Involves superficial stroma and Bowman's membrane
option_c: Opacification is easily treated with topical steroids
explanation:
The disease is characterized by the gradual appearance of a central grey disc lying in the middle layers of the stroma, usually with a denser central opacity. The slit lamp shows thickening of the cornea and often folds of the Descemet’s membrane and an immune ring of the Wessely type. It is accompanied by moderate irritation which persists for weeks or many months, leaving a permanent opacity. The cornea may become anaesthetic, but ulceration does not occur. Owing to its central situation, vision is considerably impaired. It is associated with some degree of uveitis.

It is completely a difficult condition to treat, but generally the symptoms and the extent of the permanent opacity may be ameliorated by the local administration of corticosteroids along with topical or systemic antiviral agents such as acyclovir.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Involvement of 2/3 cornea with keratomalacia indicates which stage of Xerophthalmia?
explanation:
Vitamin A deficiency and Keratomalacia

This is common in developing countries and affects poorly nourished children who are deficient in vitamin A, often early in the first year of life; the condition is usually bilateral.

The cornea becomes dull and insensitive; hazy and yellow infiltrates form until finally the whole tissue undergoes necrosis and seems to melt away (keratomalacia) within a few hours. A characteristic feature is the absence of inflammatory reaction.

Keratomalacia is often precipitated by an acute systemic illness such as measles, pneumonia or severe diarrhoea. The children are usually extremely ill and very frequently die of other systemic diseases. Owing to their apathetic condition, they do not close the lids, the cornea is continually exposed, and secondary bacterial infection can occur and complicate the clinical picture.

Staging:

question_text: What is the dosage schedule of Vit A for a 14 month baby diagnosed with keratomalacia?
option_a: Single dose of Vit A 1 lac IU
option_b: Three doses of Vit A 1 lac IU
option_c: Single dose of Vit A 2 lac IU
option_d: Three doses of Vit A 2 lac IU
explanation:
Keratomalacia must be treated as an ophthalmic emergency and the child hospitalized. Vitamin A is administered in three doses, as outlined. The first is to be given at diagnosis, the second after 24 hours and the third after 2 weeks. Oral oil-based preparations are preferred, but if the child is suffering from persistent vomiting or profuse diarrhoea, then an intramuscular injection of water-miscible vitamin A (retinyl palmitate) may be given at half these dosages as a substitute.

question_text: Which instrument is used for checking for corneal sensations?
explanation:
How do we check for corneal sensations?

This is tested by touching it with a wisp of cotton wool or a Cochet– Bonnet aesthesiometer and comparing the reaction with that in the fellow eye; the slightest touch is followed by a reflex closure of the lids if the cornea is sensitive, and absent or dull corneal reflex indicates an anaesthetic cornea.


  • It contains a thin, retractable, nylon monofilament that extends up to 6 cm in length. Variable pressure can be applied by the device by adjusting the length. The monofilament ranges from 60 mm to 5 mm and as the length is decreased the pressure increases from 11 mm/gm to 200 mm/gm
  • Extend the filament to full length of 6 cm
  • Retract the filament until the patient can feel its contact
  • Record the length (The shorter the length indicates decreased sensation.)
  • Repeat steps 1-4 in each quadrant: superior, temporal, inferior, nasal

Uses of different instruments:

  • Perkin’s Tonometer- measurement of IOP
  • Cochet-Bonnet Aesthesiometer- measurement of corneal sensations

question_text: A 47-year-old patient presents to OPD with complaints of redness, pain and loss of vision for 2/3 days. Corneal ulceration is documented, and fortified anti-microbials are started. Post a heavy bout of sneezing; patient reports to OPD with gush of fluid coming from the eye and loss of pain. What has most likely happened?
explanation:
Explanation:

Perforation of an ulcer is usually caused by sudden exertion by the patient, such as coughing, sneezing, straining at stool or spasm of the orbicularis muscle.

  • When an ulcer perforates, the aqueous suddenly escapes and the intraocular pressure falls to the atmospheric level; the iris and lens being driven forwards to meet the back of the cornea.
  • The effect upon the nutrition of the cornea is good; owing to the diminution of intraocular pressure, the diffusion of fluid through the cornea is facilitated, extension of the ulceration usually ceases, pain is alleviated, and cicatrization proceeds rapidly.

Cataract and Secondary glaucoma are known as sequelae of corneal ulcer but do not develop spontaneously in such a short span of time (Option C& D).

question_text: A 47 year old patient presents to OPD with complaints of redness, pain and loss of vision since 2/3 days. Corneal ulceration is documented and fortified anti-microbials are started. Post a heavy bout of sneezing, patient reports to OPD with gush of fluid coming from the eye and loss of pain. What has most likely happened?
explanation:
Perforation of an ulcer is usually caused by sudden exertion by the patient, such as coughing, sneezing, straining at stool or spasm of the orbicularis muscle. Any such activity causes a rise in the blood pressure, which at once manifests itself by a rise in the intraocular pressure and the weak floor of the ulcer, unable to support the sudden strain, gives way. When an ulcer perforates, the aqueous suddenly escapes and the intraocular pressure falls to the atmospheric level, the iris and lens being driven forwards to come in contact with the back of the cornea. The effect upon the nutrition of the cornea is good; owing to the diminution of intraocular pressure, the diffusion of fluid through the cornea is facilitated, extension of the ulceration usually ceases, pain is alleviated and cicatrization proceeds rapid.

Cataract and Secondary glaucoma are known sequelae of corneal ulcer but do not develop spontaneously in such short span of time.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

question_text: From where do the corneal cells derive their nourishment from?
option_c: Oxygen dissolved in the tear film
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct answer is All of the above. The cornea is a transparent, avascular structure that lacks lymphatic channels. To maintain its metabolic functions and transparency, corneal cells rely on multiple sources of nourishment:

  • Diffusion from the aqueous humor: Supplies nutrients to the posterior corneal layers.
  • Capillaries at the limbus: Provide peripheral nourishment.
  • Oxygen dissolved in the tear film: Supports the anterior corneal epithelium, especially during open-eye conditions.

This tri-source supply ensures optimal corneal health and function.

question_text: All of the following are metabolically active layers of the cornea except?
explanation:
• The metabolism of the cornea is preferentially aerobic and it can function only up to 6–7 hours anaerobically under normal conditions.
  • The metabolically active cells are the endothelium, epithelium and stromal keratocytes. The most metabolically active layer is endothelium though.
  • Oxygen is mostly derived from the tear film, with a small contribution from the limbal capillaries, and the oxygen gradient is from tears to the aqueous.
  • Glucose supply for corneal metabolism is mainly (90%) derived from the aqueous and supplemented (10%) by the limbal capillaries.
  • Bowman’s Layer is condensation of the anterior part of corneal stroma and functions as a barrier.

question_text: A 65 year old female patient reports to OPD with complaints of muco-purulent discharge, ocular irritation and lacrimation. Clinical imaging is as depicted below. Patient is being treated for face acne as well.Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are incorrect?
option_a: Local treatment with steroids has good results
option_b: Treatment of skin condition is essential
option_c: Can also present with recurrent corneal ulcers
option_d: Can also present with iritis in severe cases
explanation:
Acne Rosacea

This is generally seen in elderly women and is associated with ocular irritability and lacrimation. In addition to slight mucopurulent conjunctivitis, yellowish-white infiltrates and small ulcers appear in the cornea near the limbus, which becomes heavily vascularized. The ulcers can be intractable and frequently recur. In severe cases, iritis is also present. Local treatment is disappointing but is similar to that for phlyctenular keratitis; the greatest relief usually follows the instillation of corticosteroids as drops or ointment. The essential treatment, however, is that of the skin condition. A course of systemic tetracycline is often helpful. Patients receive 250 mg tetracycline orally four times daily or 100 mg doxycycline twice daily for 3 weeks of each month. The dosage is then slowly reduced each month and the drug is stopped if improvement is maintained.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

question_text: Which of the following conditions is/are associated with exposure keratopathy?
explanation:
This occurs in eyes insufficiently covered by the lids.

Clinical feature: The epithelium of the exposed cornea becomes desiccated and the substantia propria hazy. Owing to the drying, the epithelium is cast off and the cornea falls prey to infective organisms. The condition is due to any cause which may produce exposure of the cornea due to the following:

  • Incomplete closure of the eyelids (lagophthalmos), such as extreme proptosis as in exophthalmic ophthalmoplegia or orbital tumour or paralysis of the orbicularis (neuroparalytic keratopathy). The absence of reflex blinking and defective closure of the lids during sleep are important factors, so extremely ill patients are liable to get this form of keratitis.
  • Deep coma.

Treatment: This consists of keeping the cornea well covered. In mild cases, it is sufficient to bandage the eyes at night. If possible the cause of the exposure must be removed, but in the meantime it may be necessary to perform a tarsorrhaphy by suturing the lids together.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: What is the appropriate treatment for a patient with Bell's palsy who presents with dry eye, redness, and irritation, along with multiple punctate epithelial erosions in the cornea seen on slit lamp examination?
explanation:
Explanation:

In an elderly patient with Bell's palsy who presents with dry eye, redness, and irritation, along with multiple punctate epithelial erosions observed in the cornea on slit lamp examination, the most appropriate management is tarsorrhaphy.

Tarsorrhaphy is a surgical procedure in which the eyelids are partially sewn together to reduce corneal exposure and protect the ocular surface.

Paralytic Ectropion:

  • Cause: Facial nerve palsy (e.g., Bell's palsy), trauma, or prior surgery
  • Clinical Feature: Exposure keratopathy due to inadequate eyelid closure
  • Treatment:
    • Temporary options: Topical lubricants, eyelid taping, or suture tarsorrhaphy
    • Permanent options (if required): Horizontal lid tightening with or without middle lamellar support, or a palpebral sling procedure

Contact lenses (Option B): These are not advised, as the cornea is already compromised due to erosions.

Corneal replacement (Option C): Corneal replacement such as corneal transplantation, is not suitable, since the underlying issue of exposure keratopathy from Bell's palsy would persist.

LASIK (Option D): It is a refractive surgery used to correct myopia, hyperopia, or astigmatism, is not indicated in this scenario.

question_text: Which statement about cornea is false?
option_b: It derives nourishment from the aqueous humor
option_d: Dua's layer lies between Bowman's membrane and stroma
explanation:
• The cornea is the transparent front part of the eye which resembles a ‘watch glass’ and consists of different layers and regions:
    • Epithelium
    • Bowman’s membrane
    • Stroma (substantia propria)
    • Dua’s layer (pre-Descemet’s layer)
    • Descemet’s membrane
    • Endothelium
  • The cornea is avascular with no blood vessels with the exception of minute arcades, extending about 1 mm into the cornea at the limbus.

question_text: A corneal wisp test is performed to assess the blink reflex. Which cranial nerve carries the sensory (afferent) input responsible for initiating this reflex?
explanation:
Explanation:

The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective response that involves both sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) pathways:

  • Afferent limb (sensory input): Trigeminal nerve (CN V1 - Ophthalmic division)
    • The cornea is innervated by the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.
    • A light touch to the cornea (e.g., with a cotton wisp) stimulates sensory fibers, sending signals to the trigeminal sensory nucleus in the brainstem.
  • Efferent limb (motor response): Facial nerve (CN VII)
    • The facial nerve (CN VII) innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, which causes eyelid closure in response to the stimulus.

Facial Nerve (CN VII) (Option A): The facial nerve is responsible for the efferent limb (motor response), not the afferent limb. It causes eyelid closure by contracting the orbicularis oculi muscle.

Oculomotor Nerve (CN III) (Option C): CN III controls extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris (eyelid elevation), but it does not mediate the corneal reflex.

Abducens Nerve (CN VI) (Option D): CN VI controls the lateral rectus muscle for eye abduction but is not involved in the corneal reflex.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534247/

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Neuro-trophic keratopathy is/are incorrect?
option_a: Occurs due to paralysis of CN5-Trigeminal nerve
option_b: Occurs due to paralysis of CN-7 Facial nerve
explanation:
This occurs in cases in which the trigeminal nerve is paralysed, typically as a result of radical treatment of trigeminal neuralgia. It does not occur in all cases of peripheral lesions of the trigeminal nerve; thus, if the Gasserian ganglion is removed or the trigeminal nerve is injected with alcohol for trigeminal neuralgia with precautions, only a few cases develop into neurotrophic keratitis, the tendency being decreased if there is an adequate tear film.

Clinical features:

  • The characteristic feature of neurotrophic keratopathy is the desquamation of the corneal epithelium.
  • The surface of the cornea becomes dull and the epithelium is thrown off, first at the centre and then over the whole surface except a narrow rim at the periphery; the entire epithelium may thus peel off intact.
  • The substantia propria then becomes cloudy and finally yellow, breaking down into a large ulcer which is usually accompanied by a hypopyon.
  • There is no pain, owing to the anaesthesia, but ciliary injection is marked.
  • Relapses are the rule; the healed scar quickly breaking down again and the whole process is repeated.

question_text: Deficiency or lesion of which cranial nerve leads to lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eye)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lesion of the 7th cranial nerve leads to lagophthalmos

Lagophthalmos:

  • Defined as the inability to close the eyelids completely.
  • Most commonly occurs due to 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve) palsy.
  • Paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscleleads to incomplete eyelid closure, which can cause exposure keratitis (neuroparalytic keratitis).

Bell's Palsy:

  • The most common cause of peripheral facial palsy.
  • Characterised by idiopathic, acute lower motor neuron (LMN) facial paralysis.
  • Usually involves the labyrinthine segmentof the facial nerve.
  • Affects males and females equally.

Causes:

  • Idiopathic (most common)
  • Viral infections: HSV >> Herpes zoster
  • Vascular ischemia
  • Hereditary (6-8% of cases)
  • Autoimmune

Risk Factors:

  • Diabetes (due to microangiopathy)
  • Pregnancy (due to fluid retention)

Clinical Features:

  • Sudden facial paralysis with inability to close the eye(lagophthalmos / Bell's phenomenon)
  • Facial asymmetry, drooping mouth, drooling
  • Epiphora (excessive tearing)
  • Sometimes associated with ear pain, hyperacusis (stapedial paralysis), or loss of taste (chorda tympani involvement)

Diagnosis:

  • Primarily by exclusion of other causesof peripheral facial paralysis

Treatment:

  • General:Eye protection, physiotherapy, reassurance, pain relief
  • Medical:Prednisolone (tapered course), Acyclovir if viral
  • Surgical:Nerve decompression in selected cases

Prognosis:

  • 85-90% of patients achieve full recovery
  • Incomplete recovery occurs in recurrent or late cases

Explanation for Other Options:

6th nerve (option B): Lesion affects the lateral rectus muscle, leading to impaired abduction of the eye.

4th nerve (option C): Lesion affects the superior oblique muscle, causing vertical diplopia.

5th nerve (option D): Responsible for facial sensation and corneal reflex but does not control eyelid closure.

explanation:
Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the reconstruction or enlargement of the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal. It is performed to improve access, drainage, and ventilation of the ear canal.It is the last step of modified radical mastoidectomy.

question_text: A 43 year old male patient is suffering from recurrent episodes of vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus for last 3 years. The episode has nausea and vomiting along with vertigo. The episode settles in few hours only. What is the possible diagnosis?
explanation:
MENIERES DISEASE-ENDOLYMPHATIC HYDROPS:

  • In Meniere's disease, there is a rise in endolymph volume due to poor absorption by endolymphatic sac.

It is mostly unilateral disease. →I/L Migraine

  • Slightly more common in males. 3rd to 4th decade
  • Etiology is unknown.
  • It is an episodic disease. I/L Migraine

During Episode:

  • Episode has 3 features
    1. Tinnitus- it is the first symptom.
    2. Vertigo (With nausea, vomiting)
    3. Hearing loss.

+/- Fullness in ear

In between episodes

  1. Tinnitus may persist.
  2. Patient hears loud sounds as more loud. This is called Recruitment phenomenon
  3. Patients can get vertigo on hearing loud sounds. This is called Tullio's phenomenon
  4. Patient has a dislike for noisy areas.
  5. Patients hear the same sound in 2 frequencies. This is called Diplacusis

FEW YEARS LATER

Cochlear damage starts due to high endolymphatic pressure. (Glaucoma of ear).

This leads to hearing loss in between episodes also. This will lead to

Fluctuating hearing loss Meniere's disease causes low Frequency SNHL in early stages.

Investigations

  1. PTA (pure tone audiometry) - unilateral SNHL (Low frequencies SNHL in early stages). This will lead to a rising audiogram.
  2. RECRUITMENT PHENOMENON is positive.
  3. SHORT INCREMENT SENSITIVITY INDEX (SISI)
  4. Electrocochleography(ECOCHG)- SP:AP Ratio>30% (used for diagnostic workup of MENIERES disease.)

TREATMENT:

  1. During episode- anti vertigo medications. Eg- prochlorperazine, cinnarizine.
  2. In between episode- Acetazolamide (diuretic)

If episodes of vertigo become more frequent and disabling Further treatment options Think of 2 scenarios.

A. Residual hearing is present-

  1. VESTIBULAR NEURECTOMY- Transect the vestibular branch of 8th nerve to a control vertigo symptoms.
  2. MENIET DEVICE - Home based therapy: Everyday It is Intermittent low pressure pulse therapy for inner ear.
  3. ENDOLYMPHATIC SAC DECOMPRESSION SURGERY

B. If no residual hearing is there -

  1. Transtympanic Gentamycin Injection
  2. Surgical Labyrinthectomy.

Reference: Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery by P L Dhingra, 8th Edition, Page - 52, 119.

question_text: In the procedure indicated by the image below, what is the storage medium and suture used?
explanation:
Explanation:

The donor corneal graft is stored in McCarey–Kaufman (MK) medium, and the graft is typically secured to the host cornea using 10-0 nylon sutures.

McCarey-Kaufman medium has a pink appearance and contains Tissue Culture-199, 5 % Dextran-40, HEPES buffer to maintain a pH of 7.4, and gentamicin (0.1 mg/mL). Corneal tissue can be transplanted directly after retrieval or preserved in an eye bank for varying durations, depending on the method:

  • Short-term storage (24-96 hours): moist chamber or MK medium
  • Intermediate storage (up to about 2 weeks): medium enriched with chondroitin sulfate
  • Long-term storage (months to years): cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen or storage in glycerol, which can maintain viability for roughly a year

Corneal transplantation (keratoplasty) involves replacing a diseased or opaque cornea with a clear donor cornea. The procedure includes:

  • Trephining and removing the donor corneal button
  • Removing the corresponding portion of the recipient cornea
  • Securing the donor graft to the recipient bed with either continuous or interrupted 10-0 nylon sutures.

Explanations for other Options:

McCarey-Kaufman medium & Vicryl suture(Option B): MK medium is correct for storage, but Vicryl (polyglactin 910) is an absorbable suture that loses tensile strength rapidly and causes more inflammation, making it unsuitable for delicate, long-term corneal wound closure.

Moist chamber & silk suture (Option C): A moist chamber can temporarily keep a whole eye viable for only a few hours and is not the standard for corneal graft storage.

Ethylene glycol & Vicryl suture (Option D): Ethylene glycol is an antifreeze compound, not a corneal preservation medium. Vicryl, as noted, is absorbable and inappropriate for corneal graft fixation.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Collagen cross linking is/are incorrect?
explanation:
Corneal collagen cross-linking is a new modality of treatment introduced as an interim measure to track progression. Riboflavin (0.1%) eyedrops are instilled every 3 minutes or so for 30 minutes after removing the patient’s epithelium. Once the cornea is adequately saturated with riboflavin, it is exposed to a quantitative dose (3 mW/cm2) of UVA radiation, followed by insertion of a bandage soft contact lens to permit the epithelium to heal. Riboflavin acts as a photosensitizing agent that triggers increased crosslinking of the corneal collagen fibrils by the formation of intrafibrillar and interfibrillar covalent bonds by photosensitized oxidation to stabilize the corneal stroma,delay progression and improve contact lens tolerance.

question_text: Which of the following is commonest type of graft rejection?
explanation:
Corneal graft rejection, though its incidence is less than that in other organ transplants, can occur as early as 2 weeks and up to several years after keratoplasty.

  • Graft rejection is more common in heavily vascularized corneas (particularly those with deep vascularization in two or more quadrants) and in regrafts but can occur in all grafts except rotational autografts.
  • Rejection could be epithelial, stromal, or endothelial or a combination of all three.
  • Endothelial rejection is the commonest and the most liable to lead to graft failure.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Which of the following conditions is treated using the modality shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

INTACS (Intrastromal Corneal Ring Segments - ICRS) are small PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) semicircular ring segments, usually 2 rings, implanted into the mid-peripheral corneal stroma.

  • Mechanism of action: They flatten the central cornea by shortening the arc length of corneal lamellae in the implanted zone, thereby reducing ectasia and irregular astigmatism.
  • Indications:
    • Keratoconus (mild to moderate): Improves visual acuity in patients intolerant to contact lenses and not yet requiring keratoplasty.
    • Low myopia (up to -5.0 D): By flattening the cornea, INTACS can also correct small degrees of refractive myopia.

Note: INTACS improve vision and corneal shape but do not halt progression of keratoconus. Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) is required to prevent disease progression.

Explanation of other options:

Keratoglobus (Option B) is a diffuse thinning of the cornea with a globular shape. INTACS are not effective here; surgical options include lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty.

Vogt's limb striae (Option C) are fine vertical stress lines in the deep stroma/Descemet's membrane seen in keratoconus, which disappear with pressure on the globe. They are a sign, not a condition treated by INTACS.

Corneal dystrophy (Option D) is a genetic, bilateral, progressive condition managed with keratoplasty in advanced stages. INTACS have no role.

References:

Intracorneal Ring Segment Implantation in the Management of Keratoconus: An Evidence-Based Approach - PMC

question_text: Which corneal layer shows the characteristic 'beaten bronze' or 'beaten metal' appearance?
explanation:
Explanation:

The endothelial layer of the cornea is affected in Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy, a condition that commonly occurs in older adults. In this disorder, Descemet's membrane develops a distinctive 'beaten bronze'or 'beaten metal' appearance when examined with a slit lamp. Progressive loss of endothelial cells leads to corneal oedema and visual impairment.

Explanation for Other Options:

Stroma (option B): The stromal layer may develop opacities or haze in conditions such as macular or granular corneal dystrophies, but it does not produce a beaten bronze appearance.

Sub-epithelial layer (option C): This layer can show deposits or scarring in disorders like Reis-Bücklers or anterior basement membrane dystrophy, not the metallic sheen seen in Fuchs dystrophy.

Epithelial layer (option D): Epithelial involvement typically causes microcysts or recurrent erosions, as in epithelial basement membrane dystrophy, but not the classic beaten-metal pattern.

question_text: A 20-year-old male is found to have a golden-brown ring at the periphery of the cornea during eye examination. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Serum ceruloplasmin is the most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of Wilson's disease with the golden ring on the cornea.

  • The golden ring on the cornea seen in this 20-year-old male is characteristic of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which are typically associated with Wilson's disease.
  • Wilson's disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in various tissues, including the liver, brain, and cornea.
  • Kayser-Fleischer rings are copper deposits that form in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, appearing as a golden or greenish ring on slit-lamp examination.

Wilson's disease

  • Deficiency of ceruloplasmin leads to abnormal copper deposition in tissues.
  • Symptoms:
    • Liver disease
    • Basal ganglia dysfunction (movement disorders)
    • Psychiatric disturbances
  • Ocular Signs:
    • Kayser-Fleischer ring: Brownish-yellow golden copper deposits in the corneal Descemet membrane, visible on gonioscopy.
    • Sunflower cataract: Anterior capsular cataract in some patients.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Kayser-Fleischer rings were detected on gonioscopy.
    • Serum Ceruloplasmin levels
  • Treatment: Penicillamine therapy can reduce copper deposits and improve symptoms.

Explanation for other options:

Alpha-1-antitrypsin (Option A): This is a protein associated with lung and liver diseases (like emphysema and cirrhosis), but it is not related to copper metabolism or Wilson's disease.

Alpha-fetoprotein (Option B): This is a tumour marker, often elevated in certain cancers or during pregnancy, but not associated with Wilson's disease or corneal findings.

Serum iron (Option C): Elevated iron levels are associated with hemochromatosis or iron overload disorders, not with Wilson's disease.

Reference:

  1. Wilson Disease - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: The principle of the stenopaeic slit test is based on:
explanation:
A stenopeic slit is a slit-shaped, elongated, pinhole-like aperture positioned in the center of a disc. The slit is less than 1 mm wide and approximately 15 mm long. The stenopeic slit accurately determines the orientation and power of an astigmatic refractive error.

The stenopeic slit reduces the effective pupil size in the meridian perpendicular to it, producing an axial shift of the circle of least confusion (CLC) and, consequently, a change of the retinal blur size that depends on the orientation of the slit. The stenopeic slit removes the peripheral rays in the meridian perpendicular to the slit, isolating the meridian at which refraction is to be performed

Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

question_text: A 78-year-old man experienced unilateral sudden loss of vision 1 year previously. Currently, he complains of severe pain in that eye. Examination reveals no light-perception vision, intraocular pressure of 72 mm Hg, iris neovascularization and evidence of a central retinal vein occlusion. What would the least helpful topical therapeutic agent be at this time?
explanation:
The management of a painful blind eye with end-stage glaucoma can include topical cycloplegia (anticholinergic agent) and a corticosteroid agent for comfort. A topical beta blocker may provide relatively little intraocular pressure lowering but may provide some increased comfort. Eyes with end-stage iris neovascularization and neovascular glaucoma have completely or near completely closed angles. A cholinergic agent, such as pilocarpine, will not successfully reduce intraocular pressure in these eyes and will often increase pain and inflammation.

Reference: Parsons 22nd Edition/303

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding IIH(Idiopathic Intracranial HTN) is/are incorrect?
option_b: Symptoms include headache with transient blurring of vision and occasional photopsias
option_c: Presence of opticociliary shunts indicates poor prognosis
option_d: Neuroimaging will reveal causative space occupying lesion
explanation:
• Pseudotumour cerebri, previously often termed as benign intracranial hypertension, is a disorder associated with raised intracranial pressure in the absence of an intracranial space-occupying lesion.
  • It tends to occur in obese females in the second or third decades, producing headache with transient blurring of vision and occasional photopsia.
  • Some loss of visual function occurs in 50% of patients, especially those with a high-grade or atrophic papilloedema or peripapillary subretinal haemorrhage.
  • Transient obscurations (blurring) of vision and the presence of opticociliary shunts are bad prognostic factors for vision.
  • - Other risk factors, particularly in the older age group, are anaemia and high myopia.

question_text:
A 55 year old with known tobacco addiction reports to OPD with loss of vision. Clinical imaging is as shown.

Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are incorrect?
option_a: Mechanism of action is cyanide toxicity to optic nerve fibres directly
option_b: Mechanism of action is cyanide toxicity to retinal ganglion cells in macular area
option_c: Treatment comprises of avoidance of tobacco and folate supplementation
explanation:
• Tobacco amblyopia
  • This results from the excessive use of tobacco, either pipe smoking or chewing, and occasionally from the absorption of dust in tobacco factories. Smokers of shag and strong tobacco mixtures or cigars suffer the most; cigarette smokers are rarely affected
  • Various substances have been regarded as the toxic agent, but a potent factor may be poisoning with the cyanide in tobacco smoke associated with a deficiency of vitamin B12.
  • Pathologically, the condition is due to degeneration of the ganglion cells of the retina, particularly of the macular area where the cells show vacuolation and Nissl degeneration.
  • In the nerve, the papillomacular bundle is degenerated.
  • Clinically, the patient complains of increasing fogginess of vision, usually least marked in the evening and in dull light.
  • Central vision is greatly diminished, so that reading and near work become difficult. Although the condition is bilateral, one eye is usually more affected.
  • The fundus is normal or a slight temporal pallor may be seen in the disc. but the diagnosis is made from the characteristic defects in the central fields.
  • primarily involve the centrocaecal area between the fixation point and the blind spot.
  • Here, occupying a horizontally oval area, there is a relative scotoma to white and colours, particularly red, and in it, on the horizontal meridian, there are one or more islands of complete visual loss.
  • The scotoma gradually extends to involve the fixation area itself so that central vision may be lost but the peripheral field remains unaffected.
  • Treatment consists of abstaining from or severely curtailing the use of tobacco and alcohol.
  • If this is done, the prognosis is eventually good, although visual improvement may not be evident for a period of some months; thereafter, it may be slow.
  • Improvement may be hastened by intramuscular injections of 1000 mg hydroxycobalamin.
  • This dose should be repeated five times at intervals of 4 days and then at 2-weekly intervals for a few months.
  • Recovery may be monitored by the VEPs.
  • Recurrences are very rarely seen even if tobacco is resumed in strict moderation.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: A 20 year old male presents with complaint of diminished vision since 3 years. Fundus examination shows 'beaten-bronze' appearance at the fovea. ERG and EOG both are found to be subnormal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Stargardt disease is a recessive, progressive tapetoretinal dystrophy of the central retina and develops between the ages of 8 and 14 years.
  • In the early stages, the fovea appears normal but in the advanced stages a demarcated focus of ‘beaten bronze’ atrophy is seen in the foveal region.
  • Dark adaptation, the ERG and the EOG are subnormal while the visual fields may become slightly restricted.
  • Fluorescein angiography shows a ‘dark choroid’ in a large majority of patients. There is no leakage of dye.
  • The final result is the complete disappearance of the visual elements and the pigment epithelium in the centre of the retina.
  • By the age of 40, only 22% of patients are likely to have a vision of 6/12.
  • Once the visual acuity drops below this level, it tends to decrease rapidly and stabilize at 6/60.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the eye, 23rd edition, Chapter 17 - Diseases of retina and vitreous.

question_text: A 50 year old female came with decrease in vision since few months. She is reported to have hypertension, DM and rheumatoid arthritis since many years. there is a lesion seen in her retina for which FFA was done too. The pictures are given here. What is the likely diagnosis
explanation:
Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine can cause toxic retinopathy due to their binding of melanin in the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) as well as direct toxicity to retinal ganglion cells. Early findings include mottling of the RPE and blunted foveal reflex. The classic presentation is a bull's eye-maculopathy appearance where the fovea is surrounded by a ring of depigmentation followed by a ring of hyperpigmentation.

Chloroquine was originally used as an anti-malarial therapeutic. Chloroquine is now uncommonly used in favor of its derivative hydroxychloroquine. While early toxicity may be asymtomatic, patients with more advanced stage of toxicity may complain of color vision changes or paracentral scotomas. Advanced hydroxychloroquine toxicity presents as a bullseye maculopathy. Since retinal toxicity is usually irreversible, early detection of retinal toxicity and cessation of the offending agent is the best treatment.

Corneal toxicity presents as an intraepithelial deposition of the drug into the cornea, which rarely affects vision. Ciliary body dysfunction disturbs accommodation and is rare.

Risk Factors

Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy is most influenced by daily dose and duration of use. Risk for toxicity is less with <5.0 mg/kg real weight/day for hydroxychloroquine and <2.3 mg/kg real weight/day for chloroquine. Patients are at low risk during the first 5 years of treatment.

Other conditions causing bull's eye pattern in macula

  • Cone Dystrophy
  • Stargardt's disease
  • Chloroquine Retinopathy
  • Clofazimine Toxicity
  • Age Related Macular Degeneration
  • Leber's Congenital Amaurosis
  • Chronic macular hole
  • Inverse Retinitis pigmentosa

Reference: kanski 9/e chapter 21 pg. 884-885 retinal toxicity.

question_text: A 22-year-old patient wearing thick glasses from childhood presents with sudden onset of floaters in his eyes. What is the likely cause of this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's history of thick glasses since childhood indicates pathological myopia, and the sudden onset of flashes and floaters suggests that he has developed retinal detachment as a complication of pathological myopia.

Pathological Myopia

Pathological/degenerative/progressive myopia is a rapidly progressive refractive error that starts in childhood at 5-10 years of age and results in high myopia (>-6D) during early adult life.

Etiology

  • Rapid axial growth of the eyeball outside normal biological variations
  • Genetic factors (major role)
    • More common in women than men
    • Autosomal dominant pathological myopia
    • Heredity-
      • Familial, more common in women and in certain races
      • Autosomal Dominant - linked to genes 18p11.31 and 12q21-23
      • Sex-linked recessive - high myopia (>6D)
    • General growth process (minor role)
      • nutritional deficiency
      • endocrine disturbances

Symptoms

  • Defective vision with considerable failure in visual function
  • Muscae volitantes (floaters)
  • Difficulty in night vision in very high myopes with degenerative changes

Signs

  • Prominent eyeballs, often appear elongated
  • Exophthalmos, especially in unilateral cases
  • Cornea is large
  • The anterior chamber is deep
  • Pupils are slightly large and react sluggishly to light
  • Fundus examination reveals:
    • Large and pale optic disc
    • Characteristic myopic crescent
    • Tigroid fundus
    • Myopic crescent (temporal to disc margin)

Complications of Pathological Myopia


Explanation of other options:

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A): Rarely causes ocular symptoms; may lead to subhyaloid hemorrhage, but floaters alone without neurological signs are uncommon.

Branched retinal artery occlusion (Option D): Presents with sudden, painless, sectoral visual field loss and a cherry-red spot on fundus examination, not isolated floaters.

question_text: The most common type of refractive error is:
explanation:
Refractive error in which rays of light are focussed at more than focal points.

Astigmatism can be corneal, lenticular, or retinal. Based on the meridian, it can be with the rule, against the rule, oblique and bi-oblique astigmatism. Astigmatism can also be subdivided as simple, compound, and mixed. Various factors influence astigmatisms, such as eyelid pressure, the pressure of extraocular muscles, pupil size, and accommodation. Astigmatism usually causes asthenopic symptoms, and there can be different power in different meridians. Astigmatism is diagnosed by performing basic investigations like visual acuity, retinoscopy, slit lamp evaluation examination, keratometry, Schiempflug imaging, astigmatic fan test, and Jackson cross-cylinder.

In with-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism, there is greater refractive power (and increased curvature) along the vertical meridian than along the horizontal. Conversely, in against-the-rule astigmatism (ATR), the higher refractive power is along the horizontal meridian

With the rule” astigmatism is typically seen in children, while “against the rule astigmatism” is seen in older eyes.

question_text: A15 year old female with myopic astigmatism refuses to wear glasses; What would be the ideal management?
explanation:
The spherical equivalent is the spherical lens which places any astigmatic eye in a condition of meridional balance. That is, it changes the astigmatism into equally-mixed astigmatism and produces retinal images made up of diffusion circles.

implantable collamer lenses (ICL) are a type of posterior chamber phakic intraocular lens (pIOL). pIOL are usually used for high degrees of refractive error or when corneal refractive surgery is contraindicated. Advantages over corneal refractive surgery also include quicker recovery and reversibility. Posterior chamber pIOL provide a more cosmetically appealing alternative to anterior chamber (AC) pIOL because they are less visible externally and create less risk of endothelial cell loss (ECL) as they are placed further away from the cornea. They are a safer alternative to refractive less exchange which carries a risk of retinal detachment and loss of accommodation. There have been a number of posterior chamber phakic intraocular lenses on the market prior to the development of the implantable collamer lens. These include the Chiron Adatomed pIOL which was a rectangular, silicone plate IOL that was eventually discontinued because of high rates of AC inflammation and cataracts. The PRL Phakic Refractive Lens (CIBA Vision) was another 1-piece pIOL made of hydrophobic silicone elastomer designed so the haptics would rest on the zonules and the lens would float above the natural crystalline lens; however this lens was taken off of the market due to high incidence of subluxation of the lens into the vitreous cavity secondary to zonular dehiscence. Currently there is only one FDA approved posterior chamber pIOL in the US which is the implantable collamer lens (ICL).

The best management for a 15-year-old with myopic astigmatism who refuses to wear glasses is prescribing spherical equivalent glasses. At this age, the cornea is still developing, and refractive surgeries like LASIK, Femto LASIK, or ICL are not recommended until the refractive error stabilizes (typically after 18-21 years of age). The spherical equivalent helps correct vision without requiring astigmatism-specific glasses, making it a more acceptable option for the patient.

Incorrect Options:

  • (A) LASIK:
    LASIK (Laser-Assisted in Situ Keratomileusis) is a laser refractive surgery used to correct myopia, hyperopia, and astigmatism. However, it is not recommended for individuals under 18, as their refractive error is still changing. Performing LASIK too early can result in regression of the correction and unpredictable outcomes.
  • Femto LASIK:
    • Femto LASIK is a more advanced version of LASIK, using a femtosecond laser instead of a microkeratome to create the corneal flap.
    • Despite being safer and more precise, it is still not advised for individuals under 18 years due to ongoing corneal growth and refractive instability.
  • (C) ICL (Implantable Collamer Lens):
    • ICL is a posterior chamber phakic intraocular lens (pIOL) used for patients with high refractive errorsor those unsuitable for LASIK.
    • It is not the first-line treatment for mild-to-moderate myopic astigmatism and is not recommended for a 15-year-old due to the risk of cataracts, glaucoma, and corneal endothelial damage over time.

Key Takeaway:

For a 15-year-old with myopic astigmatism, spherical equivalent glasses are the best option because they are safe, effective, and non-invasive. LASIK, Femto LASIK, and ICL are not suitable at this age due to the unstable refractive status and the potential risks associated with early surgical intervention.

Scleritis

  • Pathologically, scleritis resembles episcleritis, but extends more deeply, the essential difference being a dense lymphocytic infiltration deep within the sclera tissue.
  • Scleritis is usually a bilateral disease, rarer than episcleritis and occurs most frequently in women (Fig. A).
  • It is associated with connective tissue disease in 50% of cases and a thorough investigation is required to eliminate active systemic disease such as polyarteritis nodosa, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis (Fig. B), Reiter syndrome, ankylosing spondylitis, non-specific arteritis, Wegener granulomatosis, dermatomyositis, polychondritis and gout.
  • Other known associations include acute or previous attacks of herpes zoster ophthalmicus, syphilis and recent ocular surgery such as cataract extraction and retinal detachment surgery.

Fig. (A) Nodular anterior scleritis. A discrete scleral nodule with displacement of the deep vessels over the nodule and surrounding inflammation overlying the unaffected sclera(By courtesy of P. Watson). (B) Anterior scleritis in a 42-yearold woman with rheumatoid.

  • One or more nodules may appear but the area affected is less circumscribed than in episcleritis.
  • The swelling is at first dark red or bluish and later becomes purple and semitransparent like porcelain.
  • It may extend entirely around the cornea, forming a very serious condition known as annular scleritis.
  • In the diffuse type, hard whitish nodules, the size of a pin's head, may develop in the inflamed zone; they disappear without disintegrating.
  • Scleritis differs from episcleritis in that the cornea and uveal tract are involved, there is some iritis but more often cyclitis and anterior choroiditis are present.
  • There is no ulceration, but the sclera is thinned and a dark purple cicatrix is formed, which occasionally becomes too weak to withstand the intraocular pressure, so that ectasia follows(ciliary staphyloma).

question_text: Arden ration normal value is
explanation:
The electrooculogram (EOG) measures the cornea-positive standing potential relative to the back of the eye. By attaching skin electrodes outside the eye near the lateral and medial canthus, the potential can be measured by having the patient move the eyes horizontally a set distance.

The voltage becomes smaller in the dark, reaching its lowest potential after 8-12min, the so-called dark trough. When the lights are turned on, the potential rises, reaching a peak by about 10min. When the size of the light peak is compared to the dark trough, the normal ratio should be near 1.85. A light peak:dark trough ratio of less than 1.5 is considered abnormal. The origin of electrooculographic potentials is the pigment epithelium of the retina interacting with the midretina. The light rise of the potential requires both a normal pigment epithelium and normal midretinal function.

An Arden Ratio is calculated by using the lowest trough and highest peak values.

Arden ratio of 1.80 or greater is normal, 1.65 to 1.80 is subnormal, and < 1.65 is significantly subnormal

The most common use of the electrooculogram is to confirm Best disease. Best disease is identified by the appearance of an egg-yellow fundus and can be confirmed by recording both an electroretinogram (ERG) and electrooculogram (EOG). The ERG will be normal and the EOG will be abnormal. The EOG is also used for tracking eye movement.

Reference: parson's 22/e section III, chapter 10. pg. 110. ARDEN index-EOG

question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with sudden, transient visual blurring in the left eye. He reports a complete, painless monocular vision loss lasting a few minutes, which then fully recovered. No headache, eye pain, or other neurological symptoms were reported. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is characteristic of amaurosis fugax, which is a form of transient monocular blindness.

  • It is classically described as a "curtain descending" over the eye.
  • Typically lasts for a few minutes and then vision recovers completely.
  • It is usually embolic in origin (commonly from carotid artery disease), but can also be due to hemodynamic, ocular, or neurologic causes.
  • Important because it is a warning sign of future stroke; it requires urgent evaluation and management.

Amaurosis Fugax:

  • Definition: Brief, painless loss of vision in one eye, commonly visualized as a curtain lowering over the eye.
  • Causes: Primarily embolic, but hemodynamic, ocular, neurologic, or idiopathic etiologies can contribute.
  • Symptoms: Short-lived visual loss (minutes), with recovery following the same pattern as onset.
  • Commonly Affects: One eye or, if both eyes are affected in sequence, suggests cerebral ischemia.
  • Associated Findings: Can coincide with an ipsilateral TIA and may present with contralateral neurological deficits.
  • Urgent Management: Needs prompt workup and treatment similar to retinal arterial occlusion due to high risk of future stroke.

Explanation of Other Options:

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (Option B) (CRAO): Leads to sudden, painless, and permanent vision loss in one eye, often with a cherry-red spot on fundus examination. Vision does not typically recover spontaneously within minutes.

Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (Option C) (CRVO): Causes visual impairment from blockage of the retinal vein, usually producing longer-lasting visual deficits and possible retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopic evaluation.

Hypertensive Retinopathy (Option D): Vision changes develop gradually over time due to chronic hypertension. Transient visual loss, as described in this patient, is not typical.

question_text: A wave of ERG represent
explanation:
ERG is mass response (electrical activity of the retina in response) to a light stimulus. The ERG arises from currents generated directly by retinal neurons in combination with contributions from retinal glia.

The ERG can be elicited by diffuse flashes or patterned stimuli.

The a-wave, negative wave, sometimes called the “late receptor potential,” reflects the general physiological health of the photoreceptors in the outer retina.

The b-wave, positive wave, reflects the health of the inner layers of the retina, including the ON bipolar cells and the Muller cells.

C-wave: The c-wave is a slow positive component that follows the b-wave and is generated from the retinal pigment epithelium.

It provides diagnostic information concerning a variety of inherited and acquired retinal disorders. Moreover, the ERG can be used to monitor disease progression and evaluate retinal toxicity due to various drugs or retained intraocular foreign bodies.

Implicit time refers to the time occurring between the initiation of the light stimulation (flash) and the peak of a-and b-waves. The a-wave amplitude was measured from baseline to a-wave trough; the b-wave amplitude was measured from a-wave trough to b-wave peak.

Tractional RD

Pathophysiology

Fibrovascular membranes in the vitreous due to long standing vitreous hemorrhage exert traction on the retina. This pulls the retina forward leading to retinal detachment.

Causes

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy(PDR)

Central retinal vein occlusion

Eales' disease

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).

Signs

Minimal mobility

question_text: In which type of retinal detachment does the retina appear concave in shape?
explanation:
Explanation:

In tractional retinal detachment, fibrous or fibrovascular tissue within the vitreous exerts mechanical pull on the retina, which gradually elevates and detaches it. This traction causes the retina to assume a concave configuration, with the maximum elevation at the point of adhesion or fibrous band.

  • There are no retinal breaks, mobility of the retina is limited, and the condition is most commonly seen in disorders involving chronic retinal ischemia and neovascularization such as PDR, CRVO, Eales' disease, and ROP.
  • Management often requires pars plana vitrectomywith relief of traction and application of laser photocoagulation.
  • Rhegmatogenous RD (Option A):Characterized by a full-thickness retinal tear, allowing liquefied vitreous into the subretinal space. The detached retina typically shows a convex / bullous appearance with corrugation and significant mobility, not concave.
  • Exudative RD (Option C):Occurs due to fluid accumulation beneath the retina without a retinal break. The retinal elevation is smooth and dome-shaped (convex) and often shifts with changes in posture, unlike tractional RD.
  • Both A and C (Option D):Both rhegmatogenous and exudative RDs present with a convex configuration, not concave. Only tractional RD demonstrates a concave pattern.

question_text: What is the presumed cause of venous obstruction in branch retinal vein occlusion?
option_b: The retinal artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath
option_d: Retinal hemorrhages result in reduced venous flow
explanation:
Explanation:

In BRVO, systemic hypertension leads to arteriosclerosis of the retinal arteries.

At arteriovenous (AV) crossing points, the retinal artery and vein lie in a common adventitial sheath, resulting in tight anatomical proximity.

  • The stiffened arteriole compresses the adjacent venule leading to narrowing of venous lumen which results in turbulent flow leading to venous thrombosis, which ultimately causes BRVO.
  • Veins develop sclerosis after occlusion (Option A): venous sclerosis is a result of chronic venous obstruction, not the primary cause. The obstruction occurs first due to compression by the sclerosed artery.
  • Embolism (Option C): Branchretinal vein occlusion is not embolic in origin. Emboli are more commonly implicated in arterial occlusions (e.g., CRAO/ BRAO).
  • Retinal hemorrhages result in reduced venous flow (Option D): Retinal hemorrhages occur secondary to venous occlusion due to increased back pressure in retinal capillaries.

question_text: Shifting fluid sign in:
explanation:
In exudative retinal detachment, the subretinal fluid is not bound by a retinal break and can freely move within the subretinal space. A hallmark of ERD is the shifting fluid sign, where the subretinal fluid relocates to the most dependent part of the retina when the patient changes position. This feature helps distinguish ERD from other types of retinal detachment.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(B) Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) - TRD occurs due to fibrovascular membranes pulling on the retina, commonly seen in conditions like proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity. Since the detachment is caused by traction rather than fluid accumulation, shifting fluid is not observed.

(C) Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RRD) - RRD is caused by a retinal tear or hole that allows vitreous fluid to seep underneath, leading to retinal separation. The fluid in RRD does not shift with body position since it is trapped under the retina due to the presence of a break.

(D) Retinal Dialysis - Retinal dialysis is a subtype of RRD where the retina is detached at the ora serrata. Like other forms of RRD, subretinal fluid does not shift with positional changes, as the fluid accumulates through a fixed retinal break.

Key Takeaways:

  • Shifting fluid sign is characteristic of exudative retinal detachment (ERD) due to freely moving subretinal fluid.
  • TRD and RRD do not exhibit shifting fluid because the detachment mechanisms involve traction or a retinal break, respectively.
  • Recognition of shifting fluid helps differentiate ERD from other types of retinal detachment.

question_text: Which of the following is the strongest indication for prophylactic treatment (cryopexy or laser surgery) to prevent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
option_a: High myopia and lattice degeneration with new onset of floaters in a phakic patient
option_b: An asymptomatic flap tear in an eye with a cataract that is about to be rendered pseudophakic
option_c: An atrophic hole in a phakic patient whose other eye developed a retinal detachment
option_d: Lattice degeneration in a pseudophakic patient with a family history of retinal detachment
explanation:
The subject of prophylaxis for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is an area of some controversy among vitreoretinal specialists. As with any surgical decision, the decision to treat must rest on an educated assessment of the risks of treatment versus the risk of leaving the patient untreated, as well as on knowledge of how much the treatment can actually reduce the risk of detachment. A thorough exploration is beyond the scope of this discussion, but factors that prompt treatment are evidence of acute onset of symptoms and the presence of vitreous traction. Less compelling indications are a history of detachment in the other eye and imminent cataract surgery, but the combination of the latter with evidence of traction becomes a strong indication to treat.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition/648

question_text: Among the following clinical situations, which one provides the strongest indication to perform prophylactic treatment (laser photocoagulation or cryopexy) to prevent a future rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
option_a: High myopia and lattice degeneration with new onset of floaters in a phakic patient
option_b: An asymptomatic flap tear in an eye with a cataract that is about to be rendered pseudophakic
option_c: An atrophic hole in a phakic patient whose other eye developed a retinal detachment
option_d: Lattice degeneration in a pseudophakic patient with a family history of retinal detachment
explanation:
Explanation:

high myopia with lattice degeneration and new onset floaters, representing acute vitreous traction in a high-risk anatomical background, making it the strongest indication for preventive treatment.

  • Prophylactic cryopexy or laser photocoagulation is considered when the risk of progression to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is high.
    The strongest risk factors include:
    • High myopia
    • Lattice degeneration
    • Acute onset symptoms such as flashes/floaters
    • Evidence of active vitreoretinal traction
  • An asymptomatic flap tear in an eye with a cataract that is about to be rendered pseudophakic (Option B): Cataract surgery increases the risk of RRD, and a pre-existing flap tear may warrant prophylaxis. However, asymptomatic tears without evidence of acute traction are not as high-risk as acute floaters in a myopic lattice retina. Treatment may be considered, but the indication is not the strongest.
  • An atrophic hole in a phakic patient whose other eye developed a retinal detachment (Option C): A previous detachment in the fellow eye DOES increase risk, but atrophic holes lack traction, and most do not progress to detachment. Usually monitored rather than routinely treated, unless additional high-risk factors exist.
  • Lattice degeneration in a pseudophakic patient with a family history of retinal detachment (Option D): Lattice degeneration alone is not a strong enough trigger for prophylaxis, even with family history. Family history is a minor risk factor, and pseudophakia increases risk only in the presence of tractional tears, not lattice alone.

Phthisis bulbi is an end stage ocular disease which can result from a variety of ocular insults including trauma, surgery, infection, inflammation, malignancy, retinal detachment and vascular lesions.

All these lead to scarring, inflammation, atrophy and eventually disorganization of the globe and intraocular contents.

Also called end-stage eye, phthisis bulbi can be described as a shrunken, collapsed in form, non-functional eye and presents with a small squared off shape, opaque and thickened cornea, thickened sclera, neovascularization of iris, cataract, cyclitic membrane, ciliochoroidal detachment and retinal detachment.

A mnemonic rule used to describe phthisis bulbi is '7S' referring to: Soft - Shrunken - Shapeless - Sightless - Structureless - Squared - Sore.

question_text: An industrial worker admitted to the hospital following an eye injury caused by cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. Which investigation is most suitable for localizing the foreign body in the eye?
explanation:
Explanation:

CT scan is the investigation of choice in case of an intraocular foreign body and MRI is contraindicated in cases where there is a risk of metallic foreign bodies.

Intraocular Foreign Bodies (IOFBs):

  • The diagnosis of an intraocular foreign body is extremely important, particularly as the patient is often unaware that a particle has entered the eye.
  • Detailed history to understand the injury mechanism of IOFB type is essential.
  • The anterior segment of the eye must be thoroughly explored with the slit lamp and the angle of the anterior chamber with the gonioscope.
  • A hole in the iris or an opaque track through the lens is pathognomonic.

Radiological investigations

CT scan

  • CT with axial and coronal cuts is used to detect and localize a metallic IOFB, providing cross-sectional images with a sensitivity and specificity superior to plain radiography and Ultrasonography. (Option A, C ruled out)

MRI

  • Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans are contraindicated in cases of magnetic or magnetizable foreign bodies, but is very useful in detecting a wooden foreign body and vascular changes. (Option D ruled out)

Ultrasonography

  • Ultrasonography allows the detection of most foreign bodies, as well as associated intraocular conditions such as retinal detachment, suprachoroidal haemorrhage and a perforating injury of the eye.

Treatment

  • If the foreign body lies within the lens, it is better to treat such particles as if they were nonmagnetic or remove the lens as a whole.
  • If a magnetic foreign body is in the vitreous or retina, an intravitreal magnet or intravitreal forceps are necessary for its removal.
  • Forceps removal may be used for non-magnetic foreign bodies and magnetic foreign bodies that cannot be safely removed with a magnet.
  • It involves pars plana vitrectomy and removal of the foreign body with forceps either through the pars plana or limbus depending on the circumstances.

question_text: Headlight in fog appearance is characteristic for
explanation:
Headlight in fog appearance is characteristic for toxoplasmosis.

Ocular manifestations of toxoplasmosis:

  • Symptoms - Unilateral acute or subacute onset of floaters, blurring and photophobia.
  • Spill-over anterior uveitis is common.
  • A single inflammatory focus of fluffy white retinitis or retinochoroiditis associated with a pigmented scar(satellite lesion) is typical. Lesions tend to involve the posterior pole.
  • De novo foci not associated with an old scar, and multiple lesions - occur more frequently in the immunocompromised.
  • Vitritis may be severe and impair fundus visualization. Headlight in the fog is the classic description of a white retinal inflammatory nidus viewed through vitritis.
  • Vasculitis is more commonly venous.
  • Optic disc oedema is common.
  • Accompanying nearby or adjacent pigmented retinochoroidal scar.
  • Extensive and fulminant retinal involvement is generally confined to the immunocompromised.
  • Neuroretinitis similar to that seen in cat-scratch disease is rare and may be a marker of acutely acquired rather than reactivated infection.
  • Visual loss - Causes of permanently reduced vision(around 25% of eyes) include macular inflammatory lesions and oedema, optic nerve involvement, vascular occlusion, serous, rhegmatogenous and tractional retinal detachment and late secondary choroidal neovascularization.
  • Healing in immunocompetent hosts usually occurs spontaneously within 6-8 weeks, although vitreous opacities take longer to clear.
  • Recurrences are seen.

Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 437.

question_text: Extra retinal fibrovascular proliferation at ridge is?
explanation: Ans. D. Stage III ROM Disease Severity (Stage) Prior to the development of ROP in the premature infant, vascularization of the retina is incomplete or "immature" (Stage 0). Stage 1: Demarcation Line: This line is thin and flat (in the retina plane) and separates the avascular retina anteriorly from the vascularized retina posteriorly. Stage 2: Ridge: The ridge arises from the demarcation line and has height and width, which extends above the plane of the retina. The ridge may change from white to pink and vessels may leave the plane of the retina posterior to the ridge to enter it. Small isolated tufts of neovascular tissue lying on the surface of the retina, commonly called "popcorn" may be seen posterior to this ridge structure and do not constitute the degree of fibrovascular growth that is a necessary condition for stage 3. Stage 3: Extraretinal Fibrovascular Proliferation: Neovascularization extends from the ridge into the vitreous. This extraretinal proliferating tissue is continuous with the posterior aspect of the ridge, causing a ragged appearance as the proliferation becomes more extensive. Stage 4: Partial Retinal Detachment: Stage 4, in the initial classification was the final stage and initially known as the cicatricial classification was the final stage and initially known as the cicatricial phase. It was later divided into extrafoveal (stage 4A) and foveal (stage 4B) partial retinal detachments. Stage 4 retinal detachments are generally concave and most are circumferentially oriented. Retinal detachments usually begin at the point of fibrovascular attachment to the vascularized retina and the extent of detachment depends on the amount of neovascularization present. Stage 5: Total Retinal Detachment: Retinal detachments are generally tractional and usually funnel shaped. The configuration of the funnel itself is used for subdivision of this stage depending if the anterior and posterior portions are open or narrowed

question_text: A Patient Presents To Emergency With History Of Trauma To Eyed With Chisel And Hammer. Which Of The Following Investigations Will Be Detrimental To The Patient?
explanation:
Diagnostic Procedures in ocular trauma

Imaging

Option B : Plain X ray: Plain X-ray AP and lateral views are essential to evaluate injured eye and orbit to assess intraocular and extra ocular injuries as well as fractures. It may also detect foreign bodies.

Ultrasonography: B-scan ultrasound is an important investigation to detect intraocular and intraorbital damage, especially when ocular media is not clear. B-scan can be used to visualize vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, intraocular foreign bodies, damage to the extraocular muscles, and scleral rupture. It can also offer information on the state of the posterior lens capsule and exudates in vitreous in case of endophthalmitis. It should be used with caution if ruptured globe is suspected, and typically deferred if ruptured globe is known.

Option C : CT scan: In the case of orbital trauma, 1.5 to 2 mm cuts should be performed in axial and coronal plains (Figure 8). CT is considered superior to ultrasound for locating foreign bodies. This is a non-invasive method that does not require direct contact with the eye and may identify damage to traumatized eye, deformed eye wall, vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment.

MRI: May be useful in case of patients with non-magnetic foreign bodies. Indications for use in those with pacemakers or implantable metallic hardware vary by type of hardware. It should be used with caution if ruptured globe is suspected, especially in cases of potential metallic foreign body. Can also be used in pregnant patients.

Electrophysiology

Full-field electroretinogram: In eyes with no light perception, the full-field ERG is an important method to evaluate the vitality of photoreceptor function.

Multifocal ERG: This modality may be used to detect which areas of the retina may have been affected by trauma.

Laboratory tests

A complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, international normalized ratio, prothrombin time (PT), and partial prothrombin time (PTT) may be required prior to surgery. Sickle cell testing should be considered in patients with hyphema.

question_text: In cases of embolic central retinal artery occlusion, which clinical finding is most useful in confirming the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In embolic CRAO, blockage of the central retinal artery leads to acute retinal ischemia, resulting in diffuse retinal whitening (retinal pallor). The fovea remains unaffected due to its choroidal circulation, giving rise to a "cherry-red spot" appearance.

Retinal pallor is therefore a key examination finding that supports the diagnosis of CRAO, although it is not exclusive to embolic causes.

Jaw claudication (Option A): Jaw claudication is a classic symptom of giant cell arteritis, which may cause arteritic CRAO, not embolic CRAO. It does not help confirm embolic etiology.

Ocular pain (Option C): CRAO due to embolism is typically painless. Presence of ocular pain raises suspicion for arteritic etiology or other ocular inflammatory/ischemic disorders.

Subacute onset (Option D): Embolic CRAO generally has a sudden, abrupt loss of vision. A subacute or fluctuating course is more typical of arteritic CRAO or ophthalmic ischemic syndrome.

question_text: Which of the following interventions is the most appropriate for treating an acute central retinal artery occlusion?
explanation:
Although not universally effective, anterior chamber paracentesis should be considered in the management of the acute phase of central retinal artery occlusion. Ocular massage has also be proposed to force retrograde or antegrade displacement of emboli. Panretinal photocoagulation and ocular antihypertensives are not useful for CRAO. Aspirin has been advocated as antiplatelet therapy to lower risk of thrombotic, but not to treat acute embolic occlusions.

question_text: A subretinal demarcation line, also known as a watershed line or high-water mark, is typically observed in which ocular condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

A subretinal demarcation line forms when retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells proliferate at the junction between attached and detached retina.

  • It appears as a pigmented or non-pigmented linear/curved band, usually concentric to the retinal break. This line indicates a long-standing (chronic) rhegmatogenous retinal detachmentand shows the previous extent of subretinal fluid before it stabilized.
  • Other features of chronic RD include:
    • Retinal thinning due to atrophy
    • Secondary intraretinal cysts
    • Reduced mobility of detached retina
  • Fresh Rhegmatogenous RD (Option A): Shows convex, elevated, and highly mobile retina, obscured choroidal pattern, fresh retinal break, and slightly opaque retina with prominent blood vessels. Demarcation line is not present in fresh RD.
  • ROP (Option C): Retinopathy of Prematurity, a disease of prematurity with retinal ridge formation, neovascularization, and possible tractional retinal detachment in later stages. Does not produce a subretinal demarcation line.
  • RP Option D): Retinitis Pigmentosa a hereditary dystrophy showing bone-spicule pigmentation, attenuated vessels, and pale disc. No demarcation (watershed) line occurs.

question_text: The type of retinal detachment seen in uncontrolled diabetes is:
explanation:
Explanation:

Advanced diabetes mellitus can lead to tractional retinal detachment (TRD).

TRD occurs when fibrous membranes in the vitreous contract and pull the neurosensory retina away from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In uncontrolled proliferative diabetic retinopathy, abnormal new vessels and fibrous tissue form on the retinal surface; as these membranes shrink, they exert traction and lift the retina.

Types of retinal detachment
Retinal detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE and is classified into three major forms:

  • Rhegmatogenous (primary): caused by a full-thickness retinal break.
  • Tractional: due to mechanical pulling by vitreoretinal membranes.
  • Exudative (serous): from accumulation of subretinal fluid without a tear or traction.

Other causes of tractional detachment include:

  • Retinopathy of prematurity
  • Eales' disease
  • Sickle-cell retinopathy
  • Incontinentia pigmenti
  • Post-haemorrhagic retinitis proliferans
  • Ocular toxocariasis
  • Vitreomacular traction syndrome
  • Retinal dysplasia

Clinical features of TRD:
The detached retina typically shows a concave configuration, with markedly reduced mobility, and there are no retinal breaks or shifting subretinal fluid. Because the process is gradual, patients usually do not experience photopsia or floaters, which are common in rhegmatogenous detachments.

Explanations for other Options:

Rhegmatogenous (Option A): Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment develops when a full-thickness break-such as a retinal hole or tear-allows liquefied vitreous to leak beneath the sensory retina, separating it from the retinal pigment epithelium.

Exudative (Option C): Exudative (serous) retinal detachment results from the build-up of fluid under the retina, which lifts the neurosensory retina away from the pigment epithelium. This fluid accumulation is typically secondary to inflammatory disorders or vascular abnormalities.
