question_text: In bagolini striated glass test what is the interpretation if patient sees only one line
explanation:
Image of bagolini's striated glasses

Bagolini glasses do not have dioptric power but have narrow striations running parallel in one meridian. This test is used to determine the direction of abnormal retinal correspondence(ARC) and suppression.

This test is mildly dissociating so it will detect small ARC even in large angle strabismus. The Bagolini glasses also simulate life-like testing conditions, which makes it the least dissociating. A disadvantage to this test is that it is difficult for young children to appreciate because it requires reliable subjective responses.

Procedure

If the examiner does not have access to a Bagolini Lens, Bagolini trial frames are placed at 135 degrees OD, 45 degrees OS. Patient is asked to look at muscle light or pen light. They will see a band of light perpendicular to the striations of the lens.

Interpretation

When a patient sees only one line at a time, the patient is suppressing. If patient sees two lines in an "A" or "V" arrangement, the patient is diplopic. You may offset the deviation with a prism and if the patient reports an X this confirms normal retinal correspondence(NRC).

Reference: Kanski, 5th Edition, Page no. 535.

question_text: Shafer’s sign is typically observed in which of the following ocular condition?
explanation:
Explanation

Shafer’s sign refers to the presence of fine pigment granules in the anterior vitreous, giving the appearance of tobacco dust.

  • It occurs when pigment from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)escapes into the vitreous following a retinal tear, indicating a fresh rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
  • Other common RD findings include:
    • Reduced visual acuity
    • Hypotony(due to absorption of liquefied vitreous through RPE)
    • Convex, corrugated, freely mobile detached retina
    • Peripheral retinal break
  • Congenital glaucoma (Option B): Thispresents corneal haze, photophobia, epiphora, buphthalmos, Haab's striae due to elevated IOP. Shafer's sign is not a feature.
  • ROP: Retinopathy of Prematurity (Option C):Seen in premature infants; features include retinal neo­vascularization, fibrovascular ridge, tractional retinal detachment in advanced stages. No tobacco-dust pigment in anterior vitreous; Shafer's sign is absent.
  • Stargardt's disease (Option D): A hereditary macular dystrophy characterized by beaten-bronze macula and pisciform flecks; ERG/EOG may be abnormal. Does not show anterior vitreous pigment cells.

question_text: A 35-year old man noticed his vision was abnormal on waking one morning: he had difficulty focusing and making out faces and could not read a newspaper because the words would disappear. A visit to the opticians revealed a visual field defect on the Humphrey chart(figure 1). An MR brain scan was done on day 15 by the ophthalmologists. This showed a lesion with T2 hyperintensity in the region of the right lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, consistent with an infarct. He was an ex-cigarette smoker with no other vascular risk factors. He was on no regular medications and denied illicit drug use. There was no recent neck trauma. Name the defect looking at this field
explanation:

Loss of the upper and lower homonymous quadrants(also known as quadruple sectoranopia) with preservation of a horizontal wedge occurs with disruption of the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the middle cerebral artery.

question_text: Earliest changes in pregnancy induced HTN is
explanation:
RETINOPATHY IN PREGNANCY-INDUCED HYPERTENSION

  • Pregnancy-induced hypertension(PIH), previously known as 'toxaemia of pregnancy', is a disease of unknown etiology characterized by raised blood pressure, proteinuria and generalized oedema.
  • Retinal changes are liable to occur in this condition when blood pressure rises above 160/100 mm of Hg and are marked when blood pressure rises above 200/130 mm of Hg.
  • Earliest changes consist of narrowing of nasal arterioles, followed by generalized narrowing. Severe persistent spasm of vessels causes retinal hypoxia characterized by appearance of 'cotton wool spots and superficial hemorrhages'.
  • If pregnancy is allowed to continue, further progression of retinopathy occurs rapidly.
  • Retinal oedema and exudation are usually marked and may be associated with 'macular star' or 'flat macular detachment'.
  • Rarely it may be complicated by bilateral exudative retinal detachment.
  • Prognosis for retinal reattachment is good, as it occurs spontaneously within a few days of termination of pregnancy.

Management:

  • Changes of retinopathy are reversible and disappear after the delivery, unless organic vascular disease is established.
  • Therefore, in pre-organic stage when patient responds well to conservative treatment, the pregnancy may justifiably be continued under close observation.
  • However, the advent of hypoxic retinopathy(soft exudates, retinal oedema and hemorrhages) should be considered an indication for termination of pregnancy; otherwise, permanent visual loss or even loss of life(of both mother and fetus) may occur.

Reference: A K Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 259.

question_text: A patient presents with sudden onset floaters and perception of a curtain in front of his right eye, what is most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Rhegmatogenous RD

Pathophysiology

The essential lesion is a rhegma (retinal break) through which the liquefied vitreous gains access to the retina. This liquefied vitreous accumulates beneath the neurosensory retina leading to RD. This is commonly seen in:

High myopes: Peripheral retinal degenerations like lattice degeneration, holes and breaks with used liquefaction of overlying vitreous predispose to RD

Retinoschisis: This is a condition where there is splitting of the neurosensory retina and vitreous degeneration. It is of two types:

  1. Typical retinoschisis: Split at the level of Outer Plexiform Layer
  2. Reticular retinoschisis: Split at the level of Nerve Fibre Layer. Seen more commonly in hyper metropes in the inferotemporal periphery of retina

Trauma

Aphakia

Pseudophakia

Symptoms

Premonitory features:

Photopsia: Flashes of light due to vitreo-retinal traction at site of break

Floaters: Due to associated vitreous haemorrhage

Visual field defect which is described by the patient as a black curtain or veil in front of the eye.

Loss of vision when the detachment involves the macula.

Signs

Decrease in visual acuity

Hypotony: The liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE leading to hypotony

Shafer's sign: Pigments in anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) is a feature of fresh RD

Detached retina is convex in configuration. Surface is corrugated with free undulation. Break is identified at the periphery.

Treatment

Prophylactic laser barrage:

It is done in Symptomatic break (associated with photopsia and floaters) Horse shoe tear.

Superior, especially supero-temporal tears Aphakia

One eyed patient

Surgery for retinal detachment

Scleral buckling: In this procedure, the sclera is indented by attaching an explant known as a buckle. This pushes the RPE inwards towards the neurosensory retina. Subretinal fluid is drained and the break is closed by laser or cryotherapy

Pneumatic retinopexy: In this procedure, the neurosensory retina is pushed towards the RPE by injecting an expansile gas in the vitreous cavity. The break is then sealed with laser. The gases commonly used are Sulphur Hexafluoride (SF6) and Perfluoropropane (C3F8)

Pars plana vitrectomy

question_text: Name the lesion seen in a 55 year old hypertensive diabetic
explanation:
Flame shaped hemorrhages: These hemorrhages are diffuse, found in the posterior pole, and last approximately 6 to 12 weeks. They occur typically in diseases affecting superficial retinal capillary plexus secondary to arterial diseases like hypertension, blood dyscrasias, and anemias.

Dot-blot hemorrhages tend to occur deeper in the retina where the cells run vertically. You associate these hemorrhages mostly with background diabetic retinopathy. Flame hemorrhages, however, are more superficial in the ganglion nerve fiber-layer, and are associated with hypertension and venous stasis.

question_text: A 20 year old male suffered from a trauma on eye a day back. He presented today with a decrease in vision. His retina showed this image. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Choroidal ruptures are breaks in the choroid, the Bruch membrane, and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) that result from blunt ocular trauma (the most common eye injury). Choroidal rupture can be secondary to indirect or direct trauma

A direct choroidal rupture occurs anteriorly at the site of impact, generally parallel to the ora serrata and peripheral retina. In contrast, an indirect choroidal rupture (MC) occurs away from the site of impact, more posterior, and often concentric to the optic disc in a crescent shape

The ruptures clinically appear as white to yellow-red crescent-shaped lesions that are often wider in the center and tapered at the ends. It may result in CNVM.

The visual prognosis may be extremely poor when involving the macular area or in cases with major comorbidities.

Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 902 choroidal rupture

question_text: A 20-year-old man experienced blunt trauma to the eye one day ago. He now presents with reduced vision. Fundus examination shows the lesion seen in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Choroidal rupture occurs when blunt trauma causes a break involving the choroid, Bruch’s membrane, and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). These injuries can happen directly at the site of impact or indirectly at a location away from the trauma.

  • Indirect choroidal ruptures, the more common type, typically appear as crescent-shaped streaks near the optic disc, usually posterior and curved around it.
    On examination, they present yellow white to reddish crescent lesions, thicker centrally and tapering at the edges. Such ruptures can later develop choroidal neovascular membranes (CNVM), and visual outcomes are especially poor if the macula is involved.
  • Angioid streak (option A): These are irregular, crack-like lines radiating from the optic disc, associated with systemic conditions such as Paget's disease, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, or sickle cell disease. They are unrelated to acute trauma and do not present immediately after injury.
  • Choroidal neovascular membrane (option C): A CNVM may occur secondary to a choroidal rupture, but it is not the acute finding just one day after trauma. It usually develops weeks to months later as a late complication.
  • Retinal detachment (option D): Retinal detachment typically shows elevation of the retina with folds or undulations, not crescent-shaped breaks at the level of Bruch's membrane. Symptoms often include flashes and floaters, which are not described here.

question_text: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient presented with blurred vision and headaches. On fundus examination, multiple flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and disc edema were noted. According to the Keith-Wagner classification, which grade of hypertensive retinopathy does this represent?
explanation:
Explanation:

The findings of hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and particularly disc edema (papilledema) correspond to Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy. This represents the most severe stage and is typically associated with malignant hypertension, which can progress to complications such as optic neuropathy and permanent vision loss.

Hypertensive retinopathy describes the retinal damage caused by systemic hypertension. The progression involves several overlapping pathological mechanisms:

  • Vasospasm:
    • Initial retinal arteriolar narrowing due to high BP.
    • More pronounced in younger patients.
    • Leads to ischemic damage in the RPE, choroid, and optic nerve head.
  • Arteriosclerosis:
    • Occurs in chronic hypertension.
    • Thickening and hardening of vessel walls.
    • Causes changes in arteriolar reflex and A–V crossings.
  • Increased Vascular Permeability:
    • Severe HTN → hypoxia → breakdown of inner blood-retinal barrier.
  • Results in hemorrhages, hard exudates, macular edema.
  • Raised Intracranial Pressure:
    • In malignant HTN, papilledema and optic nerve ischemia develop due to choroidal vessel constriction

Clinical Features:

Benign (Chronic) Hypertensive Retinopathy:

  • Generalized arteriolar narrowing: May be mild or marked, with vasoconstrictive and sclerotic phases.
  • Focal arteriolar narrowing: Localized vasoconstriction near the disc.
  • A-V nicking: Compression of veins at A-V crossings, Salus's sign (right-angle deflection of veins at arteriovenous crossings), Bonnet sign (banking of veins distal to arteriovenous crossings), and Gunn sign (tapering of veins on either side of the crossings).
  • Arteriolar reflex changes: Brightening of light reflex in younger individuals, with copper wiring (reddish-brown reflex of the arterioles occurs due to progressive sclerosis and hyalinization) and silver wiring (opaque- white reflex of the arterioles due to the continued sclerosis) seen in advanced disease.
  • Retinal hemorrhages: Flame-shaped hemorrhages at the posterior pole.
  • Hard exudates: Yellowish deposits in the retina, arranged in a macular-star pattern.
  • Cotton wool spots: Fluffy white areas representing nerve fiber infarctions.

Malignant Hypertensive Retinopathy:

  • Acute retinal changes: Marked arteriolar narrowing, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and cotton wool spots.
  • Choroidal involvement: Focal retinal pigment epithelium changes, Elschnig's spots, and Siegrist streaks due to choroidal ischemia.
  • Optic neuropathy: Disc edema and hemorrhages in the peripapillary area due to ischemia from vasoconstriction of choroidal vessels.

Staging of Hypertensive Retinopathy (Keith and Wagner Classification):

Management

  • Mild-Moderate (Grades 1-2): Optimize BP, assess vascular risk.Severe (Grade 3-4 / Malignant): Careful and gradual BP reduction to prevent ischemic injury due to sudden perfusion loss.

question_text: A 30 year old female with history of headache is sent for fundus examination. On examination she is found to have generalised arterial attenuation with multiple cotton wool spots and flame shaped hemorrhages in both eyes. The probable diagnosis is
explanation:
Retinopathy

The primary response of the retinal arterioles to systemic hypertension is vasoconstriction; this is less marked in older individuals due to involutional sclerosis conferring increased rigidity. Arteriolosclerosis refers to hardening and loss of elasticity of small vessel walls, manifested most obviously by arteriovenous (AV) nipping (nicking) at crossing points; its presence makes it probable that hypertension has been present for many years, even if the BP is currently controlled. Mild AV changes may be seen in the absence of hypertension. In sustained hypertension the inner blood-retinal barrier is disrupted, increased vascular permeability leading to flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages and oedema.

Keith-Wagner-Barker Classification

  • Grade 1. Mild generalized retinal arteriolar narrowing
  • Grade 2. Focal arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping. A 'copper wiring' opacified appearance of arteriolar walls may be seen
  • Grade 3. Grade 2 plus retinal haemorrhages (dot, blot, f lame), exudates (chronic retinal oedema may result in the deposition of hard exudates around the fovea as a 'macular star') and cotton wool spots.
  • Grade 4. Severe grade 3 plus optic disc swelling; this is a marker of malignant hypertension.
  • Markers of preclinical systemic disease.
  • Reduced retinal arteriolar calibre is an early pre-hypertensive sign and if identified should prompt BP monitoring.
  • Wider venular calibre is relatively specific for impaired glucose metabolism.
  • Low arteriolar calibre and high venular calibre are both thought to be markers of preclinical cardiovascular disease.
  • Increased venular tortuosity can be associated with chronic hypertension and prehypertension, though evidence on arteriolar tortuosity is conflicting- straightening of arterioles has been reported in some studies. Numerous other causes of retinal vascular tortuosity have been described, notably conditions associated with high and low vascular flow.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/557

question_text: A 61-year-old university professor complains of vision loss in his left eye. He compares the sensation to a curtain being pulled over his affected eye. Additionally, he experienced flashing lights and floaters a week ago. The provided image shows a B-scan of his left eye. What could be the possible diagnosis for his condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The symptom triad of flashing lights (photopsia), new floaters, and a curtain-like shadow obscuring vision is classic for acute rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. The flashing lights and floaters often represent a preceding posterior vitreous detachment that caused a retinal tear, allowing fluid to seep underneath and detach the retina.

Types of Retinal Detachment

1. Rhegmatogenous

  • Cause: Retinal break/tear with vitreous fluid seepage.
  • Symptoms:
    • Floaters (dark spots)
    • Photopsia (light flashes)
    • Gradual visual field loss (like a "dark curtain")
    • Sudden painless vision loss (if macula detached)
  • Signs:
    • Retinal breaks (horseshoe, round, dialysis)
    • Vitreous pigments ("tobacco dusting")
    • Subretinal demarcation lines (chronic cases)

2. Tractional

  • Cause: Fibrovascular bands pulling retina inward (e.g., diabetic retinopathy).
  • Symptoms:
    • Gradual, painless vision loss
    • No flashes/floaters
  • Signs:
    • Concave, localized detachment
    • Vitreoretinal bands
    • No retinal breaks
    • No shifting fluid

3. Exudative (Serous)

  • Cause: Fluid accumulation under retina (e.g., tumors, inflammation).
  • Symptoms:
    • Painless, sudden/gradual vision loss
    • No flashes/floaters
  • Signs:
    • Smooth, convex detachment
    • Shifting fluid (key feature)
    • Pigmentary changes/tumor signs
    • No retinal breaks

Key Differentiator:

  • Holes/tears: Only in rhegmatogenous.
  • Shifting fluid: Pathognomonic for exudative.
  • Vitreoretinal traction: Hallmark of tractional.

Explanation of other options:

Glaucoma (Option A): Causes gradual, painless loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision), not an acute curtain-like defect.

Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) (Option B): Causes acute floaters and flashes but does not cause a visual field defect. A PVD can be a precursor to a retinal tear.

Corneal ulcer (Option D): Causes pain, redness, photophobia, and a central corneal opacity affecting vision, not a peripheral shadow.

Key Takeaways:

  • The classic presentation of retinal detachment is flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like visual field defect.
  • This is an ocular emergency requiring urgent referral to a retinal specialist.

question_text: What feature found in embolic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is helpful in confirming the diagnosis?
explanation:
Embolic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) causes retinal pallor which is often appreciated as a "cherry red spot" due to relative retinal translucency at the fovea. However, retinal pallor is helpful to confirm a CRAO, but is not specific for embolic CRAO. Pain, intermittent or subacute onset and jaw claudication suggest an inflammatory cause of central artery occlusion. A minority of CRAOs are due to temporal arteritis, which may present with bilateral CRAO. A stat CRP and/or sedimentation rate should be obtained if an emboli or other feature confirming embolic CRAO cannot be confirmed on initial examination.

Reference: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology, 8th Edition, Page Number-552.

question_text: Cherry Red spot in children after trauma is seen in
explanation:
Commotio retinae

Commotio retinae is caused by concussion of the sensory retina resulting in cloudy swelling that gives the involved area a grey appearance. It most frequently affects the temporal fundus. If the macula is involved, a 'cherry-red spot' may be seen at the fovea. Severe involvement may be associated with intraretinal haemorrhage that can involve the macula. The prognosis in mild cases is good, with spontaneous resolution in around 6 weeks. Sequelae to more severe commotio may include progressive pigmentary degeneration and macular hole formation

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/873

question_text: Cattle Track Sign is seen in
explanation:
Central retinal artery occlusion

  • Symptoms. Sudden profound loss of vision, painless except in GCA.
  • VA is severely reduced except if a cilioretinal artery supplying a critical macular area preserves central vision (see below). Absence of light perception usually indicates either GCA or ophthalmic artery occlusion. The prognosis is poor in all cases unless recovery occurs in the first few hours.
  • RAPD is profound, sometimes total (amaurotic pupil).
  • Fundus shows similar changes to BRAO but involving all retinal quadrants
  • The orange reflex from the intact choroid stands out at the thin foveola, in contrast to the surrounding pale retina, giving rise to a 'cherry-red spot' appearance.
  • The peripapillary retina may appear especially swollen and opaque.
  • An occasional small haemorrhage is not unusual.
  • Emboli are visible in 20%, when Nd:YAG embolysis may be considered
  • In eyes with a cilioretinal artery part of the macula will remain of normal color
  • Retinal signs can sometimes be subtle; retinal oedema may take several hours to develop.
  • Over a few days to weeks the retinal cloudiness and 'cherry-red spot' gradually disappear although the arteries remain attenuated. Later signs include optic atrophy, vessel sheathing and patchy inner retinal atrophy and RPE changes
  • Around 2% of eyes with CRAO develop retinal or disc neovascularization.
  • Rubeosis iridis may occur in up to about 1 in 5 eyes, typically earlier than in CRVO (4-5 weeks compared with 3 months, though sometimes later), and along with very poor vision may indicate ophthalmic artery occlusion.
  • OCT may show a highly reflective embolic plaque within the superficial optic nerve head.
  • FA shows a variable delay in arterial filling and masking of background choroidal fluorescence by retinal oedema. A patent cilioretinal artery will fill during the early phase
  • Electroretinography may be helpful to establish the diagnosis if in doubt, particularly to distinguish from optic nerve disease, typically when signs are subtle; a diminished b-wave is present.
  • Review. The patient should be seen by an ophthalmologist after 3-4 weeks and a minimum of twice subsequently at monthly intervals in order to detect incipient neovascularization, particularly of the anterior segment. In this event, PRP should be performed as for ischaemic CRVO, and intravitreal injection of VEGF inhibitor might be considered. Appropriate systemic management is critical.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/552

question_text: The image below displays the findings of a fundoscopy. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Fundoscopy shows the typical features of pale retina and cherry-red spot, and CRAO is the most likely diagnosis in this case. CRAO often presents with sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss, and it is considered an ophthalmologic emergency because of the potential for permanent vision loss.


  • Cattle truck appearance: Due to segmentation of blood column in retinal veins

Fluorescein Angiography (FA)

  • Arterial Filling: Delayed
  • Masking of Background Fluorescence: Edematous retina blocks normal fluorescence from the choroid
  • Patent Cilioretinal Artery: Area of normal perfusion if a cilioretinal artery supplies the fovea, potentially preserving central vision

Other Diagnostic Tests

Reveals retinal edema, structural changes, and possibly an embolic plaque within the retinal artery and other systemic causes.

  • Cranial MRI or CT
  • Carotid duplex scanning
  • Echocardiography
  • Thrombophilia screening

Explanation of Other Options:

Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) (Option B): Shows diffuse retinal hemorrhages in all quadrants, venous dilation, cotton wool spots, and optic disc edema → creating the "blood and thunder" appearance. Unlike CRAO, the retina is not pale and no cherry-red spot is seen.

Diabetic Retinopathy (Option C): Findings include microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton wool spots due to chronic microvascular damage. Unlike CRAO, this is a gradual, progressive condition rather than sudden vision loss.

Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) (Option D): Characterized by cystic spaces in the macula with focal macular edema, causing blurred central vision. It does not present with retinal pallor or a cherry-red spot. CME reflects macular dysfunction, not arterial occlusion.

question_text: In which condition is a cherry red spot, like the one shown in the image below, typically observed?
explanation:
Explanation:

The sudden, painless loss of vision accompanied by a cherry-red spot at the macula strongly indicates central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

CRAO occurs when the central retinal artery becomes blocked, resulting in widespread retinal ischemia. In some cases, if a cilioretinal artery is present, it may continue to supply blood to the macula, helping to preserve central vision despite the occlusion.

Clinical Features:

Symptoms:

  • Sudden, painless, and severe vision loss
  • Pain is generally absent except in cases related to giant cell arteritis (GCA), where patients may also experience headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or temple pain

Clinical Signs:

  • Visual acuity: Markedly reduced, often to counting fingers or worse
  • Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Pronounced, sometimes leading to a total (amaurotic) pupil

Fundus Examination:

  • Retinal Whitening: The retina appears pale and opaque, especially in the posterior pole due to ischemia
  • Cherry-Red Spot: A bright red area seen at the fovea, caused by the contrast between the pale, ischemic retina and the underlying intact choroidal circulation
  • "attle Truck"Appearance: Segmentation of the blood column in the retinal veins
  • Attenuated Arteries: Retinal arterioles appear narrowed and segmented
  • Optic Disc: Becomes pale over time due to optic atrophy from prolonged ischemia, especially in chronic cases

Fluorescein Angiography (FA):

  • Arterial Filling: Delayed or absent filling of the central retinal artery
  • Masking of Background Fluorescence: Edematous retina blocks normal fluorescence from the choroid
  • Patent Cilioretinal Artery: If present, it supplies the fovea and may preserve central vision by showing normal perfusion in that area

Additional Diagnostic Tests:

  • Imaging (cranial MRI or CT)
  • Carotid duplex ultrasound
  • Echocardiography
  • Thrombophilia screening

These tests help identify retinal edema, structural changes, embolic plaques in retinal arteries, and systemic causes of CRAO.

Explanation for other options:

Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) (Option B): It occurs when the central retinal vein is obstructed. It usually presents with sudden, painless vision loss and is often accompanied by retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and retinal edema.

Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) (Option C): It happens when a branch of the central retinal artery becomes blocked, causing a localized area of retinal ischemia. The affected retinal region appears pale and may show retinal hemorrhages.

Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) (Option D): It occurs when a branch of the central retinal vein is obstructed, leading to impaired venous drainage in a specific retinal area. This condition can result in retinal hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular edema.

Reference:

Retinal Vascularization and OCT-Angiography Interpretation - EyeWikihttps://eyewiki.org/Retinal_Vascularization_and_OCT-Angiography_Interpretation

Central Retinal Vein Occlusion - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelfhttps://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525985/

question_text: Eales disease is
explanation:
Eales disease is an idiopathic occlusive peripheral periphlebitis. It is rare in Caucasians but is an important cause of visual morbidity in young males from the Indian subcontinent. It is characterized by three overlapping stages: inflammatory, occlusive and retinal neovascular, and is diagnosed principally by clinical examination. The visual prognosis is good in the majority of cases. Tubercular protein hypersensitivity may be important in the aetiology, but evidence is conflicting; some patients may have tubercular vasculitis. Diagnosis

  • Symptoms. Floaters or sudden visual reduction due to vitreous haemorrhage.
  • Systemic neurological features have been reported.
  • Mild anterior uveitis is often present.
  • Fundus. The condition is typically bilateral, though often asymmetrical.
  • Peripheral periphlebitis sheathing, superficial retinal haemorrhages and sometimes cotton wool spots. Pigmented chorioretinal scars may be seen.
  • Branch retinal vein occlusion.
  • Peripheral capillary non-perfusion; microaneurysms, tortuosity, vascular shunts and neovascularization with recurrent vitreous haemorrhage may develop at the junction of perfused and non-perfused retina. Disc new vessels can sometimes develop. The vitreous haemorrhage tends to be limited and to absorb over weeks, but can persist in some cases.
  • Macular involvement with the same changes can occur but is rare; macular oedema can develop.

Treatment

  • Steroids. Periocular, systemic, topical, and intravitreal steroids seem to be helpful in the inflammatory stage.
  • Antitubercular treatment. This is strongly advocated by some authorities but is controversial. It may be considered in selected patients in combination with steroids, either to avoid reactivation of prior tubercular infection (e.g. strongly positive skin test, QuantiFERON®) or possibly when severe ocular inflammatory signs are present.
  • Scatter photocoagulation or cryotherapy of non-perfused retina to reduce the neovascular stimulus.
  • Intravitreal VEGF inhibitors may be helpful but research is ongoing.
  • Vitrectomy for persistent vitreous haemorrhage, tractional detachment and macular epiretinal membrane.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/569-571

question_text: A 20-year-old man reports gradually worsening vision over the past three years. On fundus examination, the fovea shows a characteristic "beaten bronze" appearance. Both ERG and EOG are reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Stargardt disease is an inherited recessive macular dystrophy affecting the central retina. It typically begins in childhood or early adulthood and gradually causes central visual loss. In the advanced stage, the fundus develops a distinct "beaten bronze" appearance at the fovea, which is a hallmark feature.

  • Electrodiagnostic testing shows subnormal ERG and EOG, and fluorescein angiography classically reveals a "dark choroid" due to masking of background choroidal fluorescence. Over time, progressive loss of photoreceptors and RPE in the macula leads to further decline in central vision.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa (option B): Causes night blindness, peripheral visual field loss, arteriolar attenuation, bone-spicule pigmentation, and pale optic disc. ERG is markedly abnormal, but the macula does not show a "beaten-bronze" appearance.
  • Juvenile retinoschisis (option C): Affects boys (X-linked) and causes splitting of the retinal layers, particularly at the fovea. Fundus shows spoke-wheel pattern at the macula, not a beaten-bronze lesion. ERG classically shows selective reduction of the b-wave.
  • Leber congenital amaurosis (option D): A severe congenital retinal dystrophy presenting in infancy with profound vision loss. ERG is extinguished, and features include oculodigital reflex and nystagmus. The condition is not present in early adulthood and does not show a beaten-bronze macula.

question_text: A 40-year-old male patient, who works in an iron factory, presents to the clinic with complaints of visual disturbances. He reports that his vision has been gradually worsening and he has noticed a change in the color perception. On examination, the ophthalmologist observes the presence of iron deposits in the eye. What is the most likely ocular condition responsible for the iron deposits in the eye and the patient's visual disturbances?
explanation:
Explanation:

Siderosis bulbi results from an iron-containing intraocular foreign body (IOFB) that remains in the eye. Iron undergoes oxidation and induces toxic reactions in ocular tissues, damaging enzymes and cells. This leads to progressive iron deposition in ocular structures, causing color vision defects, cataracts, pigmentary retinal changes, and ultimately vision loss.

In this case, the patient's occupational exposure to iron (factory worker) and findings of iron deposition in the eye confirm siderosis bulbi as the correct diagnosis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hemochromatosis (Option B ruled out): A systemic iron overload disorder affecting liver, pancreas, and skin. It does not cause direct intraocular iron deposition as in siderosis bulbi.

Retinitis pigmentosa (Option C ruled out): A hereditary retinal dystrophy with progressive night blindness and peripheral vision loss. No iron deposition is seen.

Age-related macular degeneration (Option D ruled out): A degenerative disease of the macula causing central vision loss in older individuals. It is not related to iron exposure or deposits.

Key takeaway: Siderosis Bulbi vs Chalcosis

  • Siderosis bulbi (Iron foreign body):
    Iron binds cellular proteins → widespread degeneration.
  • Chalcosis (Copper foreign body):
    Copper deposits under membranes without protein binding →
    • Kayser-Fleischer ring (cornea)
    • Sunflower cataract (lens)
    • Golden plaques (retina)

Reference:

Siderosis Bulbi-NIH

question_text: Which finding best characterizes severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
option_c: Haemorrhagic component Intraretinal hemorrhages, venous beading, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities
explanation:
Explanation

Severe NPDR is defined by progressively worsening retinal ischemia. The hallmark features include:

  • Diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants
  • Venous beading in ≥2 quadrants
  • Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in ≥1 quadrant
  • These changes indicate significant retinal hypoxia and a high likelihood of progression to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), making close monitoring or treatment necessary.
  • · Vitreous hemorrhage with a subhyaloid (Option A): A subhyaloid or vitreous hemorrhage indicates bleeding into the vitreous cavity and is characteristic of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) due to rupture of fragile neovascular vessels. It is not a feature of NPDR.
  • · Tractional retinal detachment (Option B): Tractional RD occurs when fibrovascular tissue from neovascularization contracts and pulls the retina anteriorly. This is a late complication of PDR, not NPDR.
  • · Early retinal neovascularization (Option D): Neovascularization of the disc or elsewhere marks the transition from NPDR to proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Therefore, it is not a defining feature of severe NPDR.

question_text: Which of the Parameters is Decreased in Retinitis Pigmentosa?
explanation:
Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a crucial omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid found in the photoreceptor membranes of the retina, particularly in rod cells. It plays a vital role in retinal function and phototransduction. In retinitis pigmentosa (RP), there is a significant decrease in DHA levels, leading to progressive photoreceptor degenerationand abnormal electroretinographic (ERG) responses.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • A. Arachidonic Acid: A polyunsaturated omega-6 fatty acid involved in inflammatory pathways and prostaglandin synthesis. It is not significantly decreased in retinitis pigmentosa.
  • B. Trielonic Acid: This is not a commonly recognized fatty acid in relation to retinal function.
  • C. Thromboxane: A lipid mediator involved in platelet aggregation and vascular function, but it has no direct link to retinal degeneration in RP.

Key Takeaway:

Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is essential for retinal photoreceptor function, and its deficiency in retinitis pigmentosa contributes to progressive vision loss.

question_text: Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon is seen in which disorder
explanation:
Oguchi’s disease is an autosomal recessive form of congenital stationary night blindness and is caused by a disruption in the steps of inactivation of rod phototransduction. Patients with this disease often complain of static nyctalopia since childhood and a preservation of vision in bright light. Rhodopsin kinase (GRK1) and Arrestin (SAG) are two genes which act in sequence to deactivate rhodopsin to stop the phototransduction cascade.

Patients frequently claim improvement of light sensitivities when they remain for some time in a darkened environment.

On examination patients have normal visual fields but the fundi have a diffuse or patchy, silver-gray or golden-yellow metallic sheen and the retinal vessels stand out in relief against the background.

A prolonged dark adaptation of three hours or more, leads to disappearance of this unusual discoloration and the appearance of a normal reddish appearance. This is known as the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomena and is thought to be caused by the overstimulation of rod cells.

Reference: kanski 9/e chapter 15 pg. 631

question_text: A 75 year old male presents with gradual painless decrease of vision since many years. he is a smoker, hypertensive and diabetic since many years. his retina shows this picture. What is the treatment you would advice
explanation:
This is a case of dry ARMD with geographical atrophy i.e last stage of dry ARMD.

AGE RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION( ARMD)

MC cause of blindness in western world.

Etiopathogenesis -

Risk factors: Age > 50 years, hypertension, Smoking, high fat intake, Blue light exposure

Etiopathogenesis: Sheet-like deposits called basal laminar deposits, drusen (PAS positive acellular) develop between RPE and Bruch’s membrane. In normal ageing also changes occur like decreased choroidal blood flow, lumen diameter.

Age-related drusen, however, are biochemically distinct from drusen associated with ARMD. Large, confluent, or soft drusen are more likely to be a marker of ARMD than normal aging

STAGES : DRY AND WET

DRY AMD (90 %)

DRY further divided into early, intermediate, late (Geographical atrophy)

Early ARMD - Numerous small (<63 microns, “hard”) or intermediate (≥63 microns but <125 microns, “soft”) drusen

Intermediate ARMD: extensive drusen of small or intermediate size, or any drusen of large size (≥125 microns)

Late AMRD - Geographical atrophy: A large delineated area of severe chorioretinal atrophy with progressive and irreversible loss of retinal cells and marked decrease in vision. No treatment can be done

WET AMD aka Neovascular ARMD.

CNVM are new vessels from the choriocapillaris through a break in the outer aspect of Bruch’s membrane into the sub-RPE space. They are accompanied by fibroblasts, disrupts the normal architecture of the choriocapillaris, Bruch’s membrane and RPE.

Disciform scar: Photoreceptors and remaining outer retina are also damaged

Picture of CNVM

Within the sub RPE, the CNV can leak fluid and blood and may be accompanied by a serous or haemorrhagic detachment of the RPE.

Symptoms: Decreased visual acuity, Scotoma, metamorphopsia, micropsia

Reference: parson's 22/e section IV, chapter 20. pg 326-327. ARMD

question_text: A 72-year-old patient with a history of cataract surgery and diabetes presents with decreased vision one month postoperatively. Fundus examination shows a honeycomb or flower-petal pattern at the macula. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of decreased vision after cataract surgery, combined with the characteristic "flower-petal" or honeycomb appearance on fundus examination, strongly suggests cystoid macular oedema (CME).

Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME):

Causes:

  • Post-surgical: Cataract surgery, retinal detachment repair, ocular laser therapy, and certain topical medications.
  • Retinal vascular disorders: Diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusions, retinal telangiectasia, hypertensive retinopathy.
  • Intraocular inflammation: Pars planitis, uveitis.
  • Vitreomacular traction: Epiretinal membrane (ERM) or vitreomacular traction (VMT).
  • Systemic diseases: Leukaemia, chronic kidney disease, multiple myeloma.
  • Other: Niacin toxicity, prostaglandin analogues.

Clinical Features:

  • Gradual visual loss, sometimes mild initially.
  • Fundus: Loss of foveal contour, retinal thickening, yellow foveal spot, cystoid spaces creating a honeycomb/flower-petal pattern.
  • Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Leakage with a flower-petal pattern in late frames.
  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Cystoid spaces, foveal thickening, loss of foveal depression.

Complications:

  • Long-standing CME may lead to lamellar macular hole formation.

Treatment:

  • Address underlying cause: Anti-VEGF injections or photocoagulation for diabetic CME; discontinue causative drugs.
  • Topical NSAIDs: Ketorolac, diclofenac, etc.
  • Steroids: Topical or systemic, in established cases.
  • Systemic CAIs: Oral acetazolamide in select cases (e.g., retinitis pigmentosa).

Explanation for Other Options:

Central serous retinopathy (Option B): Shows "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage on FFA and neurosensory retinal detachment on OCT; does not form cystoid spaces.

Retinal detachment (Option C): Separation of neurosensory retina from RPE; vision loss is usually acute and associated with visual field defects or curtain-like symptoms, not honeycomb macular oedema.

Diabetic retinopathy (Option D): Causes diffuse retinal thickening, microaneurysms, haemorrhages, and exudates but lacks the cystoid/focal honeycomb pattern typical of CME.

question_text: What should be the subsequent course of action in managing a diabetic patient who has a visual acuity of 6/9 in one eye and further investigations reveal preretinal hemorrhages with neovascularization at the optic disc?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's features-visual acuity of 6/9, preretinal hemorrhages, and optic disc neovascularization-are characteristic of proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which is an advanced stage of diabetic eye disease.
  • In PDR, retinal ischemia triggers abnormal growth of fragile new blood vessels. These vessels are prone to rupture, resulting in preretinal hemorrhage and sometimes tractional retinal detachment.
  • The first-line therapy is pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP). This laser procedure destroys ischemic retinal tissue, lowering the drive for neovascularization.
  • The overall goal of PRP is to halt disease progression, reduce the risk of further bleeding, and protect remaining vision.

Abbreviated ETDRS Classification of Diabetic Retinopathy

  • Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR):
    • No retinopathy: review annually (12 months).
    • Very mild NPDR: only microaneurysms present; most patients can be reviewed in 12 months.
    • Mild NPDR: includes microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton-wool spots, but not reaching moderate NPDR criteria. No IRMA or marked venous beading. Follow-up in 6-12 months depending on severity, systemic control, and patient factors.
    • Moderate NPDR: shows marked retinal hemorrhages in 1-3 quadrants or mild IRMA. Venous beading may be limited to one quadrant. Cotton-wool spots often present. Review around 6 months.
    • Severe NPDR: defined by the 4-2-1 rule - severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous beading in ≥2 quadrants, or moderate IRMA in ≥1 quadrant. Review in 4 months.
    • Very severe NPDR: presence of two or more of the above criteria. Review every 2-3 months.
  • Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR):
    • Mild to moderate PDR: neovascularization at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE), but not sufficient for high-risk features. Treatment is individualized based on severity, systemic stability, and compliance with follow-up. If not treated, review within 2 months.
    • High-risk PDR: NVD >1/3-disc area, or any NVD with vitreous haemorrhage, or NVE >1/2-disc area with vitreous haemorrhage. Requires urgent intervention, ideally immediate treatment, especially in symptomatic patients with clear retinal view.
    • Advanced diabetic eye disease: characterized by tractional retinal detachment, persistent vitreous haemorrhage, or neovascular glaucoma. Requires vitreoretinal surgery along with laser treatment.
  • Management of PDR:
    • Pan-retinal Photocoagulation (PRP):
      • Aims to reduce metabolic demand by ablating ischemic retina, suppressing Vaso proliferative factor release, and converting hypoxic tissue into inert scars.
      • Commonly performed using Argon, frequency-doubled YAG, or diode lasers.
      • Treatment usually begins with the inferior quadrant.
      • The central macular area is preserved, leaving a circular zone of ~2.5 disc diameters around the fovea untouched.
      • Typically requires 2000-3000 laser burns, delivered in 2-4 sessions.
    • Anti-VEGF therapy: agents such as bevacizumab, ranibizumab, or aflibercept help control neovascularization.
    • Vitreoretinal surgery: indicated for tractional retinal detachment or persistent vitreous haemorrhage not resolving with laser or anti-VEGF.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • Intravitreal corticosteroids (Option B): Useful for diabetic macular Edema, but they do not address ischemia or regress neovascularization. They are not the treatment of choice for PDR with optic disc new vessels.
  • Focal laser photocoagulation (Option C): This is used for localized leakage in clinically significant macular Edema, not for diffuse ischemia or optic disc neovascularization.
  • Vitrectomy (Option D): Reserved for advanced disease, particularly dense non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment. It is not the initial step when active proliferative retinopathy is identified with preserved vision.

Key Takeaway:
The appearance of optic disc neovascularization in diabetic retinopathy marks progression to the proliferative stage, which carries a high risk of vision-threatening complications. The standard and most effective treatment is pan retinal photocoagulation, aimed at reducing VEGF stimulus and preventing severe sequelae.

question_text: In Fundus Fluorescein Angiography, how do microaneurysms appear?
option_d: Hyperfluorescent branching-like structure in the vessel
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Microaneurysms are the earliest clinically detectable lesions in diabetic retinopathy and appear as small, round dilations of retinal capillaries.
  • In Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA), they exhibit hyperfluorescence due to leakage of fluorescein dye from these abnormal capillaries.
  • Microaneurysms initially appear as hyperfluorescent dots in early-phase FFA due to accumulation of fluorescein dye.
  • In later phases, leakage may lead to diffuse hyperfluorescence in severe cases.

Fundus Fluorescein Angiography

Principle: Based on the detection of fluorescent light emitted by fluorescein dye in circulation.

  • Absorption & Emission Wavelengths:
    • Irradiating light: 420-490 nm.
    • Emitted fluorescence: 510-530 nm.
  • Retinal pigments and red blood cells can absorb fluorescent light, masking deeper structures. Pigment migration allows visibility of deeper layers.

Diagnostic uses

  • Diabetic Retinopathy: Reveals neovascularization, and assesses vascular tree integrity.
  • Fundus Disorders: Identifies depth of pathological involvement.
  • Optic Nerve Pathologies: Useful in detecting optic nerve issues such as papilloedema.
  • Neovascularization of Iris: Detects leakage from iris vessels, an early sign of rubeosis.

Explanation of other options:

Hypofluorescent dots (Option A): Microaneurysms are not hypofluorescent. Hypofluorescent lesions generally indicate blockages, such as hemorrhages, pigment deposits, or areas of vascular occlusion.

Hypofluorescent line (Option C): Hypofluorescent lines are seen in conditions like vascular occlusions. E.g., branch retinal artery occlusion.

Hyperfluorescent branching-like structure in the vessel (Option D): This pattern is seen in neovascularization, not microaneurysms.

Key Takeaways:

Abnormalities Detected by Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA)

question_text: Which of the following is a cause of bilateral sudden painless loss of vision?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Diabetic retinopathy often develops in stages, with initial mild symptoms that may progress to sudden vision loss due to complications.
  • Bilateral sudden painless loss of vision can be caused by diabetic retinopathy, particularly in its proliferative form, where there is a sudden onset of vision loss due macular edema, or retinal detachment.
  • Diabetic retinopathy affects both eyes and can lead to significant vision impairment if left untreated.

Clinical Features of Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR):

  • Includes all features of preproliferative diabetic retinopathy or severe NPDR: Multiple retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, vascular loops, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs), and large areas of capillary nonperfusion along with neovascularization.
  • Neovascularization
    • Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD): Arises within 1 disc diameter of the optic nerve from the optic nerve head.
    • Neovascularization Elsewhere (NVE): Arises more than 1 disc diameter from the optic nerve, along the large vessels.
    • Appears adjacent to areas of capillary closure and the accompanying fibrous tissue varies in extent.
    • Fluorescein angiography (FA): Irregular expanding hyperfluorescence.
    • Severe Vision Loss: Result in vision as poor as hand movements or worse due to severe vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment.
  • Fibrovascular Tissue Formation:
    • Formed due to condensation of connective tissue around the new vessels.
    • Lie flat on the retina or attach to the posterior vitreous face.
    • Can lead to vitreous traction, retinal separation, and blood vessel tearing.
    • The most common cause of vitreous hemorrhage in adults.
  • Rubeosis Iridis: Neovascularization of iris.
  • Neovascular glaucoma: Occurs due neovascularization of anterior segment angle.

Explanation of other options:

Acute congestive glaucoma (Option A): Acute congestive glaucoma is typically associated with painful loss of vision and is more often unilateral. The condition involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure, causing symptoms such as severe eye pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Keratoconus (Option C): Keratoconus can lead to progressive vision loss due to the distortion of the cornea, but it usually presents gradually, not suddenly, and typically affects one eye more than the other initially.

Iridocyclitis (Option D): Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis) is usually associated with pain, photophobia, and redness in the affected eye. It does not cause sudden, painless loss of vision in both eyes.

Myelinated retinal nerve fibres (MRNF) are rare congenital anomalies that appear as grey-white opaque lesions on the retina with feathery edges that obscure retina details. They may be located on the disc or elsewhere on the retina.

Retinal ganglion cell myelination proceeds from the lateral geniculate nucleus anteriorly toward the globe. Myelination along the visual pathway is first seen in the eighth month of gestation, and typically reaches the posterior globe around the time of birth with virtually all fibers reaching complete myelination by age 7 months. question_text: A 45 year old female presented with symptoms of diminished vision since five years, especially at night. Fundus examination revealed pale waxy optic disc, arteriolar attenuation and bony spicules. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Fundus changes in retinitis pigmentosa: BAP pneumonic

  • B - BONY SPICULES: Retinal pigmentary changes-These are typically perivascular (around veins) and jet black spots resembling bone corpuscles in shape. lnitially, these changes are found in the equatorial region only and later spread both anteriorly and posteriorly.
  • A - Attenuated vessels: Retinal arterioles are attenuated (narrowed) and may become thread-like in late stages.
  • P - Pale disc
  • Thinning and atrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is seen in mid and far peripheral retina with relative sparing of RPE at the macula.
  • Optic disc becomes pale and waxy in later stages and ultimately consecutive optic atrophy occurs.
  • Other associated changes which may be seen are colloid bodies, choroidal sclerosis, cystoid macular oedema, atrophic or cellophane maculopathy.

question_text: This classical fundus picture is seen in case of
explanation:
This picture is of dark choroid seen classically in this case.

Stargardt disease is the most common juvenile macular dystrophy and a frequent heritable cause of central visual dysfunction in young patients.

Stargardt disease is most commonly caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene and is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion.

The ABCA4 gene is an ATP-binding cassette transmembrane protein expressed by rod outer segments and is involved in the transport of all-trans-retinal. The mutations in ABCA4 in Stargardt disease result in the accumulation of all-transretinal in the photoreceptors as well as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

The “dark” or “silent choroid” sign results from blockage of early choroidal fluorescence by lipofuscin deposition within the RPE.

question_text: A 15 year old boy presents with history of tennis ball injury to the left eye. On examination a Red spot is seen on macula. The most likely diagnosis is

Commotio retinae

Commotio retinae is caused by concussion of the sensory retina resulting in cloudy swelling that gives the involved area a grey appearance. It most frequently affects the temporal fundus. If the macula is involved, a 'cherry-red spot' may be seen at the fovea. Severe involvement may be associated with intraretinal haemorrhage that can involve the macula. question_text: A 45-year-old woman reports gradually worsening vision over the past five years, especially difficulty seeing in dim light. Fundus examination shows a pale, waxy optic disc, narrowing of retinal arterioles, and bone-spicule-like pigment deposits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is characterised by a classic triad remembered as BAP:

  • B: Bone-spicule pigmentation: Jet-black pigment deposits clustered around retinal veins, starting in the mid-periphery.
  • A: Arteriolar attenuation: Retinal blood vessels become progressively narrow and thread-like.
  • P: Pale disc: The optic disc appears waxy or pale due to secondary optic atrophy.
  • Additional findings include peripheral RPE thinning, colloid bodies, choroidal sclerosis, and possible macular complications such as cystoid macular edema. The progressive involvement of rod photoreceptors explains the patient's night blindness.
  • Diabetic retinopathy (option A): Shows microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and neovascularisation-not bone spicules or attenuated arterioles typical of RP.
  • Hypertensive retinopathy (option B): Characterised by arterial narrowing, AV nicking, cotton-wool spots, flame haemorrhages, and macular star, not the triad of bone-spicule pigmentation, pale disc, and vessel attenuation.
  • Stargardt's disease (option C): A macular dystrophy presenting with central vision loss and "beaten bronze" macula with yellowish flecks. It does not cause night blindness or peripheral bone-spicule pigmentation.

question_text: What is the most common cause of visual loss in patients with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy?
explanation:
Diabetic macular edema is the most common cause of visual loss in patients with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy. Vitreous hemorrhage and traction retinal detachment more typically are associated with proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Macular pigmentary disturbance may be a manifestation of macular edema, but not the primary cause of visual loss.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/521

question_text: A 50-year-old woman reports gradual decline in vision over the last few months. She is a known case of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and rheumatoid arthritis. Fundus and FFA images reveal a characteristic retinal lesion. Based on clinical history and imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient is suffering from Bull's eye maculopathy based on the clinical findings and

Fundus and FFA images.

  • Hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine can induce retinal toxicity because they accumulate in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and damage the photoreceptors and ganglion cells. Early retinal changes include subtle RPE mottling and loss of foveal reflex. With progression, a classic "bull's eye maculopathy" pattern appears, characterized by a central unaffected fovea surrounded by a ring of hypopigmentation, followed by a ring of hyperpigmentation.
  • Hydroxychloroquine toxicity may initially be asymptomatic, but later patients complain of color vision defects and paracentral scotomas. The retinal damage is irreversible, hence early recognition and drug discontinuation are essential.
  • Daily dosage and duration of therapy determine the risk of retinopathy. Toxicity risk remains low during the first five years if dose is maintained below 5.0 mg/kg/day (hydroxychloroquine) or <2.3 mg/kg/day (chloroquine). Other ocular side effects like corneal deposits and accommodation issues may occur but rarely cause visual loss.
  • Conditions that may also present with a bull's-eye macular pattern include cone dystrophy, Stargardt disease, clofazimine toxicity, Leber congenital amaurosis, ARMD, chronic macular hole, and inverse retinitis pigmentosa.

CME (Option A): Cystoid macular edema occurs due to accumulation of extracellular fluid in cyst-like spaces within the macula. On FFA, it shows the characteristic petaloid / flower-petal pattern of hyperfluorescence from perifoveal capillary leakage. OCT reveals multiple hyporeflective cystic spaces in the macula.

CSR (Option B): Central serous retinopathy is caused by focal leakage at the level of the RPE, resulting in serous detachment of the neurosensory retina. FFA shows inkblot or smoke-stack pattern of leakage. It commonly affects young or middle-aged individuals and steroid users.

ARMD (Option D): Age-related macular degeneration typically occurs in older patients and may present with drusen, RPE atrophy, geographic atrophy, or subretinal neovascular membrane depending on the type. It causes metamorphopsia and central visual loss.

question_text: Which of the following is a complication of diabetic retinopathy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Tractional retinal detachment is a known complication of diabetic retinopathy, arising from fibrovascular proliferation associated with proliferative disease.
  • Contraction of these neovascular membranes exerts traction on the retina, causing it to elevate and detach from the underlying layers, potentially leading to significant vision loss.

Major Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy

  • Macular edema
  • Vitreous hemorrhage
  • Retinal detachment
  • Neovascular glaucoma
  • Rubeosis iridis

Macular Edema

  • The most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is leakage from dilated capillaries.
  • Clinically significant macular edema (CSME):
    • Retinal thickening at the center of the macula.
    • Retinal thickening and/or adjacent hard exudates at or within 500 µ of the center of the macula.
    • An area of retinal thickening greater than or equal to one disc area, any part of which is within 1 disc diameter of the center of the macula
  • Types: Focal or Diffuse macular edema
  • Diagnosis:
    • Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: Loss of foveal reflex and macular thickening
    • Fluorescein Angiography: Identifies leakage and diagnoses ischemic maculopathy.

Management:

  • Anti-VEGF Therapy: Agents like bevacizumab, ranibizumab, or aflibercept are used to regress neovascularization and reduce macular edema. Laser photocoagulation is typically deferred for 6 months after starting anti-VEGF therapy.
  • Intravitreal Triamcinolone Acetonide: Used to reduce macular edema and improve visual acuity, particularly in patients unresponsive to anti-VEGF therapy.
  • Photocoagulation:
    • Focal Photocoagulation: Preferred for focal diabetic macular edema (DME) not involving the foveal center, using diode or argon laser burns.
    • Grid Photocoagulation: Applied in diffuse or recalcitrant DME unresponsive to anti-VEGF or steroids. Burns are placed over thickened macular areas, maintaining at least 500 µm distance from the foveola and optic disc.

Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH)

  • Seen as blood floating in the vitreous, occluding the view of the retina.
  • Secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is a cause of severe vision loss in diabetic patients.
  • In PDR, fibrovascular tissue lies flat on the retina or attaches to the posterior vitreous, leading to vitreous traction, retinal separation, and vessel rupture. This is the most common cause of VH in adults.

Retinal Detachment

  • PDR causes scars to form in the back of the eye.
  • When the scars pull the retina away from the back of the eye, it's called tractional retinal detachment.

Neovascular Glaucoma:

  • PDR causes abnormal blood vessels to grow out of the retina and block fluid from draining out of the eye, leading to neovascular glaucoma.
  • Can cause vision loss and blindness.

Rubeosis Iridis:

  • Neovascularization of iris, is when blood vessels develop on the anterior surface of the iris in response to retinal ischemia.
  • Prone to spontaneous hyphema as the blood vessels are fragile.
  • Treatment: Panretinal photocoagulation with or without intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF.

Explanation of other options:

Posterior staphyloma (Option A): Posterior staphyloma is associated with pathologic myopia, not diabetic retinopathy. It involves progressive thinning and outward bulging of the sclera, primarily in high myopia.

Retinoschisis (Option B): Retinoschisis refers to the splitting of the retinal layers, commonly seen in degenerative retinoschisis or X-linked retinoschisis, rather than as a complication of diabetic retinopathy.

Progressive myopia (Option D): Progressive myopia is associated with axial elongation of the eyeball and is not associated with diabetic retinopathy.

Key Takeaways:

Complications of Diabetic Retinopathy:

  • Macular Edema
  • Vitreous Hemorrhage
  • Retinal Detachment
  • Neovascular Glaucoma
  • Rubeosis Iridis

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Optic nerve head drusen is/ are correct?
explanation:
• Drusen of the optic disc occurs in families, is typically bilateral (70%) and is inherited as an irregular dominant trait.
  • The drusen bodies evolve slowly over many years showing increasing prominence with age.
  • The appearance of the disc may mimic that of papilloedema associated with visual defects, which may not correspond to the position of the drusen..
  • Drusen are often associated with rather small optic nerve heads, and are composed of calcified concentrically laminated globular aggregates.
  • They may form as a result of altered axoplasmic transport at the optic disc secondary to local obstructing factors.
  • Optic disc drusen may be associated with angioid streaks, sub retinal neovascular membranes, vitreous haemorrhage and retinitis pigmentosa.
  • Angiographically, the vessels of the optic nerve head are normal in pseudoneuritis and drusen.

Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: A patient with a prior history of cataract surgery presents with visual disturbances. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) reveals the following findings. Which syndrome is most likely associated with this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Irvine-Gass Syndrome, also known as cystoid macular edema (CME), is a condition commonly seen after cataract surgery.
  • The OCT finding typically shows loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening, which is indicative of this syndrome.

Cystoid Macular Edema (CME)

Etiology:

  • Ocular Treatment Complications: Post-surgery (e.g., cataract extraction, retinal detachment surgery), ocular laser therapy, and topical ocular medications.
  • Retinal Vascular Disorders: Diabetic retinopathy, central and branch retinal vein occlusion, retinal telangiectasia, and hypertensive retinopathy.
  • Intraocular Inflammations: Pars planitis, uveitis.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa.
  • Vitreomacular Traction: Associated with macular epiretinal membrane (ERM) and vitreomacular traction (VMT) syndrome.
  • Systemic Diseases: Includes leukemia, chronic renal failure, and multiple myeloma.
  • Miscellaneous Causes: niacin toxicity , PG analogues (risk factor for development of CME)

Clinical Features:

  • Visual Loss: Initial minimal to moderate vision loss, potentially leading to permanent vision decrease if persistent.
  • Ophthalmoscopy: Reveals loss of foveal contour, retinal thickening, a yellow spot at the fovea, and a "honeycomb appearance" of the macula.
  • Fluorescein Angiography: Shows leakage and dye accumulation in the macular region, with a "flower petal appearance" in late frames.
  • Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Demonstrates loss of foveal depression, cystoid spaces, and overall retinal thickening.

Complications:

  • Long-standing CME may result in a lamellar macular hole.

Treatment:

  • Addressing the Cause: Intravitreal anti-VEGF or photocoagulation for diabetic CME; discontinuing causative topical medications.
  • Topical NSAIDs: Such as ketorolac, diclofenac, or profenac, are effective in preventing and treating CME.
  • Topical/Systemic Steroids: Useful in established cases.
  • Systemic Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs): Oral acetazolamide may be beneficial, particularly in cases associated with retinitis pigmentosa.

Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (Option A): This involves high IOP and mild uveitis, but is not associated with macular edema as seen in Irvine-Gass Syndrome.

Central Serous Retinopathy (Option C): is characterized by "ink-blot" or "smoke-stack" leakage patterns on FFA, and neurosensory retinal and RPE detachment on OCT. CSR typically does not present with the cystoid pattern seen in CME.

Elschnig's Pearls (Option D): Clustered, vacuolated subcapsular epithelial cells along the posterior capsule.

question_text: Which is the best test to visualize all layers of the retina?
explanation:
Explanation:

Optical coherence tomography (OCT) allows in vivo visualization of the individual retinal layers.

This non-invasive, non-contact imaging technique uses low-coherence light waves to create high-resolution cross-sectional (tomographic) scans of both the anterior and posterior segments of the eye. The resulting images resemble an "in-vivo histologic section" of the retina and are captured in the near-infrared spectrum.

In cases such as central serous retinopathy, OCT demonstrates a neurosensory retinal detachment from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium, providing detailed structural information crucial for diagnosis and monitoring.

An OCT of central serous retinopathy showing neurosensory retinal detachment from the retinal pigment epithelium is given below.

Explanations for other Options:

Perimetry (Option A): Perimetry measures the visual field, helping to detect and map any defects or areas of vision loss.

Fluorescence angiography (Option C): Fluorescein angiography visualises the retinal and choroidal vasculature by tracking the circulation of intravenously injected fluorescein dye, enabling assessment of vascular and structural abnormalities in a variety of fundus disorders.

Ultrasound B-Scan (Option D): B-scan ocular ultrasound is employed to evaluate the posterior segment of the eye when the view is obscured by opaque media. It is also valuable for identifying and localising intraocular or orbital tumours and other space-occupying lesions.

question_text: What is the most likely cause of gradually worsening vision in both eyes of a 25-year-old male who has been on long-term low-dose oral steroid therapy for the past 10 years?
explanation:
Explanation:

The progressive vision loss in a 25-year-old male with a history of long-term low-dose oral steroid use is most likely due to the development of a cataract, specifically a posterior subcapsular cataract.

Toxic Cataract and Steroids:

  • Systemic steroids are known to cause posterior subcapsular cataracts, especially with prolonged use.
  • This type of cataract is more common in children, but adults with extended exposure are also at risk.

Other Causes of Posterior Subcapsular Cataract:

  • Galactosemia
  • Myotonic dystrophy
  • Blunt trauma
  • Complicated cataracts
  • Medications: Chloroquine, Busulfan
  • Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)

Mnemonic:

  • GTCS: Glaucoma by Topical steroids, Cataract by Systemic steroids

Anterior Subcapsular Cataract- Other Drug Causes:

  • Miotics, especially long-acting cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., echothiophate, demecarium bromide, DFP)
  • Other drugs: Amiodarone, Chlorpromazine, Busulfan, Gold, Allopurinol

Mnemonic: AACG

  • Atopic dermatitis (shield cataract)
  • Amiodarone
  • Chlorpromazine
  • Gold
  • AACG - Acute Angle Closure Glaucoma

Explanation for other options:

Glaucoma (Option B): Most often associated with topical steroids, not systemic ones.

Cystoid Macular Edema (Option C):Though possible with steroid use, it typically causes blurry central vision, distortion, and not classic progressive bilateral vision loss.

Retinal Detachment (Option D): Leads to sudden or rapidly progressive vision loss and doesn't match the slow, bilateral pattern described here.

question_text: Two months after developing a vitreous hemorrhage, a patient is found to have intraocular pressure of 50 mmHg. Khaki-colored cells are noted in the anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Ghost cells are red blood cells that have lost their intracellular hemoglobin and appear as small, khaki-colored cells. Ghost cells are less pliable than normal red blood cells and obstruct the trabecular meshwork, causing secondary intraocular pressure elevation, known as ghost-cell glaucoma. The cells develop within 1-3 months following a vitreous hemorrhage and gain access to the anterior chamber through a disruption of the hyaloid face.
  • Schwartz's syndrome is a rare secondary open-angle glaucoma that develops in the setting of a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in which photoreceptor outer segments migrate through a retinal break to the anterior chamber, where they impede aqueous outflow.
  • Phacolytic glaucoma is an inflammatory glaucoma caused by leakage of lens proteins through the capsule of a mature or hypermature cataract, resulting in obstruction of trabecular outflow. Glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome) is an inflammatory glaucoma characterized by recurrent attacks of mild anterior uveitis associated with marked intraocular pressure elevation. In the anterior chamber of Schwartz's syndrome, phacolytic glaucoma, and glaucomatocyclitic crisis are not khaki-colored, the cells that are seen are not khaki-colored.

Reference: AAO GLAUCOMA 133/134

question_text: Candle wax dripping type of vasculitis is a feature of
explanation:
Candle wax dripping is seen in severe sarcoid periphlebitis.

Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory disease of unknown etiology characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas. The disease most commonly affects the skin, lungs, lymph nodes and eyes but can affect virtually any organ.

The International Workshop on Ocular Sarcoidosis(IWOS), reporting in 2009, identified seven key signs in the diagnosis of intraocular sarcoidosis:

  • Mutton fat keratic precipitates(KPs) and/or small granulomatous KPs and/or iris nodules(Koeppe and/or Busacca).
  • Trabecular meshwork(TM) nodules and/or tent-shaped peripheral anterior synechiae.
  • Vitreous opacities: snowballs and/or strings of pearls
  • Multiple chorioretinal peripheral lesions(active and/or atrophic) - Multiple small pale-yellow infiltrates, sometimes with a punched-out appearance are the commonest; they are often most numerous inferiorly.
  • Nodular and/or segmental periphlebitis(± candle wax drippings) and/or retinal macroaneurysm in an inflamed eye.
    • Periphlebitis appears as yellowish or grey-white perivenous sheathing.
    • Perivenous exudates referred to as 'candle wax drippings'(en taches de bougie) are typical of severe sarcoid periphlebitis.
  • Optic disc nodule(s)/granuloma(s) and/or solitary choroidal nodule.
  • Bilaterality.

Other ocular manifestations include conjunctival nodules resembling those of follicular conjunctivitis, lacrimal gland infiltration and dry eye, eyelid skin nodules, orbital and scleral lesions. Complications are those typically seen in idiopathic uveitis, including cataract, glaucoma, posterior and peripheral anterior synechiae, band keratopathy, vitreous haemorrhage, maculopathy(cystoid macular oedema, epiretinal membrane, choroidal neovascularization), retinal detachment and phthisis.

Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 432.

question_text: Dalen Fuch nodules are seen in
explanation:
DF nodules are nodular clusters of epithelioid cells containing pigment lying between the RPE and Bruch's membrane

They are clinically seen as yellow-white lesions in the peripheral retina, which may extend towards the optic disc or even involve the posterior pole.

In SO - Anterior segment examination often reveals bilateral acute anterior uveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium. However, non-granulomatous reaction involving the anterior segment may also be noted. Lymphocytic infiltration of the iris may result in thickening and synechiae while variation in the intraocular pressure may be attributed to ciliary body shutdown or blockage of the trabecular meshwork.

Posterior segment examination often reveals multifocal serous retinal detachment, exudative retinal detachment, moderate-to-severe vitritis, choroiditis, thickening of the peripapillary choroid, and edema or hyperemia of the optic nerve in the acute phase. Yellow-white lesions beneath the level of RPE signify Dalen Fuch nodules that are not specific to SO

Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 12 uveitis pg. 448 sympathetic ophthalmitis

explanation:
it is formed as a result of the concussive force, which pushes the cornea and iris inward and causes the pupillary ruff to press against the anterior lens capsule, thereby leading to rupture of cells and deposition of pigments

Rupture of the cells causes deposition of a circular line of melanin pigment on the lens capsule. The ring of pigment is generally the same diameter as the undilated pupil.
