Explanation:

Macular opacity refers to a opacity in the lens or cornea that affects the passage of light and vision. In macular opacity, iris details are visible but blurred due to moderate corneal scarring.

Types of corneal opacity

Management of corneal opacity

  • Optical Iridectomy: Performed in cases of central macular or leucomatous opacities when vision improves with pupil dilation, allowing light to pass through a clear peripheral corneal area.
  • Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK): Utilizes an excimer laser to remove superficial opacities such as nebulae and improve corneal smoothness and vision.
  • Keratoplasty: Indicated for deeper or extensive corneal opacities to restore corneal clarity and vision.
  • Cosmetic Coloured Contact Lenses: Used to mask unsightly corneal scars in eyes without significant visual potential.
  • Corneal Tattooing: A cosmetic procedure reserved for dense, stable corneal scars in blind eyes to improve appearance.

Only pupillary margin is visible (Option B): Not a known description for any corneal opacity.

question_text: Bonnet sign is seen in
explanation:
Grading of hypertensive retinopathy:

Keith and Wegner(1939) have classified hypertensive retinopathy changes into following four grades:

  • Grade I: It consists of mild generalized arteriolar attenuation, particularly of small branches, with broadening of the arteriolar light reflex and vein concealment.
  • Grade II: It comprises marked generalized narrowing and focal attenuation of arterioles associated with deflection of veins at arteriovenous crossings (Salu's sign).
  • Grade III: This consists of Grade II changes plus copper-wiring of arterioles, banking of veins distal to arteriovenous crossings(Bonnet sign), tapering of veins on either side of the crossings(Gunn sign) and right-angle deflection of veins(Salu's sign). Flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates are also present.
  • Grade IV: This consists of all changes of Grade III plus silver-wiring of arterioles and papilledema.

Reference: A.K. Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 258.

question_text: What is the remnant of primary vitreous on posterior capsule of the lens known as?
explanation:
During the development of eye, a blood vessel runs between the optic nerve and the back of the lens, called hyaloid vessel.

  • This vessel carries nutrients and oxygen to the developing parts of anterior section of eye.
  • This hyaloid vessel along with surrounding embryonic material is called primary vitreous.
  • Hyaloid vessels and primary vitreous begin to involute in the second month of gestation giving way to the secondary vitreous (the vitreous humor).
  • Small remnants of the system are common findings in healthy adults, e.g. Bergmeister papilla (tuft of tissue at the optic disc) and Mittendorf dot (tag of tissue on the posterior capsule of lens).
  • However, extensive remnants of this "hyaloid vessel - primary vitreous" system are called persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous.

question_text: A patient presented with a breast lump. On biopsy, it came out to be breast cancer with ER positivity. Tamoxifen was given to the patient. Tamoxifen increases the risk of:
explanation:
The most common side effects of tamoxifen are:

Hot flashes, vaginal discharge, nausea, mood swings, fatigue, depression, hair thinning, constipation, loss of libido, dry skin.

Tamoxifen also may cause serious side effects, including:

Endometrial cancer: Tamoxifen may cause changes to the lining of your uterus, which can lead to endometrial cancer.

Blood clots: Tamoxifen is known to increase the risk of blood clots. Tell your doctor right away if you have: sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing that brings up blood pain, tenderness, or swelling in one or both of your legs. Stroke: Tamoxifen also can increase the risk of having a stroke.

Cataracts: Tamoxifen can increase the risk of needing cataract surgery, clouded, blurry, or dimmed vision trouble seeing at night sensitivity to light and glare a need for brighter light for reading and other activities seeing halos around lights

Liver problems: yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes dark or brown urine feeling very tired loss of appetite pain on the upper right side of the abdomen bleeding or bruising more easily than normal

question_text: Which virus has following pathophysiology and causes microcephaly in fetus?
explanation:
Zika virus infection during pregnancy can cause infants to be born with microcephaly and other congenital malformations as well as preterm birth and miscarriage. Zika virus infection is associated with Guillain- Barré syndrome, neuropathy and myelitis in adults and children. Zika infection during pregnancy causes a birth defect called microcephaly and other brain problems. It also may be linked to other serious problems for a baby.

B. Rubella Virus (German Measles)

  • Teratogenic Effects: Rubella is highly teratogenic and can cause Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS), which includes:
    • Heart Defects: Patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery stenosis.
    • Eye Abnormalities: Cataracts, retinopathy, and glaucoma.
    • Hearing Loss: Often the most common defect.
    • Neurodevelopmental Defects: Intellectual disabilities, microcephaly, and behavioral disorders.
    • Others: Hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura, growth retardation.
  • Highest Risk Period: Infection during the first 12 weeks is associated with the highest risk of severe congenital defects. Risk decreases but persists in the second trimester.

C. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

  • Teratogenic Effects: CMV is the most common congenital viral infection and can lead to:
    • Sensorineural Hearing Loss: Often progressive and bilateral.
    • Neurodevelopmental Issues: Intellectual disability, microcephaly, and seizures.
    • Vision Problems: Chorioretinitis, optic nerve atrophy.
    • Growth Restriction: Low birth weight and small for gestational age.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly, Thrombocytopenia, Jaundice: Symptoms that may indicate congenital CMV at birth.
  • Highest Risk Period: Primary maternal CMV infection in the first and second trimesters poses the highest risk for fetal abnormalities. Recurrent infections tend to be less severe.

D. Parvovirus B19

  • Teratogenic Effects: Parvovirus B19 primarily affects fetal red blood cells, which can lead to:
    • Fetal Anemia: Can be severe and lead to hydrops fetalis, a potentially fatal condition marked by fluid accumulation in fetal compartments.
    • Heart Failure: Due to the anemia-induced increased cardiac workload.
    • Miscarriage and Stillbirth: High risk, particularly with infection during the first 20 weeks.
  • Highest Risk Period: Infection during the first half of pregnancy poses the highest risk of adverse effects; later infections may still cause complications but with reduced risk.

question_text: A female patient with postpartum hemorrhage has received oxytocin and ergometrine, but bleeding persists. Which prostaglandin derivative is appropriate to control the ongoing hemorrhage?
explanation:
Explanation :

Carboprost Tromethamine is a prostaglandin F2α analogue indicated for refractory postpartum hemorrhage after oxytocin and ergometrine. It stimulates strong tetanic uterine contractions, effectively controlling bleeding that persists despite first- and second-line therapy.

Dosage: 250 µg IM, repeatable every 15-90 min (maximum 8 doses)

Side Effects:

  • Diarrhea, vomiting, fever, flushing
  • Tachycardia, pulmonary constriction

Contraindications:

  • Asthma
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Severe renal, hepatic, or cardiac disease
  • Suspected amniotic fluid embolism

Uterotonic Agents for PPH Management

First-Line Agent:
Oxytocin

  • WHO recommended first-line prophylaxis for PPH
  • Dosage:20 units in 1000 mL crystalloid IV at 10 mL/min (200 mU/min)
  • IM administration alternative if IV access unavailable
  • Avoid undiluted IV bolus (risk of hypotension, arrhythmias)
  • Indicated for initiation or ongoing uterine atony

Second-Line Agents:
Ergot Alkaloids (Ergonovine / Methylergonovine - Methergine)

  • Induce rapid tetanic uterine contractions (~45 min)
  • Dosage:2 mg IM, repeatable every 2-4 h
  • Contraindications:Hypertension, preeclampsia, concomitant HIV protease inhibitors

Prostaglandins:

  • Carboprost:Effective in refractory PPH (see above)
  • Misoprostol (Prostaglandin E1 analogue):600-1000 µg rectally, orally, or sublingually; mainly prophylactic, limited role in treatment
  • Dinoprostone (Prostaglandin E2):20 mg rectally/vaginally every 2 h; hypotension risk; rarely used for PPH
  • Latanoprost:Ophthalmic prostaglandin F2α analogue; no role in PPH management

Explanation of Other Options:

Dinoprostone (Option A):Prostaglandin E2 derivative, mainly used for labor induction; hypotension risk limits its use in PPH.

Misoprostol (Option B): Prostaglandin E1 analogue; used prophylactically or for prevention of PPH but less effective for treatment after oxytocin and ergometrine.

Latanoprost (Option C): Prostaglandin F2α analogue designed for ophthalmic use (glaucoma); not used in PPH.

question_text: What substance is responsible for the development of a diabetic cataract in a 68-year-old female patient, which has been present for 3 months?
explanation:
Explanation:

In diabetic patients, the accumulation of sorbitol in the lens is the major cause of diabetic cataract formation. This process is mediated by the polyol pathway, where:

  • Glucose → (aldose reductase) → Sorbitol
  • Sorbitol is poorly diffusible across the lens capsule, leading to osmotic imbalance, swelling of lens fibers, and eventual opacification.

Glucose Metabolism in the Lens:

  • Glycolytic pathway: ~80% of glucose is metabolized anaerobically.
  • Pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt): ~15% of glucose is metabolized here.
  • Krebs' cycle: Only a small proportion enters oxidative metabolism.
  • Sorbitol pathway: Normally minor, but in diabetes and galactosemia, excess glucose (or galactose) is shunted here. In diabetes, sorbitol builds up and produces osmotic stress → cataract formation.

Explanation of Other Options:

Glucose (Option A): Although glucose is involved in cataract formation, it is not directly responsible for the development of diabetic cataracts. In the lens, glucose is metabolized via several pathways, but it is the conversion of glucose to sorbitol (via the polyol pathway) that leads to osmotic stress and cataract formation in diabetes.

Fructose (Option B): Fructose does not significantly contribute to diabetic cataracts. While fructose is metabolized in the body, it is not the primary substance implicated in lens opacity in diabetic patients. The key factor in diabetic cataracts is sorbitol accumulation.

Lactose + Glucose (Option C): Lactose is not involved in the formation of diabetic cataracts. Although glucose plays a role in cataract formation, lactose is more relevant in galactosemic cataracts and not in diabetes-induced cataracts.

question_text: If the numerical aperture of objective lens is increased, what is the change in the image observed?
explanation:
In optics, the numerical aperture (NA) of an optical system is a dimensionless number that characterizes the range of angles over which the system can accept or emit light. By incorporating index of refraction in its definition, NA has the property that it is constant for a beam as it goes from one material to another, provided there is no refractive power at the interface. The exact definition of the term varies slightly between different areas of optics. Numerical aperture is commonly used in microscopy to describe the acceptance cone of an objective (and hence its light-gathering ability and resolution), and in fiber optics, in which it describes the range of angles within which light that is incident on the fiber will be transmitted along it.

In microscopy, NA is important because it indicates the resolving power of a lens. The size of the finest detail that can be resolved (the resolution) is proportional to λ/2NA, where λ is the wavelength of the light. A lens with a larger numerical aperture will be able to visualize finer details than a lens with a smaller numerical aperture. Assuming quality (diffraction-limited) optics, lenses with larger numerical apertures collect more light and will generally provide a brighter image, but will provide shallower depth of field.

Numerical aperture is used to define the "pit size" in optical disc formats.

Increasing the magnification and the numerical aperture of the objective reduces the working distance, i.e. the distance between front lens and specimen.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

Option A: Increased magnification - While NA is related to image clarity, magnification depends more on focal length and optical design, not just NA.

Option B: Increased contrast - Contrast is influenced by staining, illumination, and optical coatings rather than NA.

Option D: Increased field - A higher NA typically reduces the depth of field and field of view instead of increasing it.

Key Takeaways:

  • Higher NA improves resolution by capturing finer details.
  • It does not significantly affect magnification, contrast, or field of view.
  • Increased NA also reduces working distance and depth of field.

Reference: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_aperture

question_text: Angle subtended by 6/6 letter in Snellen's chart from a distance of 6 meters?
explanation:
The normal Snellen chart is printed with eleven lines of block letters. The first line consists of one very large letter, which may be one of several letters, for example E, H, or N. Subsequent rows have increasing numbers of letters that decrease in size. A person taking the test covers one eye from 6 metres or 20 feet away, and reads aloud the letters of each row, beginning at the top. The smallest row that can be read accurately indicates the visual acuity in that specific eye. The symbols on an acuity chart are formally known as "optotypes".

Variation of Snellen chart with another letter sequence. Australia, 1946

In the case of the traditional Snellen chart, the optotypes have the appearance of block letters, and are intended to be seen and read as letters. They are not, however, letters from any ordinary typographer's font. They have a particular, simple geometry in which:

the thickness of the lines equals the thickness of the white spaces between lines and the thickness of the gap in the letter "C"

the height and width of the optotype (letter) is five times the thickness of the line.

Only the nine letters C, D, E, F, L, O, P, T, Z are used in the common Snellen chart. The perception of five out of six letters (or similar ratio) is judged to be the Snellen fraction. Wall-mounted Snellen charts are inexpensive and are sometimes used for approximate assessment of vision, e.g. in a primary-care physician's office. Whenever acuity must be assessed carefully (as in an eye doctor's examination), or where there is a possibility that the examinee might attempt to deceive the examiner (as in a motor vehicle license office), equipment is used that can present the letters in a variety of randomized patterns. BS 4274-1:1968 (British Standards Institution) "Specification for test charts for determining distance visual acuity" was replaced by BS 4274-1:2003 "Test charts for clinical determination of distance visual acuity - Specification". It states that "the luminance of the presentation shall be uniform and not less than 120 cd/m2. Any variation across the test chart shall not exceed 20%." According to BS 4274-1:2003 only the letters C, D, E, F, H, K, N, P, R, U, V, and Z should be used for the testing of vision based upon equal legibility of the letters

Snellen defined "standard vision" as the ability to recognize one of his optotypes when it subtended 5 minutes of arc. Thus the optotype can only be recognized if the person viewing it can discriminate a spatial pattern separated by a visual angle of one minute of arc.

Outside the United States, the standard chart distance is 6 metres (20 ft), and normal acuity is designated "6/6". Other acuities are expressed as ratios with a numerator of 6. Some clinics do not have 6-metre eye lanes available, and either a half-size chart subtending the same angles at 3 metres (9.8 ft), or a reversed chart projected and viewed by a mirror is used to achieve the correct sized letters.

In the most familiar acuity test, a Snellen chart is placed at a standard distance: 6 metres. At this distance, the symbols on the line representing "normal" acuity subtend an angle of five minutes of arc, and the thickness of the lines and of the spaces between the lines subtends one minute of arc. This line, designated 6/6 (or 20/20), is the smallest line that a person with normal acuity can read at a distance of 6 metres. This definition is arbitrary, since human eyes typically have higher acuity, as Tscherning writes, "We have found also that the best eyes have a visual acuity which approaches 2, and we can be almost certain that if, with a good illumination, the acuity is only equal to 1, the eye presents defects sufficiently pronounced to be easily established."

Three lines above, the letters have twice the height of those letters on the 6/6 (or 20/20 in the US) line. If this is the smallest line a person can read, the person's acuity is "6/12" ("20/40"), meaning that this person needs to approach to a distance of 6 metres (20 ft) to read letters that a person with normal acuity could read at 12 metres (39 ft). In an even more approximate manner, this person could be said to have "half" the normal acuity of 6/6.

At exactly 6 metre's distance from the patient, the letters on the 6/6 line shall subtend 5 minutes of arc (such that the individual limbs of the letters subtend 1 minute of arc), which means that the chart should be sized such that these letters are 8.73 mm tall and the topmost (6/60) "E" should be 87.3 mm tall. Putting it another way, the eye should be at a distance 68.76 times the height of the top (6/60) letter

Acuity charts are used during many kinds of vision examinations, such as "refracting" the eye to determine the best eyeglass prescription.

The largest letter on an eye chart often represents an acuity of 6/60 (20/200), the value that is considered "legally blind" in the US. Many individuals with high myopia cannot read the large E without glasses, but can read the 6/6 (20/20) line or 6/4.5 (20/15) line with glasses. By contrast, legally blind individuals have a visual acuity of 6/60 (20/200) or less when using the best corrective lens.

A 75 year old female patient reports to OPD with sudden loss of vision in one eye. Visual acuity: Cf 3 mts (affected eye)/ 6/12 (non-affected eye).

question_text: A 70-year-old patient, previously reliant on reading glasses for presbyopia, now reports being able to read the newspaper comfortably without them. What is the most likely explanation for this change?
explanation:
Explanation:

Myopia (shortsightedness) is a refractive error where parallel light rays from distant objects focus in front of the retina when accommodation is relaxed.

Index Myopia:

  • Occurs in older adults due to age-related changes in the crystalline lens.
  • The refractive index of the lens increases, shifting the focal point forward and improving near vision.
  • This explains why the patient, previously using presbyopia glasses, can now read without them.

Clinical Features of Index Myopia:

  • Asthenopic symptoms (eye strain)
  • Squinting or half-closing eyes to see clearly
  • Prominent eyeballs and slightly sluggish pupils
  • Slightly deeper anterior chamber
  • Fundusis usually normal; occasionally, a temporal myopic crescent

Management:

  • Prescription of appropriate concave lenses
  • Surgical correction if needed

Explanation of Other Options:

Index hypermetropia (Option B): Lens becomes more farsighted, making near vision worse. This would not explain the patient’s improved reading ability.

Presbyopia (Option C): Normal age-related loss of accommodation causing difficulty with near tasks. Since the patient’s near vision improved, presbyopia alone cannot explain the findings.

None of the above (Option D): Incorrect because index myopia provides a plausible mechanism for the observed improvement in near vision.

Reference:

Defining and Classifying Myopia

explanation:
AMBLYOPIA

  • Amblyopia is a unilateral or bilateral reduction of best corrected visual acuity in the absence of any organic cause.

Clinical Features:

  • Unilateral or bilateral reduced vision
  • Crowding phenomenon may be seen: The patient is able to identify a Snellen's chart character with the amblyopic eye when the character is presented in isolation.
  • If the character is shown along with other letters, the patient may not be able to recognize it.
  • Neutral Density Filter Test(NDF): When the patient is asked to read through a NDF, the amblyopic eye shows no change, while in the normal eye, there is a drop in visual acuity

question_text: Based on the image findings, what is the likely associated refractive error observed?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows Munson's sign - a V-shaped conformation of the lower lid produced by the cornea in downgaze seen in Keratoconus. The refractive error seen in keratoconus is myopia and irregular astigmatism leading to defective vision.

Keratoconus:

  • Progressive, non-inflammatory bilateral ectatic corneal condition affecting the axial part.
  • Involves progressive thinning and ectasia of the cornea due to defective synthesis of mucopolysaccharides and collagen.

Clinical Features

  • Defective vision due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism (uncorrectable by glasses) (Option B)
  • Blurred and distorted vision, glare, and halos around lights
  • Light sensitivity and ocular irritation
  • Visual loss primarily from irregular astigmatism and myopia, secondary loss from corneal scarring

Examination Findings

  • Distorted Window Reflex: Visual irregularity on corneal reflection.
  • Placido Disc Irregularity: Irregular circles.
  • Slit-Lamp Examination:
    • Thinning and ectasia of the central cornea.
    • Opacity at the apex, Fleischer Ring (brownish ring around the cone due to hemosiderin in the epithelium).
    • Folds in Descemet's and Bowman's membranes.
  • Vogt Striae:
    • Fine, parallel striae at the apex, disappearing with external pressure.
  • Oil Droplet Reflex:
    • Annular dark shadow separating central and peripheral cornea in distant direct ophthalmoscopy.
  • Retinoscopy:
    • Yawning reflex (scissor reflex) with high oblique/irregular astigmatism.
  • Ophthalmoscope Findings:
    • Irregular astigmatism and progressive myopia, poorly corrected by glasses in later stages.
  • Munson's Sign:
    • Localized bulging of the lower lid when looking down (seen in late stages).
  • Corneal Topography: Sensitive method for early detection, shows corneal surface shape.

Management

  • Spectacle Correction:
    • Effective in the early stages, but contact lenses are more beneficial.
    • Less effective in later stages due to irregular astigmatism.
  • Contact Lenses:
    • Rigid gas permeable lenses improve vision in early cases.
    • Specially designed scleral lenses (e.g., Rose-K) are useful in early to moderate cases.
  • Corneal Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL):
    • New treatment modality to slow disease progression.
    • Involves Riboflavin (0.1%) eye drops and UVA radiation.
    • Riboflavin induces cross-linking of corneal collagen to stabilize the stroma and improve contact lens tolerance.
  • Keratoplasty :
    • Recommended if disease progresses or in cases of acute hydrops (Descemet's membrane tear).
    • Reserved for more advanced diseases or when other treatments fail.
    • Penetrating keratoplasty is common, but Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) is preferred if Descemet's membrane and endothelium are intact, reducing rejection risk.
  • Intracorneal Ring Segments (INTACS) :
    • Effective in early to moderate cases by flattening the cornea.
    • Less effective in halting progression.

option_a: Curves that flatten away from the Centre

• Optical correction for refractive errors can be done with spectacles, contact lenses and refractive surgeries.
  • Aspheric lenses have curves that flatten away from the centre, reducing the peripheral prismatic effects.

question_text: Contact lens is best used in:
explanation:
Astigmatism is a refractive error caused by irregular corneal curvature, resulting in blurred and distorted vision.

In irregular astigmatisms, the meridians having the maximum and minimum refractive power are separated by an angle other than 90°. In these cases, the principal meridians are not perpendicular to one another

The single best technique to diagnose irregular astigmatism and determine its clinical significance is trial of a rigid contact lens.

If the vision loss is secondary to irregular astigmatism, the rigid lens will correct it by creating a new optical surface on the cornea. By contrast, a soft lens tends to mold to the shape of the cornea, so it masks some but not all of the irregular astigmatism.

Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

question_text: Shield ulcer is most commonly seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic allergic condition affecting the eyes, often associated with shield ulcers. These ulcers are corneal microerosions, usually located on the upper third of the cornea, resulting from mechanical trauma by giant papillae and ongoing inflammation. Patients may present with itching, photophobia, and blurred vision, often worsened by eye rubbing.

Explanation for other options:

Spring catarrh (option A): Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) / Spring catarrh (option A ruled out):

  • Recurrent bilateral conjunctivitis, more common in children and adolescents during warm weather
  • Symptoms: burning, itching, photophobia, tearing
  • Palpebral form: hypertrophied conjunctiva with cobblestone papillae
  • Limbal form: gelatinous limbal thickening with Horner-Trantas dots
  • Shield ulcers can occur in severe VKC, particularly with the palpebral form
  • Mixed form: Exhibits characteristics of both the tarsal (palpebral) and limbal subtypes, typically presenting in only one eye.

Maxwell Lyon's sign is a pseudo membrane formed due to excessive mucus deposition on the papilla resulting in cobblestone papillae.

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option B):

  • Allergic reaction to bacterial antigens (Staphylococcus aureusor Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
  • Clinical features: conjunctival nodules near the limbus, redness, watering, and mild discomfort
  • Does not typically cause shield ulcers

Autoimmune conditions (Option D):

  • Diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or Sjögren's syndrome may involve the eyes, leading to dry eye, scleritis, or uveitis
  • Shield ulcers are not commonly associated with these conditions

Key takeaway:

Additional Features in Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis / VKC:

  • Dennie-Morgan folds under the eyes
  • Madarosis(loss of eyelashes)
  • Hertoghe's sign (eyebrow thinning) may be present
  • Treatment includes:
    • Topical antihistamines(e.g., levocabastine, emedastine)
    • Mast cell stabilizers(e.g., sodium cromoglicate)
    • Mild steroids(e.g., fluorometholone, loteprednol)
    • Acetylcysteine for mucus control
    • Subtarsal steroid injections or cryotherapy in severe cases
    • Surgical intervention for shield ulcers: debridement, amniotic membrane, or bandage contact lens
    • Supportive care: cold compresses, tinted glasses, and avoiding eye rubbing

question_text: What is the most likely risk in a 37-year-old man presenting with blurred vision and severe pain in his right eye, following recent pond water exposure while swimming? Examination revealed a ring-shaped lesion, as shown in the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of blurred vision, severe eye pain, and a ring-shaped corneal lesion following exposure to pond water strongly suggests a diagnosis of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Acanthamoeba Keratitis

Acanthamoeba is a free-living amoeba commonly found in water and soil, capable of causing severe corneal infections.

Risk Factors:

  • Contact lens use (especially with poor hygiene) - M/c risk factor
  • Exposure to contaminated water (e.g., ponds, hot tubs)
  • Corneal trauma
  • Immunosuppression
  • Use of non-sterile homemade saline solutions
  • Improper lens storage or disinfection

Clinical Features:

Symptoms:

  • Blurred vision due to disruption of corneal clarity
  • Significant discomfort
  • Severe ocular pain-often disproportionate to the clinical findings, which is a key diagnostic clue

Signs:

Early Stage:

  • Irregular, greyish epithelium - an early sign of amoebic involvement
  • Pseudodendrites- may resemble herpetic keratitis lesions
  • Limbitis and stromal infiltrates - inflammation around the corneal periphery with diffuse or focal stromal changes
  • Perineural infiltrates (radial keratoneuritis): Pathognomonic sign, appearing as radial lines extending centrally from the limbus

Advanced Stage:

  • Ring-shaped corneal abscess - classic finding in progressive Acanthamoeba infection
  • Stromal opacification and neovascularization - leads to visual impairment
  • Corneal melting - localized tissue destruction, often at the edge of the infiltrate
  • Scleritis - reactive inflammation of the sclera, not due to direct amoebic invasion

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding histologic features of Bowman membrane dystrophy is/are correct?
option_a: Irregular thickening of epithelium basement membrane
option_b: Fibro-cellular layer with saw-tooth pattern between epithelium and stroma
explanation:
Histopathology shows irregular thickening of the epithelium with focal deficiencies in the epithelial basement membrane and replacement of the Bowman layer by a fibro cellular layer with a saw-toothed wavy pattern visible between the epithelium and stroma in Thiel–Behnke corneal dystrophy and a sheet of connective tissue with fibrillar or granular hyaline deposits of protein that stain red with Masson trichrome.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Edition 23rd- Chap 12- Diseases of the cornea

question_text: A 45-year-old man presents with a history of ocular trauma involving vegetative material. He reports severe eye pain, redness, tearing, and sensitivity to light. Microscopic analysis of corneal scrapings reveals septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation-eye trauma involving vegetative material, severe eye pain, redness, tearing, and photophobia-suggests an infectious cause of a corneal ulcer. The key clue in this case is the microscopic examination of the corneal scraping showing septate hyphae at an acute angle, which is characteristic of fungal infection.

The combination of trauma with vegetative matter, intense ocular pain, redness, tearing, and photophobia points toward an infectious corneal ulcer. The definitive clue is the presence of septate hyphae on microscopy, which is indicative of fungal involvement.

Keratomycosis (Fungal Corneal Ulcer):

Clinical Features:

  • Eye pain and foreign body sensation
  • Excessive tearing
  • Photophobia
  • Blurred vision
  • Redness

Examination Findings:

  • Corneal Ulcer: Grey-white, dry-appearing, with elevated or rolled margins
  • Pigmented Ulcer: Brownish discoloration, seen with dematiaceous fungi
  • Feathery Edges: Finger-like extensions into the surrounding stroma
  • Sterile Immune Ring: Yellow demarcation from the interaction of fungal antigens and host antibodies
  • Satellite Lesions: Small secondary lesions surrounding the main ulcer
  • Hypopyon: Large, non-sterile, may appear even with a small ulcer
  • Endothelial Plaque: Underlying stromal fibrin and leukocytes
  • Corneal Vascularization: Usually absent in isolated fungal ulcers
  • Perforation: Rare but possible

Investigations:

  • Corneal Scraping: Performed under topical anesthesia for microbiology
  • Wet KOH Mount: Detects filamentous fungi (septate hyphae) or yeast-like fungi (Candida)
  • Gram & Giemsa Stains: Identify hyphae and inflammatory cells
  • Culture: Sabouraud's agar medium
  • PCR: Rapid detection of fungal pathogens
  • Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: If intraocular involvementis suspected
  • Corneal Biopsy: For deep stromal abscesses or negative cultures
  • Confocal Microscopy: Confirms the presence of fungi within the cornea

Explanation of Other Options:

Bacterial corneal ulcer (Option B): Bacterial infections, such as those caused by Pseudomonas or Staphylococcus, can also cause pain, redness, and photophobia. However, cultures reveal bacteria rather than hyphal elements. The acute-angle branching pattern is unique to fungi.

Viral corneal ulcer (Option C): Herpes simplex (HSV) or varicella-zoster (VZV) may produce corneal ulcers with photophobia and pain, but these lack septate hyphae. Viral ulcers are typically dendritic or geographic and often linked to reactivation, not trauma with plant material.

Acanthamoeba corneal ulcer (Option D): Acanthamoeba infections are usually seen in contact lens users or after exposure to contaminated water. They cause severe pain and photophobia, but clinical examination often shows a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate, and microscopy reveals cysts and trophozoites rather than hyphae.

Key takeaway:

question_text: What is the likely reason for a 21-year-old student to have ocular redness, feeling of a foreign object in the eye, and excessive tearing after wearing a soft contact lens, as indicated by the corneal scraping interface contrast microscopy image?
explanation:
Explanation:


The history of soft contact lens wear coupled with severe pain and the microscopic findings point to Acanthamoeba keratitis.

Acanthamoeba Keratitis

  • Acanthamoeba keratitis is a severe, vision-threatening corneal infection caused by a free-living amoeba, primarily affecting contact lens users. It is characterized by excruciating pain disproportionate to clinical signs, which is a hallmark feature.
  • Key Clinical Features:
    • Pathognomonic Sign: Radial keratoneuritis (perineural infiltrates).
    • Classic Sign: Ring-shaped stromal infiltrate or abscess.
    • Early Signs: Epithelial irregularities, pseudodendrites, limbal inflammation (limbitis).
    • Advanced Disease: Stromal opacification, melting, perforation, and scleritis.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Microscopy: Corneal scrapings stained with Calcofluor white or PAS to identify cysts.
    • Culture: On non-nutrient agar with E. coli.
    • Confocal Microscopy: In vivo visualization of corneal cysts and trophozoites.
  • Management:
    • Topical Amoebicides: First-line treatment with biguanides (e.g., 0.02% Polyhexamethylene biguanide - PHMB) or diamidines.
    • Adjunct Therapy: Epithelial debridement, oral NSAIDs for pain control.
    • Corticosteroids: Controversial; use only after effective anti-amoebic therapy is established to control significant inflammation.
    • Surgery: Therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty for impending perforation or medical treatment failure.

Explanation of other options:

Naegleria fowleri (Option B): Causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a fatal brain infection, not keratitis.

Entamoeba histolytica (Option C): Causes amoebic dysentery and liver abscesses, not corneal infections.

Balamuthia mandrillaris (Option D): Causes granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE), not keratitis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Acanthamoeba keratitis is a vision-threatening infection linked to contact lens use.
  • Severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs is a hallmark.
  • Radial keratoneuritis is a pathognomonic sign.

question_text: A 23-year-old male presents with eye pain, photophobia, and redness for the past 2 days. He gives a history of ocular trauma while gardening, when his eye came in contact with leaves and thorns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario of pain, redness in eyes following trauma with vegetative matter is suggestive of Fungal Keratitis.

Fungal Keratitis

  • Mycotic or fungal keratitis is frequently seen in tropical countries, rural areas and in immunocompromised individuals.
  • Causative organisms:
    • Aspergillus, Fusarium or Candida albicans.
  • Predisposing factor:
    • Injury with vegetable matter such as a thorn or wooden stick

Clinical features

  • Relatively indolent course.
  • Compared to bacterial ulcers, symptoms are much milder than the clinical signs would suggest.
  • Symptoms: Marked ciliary and conjunctival congestion with pain, watering and photophobia
  • Signs
    • Ulcers appears greyish-white and dry with feathery borders.
    • Hypopyon:
      • If present is thick and immobile and is due to direct i into anterior chamber.
    • Wessely immune ring:
      • Yellow line of demarcation which gradually deepens into a gutter.
      • Due to deposition of immune complexes and inflammatory cells around the ulcer.
    • Satellite lesions may also be seen.

Fig: (A) Fungal corneal ulcer showing a dry looking ulcer with feathery margins and thick hypopyon. (B) Fungal corneal ulcer with satellite lesions.

Treatment

Medical management:

  • Topical Antifungal Agents
    • Treatment is by means of local natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium.
    • Nystatin is effective against Candida.
  • Oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole may be needed if the ulcers are severe with hypopyon, perforated, or there is a suspicion of endophthalmitis.

Surgical Management: If the ulcer progresses despite therapeutic measures,

  • Repeated Scraping of the floor of ulcer with a spatula for removal of necrotic material
  • Cauterization: Performed with Carbolic acid (100%), Trichloroacetic acid (10%-20%), Povidone-iodine (5%)
  • Therapeutic Keratoplasty: Corneal transplantation

Explanation of other options:

Simplex Keratitis (Option A): Simplex keratitis is caused by Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1). Unlike Fungal keratitis, Simplex keratitis is acquired by kissing or in close contact with an infected person. A dendritic ulcer with a budding patterns suggestive of simplex keratitis.

Bacterial keratitis (Option B): Bacterial keratitis commonly follows corneal trauma, contact lens use, or ocular surface disease, where epithelial breaches allow bacterial entry.
Other risk factors include prolonged steroid use, dry eyes, eyelid malpositions, bullous keratopathy, and poor local hygiene.

Acanthamoeba keratitis (option D): Usually seen in contact lens users; pseudodendritic pattern with tapering ends is suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 30-year-old man with a history of contact lens use who presents with pain, redness, and pus discharge from his right eye? On examination, a greyish-white, snake-shaped ulcer is noted on the lower part of the cornea, along with a 4 mm hypopyon in the anterior chamber and a moderate flare reaction.
explanation:
Explanation:

Bacterial corneal ulcers typically present with redness, pain, and discharge. A key sign is the presence of a greyish-white serpiginous (snake-shaped) ulcer on the lower third of the cornea, which is characteristic of bacterial infection.

Aetiology of Purulent Corneal Ulcer:

  • Corneal Epithelial Damage: This can result from corneal abrasion, epithelial drying (xerosis, exposure keratitis), necrosis (keratomalacia), desquamation (bullous keratopathy), or trophic changes (neuroparalytic keratitis).
  • Pathogens Invading Intact Epithelium: Some bacteria like Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus aegyptius, and Listeria species can invade even without epithelial damage.
  • Sources of Infection:
    • Exogenous sources such as conjunctival sac, lacrimal sac infections (dacryocystitis), infected foreign bodies, vegetative material, and waterborne or airborne pathogens.

Common Bacteria Causing Corneal Ulceration:

  • General: Staphylococci, Pseudomonas, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Enterobacteriaceae, Neisseria.
  • In Contact Lens Wearers: Pseudomonas is the most frequent cause. Acanthamoeba should also be considered, especially in cases of contact lens misuse.

Bacteria Groupings:

  • Gram-positive Cocci: Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae.
  • Gram-negative Cocci: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis.
  • Gram-positive Bacilli: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, C. xerosis, Bacillus cereus, Propionibacterium acnes, Listeria, Clostridium.
  • Gram-negative Bacilli: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., Klebsiella, Proteus, E. coli, Serratia), Moraxella lacunata, Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Gram-positive Filamentous Bacteria: Actinomyces, Nocardia.
  • Mycobacteria: Non-tuberculous Mycobacteria, M. tuberculosis.

Clinical Features of Bacterial Corneal Ulcers:

Symptoms:

  • Pain and foreign body sensation
  • Watery eye (reflex hyperlacrimation)
  • Photophobia (light sensitivity)
  • Blurred vision
  • Redness

Signs:

  • Lid swelling
  • Blepharospasm (involuntary eyelid twitching)
  • Conjunctival chemosis and hyperemia
  • Corneal ulcer:
    • Early stage: Epithelial defect with greyish-white infiltrate
    • Established: Yellowish-white ulcer with swollen margins, necrotic base, and stromal edema
  • Specific bacterial features:
    • Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae: Oval, yellowish-white ulcer with clear corneal margins
    • Pseudomonas: Irregular ulcer with greenish exudate, rapid progression, often with hypopyon
    • Enterobacteriaceae: Shallow ulcer with greyish-white suppuration and ring-shaped infiltrate
  • Hypopyon (pus in anterior chamber)
  • Muddy iris color
  • Small pupil due to iritis
  • Possible raised intraocular pressure (inflammatory glaucoma)

Explanation for other options:

Viral Corneal Ulcer (Option A): Usually occurs in immunocompromised patients, presenting with red, watery, bloodshot eyes, severe pain, and discharge. It can lead to vision loss.

Fungal Corneal Ulcer (Option C): Often caused by trauma. Pain is typically less severe, and hypopyon, if present, is thick and immobile.

Parasitic Corneal Ulcer (Option D): Characterized by disproportionately severe pain, commonly linked to contact lens wear or exposure to contaminated water.

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis in a 65-year-old female patient with a history of chickenpox who presents with the clinical features shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of a 65-year-old patient with a history of chickenpox and cutaneous lesions distributed along the trigeminal nerve strongly points to a diagnosis of Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO).

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)

  • Involves the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V)
  • Anterior uveitis develops in approximately 40-50% of cases, typically within two weeks after the appearance of the skin rash

Clinical Features:

  • Mild iritis
  • Vesicular rash, especially on the nose (Hutchinson's sign)
  • Small keratic precipitates (KPs)
  • Mild aqueous flare
  • Occasionally, hemorrhagic hypopyon

Potential Complications:

  • Iris atrophy
  • Secondary glaucoma
  • Complicated cataracts

Explanation for other options:

Chickenpox exacerbation (Option A): This is caused by primary varicella-zoster virus infection, typically seen in children, presenting with a generalized vesicular rash. In adults, reactivation of the virus leads to herpes zoster, not a recurrence of chickenpox.

Drug allergy to acyclovir (Option B): Allergic reactions to this antiviral may include skin rash, itching, or swelling, but would not cause dermatomal vesicular lesions or ocular symptoms consistent with HZO.

Herpes Zoster Oticus (Option D): (Ramsay Hunt Syndrome) This involves reactivation of the virus in the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), leading to ear pain, vesicles in the ear canal, and often facial paralysis. It does not primarily affect the eye or result in keratitis.

question_text: What does this image indicate?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image shows corneal thinning with conical protrusion, a hallmark feature of keratoconus.
  • This condition leads to irregular astigmatism and progressive myopia, resulting in distorted vision that cannot be corrected with glasses.
  • Associated signs include Fleischer's ring, Vogt's striae, and in advanced cases Munson's sign.

Keratoconus

Definition

  • Progressive, bilateral, non-inflammatory ectasia of the cornea, typically central or paracentral.

Pathology

  • Abnormal synthesis of collagen and mucopolysaccharides causes stromal thinning and anterior protrusion.

Clinical Features

  • Symptoms: Blurred vision, glare, halos, photophobia, foreign body sensation.
  • Vision loss: Mainly from irregular astigmatism, later from scarring.

Examination Findings

  • Thinning and cone-shaped bulging of the cornea, with apex usually just below centre.
  • Fleischer's ring: Iron deposition encircling the cone.
  • Vogt's striae: Vertical stress lines that disappear on pressure.
  • Oil droplet reflex on ophthalmoscopy.
  • Munson's sign: Lower lid bulge in downgaze.
  • Distorted mires on keratometry.
  • Corneal topography: Most sensitive test, detects early/forme fruste keratoconus.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Vogt's limbal girdle (Option B): Represents an age-related chalky crescent at the corneal periphery, without thinning or protrusion.

Keratoglobus (Option C): Characterised by uniform corneal thinning and a globular shape, not the conical deformity of keratoconus.

Corneal dystrophy (Option D): Inherited disorders with abnormal corneal deposits, but they do not show thinning with cone-shaped ectasia.

Key Takeaway:

Keratoconus is a bilateral, progressive corneal thinning disorder producing irregular astigmatism, diagnosed clinically with signs like Fleischer's ring, Vogt's striae, and confirmed with corneal topography.

question_text:
A patient previously diagnosed with keratoconus reports to OPD with sudden loss of vision.

Clinical imaging is as shown below. What is next step of management in this scenario?
explanation:
Sometimes ruptures develop in the Descemet’s membrane in which case the stroma becomes suddenly oedematous and opaque (acute hydrops). In the early stages, vision may be improved with spectacles but contact lenses are more beneficial as they eliminate the irregular corneal curvature and are said to have a supporting effect.

Corneal collagen cross-linking is a treatment introduced as an interim measure to track progression. If despite all measures the disease progresses or the cone becomes hydrated due to a sudden tear of the Descemet’s membrane (acute hydrops), the most satisfactory treatment is corneal transplantation (keratoplasty).

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text:
A 17 year old male patient reports to OPD with diminution of vision in one eye and frequent change in glasses with poor visual result. Clinical imaging is as shown below.

Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are correct?
option_a: Corneal ectasia is caused due to inflammation
option_c: Lower lid notching on downward gaze is called Fleischer's sign
option_d: Formation of Vogt striae indicates folds in Descemet's membrane
explanation:
Inferior bulging of cornea with notching of lower eyelid in down gaze in male patient post – puberty : pathgnomonic of KERATOCONUS

Etiology

This is frequently due to a congenital weakness of the cornea, though it manifests only after puberty.

  • However, it can also occur secondarily following trauma, in which case it is unilateral, or in patients with vernal keratoconjunctivitis or Down syndrome due to repeated rubbing of the eye.

Clinical Features

  • The condition is almost invariably bilateral, though frequently more advanced on one side than on the other. It may be slight and progress very slowly, or the reverse.
  • If the condition is marked, the conical shape is easily recognized in profile, particularly by the acute bulge given to the lower lid when the patient looks down (Munson sign) not Fleischer’s sign
  • In the later stages, the apex shows fine, more or less parallel striae (Vogt striae), best seen with the slit lamp, and also discrete opacities which become confluent-formed due to folds in Descemet’s membrane In the early stages, vision may be improved with spectacles but contact lenses are more beneficial as they eliminate the irregular corneal curvature and are said to have a supporting effect

Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 - Diseases of Cornea

question_text: Sunflower Cataract is seen in
explanation:
Sunflower cataracts are seen in conditions which result in excessive copper deposition in the eye. These include -

  • Wilson's disease, an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism.
  • Copper containing alloys with less than 85% copper cause chalcosis. Chalcosis can result in a Kayser-Fleischer ring, greenish heterochromia, sunflower cataract of the anterior capsule, and refractile deposits in the macular region often with peripheral sparing.

Copper alloys of greater than 85% result in a sterile endophthalmitis.


Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

Monocular Diplopia

question_text: A child with elevated liver enzymes is examined in the OPD and a gonioscopic eye finding is noted. Which element is implicated in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Wilson's Disease is caused by defective copper metabolism due to caeruloplasmin deficiency, leading to copper accumulation in multiple tissues.

Ocular Finding:

  • Kayser-Fleischer ring: Brownish-yellow copper deposits in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, detectable via gonioscopy.
  • This ring is a hallmark of Wilson's disease and strongly suggests copper accumulation.
  • Sunflower cataract: Some patients may also develop anterior capsular cataracts with a characteristic pattern.

Clinical Features of Wilson's Disease

  • Hepatic: Elevated liver enzymes, chronic liver disease
  • Neurological: Basal ganglia involvement → movement disorders, tremors, dystonia
  • Psychiatric: Behavioral changes, mood disorders
  • Ocular: Kayser-Fleischer ring, sunflower cataract 

Diagnosis and Management:

  • Detection: Kayser-Fleischer rings are visible on slit-lamp or gonioscopic examination
  • Treatment: Copper chelation with penicillamine or zinc therapy to reduce copper deposition and improve symptoms 

Explanation of Other Options:

Zinc (Option B): Used therapeutically to reduce copper absorption but not responsible for Kayser-Fleischer rings.

Selenium (Option C) and Iron (Option D): Not associated with this ocular finding or Wilson disease symptoms.

Reference:

Wilson Disease - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: All of the following antioxidants are present in the lens except:
explanation:
Vitamin D does not have an antioxidant role.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) have the capacity to damage the lens in many ways:

  • Peroxidizing membrane lipids results in the formation of aldehydes, which in turn can form cross-links between membrane lipids and proteins.
  • Introducing damage into the bases of the DNA (e.g base modifications) and reducing DNA repair efficiency
  • Polymerizing and crosslinking proteins result in crystallin aggregation and inactivation of many essential enzymes, including those with an antioxidant role.

Protection against damage induced by ROS is achieved in a number of ways. These include the antioxidant effects of -

  • Superoxide dismutase
  • Catalase - present in epithelial cells at higher levels than in fibers.
  • Glutathione peroxidase - found in significant amounts in both epithelial cells and fibers.
  • Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) - present at high levels in the outer layers of the lens but virtually absent from the nucleus.
  • Vitamin E also has a role

This system, however, is not 100% efficient and a low level of cumulative damage occurs throughout life.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition/330

question_text: Rubella in pregnancy is important cause in causing which of the following cataracts?
explanation:
Nuclear cataract usually affects the embryonic nucleus. Rubella in pregnancy is an important cause.

In maternal rubella infection, after 6 weeks of gestation, the virus can penetrate the lens capsule causing unilateral or bilateral, dense, nuclear opacities at birth, or they may develop several weeks or months later.

Extra information - lamellar/ zonular cataract can also be seen in rubella. The congenital rubella retinitis may present as a salt and-pepper fundus appearance.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

question_text: Oil droplet cataract is seen in
explanation:
Central oil droplet opacities are characteristic of galactosaemia


Galactosemia is a rare autosomal recessive condition caused by one of the three defective enzymes, galactose 1 phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT), galactokinase and/or epimerase, involved in galactose metabolism. Cataract formation is consequent to accumulation of galactitol in the crystalline lens.

An impairment or deficiency in the enzyme, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), results in classic galactosemia, or Type I galactosemia. Classic galactosemia is a rare (1 in 47,000 live births), autosomal recessive disease that presents with symptoms soon after birth when a baby begins lactose ingestion. Symptoms include life-threatening illnesses such as jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly (enlarged spleen and liver), hypoglycemia, renal tubular dysfunction, muscle hypotonia (decreased tone and muscle strength), sepsis (presence of harmful bacteria and their toxins in tissues), and cataract among others. The prevalence of cataract among classic galactosemics is markedly less than among galactokinase-deficient patients due to the extremely high levels of galactitol found in the latter

Although a rare cause of cataract, timely recognition is important as dietary restriction of lactose-containing foods in early stages can reverse cataract formation and minimize adverse effects of galactitol on liver and brain. Diagnosis of galactosemia rests on the presence of galactose metabolites in urine and blood, enzymatic assay, and mutation analysis.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

Galactosemia & Oil-Droplet Cataract

  • Cause: Defects in
    • Galactokinase (GALK1)
    • Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT)
    • UDP-galactose epimerase
  • Mechanism: Accumulation of galactitol → osmotic lens swelling → cataract.

Clinical Notes

  • Galactokinase deficiency: Often causes isolated congenital cataracts.
  • Other enzyme defects: Produce systemic features such as vomiting, failure to thrive, liver disease, intellectual disability.

Cataract Characteristics

  • May be nuclear or subcapsular.
  • Classic appearance: "Oil-droplet cataract."
  • Reversible with early dietary galactose restriction (some subcapsular opacities may persist).

Snow flake cataract (Option A): Classically in juvenile diabetes.

Sunflower cataract (Option C): Associated with Wilson disease.

Shield cataract (Option D): Associated with atopic dermatitis.

Key Takeaways:

Oil-droplet cataract + gastrointestinal failure to thrive → galactosemia; dietary management critical early.

question_text: A long-term diabetic patient presents with cataract. Which metabolic byproduct is most directly implicated in the pathogenesis of diabetic cataracts?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In individuals with diabetes, high blood glucose levels can lead to increased activity of the enzyme aldose reductase. This enzyme converts glucose to sorbitol.
  • Sorbitol is poorly metabolized and can accumulate within the lens of the eye.
  • The accumulation of sorbitol leads to osmotic changes, drawing water into the lens and causing it to swell. This swelling and disruption of lens fibers leads to cataract formation.

Pathophysiology of Diabetic Cataract Formation:

  1. Glucose enters the lens (insulin-independent uptake).
  2. Aldose reductase converts glucose → sorbitol .
  3. Sorbitol accumulates (since its conversion to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase is slow in the lens).
  4. Sorbitol is osmotically active, causing lens swelling, oxidative stress, and crystallin protein aggregation → cataract formation.

Mannitol (Option A): Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic and is not involved in cataract formation. 

Galactitol (Option B): Galactitol (dulcitol) accumulates in the lens in galactosemia, leading to early-onset cataracts, but not in diabetic cataracts. 

Fructose (Option D): While sorbitol is eventually converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase, the rate is slow in the lens, making sorbitol the primary culprit in diabetic cataracts. 

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2903955/#:~:text

question_text: Which type of cataract is commonly seen following blunt ocular trauma?
explanation:
Explanation:

Rosette cataract is a cortical cataract that typically arises from the posterior cortex along lens suture lines after blunt trauma. It is often feathery in appearance in the early stage and may become more compact over time.

Traumatic cataracts are acquired cataracts resulting from ocular trauma (blunt or penetrating) and occur due to degeneration of previously normal lens fibres.

Morphological forms of traumatic cataracts:

  • Rosette cataracts: Feathery opacities along posterior cortex suture lines; early stage seen soon after concussion, late stage develops 1-2 years post-injury.
  • Subepithelial opacities: Most common, but do not form feathery sutural patterns.
  • Diffuse concussion cataract: Widespread lens opacity, often total cataract following blunt trauma, may accelerate senile cataract formation.

Explanation for other options:

Toxic cataract (option B): Typically, posterior subcapsular type. It is caused by steroids, phenothiazines, long-acting miotics, amiodarone, busulfan, gold, and chloroquine. Not specifically associated with trauma.

Metabolic cataract (option C): Caused by systemic metabolic disorders, e.g., diabetes mellitus

  • Enzyme deficiencies:
    • Galactokinase deficiency: lamellar cataract
    • GPUT deficiency: oil drop cataract
  • Not trauma-related

Nuclear cataract (option D): It is due to nuclear sclerosis. It results from protein denaturation, insoluble protein accumulation, and pigment deposition (melanin, urochrome). It is Age-related rather than traumatic.

question_text: Oil droplet Cataract is characteristic feature of:
explanation:
METABOLIC CATARACTS

These cataracts occur due to endocrine disorders and biochemical abnormalities. A few common varieties of metabolic cataracts are described here.

  • Diabetic cataract: Diabetes is associated with two types of cataracts:
    1. Senile cataract in diabetics appears at an early age and progresses rapidly.
    2. True diabetic cataract. It is also called 'snow flake cataract' or 'snow-storm cataract'. It is a rare condition, usually occurring in young adults due to osmotic over-hydration of the lens. Initially a large number of fluid vacuoles appear underneath the anterior and posterior capsules, which is soon followed by appearance of bilateral snowflake-like white opacities in the cortex.
  • Galactosemic cataract: It is associated with inborn error of galactose metabolism. Galactosaemia occurs in two forms:
    1. Classical galactosaemia occurs due to deficiency of galactose-1 phosphate uridyl-transferase(GPUT); and
    2. A related disorder occurs due to deficiency of galactokinase(GK).
  • Characteristic features: Galactosaemia is frequently associated with the development of bilateral cataract(oil droplet central lens opacities). The lens changes may be reversible and occurrence of cataract may be prevented, if milk and milk products are eliminated from the diet when diagnosed at an early stage.
  • Hypocalcemia cataract: Cataractous changes may be associated with parathyroid tetany, which may occur due to atrophy or inadvertent removal (during thyroidectomy) of parathyroid glands.
  • Multicolored crystals or small discrete white flecks of opacities are formed in the cortex which seldom mature.
  • Cataract due to error of copper metabolism:
  • Inborn error of copper metabolism results in Wilson's disease(hepatolenticular degeneration). The green 'sunflower cataract' may be observed rarely in such patients. The more commonly observed ocular feature of Wilson's disease is 'Kayser-Fleischer ring'(KF ring) in the cornea.
  • Cataract in Lowe's syndrome

Lowe's(Oculo-cerebral-renal) syndrome is a rare inborn error of amino acid metabolism. Ocular features include congenital cataract and glaucoma. Systemic features of this syndrome are mental retardation, dwarfism, osteomalacia, muscular hypotonia and frontal prominence.

Reference: A K Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 181.

question_text: Riders are seen in
explanation:
Hypocalcemia or Vitamin D deficiency in pregnancy gives rise to spoke like opacities which are called riders. It is a type of zonular cataract.

CONGENITAL AND DEVELOPMENTAL CATARACT

This is due to disturbance in the growth and development of the lens. Disturbance in development during the period of gestation leads to congenital cataract and usually affects the embryonic or foetal nucleus. Developmental cataract is due to disturbance in development after birth and hence affects the infantile or adult nucleus and cortex. The different morphological varieties are -

  • Punctate cataract or blue dot cataract: It consists of minute white dots throughout the lens but causes no visual disturbance. It is the most common type of congenital cataract.
  • Zonular or lamellar cataract: This is the most common type of congenital cataract associated with diminished vision. A zone in the foetal nucleus is usually affected. Hypocalcemia in pregnancy is an important cause.
  • Nuclear cataract: This usually affects the embryonic nucleus. Rubella in pregnancy is an important cause.
  • Fusiform or coralliform cataract: Consists of round and oblong opacities, grouped toward the center of the lens; they resemble coral.
  • Coronary cataract: It usually occurs around puberty of and is characterized by opacities in the periphery of the lens.
  • Anterior polar cataract: Presents as well-defined opacities of the anterior capsule which may affect the vision.
  • Posterior polar cataract: Begin as posterior subcapsular opacities and spread toward the periphery.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

question_text: A newborn presents with excessive tearing and symptoms of photophobia. On ocular examination revealed a normal tear passage and findings as shown in the image. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows an abnormally enlarged cornea suggestive of megalocornea, blue sclera and when associated with excessive tearing and photophobia, it is indicative of buphthalmos a feature of congenital cataract.

Primary Congenital Glaucoma

  • Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is rare, with an incidence of 1: 10 000 in many populations.
  • Boys are more commonly affected than girls.
  • Involvement is more often bilateral, but frequently asymmetrical.
  • Thought to be caused by impaired aqueous outflow due to maldevelopment of the anterior chamber angle trabeculodysgenesis.

Clinical features:

  • Classic triad
    • Lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm; often accompanied by eye rubbing.
  • Buphthalmos
    • Presents as a large eye as a result of stretching due to elevated IOP prior to the age of 3 years. The thinned sclera often appears blue due to increased visualisation of the underlying uvea. Complications include myopia and lens subluxation.
  • Corneal Signs:
    • Corneal haze is due to diffuse oedema secondary to raised IOP, or localized oedema due to breaks in Descemet membrane.
    • Enlargement: Corneal diameter >13 mm confirms enlargement; >16 mm indicates poor prognosis.
  • Haab's Striae: Tears in Descemet's membrane, visible as opaque lines.
  • Other Features:
    • Deep Anterior Chamber: Indicates elevated IOP.
    • Optic Disc Changes: Variable cupping and atrophy.
    • Raised IOP: Elevated but not acute.
    • Axial Myopia: Due to increased axial length.

Management

  • Direct Goniotomy followed by Trabeculotomy is the preferred management for Congenital Glaucoma

Explanation of other options:

Megalocornea (Option A): Megalocornea is not associated with photophobia or watering.

Congenital cataract (Option C): Presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), decreased vision, or nystagmus. There is no corneal enlargement or photophobia in congenital cataract.

Congenital dacryocystitis (Option D): Presents with watering due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction, but there is no associated enlarged cornea or photophobia.

question_text: A 3-year-old male child was brought by parents with complaints of recurrent episodic abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive since early childhood. Elsewhere, the child was diagnosed to have malabsorption syndrome and was thoroughly investigated including jejunal biopsy to rule out celiac sprue. Lately, parents had noticed a white reflex in both eyes which kept on progressing. On general examination, the child was drowsy, apathetic with generalised wasting. Mental functions seemed age appropriate. The lens showed THIS slit lamp picture in both eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis
explanation:
Oil droplet cataract. This is suggestive of galactosemia and the slit lamp picture shows typical oil droplet cataract.

Galactosemia is a condition caused by abnor- mally high serum level of galactose. It is caused by mutations in galactokinase (galk1), galactose-1- phosphate uridyl transferase or uridine diphosphate 1–4 epimerase. In these conditions, galactitol accumu lation occurs that causes osmotic swelling of the lens leading to cataracts. While galactokinase deficiency is associated with isolated congenital cataracts, deficiency in the other two enzymes is associated with systemic manifestations such as vomiting, failure to thrive, liver disease and mental retardation. The galactosemic cataract presents as nuclear cataracts, but can also be anterior or posterior subcapsular. The classic description of the galactosemic cataract is "oil droplet" owing to increased refractive power of the lens (fig. 3). The changes are initially reversible by eliminating galactose from the diet, but the anterior or posterior subcapsular component of the cataract usually persists

question_text: A patient presents with a sudden decrease in vision, photophobia, circumcorneal congestion, and a visible hypopyon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of sudden vision loss, photophobia (difficulty looking at light), circumcorneal congestion, and hypopyon strongly suggests acute anterior uveitis.

  • Anterior uveitis is characterised by the presence of fine, grey keratic precipitates (KPs) on the corneal endothelium, a hazy anterior chamber (aqueous flare), and a constricted pupil.

Anterior Uveitis

Definition: The most common type of uveitis affecting the anterior segment of the eye.

Clinical Features:

  • Pain
  • Redness
  • Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
  • Blepharospasm (involuntary blinking)
  • Serous discharge
  • Blurring and diminished vision

Examination Findings:

  • Keratic Precipitates (KPs):
    • Non-Granulomatous: Fine, grey deposits; composed of lymphocytes
    • Granulomatous: Large, greasy-looking deposits known as "mutton fat KPs"; composed of macrophages
    • Location: Typically found in the lower cornea due to convection currents in aqueous humour; this area is known as Arlt's triangle
  • Aqueous Cells:
    • Indicator of active inflammation
  • Aqueous Flare:
    • Haziness in the anterior chamber due to leakage of proteins from inflamed tissues
  • Muddy Iris:
    • Oedema in the iris caused by protein leakage
  • Miosis:
    • Constricted pupil due to toxins released from the inflamed tissue
  • Nodules on the Iris:
    • Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary border; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis
    • Busacca Nodules: At the base of the iris; seen in granulomatous uveitis

Complications: (Findings)

  • Posterior Synechiae: Iris adheres to the lens; may lead to a festooned-shaped pupil
  • Secclusio Pupil/Ring Synechiae: Adhesion along the entire pupillary border; can lead to Iris Bombe and peripheral anterior synechiae, causing angle closure glaucoma
  • Occlusio Pupil: Covers the whole surface of the lens
  • Cyclitic Membrane
  • Rubeosis Iridis: New vessel formation on the iris

Explanation for other options:

Acute conjunctivitis (Option A): Conjunctivitis typically presents with diffuse conjunctival redness, watery/mucoid discharge, and itching (especially in allergic conjunctivitis).

Acute angle closure glaucoma (Option B): Presents with severe ocular pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, and blurred vision with halos around lights. The eye appears hazy with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, not a hypopyon. IOP is significantly elevated (>40 mmHg), which is a distinguishing feature.

Episcleritis (Option C): Episcleritis causes localised redness without circumcorneal congestion or hypopyon. It is not associated with vision loss or photophobia.

question_text: Capsule of the crystalline lens is thinnest at
explanation:
The capsule of the crystalline lens is thickest in the pre-equatorial region and thinnest at the posterior pole.

The lens is a biconvex, transparent crystalline structure which divides the eye into anterior and posterior segments. It is placed in a saucer shaped depression called patellar fossa.

The lens has two surfaces - anterior and posterior. The anterior surface is less convex than the posterior.

The lens is made up of:

  • Lens capsule - It is a transparent membrane covering the lens. It is thickest in the pre-equatorial region and thinnest at the posterior pole.
  • Lens epithelium - There is a single layer of epithelium on the anterior surface of the lens but no epithelium on the posterior surface.
  • Lens fibres- These are protein fibres arranged closely in concentric layers. They are formed throughout life so that the oldest fibres are at the centre and the newest fibres are most superficial. Hence the lens fibres may be divided into -
  • Nucleus: It is the central part of the lens containing the older fibres. It is again subdivided into -
    • Embryonic nucleus → Formed in first 3 months of gestation.
    • Foetal nucleus → Formed till birth.
    • Infantile nucleus → Formed from birth to puberty.
    • Adult nucleus → Formed after puberty.
  • Cortex: It is the peripheral part containing the new formed fibres.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition/329-330

Other Types of Cataracts by Cause:

  • Toxic cataract:Long-term use of steroids can cause posterior subcapsular cataracts, particularly in children. Other causes of posterior subcapsular cataracts include galactosemia, myotonic dystrophy, complicated cataracts, chloroquine, busulfan, and NF2.

Cavernous hemangioma (Option D): A benign, slow-growing orbital tumour in adults that can cause gradual, painless proptosis, but it is less common than thyroid eye disease.

question_text: All are features of cavernous sinus thrombosis except
option_a: Loss of direct and indirect light reflex
explanation:
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a rare, life-threatening disorder that can complicate facial infection, sinusitis, orbital cellulitis, pharyngitis, or otitis or following traumatic injury or surgery, especially in the setting of a thrombophilic disorder

Cavernous sinus thrombosis has a distinctive clinical picture that includes, in classic acute cases, chemosis, proptosis, and painful ophthalmoplegia, initially unilateral but frequently becoming bilateral.

Patients with cavernous sinus thrombosis most commonly complain of fever, headache (50% to 90%), periorbital swelling and pain, vision changes, such as photophobia, diplopia, loss of vision. Symptoms may be present at onset or progress subacutely over days. The headache is usually sharp, increases progressively, and is usually localized to the regions innervated by the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the fifth cranial nerve

  • Diplopia from partial or complete external ophthalmoplegia due to compression of the sixth (abducens), third (oculomotor) and fourth (trochlear) nerves. Limited eye abduction from abducens palsy is most common early finding, often progressing to inability to move the eye in any direction when III, IV and VI are involved
  • Internal ophthalmoplegia (non-reactive pupil) occurs from loss of sympathetic fibers from the short ciliary nerves (resulting in miosis) and/or from loss of parasympathetic fibers from cranial nerve III (resulting in mydriasis)
  • Numbness or paresthesias (around the eyes, nose, forehead) and loss of corneal blink reflex from the ophthalmic nerve, a branch of the trigeminal nerve (V)
  • Facial pain, paresthesias or numbness from compression of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve.

Reference: Parson 21st edition pg 483

question_text: True about hard contact lens
option_a: Hard contact lenses are made of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA).
option_b: These lenses allow enough oxygen to reach the eye and patients find it easy to adapt to them
explanation:
• Hard contact lenses are made of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA).
  • These lenses do not allow enough oxygen to reach the eye and patients find it difficult to adapt to them.
  • However, visual clarity is good and they can be used in astigmatic corneas.
  • Soft contact lenses are made from a gel-like plastic, hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA) that contains as much as 79% water.
  • They offer better initial comfort, but are prone to deposits, are difficult to keep clean and are difficult to handle.
  • Deposit problems with soft lenses can lead to discomfort in the long term and therefore they are now used as disposables, being discarded every day, weekly or monthly.
  • Daily disposables are designed to be worn for just a day, up to 15 hours.
  • Weekly or monthly disposal programmes allow for the use of soft contact lenses on a daily basis with the necessity to clean them rigorously every day; however, they are discarded before excessive deposits make them unsuitable for wear.
  • Continuous-wear lenses have an increased water content and oxygen permeability and allow up to six times more oxygen to the cornea than ordinary soft contact lenses.
  • They can be worn continuously for up to 30 nights and days, but are associated with a higher risk of infection compared to daily-wear lenses.

Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 88

explanation:
• Pupillary dysfunction from syphilis is characterized by light-near dissociation.
  • Syphilitic pupils constrict better to a near target than to direct light stimulation.
  • Pharmacologic constriction with pilocarpine stimulates the iris constrictor muscle.
  • Therefore activity of the pupil is affected both at near and to light. The appearance of the iris stroma and sphincter may be normal or restricted by synechia, in both conditions.

explanation:
• Pharmacologic iris blockade with pilocarpine, which is a parasympathomimetic, would constrict the pupil and produce poor or no reaction to light or near stimuli.
  • A small pupil that is unreactive to light but reactive to near is a sign of the Adie's tonic pupil(i.e., the "little old Adie's pupil").
  • The pupil sphincter would remain round from parasympathomimetic stimulation equally to the pupil and an irregular pupil is a sign of the Adie's tonic pupil or a structural defect in the iris itself.
  • A myopic rather than hyperopic shift occurs with pilocarpine use.

Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 222/424.

question_text: Paralysis of convergence, Pseudobulbar palsy, Extrapyramidal rigidity, gait ataxia and dementia is seen in
explanation:
Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Also known as the Steele - Richardson - Olszewski syndrome.

  • This neurodegenerative condition is associated with neuronal loss, NFTs(different from the type seen in Alzheimer disease) and gliosis in the mid-brain, pons, basal ganglia and cerebellar dentate nuclei.
  • Seen twice as often in males than females, it begins in those who are 45-75 years old and is characteristically associated with supranuclear ophthalmoplegia.
  • Voluntary saccadic gaze and the fast phase of optokinetic nystagmus are absent first in the vertical plane(downgaze is more severely affected) and then in the horizontal plane as well.
  • Reflex conjugate eye movements such as the oculocephalic(doll's head) and oculovestibular(caloric) reflexes are preserved.
  • Additional features include rigidity and bradykinesia which may resemble Parkinson disease, but in progressive supranuclear palsy tremor is uncommon and the dystonic axial posture is in extension rather than flexion.
  • Axial rigidity combined with a disturbance of downgaze is often present with a history of frequent falls.
  • Dysarthria, dysphagia and exaggerated jaw jerks complete the clinical picture of pseudobulbar palsy.
  • Dopaminergic and anticholinergic preparations are partly effective.

Reference: Kanski, 8th edition, Pg: 831/832.

question_text: which of the following features helps differentiate papillitis from papilledema?
explanation:
• In optic neuritis due to inflammation (papillitis), the appearance of the disc is often ophthalmoscopically indistinguishable from that in papilloedema.
  • The swelling is usually moderate (2-3 D), shelving off gradually into the surrounding retina. Vision in papilledema is normal, but in papillitis it is lost
  • Vitreous opacities are usual, although they may be very fine. The visual symptoms are usually marked in papillitis.
  • The acute depression of central vision, presence of a definite afferent pupillary defect or a relative afferent pupillary defect and the absence of signs of an intracranial space-occupying lesion form the most important differentiating features.
  • Involvement in papillitis is usually unilateral whereas in papilledema it is bilateral.

Reference: Parson's diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 - Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text:
A 26 year old male patient suffering from Insulin dependent diabetes has come to OPD for routine fundus examination. Clinical imaging is as follows in both eyes.

option_a: Visual field analysis may reveal central/arcuate scotoma
option_b: Visual field defects will reverse with treatment
