explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has acute diabetic papillopathy, an uncommon condition seen in young insulin-dependent diabetics. It presents with bilateral or unilateral swollen discs with telangiectatic vessels on the disc surface(characteristic and useful in diagnosis).

and only mild visual symptoms. Visual field defects like central or arcuate scotomas (A) can be seen, but importantly, these field defects tend to be irreversible. Also, although disc edema usually resolves over months, it does not typically progress to optic atrophy. Instead, the disc swelling may resolve completely or sometimes progress to disc neovascularization. Therefore, statements B and C are incorrect.

question_text: What is the diagnosis
explanation:
Duane retraction syndrome(DRS), previously known as Stilling-Turk-Duane syndrome, is caused by the absence or partial development of the abducent nucleus and nerve. As a result, there is aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus(LR) by the oculomotor nerve.

Clinical features of DRS include:

  1. Abduction limitation - One of the prominent features of DRS is due to subnormal innervation of the LR. This helps distinguish it from sixth nerve palsy, where the abduction limitation and primary position deviation are in proportion to each other.
  2. Abnormal head posture(AHP) - Commonly seen in unilateral cases, the AHP aims to center, enlarge and maintain binocular single vision and compensate for the duction deficit. The head turn will be toward the side of the affected eye in esotropic DRS and away from the affected eye in exotropic DRS.
  3. Globe retraction - A characteristic feature of DRS and is usually accompanied by a narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction.
  4. Upshoots and downshoots - While mechanical shoots are characterized by a sudden abrupt movement following a small vertical movement in adduction, innervational shoots are characterized by gradual elevation or depression of the eye as it adducts.

Huber classified the condition into three types:

Type 1 - Marked limitation of abduction with minimally defective or normal adduction. This is the most common type, accounting for 70-80% of cases.

Type 2 - Limitation of adduction with normal or slightly limited abduction. This is the least common type, accounting for 7% of the cases. EMG recordings showed innervation of LR in both abduction and adduction, while MR was innervated normally.

Type 3 - Limitation or complete absence of adduction and abduction. EMG recordings showed simultaneous innervation of LR and MR in primary position, adduction and abduction.

Reference: Kanski, 5th Edition, Page no. 549.

question_text: Patient had a fight, following which he presents with non-reactive pupil and painful ocular movements. The most probable diagnosis is
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario of a non-reactive pupil and painful eye movements following trauma is most likely due to optic neuritis.

Optic neuritis

  • An inflammation of the optic nerve is known as optic neuritis. The optic nerve may be affected by inflammation in any part of its course, but for clinical convenience it is usual to divide inflammatory conditions into two categories:
    • Those affecting the part of the nerve ophthalmoscopically visible at the disc and therefore showing obvious signs of disease:
      • Papillitis
      • Neuroretinitis
    • Those which attack the nerve proximal to this region and therefore show no ophthalmoscopic changes, so that the diagnosis has to be made on the basis of symptoms alone:
      • Retrobulbar neuritis
  • The most common associated cause is a demyelinating disorder of the nerve, as occurs in other tracts of the white matter of the central nervous system (multiple sclerosis).

Clinical features

  • Monocular sudden, progressive and profound visual loss is the hallmark of acute optic neuritis.
  • Dark adaptation may be lowered.
  • Visual obscuration in bright light is a typical symptom of acute optic neuritis.
  • Impairment of color vision is always present in optic neuritis.
  • Presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect or Marcus Gunn pupil is of greater diagnostic significance, indicating a defect in the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex due to a pathological lesion in the optic nerve.
  • Depth perception may be impaired, particularly for the moving object.
  • Visual acuity is usually reduced markedly.
  • Visual field changes
    • The most common field defect in optic neuritis is a relative central or centrocecal scotoma.
  • Contrast sensitivity is impaired.

Treatment:

  • Conservative management:
    • Observation and Monitoring.
    • Only for mild symptoms but not recommended for severe cases or first episodes.
  • High-dose corticosteroids: Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) followed by oral prednisolone taper as established by the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial). Indications:
    • Severe vision loss
    • No history of previous episodes
    • MRI evidence of demyelination

Explanation of other options:

Cataract (Option A): Cataract is a gradual opacification of the lens, most commonly due to aging, leading to blurred vision; it is not associated with painful eye movements and does not typically occur following trauma.

Glaucoma (Option C): Glaucoma is less likely because it is a chronic condition that develops gradually, usually associated with raised intraocular pressure, optic nerve damage, and visual field loss, and it does not typically present acutely after trauma with a non-reactive pupil and painful eye movements.

Pupil sphincter tear (Option D): Tears in the sphincter may occur after blunt eye trauma and results in persistent pupillary dilation, but are not assocated with painful ocular movements.

question_text: Which of the following is the first clinical sign of IIH?

• Signs vary but one of the first is a blurring of the margins of the optic disc.

  • The disc becomes hyperaemic and gradually, progressive oedema extends over the surface of the disc reducing the size of the physiological cup, blurring the temporal margin and spreading into the surrounding retina.
  • The disc swells, the veins become congested and turgescent; their pulsations may be absent even on applying pressure on the globe.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Thyroid related optic neuropathy is/are incorrect?
option_a: Irradiation has no role in management
option_b: Optic neuropathy is more likely to develop in patients with proptosis
option_c: High dose IV Methyl prednisolone is indicated in all cases
explanation:
Thyroid-related optic neuropathy

  • In Graves disease, optic neuropathy is caused by compression of the nerve at the apex of the orbit by enlarged extraocular muscles.
  • Though visual loss is usually gradual, a rapid deterioration has also been seen to occur. The severity of optic neuropathy and the amount of proptosis are not directly interrelated and, in some patients, optic neuropathy occurs in the absence of any apparent proptosis.
  • In fact, proptosis is often a natural mechanism to decompress the orbit and those patients with tight orbits and no proptosis are more likely to develop features of optic nerve dysfunction.
  • When examined at presentation, the optic nerve head may be normal, swollen or even pale.
  • Clinical workup for evidence of neuropathy includes recording the visual acuity, colour vision and visual fields.
  • Additional tests include measuring the degree of proptosis and lagophthalmos, slit-lamp examination for exposure keratopathy, recording of intraocular pressure and testing of ocular motility.
  • Treatment depends on the extent of nerve involvement and is tailored to the individual.
  • Options include systemic steroids, orbital decompressive surgery or orbital radiation.
  • If visual loss is mild with a minimal field defect, oral steroids with careful monitoring are the norm.
  • Additional measures such as sleeping propped up, avoiding smoking and eye protection are advised.
  • If visual loss is not controlled by these measures or is severe from the outset, high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/day is administered.
  • If vision does not improve within 24–48 hours, orbital decompression is required.
  • Surgery remains an option for patients who cannot be given systemic steroids for any reason.
  • In those not considered fit for surgery, or in whom other measures are only partially effective, orbital radiation (2000 rad in 10 divided doses over a fortnight) is an alternative.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: A 30-year-old woman has bilateral optic atrophy, bilateral deafness, cataracts, and epiretinal membranes. Assuming that all of these findings are due to a single underlying condition, for which diagnosis should she be evaluated?
explanation:
Explanation:

This constellation of findings is characteristic of Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), a tumor-predisposition syndrome. The diagnosis is strongly suggested by:

  • Bilateral deafness: The hallmark of NF2, caused by bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas).
  • Cataracts: Juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts are a very common and early ocular finding.
  • Epiretinal membranes: A known ocular association.
  • Optic atrophy: Can be a secondary sign resulting from optic nerve sheath meningiomas or optic nerve gliomas, which are also associated with NF2.

Explanation of Other Options:

(A) Pseudotumor cerebri: This condition causes optic disc edema (papilledema) from elevated intracranial pressure, which can lead to secondary optic atrophy. However, it is not associated with deafness or cataracts.

(C) Multiple sclerosis: Associated with inflammatory optic neuropathy (optic neuritis), which can lead to optic atrophy, but it does not typically cause deafness or the specific type of cataracts seen in NF2.

(D) Joubert's syndrome: This is a rare genetic disorder characterized by cerebellar abnormalities and ocular motor apraxia. Its clinical features do not match the patient's presentation.

question_text: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a history of rapidly progressing, painless swelling and forward displacement of his right eye over the past two weeks. The clinical presentation is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The key feature in this case is the rapid onset of unilateral proptosis in a young child. This clinical presentation is the classic hallmark of orbital rhabdomyosarcoma.
  • Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor of childhood, typically presenting in the first decade of life. It arises from primitive mesenchymal cells and grows very quickly, causing a dramatic forward displacement of the eyeball. The embryonal subtype is the most common variety.

Explanation of Other Options:

Retinoblastoma (Option B): Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular (inside the eyeball) malignancy in children. Proptosis is a late sign that occurs when the tumor has grown to a very large size and has extended outside of the globe. The initial signs are typically leukocoria (white pupil) and strabismus.

Orbital varices (Option C): These are congenital venous malformations that cause intermittent proptosis. The proptosis characteristically increases with any Valsalva maneuver (e.g., crying, coughing, or straining), which raises venous pressure. The swelling in this patient is constant and rapidly progressive, not intermittent.

Lymphoma (Option D): While lymphoma can occur in the orbit in children, it typically presents with a more subacute or slowly progressive proptosis, not the rapid evolution described in this case.

Reference: Parson's Diseases of the Eye, 22nd Edition, Page Number-495.

question_text: A mother brings her child to eye OPD with complaint of difficulty in watching blackboard. What could be the most probable reason?
explanation:
Explanation:

A child with difficulty reading the blackboard is unable to see distant objects clearly, which indicates nearsightedness (myopia).

Myopia

  • Also known as short-sightedness, it is the condition in which parallel light rays from infinity, as they refract on cornea and lens, converge at a focus in front of the retina.
  • Based on the degree of refractive error myopia can be:
    • Low: < 3D
    • Medium: -3 to -6D
    • High: > 6D
  • The only symptom in low myopia may be indistinct distant vision.
  • In other cases and in high myopia, there is often, in addition, discomfort after near work, due largely to disproportion between the efforts of accommodation and convergence often leading to exophoria.
  • The eyes may be sensitive to light and black spots may be seen floating before them, and sometimes flashes of light are noticed.

Management:

  • Concave lens in the form of spectacle or contact lenses are used to correct myopia.

Surgical management

Surgical correction is only undertaken in individuals 21 years and older who have a stable refractive error for at least 1 year.

  • Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis
    • Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis or LASIK with the excimer laser is the most popular and widely accepted treatment modality among all the choices available at present.
  • Refractive Lenticule Extraction (SMILE):
    • A minimally invasive laser procedure where a small lenticule is removed to reshape the cornea.
    • Effective for myopia up to -10 D, with or without astigmatism.
  • Phakic Intraocular Lens (IOL) Implantation:
    • Implantable lens placed without removing the natural lens.
    • Best for myopia exceeding -8 D, especially in patients unsuitable for laser surgery.

Explanation of other options:

Hypermetropia (Option B): Hypermetropia, also called farsightedness, is a condition in which, when the eye is at rest, parallel light rays focus behind the retina. Because the eye can use accommodation to adjust, distant objects are seen more clearly than near objects.

Ambylopia (Option C): Amblyopia refers to the partial loss of vision, in one or both eyes, in the absence of ophthalmoscopic or other marked objective signs.

Anisometropia (Option D): This is the condition in which the refractive state of the two eyes shows a considerable difference. Hypermetropia can cause eye strain; mild cases retain imperfect binocular vision, while higher degrees result in monocular vision.

question_text: When selecting the strength of an intraocular lens (IOL) for a child under 1 year old, what factors should be considered?
explanation:
Explanation:

The primary factor is the myopic shift. A child's eye continues to grow and elongate after birth. This axial elongation naturally induces a myopic shift, meaning the eye becomes more nearsighted over time. To compensate for this anticipated change and avoid high myopia in adulthood, a lower-power IOL is intentionally implanted. This strategy aims for initial hypermetropia, expecting the eye's growth to shift the refraction towards emmetropia.

Explanation of other options:

Hypermetropic shift (Option B): This is not a typical phenomenon in a growing child's eye; the natural progression is towards myopia (myopic shift).

Length of the lens capsule and Growth of the lens capsule (Options C and D): While the overall size and growth of the eye (axial length) are critical for IOL power calculation, the specific dimensions of the lens capsule itself are not the primary deciding factor for the power of the IOL.

Key Takeaways:

  • The infant eye undergoes a predictable myopic shift due to axial growth.
  • IOL power selection in infants aims for initial hypermetropia to accommodate this future growth.

References: Choice of IOL power in pediatric cataract

question_text: Presently surgical treatment of choice in a 22 year male with - 10D myopia is:
explanation:
Phakic intraocular lenses, or phakic lenses, are lenses made of plastic or silicone that are implanted into the eye permanently to reduce a person's need for glasses or contact lenses. Phakic refers to the fact that the lens is implanted into the eye without removing the eye's natural lens. During phakic lens implantation surgery, a small incision is made in the front of the eye. The phakic lens is inserted through the incision and placed just in front of or just behind the iris.

Implantation of phakic intraocular lenses (pIOLs) is a reversible refractive procedure, preserving the patient’s accommodative function with minimal induction of higher order aberrations compared with corneal photoablative procedures.

The PRL is a pIOL indicated for the correction of moderate-to-high myopia as well as some degrees of hyperopia. It is a monofocal spherical lens with two different geometries: biconcave for myopia correction and concave–convex for hyperopia correction.

Reference: Khurana Optics 2/e

question_text: True about aphakia
option_b: Spherical aberrations producing a 'pin cushion effect'
option_c: A 'jack-in-the-box' ring scotoma from prismatic effects at the edge of the lens
explanation:
Aphakia

  • The retinal image of the aphakic eye wearing spectacles is about a quarter (25%) larger than the emmetropic retinal image.
  • Hence vision of 6/6 with a correcting lens after extraction is not quite as good as it seems.
  • Owing to the disparity of the images, any attempt to correct unilateral aphakia with spectacles when there is good vision in the other eye leads to an intolerable diplopia.
  • With contact lenses, comfortable binocular vision may be attained.
  • However, IOLs are by far the best method for optical correction of aphakia.
  • In addition to the hypermetropia, there is always some astigmatism in those cases in which a corneal or corneoscleral section has been made.
  • If the sutureless, phacoemulsification incision is in the upper part of the cornea, the astigmatism is 'against the rule' since the cornea is flattened in the vertical meridian.
  • The astigmatism usually amounts to 0.5-1 D. If an extracapsular cataract surgery is performed with sutures, and the section is in the upper part of the cornea, 'with the rule' astigmatism, generally from 1 D to 3 D, is common.
  • This reduces after suture removal and gradually diminishes thereafter. The difficulties of aphakia and its correction by spectacles include the following:
  • An image magnification of about 25-30%.
  • Spherical aberrations producing a 'pin cushion effect'.
  • Lack of physical coordination.
  • A 'jack-in-the-box' ring scotoma from prismatic effects at the edge of the lens.
  • Prismatic errors resulting from displaced optical centres of the lenses.
  • Reduced visual fields and poor eccentric acuity.
  • Inaccurate correction because of erroneous vertex distances and Physical inconvenience and cosmetic deficiency of heavy spectacle lenses.

Reference: Parson 22/e section II chapter 8 pg. 76-77 aphakia

question_text: Refraction a point of light cannot be made to produce a punctate image upon the retina by any spherical correcting lens is called as
explanation:
• In this condition of refraction, a point of light cannot be made to produce a punctate image upon the retina by any spherical correcting lens.
  • Regular astigmatism, the only form susceptible to optical correction by spectacle lenses, invariably produces some defect in visual acuity.
  • It is particularly liable to cause the worst forms of asthenopia or eye strain; the asthenopia in these cases is only in part accommodative.
  • It is often worse in the lower degrees of astigmatism than in the higher because of endeavors to accommodate so as to produce a circle of least diffusion upon the retina.
  • Aching of the eyes and headache are common symptoms; the eyes quickly become fatigued with reading and the letters are described as 'running together'.
  • Regular astigmatism is usually a congenital defect, due in most part to differences in the curvature of the cornea in different meridians.
  • It must be remembered that frequently it is not the cornea alone which is at fault, for corneal astigmatism may be increased or partially corrected by lenticular astigmatism.
  • Regular astigmatism may be traumatic following a wound, frequently surgical such as in the corneoscleral margin following cataract surgery, since contraction of the scar after extracapsular cataract extraction causes flattening of the cornea in the meridian at right angles to the wound.
  • Tight sutures further accentuate this effect by causing corneal steepening in the same axis as the tight suture. Astigmatism due to this cause continues to alter for some weeks after the injury; therefore, final spectacles should not be ordered for at least 6 weeks thereafter.
  • Following sutureless surgery by phacoemulsification there is usually some flattening of the cornea in the axis of the wound.
  • Higher degrees of astigmatism cause a lowering of visual acuity; this is usually least in mixed astigmatism, probably because the circle of least diffusion falls upon or near the retina

Reference: Parson ch 8, P. 80

question_text: What is not True about these IOLs?
option_a: Good for both correcting near and distance vision
option_c: Best for persons who have astigmatism
option_d: Can be placed in FLACS surgery
explanation:
Explanation:

The pictured lens is a multifocal IOL, useful for correcting both near and distance vision (Option A) but associated with glare and haloes (Option B). For preexisting astigmatism, toric lenses are used (not necessarily multifocal), so statement C is not True. Multifocal IOLs can be implanted during femtosecond-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS).

Multifocal IOLs

  • Toric IOLs are used for pre-existing astigmatism.
  • The lens shown is a multifocal IOL, used to correct both near and distance vision.

Refractive Multifocal IOLs

  • "Bull's-eye" design
  • Concentric rings with different refractive powers

Diffractive Multifocal IOLs

  • Anterior aspheric surface
  • Provides basic refractive power
  • Multiple grooves on the posterior surface enabling diffractive optics

Key Takeaways:

Multifocal IOLs provide spectacle independence for near and distance but are not inherently ideal for uncorrected high astigmatism unless toric-multifocal variants used.

question_text: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the SAFE strategy for controlling trachoma. In this acronym, what does the letter S represent?
explanation:
Explanation:

Surgery addresses tertiary prevention by treating advanced complications of trachoma, such as trichiasis and entropion, which, if left untreated, may cause corneal scarring and permanent blindness. Therefore, the S in SAFE stands for Surgery.

Management of Trachoma:

Investigations:

  • Micro-immunofluorescence (micro-IF): Uses pooled antigens; primarily for routine diagnosis.
  • Culture of Chlamydia trachomatis: Grown in irradiated McCoy cells; expensive and technically demanding.
  • Monoclonal antibody direct tests: IgA-IPA light microscopy offers a reliable diagnostic combination.

SAFE Strategy (WHO-recommended interventions):

  • Surgery (Tertiary prevention): Corrects cicatricial entropion and trichiasis
  • Antibiotics (Secondary prevention): Eliminate C. trachomatis infection.
  • Facial cleanliness (Primary prevention): Prevents transmission.
  • Environmental improvements (Primordial prevention):
    • Access to clean water and latrines
    • Proper disposal of refuse
    • Controlling fly populations
    • Keeping animal pens away from living areas
    • Health education

Facial Cleanliness (Primary prevention):

  • Frequent washing of the face with clean water
  • Avoid sharing towels, handkerchiefs, or cosmetic tools (e.g., Surma rods)

Community-Based Mass Antibiotic Therapy:

  • ≥10% prevalence (active trachoma in 1–9 years):
    • Single oral dose of azithromycin 20 mg/kg for all community members
    • Tetracycline 1% eye ointment BD for 6 weeks for pregnant women, children, or macrolide-allergic individuals
    • Continue until prevalence drops below 5%
  • 5–10% prevalence: Targeted therapy for affected families and close contacts
  • <5% prevalence: Only treat affected patients

Blanket (Intermittent) Therapy:

  • Indicated when >5% of children (1–9 years) have moderate to severe trachoma
  • Apply 1% tetracycline ointment to all children:
  • Twice daily for 5 consecutive days each month, for 6 months, OR
  • Once daily for 10 consecutive days each month, for 6 months, OR
  • Continuous application for 60 days
  • Alternative: Erythromycin

Surgery Techniques (Tertiary prevention):

  • Simple epilation
  • Repair procedures
  • Bilamellar tarsal rotation

Explanation of Other Options:

Symptom (Option B): Not part of the SAFE acronym; symptomatic relief alone does not prevent blindness.

Spectacles (Option C): Not included in the SAFE strategy, and does not address the underlying cause or complications.

Symbol (Option D): Not relevant; SAFE interventions are practical public health measures, not symbolic actions.

Reference:

  1. Antibiotics for trachoma - PMC
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559035/
  3. Intermittent trachoma chemotherapy: a controlled trial of topical tetracycline or erythromycin - PMC

question_text: A patient presents with orbicularis oculi paresis, lagophthalmos & insensitive cornea leading to blindness, which of the following condition may be responsible for the same?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely cause is leprosy in this patient; in leprosy, Mycobacterium leprae invades peripheral nerves, including the facial nerve and ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerves, causing orbicularis oculi paralysis (lagophthalmos) and corneal anaesthesia.

Ocular Involvement in Leprosy

  • Eye involvement in leprosy is usually indirect, resulting from neuroparalytic and neurotrophic keratopathy due to involvement of the facial (VII) and trigeminal (V1)
  • The eyes may also be affected during lepra reactions (Type I and II).
  • Lepromatous leprosy
    • Ocular disease occurs late and may begin with conjunctivitis, episcleritis, or keratitis.
    • May progress to uveitis, iris atrophy, small non-reacting pupils, corneal and lens opacities, and eventual visual loss.
    • These changes are due to heavy bacillary load and immune complex-mediated inflammation (e.g., erythema nodosum leprosum).
  • Tuberculoid leprosy
    • Uveitis is rare, but granulomatous inflammation around peripheral nerves can cause facial nerve palsy or trigeminal nerve damage.
    • Facial nerve palsy leads to lagophthalmos and exposure keratopathy, or trigeminal nerve damage, results in corneal anesthesia and neurotrophic keratitis.
  • Complications: Corneal ulceration, perforation, and blindness.

Explanation of other options:

Lyme's disease (Option A): Lyme's disease is caused by borrelia burgdorferi, a spirochete. It can cause facial nerve palsy, leading to lagophthalmos, but corneal anaesthesia or blindness are not uncommon.

Ophthalmia neonatorum (Option C): Refers to severe conjunctivitis in newborns, usually due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis, presenting as purulent discharge. It shows no nerve involvement.

Trachoma (Option D): Trachoma, caused by chlamydia trachomatis, causes blindness due to corneal scarring and is not associated with corneal anaesthesia or lagophthalmos.

question_text: On examination, a patient was found to have orbicularis oculi paresis, lagophthalmos, insensitive cornea. Which of the following might be responsible for the scenario?
explanation:
Ocular involvement in leprosy

The eye may be involved in leprosy in several ways, depending on the immune status of the patient. Ocular involvement is more common in lepromatous leprosy, where direct invasion of the globe by M. leprae can occur, probably through the bloodstream.

M. leprae has a known affinity for cooler parts of the body and therefore has a particular attraction to the superficial structures of the face and the anterior segment of the eye. Rarely there is involvement of structures posterior to the equator.

The most frequent ocular manifestation in lepromatous leprosy is uveitis, commonly in the form of chronic low-grade iridocyclitis. In such cases, the presence of iris pearls is pathognomonic, representing dead M. leprae bacillus that progressively enlarged, coalesce, become pedunculated and lodge in the anterior chamber. Inflammation also promotes cataract development and intraocular hypotony. In later stages of the disease large areas of iris atrophy and miotic pupils may be noted, as a result of chronic inflammation and of sympathetic nerve involvement of the pupillary dilator muscle.

Corneal involvement in leprosy can also occur, in the form of visible beaded corneal nerves, interstitial keratitis, avascular keratitis and corneal leproma.

In tuberculoid leprosy, ocular manifestations result from lid closure impairment and reduced corneal sensation, through involvement of the facial nerve and of the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve. Corneal opacification resulting from exposure keratopathy and chronic neurotrophic keratitis can cause significant visual impairment. Lacrimal gland involvement can result in dry eye and conjunctival keratinization. Miotic pupils in multibacillary leprosy, combined with cataract can also contribute to low visual acuity.

Scleritis can also happen, as a result of direct infiltration by M. leprae or due to a lepromatous erythema nodosum reaction, although episcleritis is more common than scleritis.

Acute inflammatory reactions affecting the facial nerve, cornea and iris are a feature of Type I and Type 2 reactions and may cause severe damage to the eye either directly or indirectly.

List of possible ocular complications in leprosy:

Lids: madarosis, blepharochalasis, nodules, ectropion, entropion, lagophthalmos, reduced blinking, trichiasis

Cornea: thickened corneal nerves, superficial stromal keratitis, corneal anesthesia, pannus, exposure keratopathy, intersticial keratitis, band shaped keratopathy, corneal leproma.

Iris: acute iritis (synechiae, secondary glaucoma, secondary cataract, seclusio pupillae), chronic iritis (iris pearls, iris atrophy, miosis, corectopia, polycoria, secondary cataract), iris leproma.

Ciliary body: loss of accommodation, hypotonia, phthisis.

Sclera: episcleritis, scleritis, nodules, staphyloma.

Lens: cataract.

Fundus: peripheral choroidal lesions, retinal vasculitis, papillitis

Lacrimal system: acute dacryocystitis, chronic dacryocystitis.

Clinical diagnosis

Diagnosis of leprosy is made through clinical criteria, namely the existence of: hypopigmented or reddish skin lesions with definite sensory loss, with or without thickened peripheral nerves and acid-fast bacilli identified on skin smears or biopsy samples. There is also a classification of disease based on bacteriological criteria, distinguishing between paucibacillary leprosy and multibacillary leprosy and this distinction has implications on which treatment regimen to choose. Regarding skin smears: patients with negative smears at all sites are considered to have paucibacillary leprosy, while those with positive smears at any site are considered to have multibacillary leprosy. However, in practice, clinical criteria are usually used to distinguish between paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy, since skin smears are not always available. Regarding the number of skin lesions: one to five skin lesions corresponds to paucibacillary leprosy and more than five skin lesions corresponds to multibacillary leprosy. Paucibacillary leprosy includes the tuberculoid form of the disease and the borderline tuberculoid form, while multibacillary leprosy includes the remaining borderline forms and the lepromatous form of the disease.

Management

Treatment of leprosy includes multidrug oral therapy and its duration depends on the type of infection (paucibacillary vs multibacillary). First line drugs are rifampin, dapsone and clofazimine, but minocycline and ofloxacin are occasionally used in cases where only one skin lesion exists.

WHO recommended multidrug treatment regimens are the following:

For Multibacillary leprosy, the standard regimen in adults has a 12 months duration and includes: Rifampin 600 mg once a month, Dapsone 100 mg daily and Clofazimine 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily. For Paucibacillary leprosy the regimen as a 6 months duration and includes: Rifampin 600 mg once a month and Dapsone 100 mg daily. If only a single skin lesion exists, the regimen includes a single dose of: Rifampin 600 mg, Ofloxacin 400 mg and Minocycline 100 mg.

Management of uveitis requires topical corticosteroids and eventually oral corticosteroids to manage acute exacerbations. Phenylephrine is used to keep pupils mobile, in order to prevent miosis

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Option A: Acanthamoeba castellanii - Causes Acanthamoeba keratitis, associated with contact lens wear and severe corneal ulceration, but does not cause nerve palsy or corneal anesthesia.

Option B: Onchocerca volvulus - Causes river blindness (onchocerciasis), leading to punctate keratitis, sclerosing keratitis, and chorioretinitis, but does not cause lagophthalmos or orbicularis paresis.

Option D: Chlamydia A-C - Causes trachoma, leading to chronic follicular conjunctivitis and corneal scarring, but does not affect facial or trigeminal nerves.

Key Takeaway:

The combination of orbicularis paresis, lagophthalmos, and corneal anesthesia strongly suggests ocular leprosy due to Mycobacterium leprae

question_text: In the image, what are the associated complications observed in a 35-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The scenario is consistent with scleromalacia perforans, a severe ocular manifestation of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
  • It presents as painless scleral thinning with a bluish hue due to visibility of the underlying uveal tissue.
  • The pathogenesis is related to type III hypersensitivity-mediated vasculitis causing ischemia and progressive scleral melt.

Scleromalacia Perforans

  • Epidemiology: More common in elderly women with established RA.
  • Pathophysiology: Obliteration of the episcleral and scleral vasculature → ischemia → thinning and softening of sclera.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Painless thinning of sclera
    • Dark uveal tissue visible beneath
    • Rarely progresses to perforation of the globe
  • Treatment:
    • Protective measures to avoid trauma
    • Artificial tears for lubrication
    • Systemic NSAIDs or corticosteroids
    • Immunomodulatory therapy for refractory cases
    • Surgical scleral patch grafting in advanced thinning

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Ciliary staphyloma (Option B): Refers to localized bulging of the uveal tissue through weakened sclera near the ciliary body, often secondary to trauma or severe inflammation, not directly linked to rheumatoid arthritis.

Coloboma (Option C): A congenital defect due to incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure; unrelated to autoimmune conditions like RA.

Malignant melanoma (Option D): A pigmented intraocular tumor arising from uveal melanocytes; not an autoimmune complication and not associated with RA.

Key Takeaway:

Patients with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis are at risk of developing scleromalacia perforans, a painless but vision-threatening scleral thinning disorder caused by ischemic necrosis from autoimmune vasculitis.

Scleromalacia Perforans - EyeWiki

Parotid tumour surgery on the same side can lead to damage of facial nerve which can itself cause lagophthalmos on same side (inability to close eyelid). Hence corneal exposure in the lower half of cornea can occur leading to exposure / neuroparalytic ulcer.

question_text: A 64-year-old woman with a history of trauma to the left eye 5 days back now presented with complaints of complete loss of vision. Upon examination the following findings were seen. What should be the subsequent course of action to manage this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The history of ocular trauma, accompanied by complete vision loss and clinical findings such as congestion and corneal perforation, strongly suggests uncontrolled keratitis most commonly due to a bacterial infection. In such cases, when the infection has penetrated the cornea, the preferred treatment is keratoplasty.

Penetrating Keratoplasty (PK):

This is a type of allograft (also referred to as Allo-Keratoplasty), where a full-thickness section of the patient's damaged cornea is replaced with a healthy donor cornea.

It is indicated when there is:

  • Corneal perforation
  • Severe infection
  • Loss of corneal transparency that is not manageable by medical therapy

PK helps restore vision, maintain globe integrity, and eliminate the infectious source when medical therapy alone is insufficient.

Indications for Penetrating Keratoplasty:

Complications:

  • Early Complications:
    • Flat anterior chamber
    • Iris prolapse
    • Infection
    • Secondary glaucoma
    • Epithelial defects
    • Primary graft failure
  • Late Complications:
    • Graft rejection
    • Recurrence of disease
    • Astigmatism

Explanation for other options:

Keratotomy (Option B): It is a surgical procedure primarily used to correct refractive errors. It works by flattening the cornea, thereby reducing its focusing power, and is typically performed in cases of myopia (nearsightedness).

LASIK (Option C): It stands for Laser-Assisted In Situ Keratomileusis. It is commonly performed for refractive correction and involves reshaping the curvature of the cornea to improve focus and reduce dependency on glasses or contact lenses.

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) (Option D): IT is a procedure done to treat chronic dacryocystitis, which is inflammation or infection of the lacrimal sac. The surgery creates a new drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity to relieve the blockage

question_text: Which of the following is/are not complications noted in early post-operative period of keratoplasty?
explanation:
Complications in the early postoperative period include wound leak, shallow anterior chamber, persistent or nonhealing epithelial defect, secondary glaucoma, graft oedema, uveitis, graft infection, inflammatory ‘sterile’ suture infiltrates and primary graft failure.

  • In the late postoperative period (after 3 weeks), complications include graft
  • rejection, graft infection, secondary glaucoma, loose sutures and high astigmatism.
  • Very late complications (after 1 year) include graft rejection and wound dehiscence from minor trauma and recurrence of the primary disease.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

question_text: What is the most common cause of cystoid macular edema that demonstrates a fluorescein angiographic hyperfluorescent cystic ("petaloid") pattern?
explanation:
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) as retinal thickening of the macula due to a disruption of the normal blood-retinal barrier; this causes leakage from the perifoveal retinal capillaries and accumulation of fluid within the intracellular spaces of the retina, primarily in the outer plexiform layer

Of the causes listed, cataract surgery is the most common cause of clinical and angiographic cystoid macular edema. Retinitis pigmentosa is a rare cause of CME. Although choroidal neovascularization may be associated with cystic retinal thickening on optical coherence tomography, it rarely demonstrates a hyperfluorescent cystic pattern.

Blurry vision associated with CME has been reported in doses greater than 1.5g/day

CME occurs with niacin but leakage is not reported.

Niacin toxicity does not demonstrate retinal cystic hyperfluorescence.

CME that does not demonstrate leakage on FA include:

  • Juvenile retinoschisis
  • Goldmann-Favre disease
  • Certain types of RP
  • Nicotinic Acid maculopathy
  • Phototoxicity
  • Antimicrotubule agents

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/630

question_text: Which condition most commonly leads to cystoid macular edema that shows a classic "petaloid" hyperfluorescent pattern on fluorescein angiography?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the listed causes, post-cataract surgery CME (Irvine Gass syndrome) is the most common clinical and angiographic cause and classically demonstrates the petaloid hyperfluorescent pattern on fluorescein angiography.

  • Cystoid macular edema results from breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, leading to leakage from perifoveal capillaries and fluid accumulation within the outer plexiform layer of the retina.
  • Retinitis pigmentosa (Option A): CME can occur in retinitis pigmentosa but it is an uncommon cause, and when present may not always show the typical hyperfluorescent petaloid leakage patternon FFA.
  • · Niacin (Option B): High doses of niacin can cause CME, but FFA usually does NOT show leakage, so the petaloid hyperfluorescence pattern is typically absent.
  • · Choroidal neovascularization (Option D): CNV can lead to macular edema and cystic changes on OCT, but the pattern is due to leakage from neovascular membranes, and does not characteristically produce a petaloid cystic pattern on fluorescein angiography.

question_text: Which vitamin in supraphysiologic doses causes macular oedema and a a macular cyst ?
explanation:
CME is a disorder that involves the central retina, caused by an accumulation of extracellular fluid in the macular region with secondary formation of multiple cystic spaces. Histological studies show that radially orientated cystoid spaces consisting of ophthalmoscopically clear fluid are often clinically detectable in the macula area. These cysts seem to be areas of the retina in which the cells have been displaced. It is the result of cystic accumulation of extracellular intraretinal fluid in the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers of the retina.

The exact pathogenesis of CME remains uncertain. CME following disruption of the blood-retinal barrier (BRB). When the BRB is damaged, fluid accumulates within the retina both intra- and extracellularly . Müller cells are thought to play an important role in acting as metabolic pumps that keep the macula dehydrated. However, intracellular fluid accumulation in the Müller cells may also occur in CME and further reduce macular retinal function. Vitreous traction may also play a part in the development of CME . Macular edema is the most frequent and severe complications of pars planitis, HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis, sarcoidosis, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, Behcet's syndrome, toxoplasmosis, Eales' disease, idiopathic vitritis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and scleritis. CME can follow cataract surgery in the Irvine-Gass syndrome, because after cataract surgery, inflammatory mediators from the anterior chamber diffuse posteriorly into the vitreous, causing leakage from the retinal vasculature.

CME is the consequence of diabetic retinopathy. The edema in the macular area occurs secondary to an abnormal permeability of the capillaries surrounding the macula (failure of inner retinal blood barrier), and in turn to a failure in the outer retinal barrier (formed by the retinal pigmented epithelium). Retinal vein obstructions (RVO) represent another cause of CME. Increased rigidity of a crossing artery because an atherosclerotic process has been suggested to cause compression of the underlying vein, provoking turbulent blood flow, endothelial damage, and thrombus formation. Likewise, a common vitreous adhesion at the obstruction site has also been reported, suggesting a possible role of vitreovascular traction in the etiology of some cases of BRVO. Atherosclerosis is a chronic low-grade inflammatory disorder and inflammation within the vascular wall contributes to the development of CME . Due to BRB breakdown secondary to damage at the tight junctions of endothelial cells, fluid diffusion from the occluded veins into the tissue can lead to CME. In addition, through such mechanisms, inflammatory responses and vascular dysfunction can all interact to cause retinal ischemia, which induces the expression of VEGF and others inflammatory agents, which participate in a complex chain of events that has yet to be fully defined.

Many authors reported ocular side effect after therapy with niacin. Fraunfelder et al. reported that 3 g or more per day of nicotinic acid, could cause blurred vision, eyelid edema, toxic amblyopia, proptosis, loss of eyelashes or eyebrow, superficial punctate keratitis and CME. Some cases of blurred vision were reported in the literature , and 18 cases were reported to the National Registry or the FDA spontaneous reporting system. In these cases, the average dose of niacin was 1.5-2 g per day, with a duration of therapy varying from 6 weeks to 1 year. Follow-up reported complete resolution of visual symptoms after discontinuing niacin. Dry eye was explained because this vitamin may be secreted and concentrated in human tears, thereby irritating an already dry eye. Niacin can cause ocular signs and symptoms reversible dose related, so if the patient wishes to continue this therapy, it may be feasible to reduce the dose of the drug . Cases of niacin related maculopathy there is a 10:1 male: female ratio. Most cases were in their third to fifth decade of life and were being treated with an average dose of 3-6 g of niacin per day. The etiology of niacin's effect on the macula is unknown, A first hypothesis suggests that, in patients with vascular or inflammatory diseases, niacin induces the release of prostaglandins, causing the blood-retinal barrier compromise with extracellular accumulation of fluid in many cystic spaces. This theory is not entirely accepted for the absence of fluorescein leakage.

The second and the most reliable hypothesis supports that the niacin has a direct toxic effect on Müller cells, without disruption of the blood-retinal-barrier. Alterations in cellular metabolism cause intracellular fluid increase and swelling of these cells, with secondary formation of cysts between the glial spaces. After the discontinuation of niacin therapy, there is a complete regeneration of the Müller cells and their normal function . Reports from the literature suggest that the onset of maculopathy ranges from 1 to 36 months after initiation of relatively high-dose therapy (3 g or more daily). There have also been reports of this condition with lower dosages (1.5 g daily). This patient had increased the dosage of niacin to 3 g daily nearly 2 months before documentation of CME. In a previous case report a very low dose of niacin was administered (18 mg) and niacin maculopathy appears 4 weeks later with a complete resolution after discontinuation of drug, confirming the relationship between drug administration and macular edema appearance. In this patient, funduscopic examination showed bilateral macular edema, but no signs of diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy excluding the presence of other factors that may contribute to the capillary dysfunction associated with edema onset. At funduscopic examination, the foveomacular area had a peculiar aspect: the foveola takes on a bright yellow hue, similar to an exudate. Cysts primarily involve the foveal area, and they are smaller than those seen in post-surgical or inflammatory CME . FA and OCT are useful to confirm the diagnosis. FA showed the absence of fluorescein leakage or vascular alteration, whereas OCT confirms the presence of cystic hyporeflective spaces in the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers. The cystoid spaces were more numerous and larger in the outer plexiform layer compared with the inner nuclear layer. Indeed previous studies reported that the fluor-angiographic pattern is atypical.

On the left, there is an image of Stratus OCT 2 weeks after the start of niacin treatment. On the right fluorescein angiography of the same patient after 3 weeks after the beginning of niacin treatment with the typical absence of leakage also in later phases

Gass described reversible bilateral CME with no angiographic fluorescein leakage in 3 patients taking doses of niacin greater than 1.5 g daily to treat hyperlipidemia . Although Gass described transmitted hyper-fluorescence with a cartwheel pattern in the fluorescein angiograms of his patients, later reports described typical fluorescence in similarly affected patients. In all these cases, symptoms resolved over 4 to 8 weeks following discontinuation of niacin. First-line treatment for CME of toxic origin, such as that induced by niacin, is the removal of the offending agent. In milder cases of maculopathy, symptoms have resolved within a few days of drug discontinuation.

Incorrect Options:

A. Vitamin-A

While Vitamin-A deficiency can lead to night blindness and other vision issues, it is not typically associated with macular edema or macular cysts. However, excessive intake of Vitamin A can lead to toxicity, but this primarily causes other issues such as hypervitaminosis A and does not generally result in macular edema or cysts.

B. Vitamin-D

While Vitamin-D toxicity is associated with hypercalcemia, which can lead to kidney stones, bone pain, and other systemic effects, but it is not typically linked to macular edema or macular cyst formation.

C. Vitamin-E

While Vitamin E is a potent antioxidant, excessive intake generally leads to bleeding and other side effects but is not commonly associated with macular edema or cyst formation.

Key Takeaway: Niacin (Vitamin B3) in supraphysiologic doses can cause macular edema and the formation of macular cysts, which is an important consideration when using niacin for treating high cholesterol or other conditions requiring high doses of this vitamin.

question_text: A 65-year-old woman with diabetes presents with a painless loss of vision. The accompanying image shows her ocular findings. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what would be the appropriate management?
option_d: Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient is a 65-year-old diabetic woman with painless loss of vision, which points towards cataracts, a common cause of visual impairment, especially in older individuals and those with diabetes.

  • Immature senile cataract refers to the early stages of cataract formation, where the lens becomes cloudy but is not yet completely opaque. This typically leads to a gradual loss of vision without pain.
  • The standard treatment for cataracts, particularly in cases with significant visual impairment, is phacoemulsification -a surgical procedure that utilises ultrasound to break up the lens, followed by its removal and the placement of an intraocular lens (IOL) to restore clear vision.

Explanation for other options:

Zonular cataract and lensectomy (Option A): Zonular cataract is a specific type of cataract involving changes to the lens fibres and zonules (the ligaments that hold the lens in place). While lensectomy (removal of the lens) can be performed, it is typically not the preferred term for routine cataract surgery, and this condition is not as commonly associated with the age and symptoms described here.

Rosette cataract and sugar control (Option B): A rosette cataract is a rare type of cataract that forms as a star-shaped pattern, usually associated with trauma or certain diseases, but it is not typically seen in diabetic patients or with the presentation described here. Sugar control is important for diabetes management, but it doesn't directly address the cataract-related vision loss.

Sunflower cataract and lesion extraction (Option C): A sunflower cataract is typically associated with Wilson's disease, a condition characterised by copper accumulation in tissues, leading to a distinctive appearance of the cataract. The patient does not have signs of Wilson's disease, and lesion extraction would not be appropriate for a cataract.

question_text: Rubella in pregnancy is an important cause in causing which of the following cataracts?
explanation:
Explanation:

Nuclear cataract usually affects the embryonic nucleus. Rubella in pregnancy is an important cause.

Congenital Rubella Nuclear Cataract

  • Early developmental inhibition of the lens → embryonal nuclear cataract
    • Central nucleus remains opaque
    • Often of limited visual significance unless progressive
  • Progressive congenital nuclear cataract is associated with maternal rubella infection (especially 2nd month, sometimes 3rd month of pregnancy)
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Virus reaches fetus before immune system develops → extensive cellular parasitism
    • Interferes with DNA → RNA translation
    • Lens nucleus becomes necrotic → entire lens may become opaque
  • Ocular findings:
    • Dense, unilateral or bilateral nuclear opacities present at birth or developing within weeks-months
    • Congenital rubella retinitis: fine pigmentary "salt-and-pepper" appearance at posterior pole
  • Systemic associations:
    • Congenital heart disease (PDA)
    • Microphthalmos
    • Microencephaly
    • Mental retardation
    • Deafness
    • Dental anomalies
  • Complications:
    • Chronic inflammatory endophthalmitis if residual lens matter remains after aspiration
  • Prevention:
    • MMR vaccination in primary schedule
    • Rubella vaccine for prepubertal girls and rubella-antibody-negative women planning pregnancy
  • Additional note:
    • Lamellar (zonular) cataract may also occur with congenital rubella

Key Takeaways:

Maternal rubella (first trimester especially) → nuclear (embryonic) cataract; can present at birth or later.

question_text: A patient develops endophthalmitis after cataract surgery, with vision reduced to hand movements. What is the appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

Acute endophthalmitis is an inflammation of the internal structures of the eye, including the uveal tissue and retina, often with purulent exudates in the vitreous and anterior/posterior chambers, but sparing the sclera. It commonly occurs 1-7 days after intraocular surgery, such as cataract extraction.

Most common causative organism:

  • Staphylococcus epidermidis

Clinical presentation:

  • Severe ocular pain and redness
  • Photophobia and lacrimation
  • Loss of vision (often sudden)
  • Swollen eyelids, conjunctival chemosis, and corneal congestion
  • Cloudy cornea, ring infiltration, yellow necrotic wound edges
  • Hypopyon and edematous iris
  • Vitreous exudation causing an amaurotic "cat's-eye" reflex
  • Raised intraocular pressure initially

Treatment:

  • Intravitreal antibiotics: Immediate injection is the first-line therapy, e.g.:
    • First choice: Vancomycin 1 mg + Ceftazidime 2.25 mg
    • Second choice: Vancomycin 1 mg + Amikacin 0.4 mg
  • Topical and systemic antibiotics are adjuncts.
  • Steroids may be used under supervision.
  • Pars plana vitrectomy: Indicated if no improvement within 48-72 hours or in severe cases with vision reduced to hand movements or worse. (Option B ruled out)
  • Redo surgery is not indicated. (Option C ruled out)
  • Topical antibiotics alone are insufficient for intraocular infection. (Option D ruled out)

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559079/

question_text:
True statement regarding KF ring:
A. Seen in all patients with neurological involvement
B. Is pathognomonic for Wilson's disease
C. Resolves with desferrioxamine
D. Seen in all patients with hepatic involvement
E. Seen in superior and inferior descemet's membrane
option_c: A, B, C, D and E
explanation:
Wilson's disease is a genetic disorder in which excess copper builds up in the body. Symptoms are typically related to the brain and liver. Liver-related symptoms include vomiting, weakness, fluid build up in the abdomen, swelling of the legs, yellowish skin and itchiness. Brain-related symptoms include tremors, muscle stiffness, trouble in speaking, personality changes, anxiety, and psychosis.

Wilson's disease is caused by a mutation in the Wilson disease protein (ATP7B) gene. This protein transports excess copper into bile, where it is excreted in waste products. The condition is autosomal recessive; for a person to be affected, they must inherit a mutated copy of the gene from both parents. Diagnosis may be difficult and often involves a combination of blood tests, urine tests and a liver biopsy. Genetic testing may be used to screen family members of those affected.

Wilson's disease is typically treated with dietary changes and medication. Dietary changes involve eating a low-copper diet and not using copper cookware. Medications used include chelating agents such as trientine and d-penicillamine and zinc supplements. Complications of Wilson's disease can include liver failure, liver cancer and kidney problems. A liver transplant may be helpful to those for whom other treatments are not effective or if liver failure occurs.

Eyes: Kayser-Fleischer rings (KF rings) may be visible in the cornea of the eyes, either directly or on slit lamp examination as deposits of copper form a ring around the cornea. This is due to copper deposition in Descemet's membrane. These rings can be either dark brown, golden, or reddish-green, are 1 to 3 mm wide, and appear at the corneal limbus. They do not occur in all people with Wilson's disease and may be seen in people with chronic cholestasis. Wilson's disease is also associated with sunflower cataracts exhibited by brown or green pigmentation of the anterior and posterior lens capsule. Neither causes significant visual loss. KF rings occur in approximately 66% of diagnosed cases (more often in those with neurological symptoms rather than with liver problems).

Diagnosis

Location of the basal ganglia, the part of the brain affected by Wilson's disease

Wilson's disease may be suspected on the basis of any of the symptoms mentioned above, or when a close relative has been found to have Wilson's. Most have slightly abnormal liver function tests such as a raised aspartate transaminase, alanine transaminase and bilirubin level. If the liver damage is significant, albumin may be decreased due to an inability of damaged liver cells to produce this protein; likewise, the prothrombin time (a test of coagulation) may be prolonged as the liver is unable to produce proteins known as clotting factors. Alkaline phosphatase levels are relatively low in those with Wilson's-related acute liver failure. If there are neurological symptoms, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is usually performed; this shows hyperintensities in the part of the brain called the basal ganglia in the T2 setting. MRI may also demonstrate the characteristic "face of the giant panda" pattern.

There is no totally reliable test for Wilson's disease, but levels of ceruloplasmin and copper in the blood, as well of the amount of copper excreted in urine during a 24-hour period, are together used to form an impression of the amount of copper in the body. The gold standard-or most ideal test-is a liver biopsy.

Ceruloplasmin

Ceruloplasmin

Levels of ceruloplasmin are abnormally low (<0.2 g/L) in 80-95% of cases. It can, however, be present at normal levels in people with ongoing inflammation as it is an acute phase protein. Low ceruloplasmin is also found in Menkes disease and aceruloplasminemia, which are related to, but much rarer than Wilson's disease.

The combination of neurological symptoms, eye signs and a low ceruloplasmin level is considered sufficient for the diagnosis of Wilson's disease. In many cases, however, further tests are needed.

Serum and urine copper

Serum copper is low, which may seem paradoxical given that Wilson's disease is a disease of copper excess. However, 95% of plasma copper is carried by ceruloplasmin which is often low in Wilson's disease. Urine copper is elevated in Wilson's disease and is collected for 24 hours in a bottle with a copper-free liner. Levels above 100 μg/24h (1.6 μmol/24h) confirm Wilson's disease, and levels above 40 μg/24h (0.6 μmol/24h) are strongly indicative. High urine copper levels are not unique to Wilson's disease; they are sometimes observed in autoimmune hepatitis and in cholestasis (any disease obstructing the flow of bile from the liver to the small bowel).

In children, the penicillamine test may be used. A 500 mg oral dose of penicillamine is administered, and urine collected for 24 hours. If this contains more than 1600 μg (25 μmol), it is a reliable indicator of Wilson's disease.[clarification needed] This test has not been validated in adults.

Slit-lamp examination

The eyes of the patient are examined using a slit-lamp to look for Kayser-Fleischer rings, which are strongly associated with Wilson's Disease and are caused by copper deposition on the inner cornea in Descemet's membrane.

Liver biopsy

Once other investigations have indicated Wilson's disease, the ideal test is the removal of a small amount of liver tissue through a liver biopsy. This is assessed microscopically for the degree of steatosis and cirrhosis, and histochemistry and quantification of copper are used to measure the severity of the copper accumulation. A level of 250 μg of copper per gram of dried liver tissue confirms Wilson's disease. Occasionally, lower levels of copper are found; in that case, the combination of the biopsy findings with all other tests could still lead to a formal diagnosis of Wilson's.

In the earlier stages of the disease, the biopsy typically shows steatosis (deposition of fatty material), increased glycogen in the nucleus, and areas of necrosis (cell death). In more advanced disease, the changes observed are quite similar to those seen in autoimmune hepatitis, such as infiltration by inflammatory cells, piecemeal necrosis and fibrosis (scar tissue). In advanced disease, finally, cirrhosis is the main finding. In acute liver failure, degeneration of the liver cells and collapse of the liver tissue architecture is seen, typically on a background of cirrhotic changes. Histochemical methods for detecting copper are inconsistent and unreliable, and taken alone are regarded as insufficient to establish a diagnosis.

Genetic testing

Mutation analysis of the ATP7B gene, as well as other genes linked to copper accumulation in the liver, may be performed. Once a mutation is confirmed, it is possible to screen family members for the disease as part of clinical genetics family counseling. Regional distributions of genes associated with Wilson's disease are important to follow, as this can help clinicians design appropriate screening strategies. Since mutations of the WD gene vary between populations, research and genetic testing done in countries like the USA or United Kingdom can pose problems as they tend to have more mixed populations.

question_text: Which of the following is true about viscoelastic substances?
option_a: Cause mechanical injury to corneal endothelium
option_b: Prevents anterior chamber from collapsing during crucial steps like capsulorrhexis and IOL placement
option_c: It is inert and can be left behind after surgery
option_d: Silicone oil, perfluoropropane, and sodium hexafluoride are most commonly used substances
explanation:
Explanation:

Viscoelastic substances maintain anterior chamber stability during critical steps like capsulorrhexis and IOL implantation, preventing chamber collapse and protecting intraocular structures.

Viscoelastic substances:

  • Viscoelastic Substances are ophthalmic agents commonly used in anterior segment surgeries, such as cataract phacoemulsification.They help to:
    • Maintain anterior chamber stability
    • Protect intraocular tissues
    • Facilitate intraocular lens implantation

Common Ophthalmic Viscoelastic Devices:

  • Sodium hyaluronate (Healon, ProVisc)
  • Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC)
  • Chondroitin sulfate-based OVDs (Viscoat)

Uses of Viscoelastics in Ophthalmic Surgery:

  • Cataract Surgery: Capsulotomy, nucleus manipulation, endothelial protection
  • Corneal Surgery: Keratoplasty, DALK, DSEK, DMEK
  • Glaucoma Surgery: Trabeculectomy, viscocanalostomy
  • Retinal Surgery: Membrane separation, traction release
  • Other Uses: Strabismus surgery, pediatric cataract surgery, open globe repair, oculoplasty

Ideal Properties of Viscoelastics:

  • Clear, sterile, non-toxic, non-inflammatory, non-immunogenic
  • Good viscosity: To prevent anterior chamber collapse
  • Elastic and shock-absorbing: To protect intraocular structures
  • Retention under pressure with high cohesion and minimal surface activity
  • Easily removable to avoid obstructing aqueous outflow
  • Coatability: To protect endothelium and prevent cell loss

Complications assocaited with viscoelastics

Explanation of other options:

Cause mechanical injury to corneal endothelium (Option A): Viscoelastic substances are protective to the corneal endothelium, not damaging; however, high-viscosity OVDs (e.g., Healon GV) can elevate intraocular pressure if not fully removed, but they do not directly injure the endothelium.

It is inert and can be left behind after surgery (Option C): Viscoelastics are not inert and must be completely removed at the end of surgery to prevent postoperative IOP spikesfrom obstruction of aqueous outflow.

Silicone oil, perfluoropropane, and sodium hexafluoride are most commonly used substances (Option D): These are tamponade agents used in retinal surgeries like retinal detachment repair and are not viscoelastic substances.

Reference:

  1. Viscoelastics - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  2. Agents for Vitreous Tamponade - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: Identify the investigation being done
explanation:
Ocular biometry refers to measurement of anatomic dimensions of the eye, which include corneal curvature (keratometry), axial length, and anterior chamber depth. These measurements are primarily used to calculate the appropriate power of the IOL to be implanted during cataract surgery. In addition to axial length, ultrasound biometry can measure anterior chamber depth and lens thickness.

There are two main types of ultrasound used in ophthalmologic practice currently, a-scan and b-scan. In a-scan, or time-amplitude scan, sound waves are generated at 8 MHz and converted into spikes that correspond with tissue interface zones. In b-scan, or brightness amplitude scan, sound waves are generated at 10 MHz. The data collected by the transducer produces a corresponding image

Hydrodissection is a technique to separate the lens nucleus from the cortex and the capsule by injecting fluid, under the anterior capsule leaflet. A fluid wave can be seen as the balance salt solution (BSS) passes between the nucleus and cortex.

HHYDRODILINEATION

question_text: This golden ring sign as shown in picture is suggestive of
option_d: Usage of Femtolaser in cataract surgery
explanation:
Explanation:

Hydrodelineation separates endonucleus from epinucleus; the golden ring sign ensures complete hydrodelineation i.e., separation of endonucleus allowing easier nucleus management during phacoemulsification.

Hydrodissection & Hydrodelineation

Hydrodissection

  • Technique to separate the lens nucleus from the cortex and capsule
  • Done by injecting BSS under the anterior capsule leaflet
  • A fluid wave is seen as BSS passes between nucleus and cortex

Hydrodelineation

  • Separates the endonucleus from the epinucleus
  • Reduces the overall size of the nucleus → allows less deep and less peripheral grooving
  • Results in smaller, easily mobilized quadrants after cracking or chopping
  • Epinucleus acts as a protective cushion, containing phacoemulsification forces
  • Presence of a "golden ring sign" indicates complete hydrodelineation

Hydrodissection (Option B): Related technique (fluid wave under anterior capsule) but the golden ring indicates hydrodelineation completion.

Anterior capsulotomy (Option C): Not indicated by golden ring sign.

Usage of Femtolaser (Option D): Not represented by golden ring.

Key Takeaways:

Golden ring sign = confirms complete hydrodelineation (endonucleus separated from epinucleus) during cataract surgery.

question_text: Which dye is utilized to stain the anterior lens capsule during cataract surgery?
explanation:
Explanation:

Trypan blue is the preferred dye for highlighting the anterior lens capsule in cataract procedures, especially when visualization is challenging due to factors such as mature white cataracts or a weak red reflex.

Trypan Blue in Ophthalmic Procedures:

  • Primary Use: Improves visualization of the anterior capsule in cataract surgery, particularly in dense white cataracts or when the red reflex is poor (e.g., corneal opacities, asteroid hyalosis, vitreous hemorrhage).
  • Other Applications:
    • Stains posterior stromal fibers during Deep Lamellar Endothelial Keratoplasty (DLEK).
    • Highlights the endothelium in Descemet's Stripping Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSEK).
    • Assists in vitreoretinal surgeries by marking epiretinal membranes, internal limiting membrane, and posterior hyaloid.
    • Stains Tenon's capsule in oculoplastics, such as during enucleation.

Application Techniques:

  • Under Air Bubble: Dye is introduced beneath an air bubble in the anterior chamber.
  • Under Viscoelastic: Dye is delivered along with a viscoelastic material in theanterior chamber.
  • Both approaches are considered safe and effective, with no significant differences in surgical outcomes such as phacoemulsification time, visual recovery, corneal thickness, or endothelial cell count.

Advantages:

  • Provides more intense staining of the anterior lens capsule compared to other dyes like indocyanine green or fluorescein.
  • Convenient to use as a premixed solution and cost-effective.

Explanation of Other Options:

Brilliant blue (Option B): Although used in ophthalmic surgeries, particularly for retinal procedures, it is not the primary dye for anterior capsule staining.

Fluorescent green (Option C): Primarily utilized in fundus imaging rather than anterior lens capsule visualization.

Lissamine green (Option D): Commonly applied in ocular surface evaluations and dry eye testing, not for anterior capsule staining.

Reference:

Trypan Blue Dye: Capsular Staining for Cataract Surgery and More - American Academy of Ophthalmology

question_text: In which type of cataract surgery is suturing with 10-0 nylon commonly performed?
explanation:
Explanation:

Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) involves removal of the lens nucleus while leaving the posterior capsule intact. Since the incision is relatively large (8-10 mm at the limbus), closure with 10-0 nylon sutures is commonly performed to ensure proper sealing and prevent wound leakage.

10-0 nylon is a very fine, non-absorbable suture, ideal for ophthalmic procedures as it maintains wound strength while minimizing scarring.

ECCE Techniques

  • Conventional ECCE → Large incision (8-10 mm), nucleus expressed, sutures needed.
  • Manual SICS (Small Incision Cataract surgery) → Smaller scleral tunnel (5-7 mm), usually self-sealing and sutureless.
  • Phacoemulsification → Corneal incision (2.2-3.2 mm), self-sealing, no sutures required.
  • Microincision (MICS) → <1.8 mm incision, advanced phaco technique.

Surgical Steps of Conventional ECCE

  1. Eye stabilization with superior rectus bridle suture.
  2. Conjunctival flap creation to expose limbus.
  3. Limbal incision (partial-thickness groove).
  4. Capsulotomy → can-opener, linear, or CCC.
  5. Hydrodissection to separate nucleus.
  6. Nucleus removal (pressure/counter pressure or vectis).
  7. Cortex aspiration (I/A cannula).
  8. Posterior chamber IOL
  9. Closure with 10-0 nylon sutures.
  10. Conjunctival flap reposition + subconjunctival injections.

Advantages of ECCE over ICCE

  • Allows posterior chamber IOL placement.
  • Safer with intact zonules at any age.
  • Lower risk of vitreous loss, retinal detachment, and CME.
  • Reduced risk of postoperative astigmatism.
  • Better outcomes in diabetics and in eyes needing later glaucoma/corneal surgery.

Explanation of Other oOtions:

Phacoemulsification (Option A): Uses ultrasonic fragmentation with a very small self-sealing corneal incision. Sutures are rarely needed.

Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE) (Option C): Removes entire lens + capsule through a large incision. While sutures are used, they are not typically 10-0 nylon, as larger, stronger sutures are preferred.

Manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS) (Option D) : Designed as a sutureless, self-sealing technique. If sutures are placed, they are not as commonly 10-0 nylon as in ECCE.

question_text: Which laser is regarded as the most suitable choice for cataract surgery?
explanation:
Explanation:
The femtosecond laser is currently considered the most appropriate laser for cataract surgery, particularly in a technique known as Femtosecond Laser-Assisted Cataract Surgery (FLACS).

Femtosecond Lasers:

  • Mechanism:
    Utilizes ultra-short laser pulses to precisely cut tissue by creating plasma bubbles that gently separate the targeted tissue with minimal collateral damage.
  • Advantages:
    • Offers exceptional precision
    • Reduces thermal injury to surrounding tissues
    • Enhances surgical safety and reproducibility compared to conventional techniques
  • Limitations:
    • High cost of equipment
    • Requires specialized training for surgeons
    • Can increase the overall cost of the procedure
  • Applications:
    • FLACS: Precise corneal incisions, capsulotomy, and lens fragmentation in cataract surgery
    • LASIK: Creation of corneal flaps
    • PRK and SMILE: Refractive correction for myopia
    • Intracorneal ring tunnel creation
    • Arcuate incisions: For corneal astigmatism correction
    • Keratoplasty: Both lamellar and full-thickness corneal transplants

Explanation for other options:

Nd:YAG Laser (Option A): Mainly used for posterior capsulotomy in cases of posterior capsule opacification following cataract surgery, not for the removal of the cataract itself.

Diode Laser (Option B): Commonly used in laser iridotomy and cyclophotocoagulation for glaucoma management, but not for cataract surgery.

Excimer Laser (Option C): Primarily utilized in refractive procedures like LASIK and PRK to reshape the cornea, not for cataract extraction.

question_text: A patient reports progressive visual decline three years following ocular surgery and presents with the condition shown. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Posterior capsular opacification (PCO) is a common complication after cataract surgery.

  • It occurs when the posterior capsule of the lens becomes opacified, leading to decreased visual acuity and glare, particularly at night.
  • The symptoms of glare and decreased visual acuity, along with the fact that the patient has had cataract surgery within the last year, make PCO the most probable diagnosis.

Explanation for other options:

Pseudo-bullous keratopathy (Option A): This condition is due to endothelial dysfunction, leading to corneal oedema and bullae formation. Unlike PCO, it presents earlier and is associated with pain and photophobia rather than progressive vision loss.

Corneal dystrophy (Option B): Corneal dystrophies are bilateral, progressive, and hereditary corneal disorders affecting various corneal layers. They do not occur secondary to cataract surgery.

Posterior subcapsular cataract (Option C): PSC affects the posterior lens but occurs before cataract surgery, whereas PCO develops after cataract surgery.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy is/are incorrect?
option_b: Caused due to damage to Descement's membrane
option_c: Patients of Fuch's dystrophy are at greater than normal risk for development
option_d: Use of good quality visco-elastic during surgery is helpful in prevention
explanation:
Aphakic/ Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy

Often incorrectly called ‘secondary Fuchs dystrophy’, aphakic and pseudophakic bullous keratopathy is a condition akin to primary Fuchs dystrophy, which is due to endothelial damage.

  • It is known to occur after complicated cataract surgery during which there is damage to the corneal endothelium leading to functional decompensation and consequent corneal oedema.
  • It is estimated that an endothelial cell density of approximately 500 cells/mm2 is required to maintain normal transparency of the cornea, and the average loss of cells after routine cataract surgery varies from 2% to 10%.
  • However, following complicated cataract surgery, a cell loss of 16%– 20% is possible.
  • If the patient has an unhealthy endothelium to begin with, as in Fuchs endothelial dystrophy or following an attack of acute glaucoma, the counts may be low and the cell loss induced by surgery—which might have had little effect on a healthy cornea—may lead to corneal oedema postoperatively.
  • Measures to minimize cell damage during surgery include adequate anaesthesia, hypotension and the use of good-quality viscoelastic and physiological solutions.
  • Treatment is difficult unless the primary cause of the oedema can be eliminated.
  • Some comfort may be obtained by the application of a bandage contact lens and the frequent instillation of a concentrated saline solution (5%) or an ointment containing 6% sodium chloride.
  • An alternative which is frequently effective is to strip off the entire epithelium and to replace it with a thin flap of the conjunctiva.
  • Visual improvement depends on full thickness keratoplasty.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea

  • The upper blade features a sharp cutting edge and a small hole, while the lower blade has a cup-shaped indentation.
