question_text: Identify the sign in the given picture?
explanation:
vossius ring is a well-circumscribed complete or incomplete ring of pigment deposition on the anterior lens capsule surface, usually as a result of significant blunt eye trauma. The disease was first described by Vossius in 1903, at which time he discussed both a pigmented variety of the ring and a non-pigmented variety that he thought was the result of degeneration of anterior lens epithelial cells. The non-pigmented form is no longer considered to be a Vossius ring.

Etiology

A Vossius ring is a result of compression of the pigmented posterior iris epithelial cells and/or pupillary ruff against the anterior lens capsule with abrupt blunt force to the eye. Rupture of the cells causes deposition of a circular line of melanin pigment on the lens capsule. The ring of pigment is generally the same diameter as the undilated pupil. Interestingly, when evaluating a series of injured combat soldiers who sustained injury at various times of day and night, Gunderson noted in 1945 that the rings were of fairly uniform in size despite variable pupil size at the time of injury. Although his measurement system was relatively crude (a transparent ruler held close to the cornea while looking through a direct ophthalmoscope with +8.00 sphere), the rings in all of his patients were a consistent 2.25 to 2.75 mm in diameter.

Risk Factors

The major risk factor for Vossius ring formation is sudden, blunt trauma to the eye.

General Pathology

Deposition of melanin and cellular debris, from ruptured iris epithelial cells in a concentric ring on the anterior lens capsule.

Pathophysiology

Compression of pigmented iris epithelium and/or pupillary ruff cells during blunt compression of the eye results in cellular rupture with deposition of cellular contents and melanin pigment onto the lens capsule surface.

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is made at the slit lamp by observing a complete or incomplete ring of pigment on the anterior lens capsule. The ring is seen most easily with a dilated pupil.

History

A history of blunt eye trauma is critical to making this diagnosis. The shortest interval between injury and appearance of a Vossius ring was two hours, but typically it is not observed until four or more days post injury

Previously, there was some debate as to the origin of the pigment. Some authors believed that the pigment was a result of hemoglobin deposition on the lens surface as hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage were frequently associated with the condition. These theories are no longer widely accepted as Vossius rings are known to form without hemorrhage, and a Vossius ring does not form after an atraumatic vitreous hemorrhage.

Signs

A thin, circular line of pigment on the lens capsule is observed. The circle may be incomplete depending on the vector of the blunt trauma.

Symptoms

A Vossius ring is asymptomatic and generally will improve or resolve with time.

Clinical diagnosis

The diagnosis is made by clinical examination only.

Diagnostic procedures

Dilation can assist in making the diagnosis. Generally, no other procedures are necessary.

Laboratory test

No laboratory tests are typically indicated in the evaluation of a Vossius ring.

Differential diagnosis

Anterior lens capsule pigment deposition can be observed in other conditions without a history of trauma and can mimic the appearance of a Vossius ring. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome (PXS) is characterized by a defect in the LOXL-1 gene at locus 15q22, which results in deposition of fibrillar, exfoliative material on the pupillary margin, lens capsule and zonules. The fibrillar material can be differentiated from Vossius ring by absence of trauma by history as well as lack of pigmentation. Additionally, pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS) is characterized by release of pigment granules by the iris pigment epithelium. The granules distribute throughout the anterior segment including the lens surface where they can form a ring of posterior pigment peripherally known as a Scheie stripe or line. Location of the line, iris transillumination defects and increased pigment on other anterior segment structures differentiates PDS from Vossius ring.

Uveitis is another well-known cause of pigment deposition on the lens surface. Intraocular inflammation can result in formation of posterior synechiae. With resolution of inflammation or pharmacologic mydriasis, the synechiae can leave patchy clumps and fragments of pigment on the anterior lens capsule. Uveitis can be distinguished from Vossius ring based on history and presence of other ocular signs of inflammation including cell and flare in the anterior chamber, hypopyon, keratic precipitates, presence of systemic inflammatory disease, etc.

Management

No medical or surgical treatment is necessary for a Vossius ring, which is usually of little clinical significance but can be an important diagnostic tool if history of blunt trauma is in question

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(Option A) Kayser-Fleischer Ring:

  • Found in Wilson's disease, caused by copper deposition in Descemet's membrane of the cornea, not the lens.
  • It appears as a golden-brown ring around the cornea, unlike the pigmented ring on the anterior lens capsule seen in a Vossius ring.

(Option C) Fleischer's Ring:

  • Seen in Keratoconus, due to iron deposition at the base of the cone-shaped cornea.
  • It is a brownish ring located in the corneal epithelium, not on the lens.

(Option D) Weiss Ring:

  • Seen in posterior vitreous detachment (PVD).
  • It is a circular, white or grayish floater, representing detachment of the vitreous from the optic nerve head.
  • Unlike the Vossius ring, it is not attached to the lens and is visible in the vitreous cavity.

Key Takeaway:

  • Vossius ring is caused by blunt trauma and results in pigment deposition on the anterior lens capsule.
  • It is asymptomatic and requires no treatment as it fades over time.
  • Other rings (Kayser-Fleischer, Fleischer, Weiss) are not related to trauma and occur in different conditions affecting the cornea or vitreous.
  • Diagnosis is made using a slit lamp examination.

Reference: https://eyewiki.aao.org/Vossius_Ring

question_text: One week after a trabeculectomy a patient has a flat peripheral anterior chamber with iris to cornea touch, but no lens to cornea touch, applanation tension near 0 mm Hg, large choroidal effusions, and a positive Seidel test with a flat bleb. What would the single most important step be at this time?
explanation:
For any patient with a flat bleb and a visible leak, with or without a shallow anterior chamber, measures should be undertaken to close the leak. If bleb function is not severely compromised, conservative maneuvers, such as pressure patching and aqueous suppressant therapy, may succeed. However, if the bleb is completely flat with a large leak, it is usually necessary to close the leak surgically. Glue with a contact lens would be another alternative, but this technique can compromise bleb function. Simply reforming the anterior chamber or draining the choroidal effusions will not solve the important problem of the bleb leak. If there is no lens to cornea touch, anterior chamber reformation may not be necessary.

Reference: AAO GLAUCOMA/242

question_text: Which of the following statements is true about ciliary body?

option_b: Contraction of ciliary body helps in accommodation
explanation:
The ciliary body has three basic functions:

  • Aqueous production and removal
  • Helps in accommodation
  • Formation of vitreous mucopolysaccharide

The inner surface of the ciliary body is divided into two regions.

  • The anterior part (pars plicata) is corrugated with a number of folds running in an anteroposterior direction.
  • The posterior part(pars plana) is smooth.

The arterial supply to the ciliary body is via the long posterior ciliary and anterior ciliary arteries.

question_text: What is the most common cause of anterior uveitis associated with arthritis?

AS is a chronic, progressive, pauciarticular(involvement of four or less than four joints) disorder involving the sacroiliac and the posterior intervertebral joints.

  • The onset is insidious with intermittent attacks of arthralgia.
  • Males, in the third decade, are more frequently affected than females.
  • There is a strong association with the HLA-B27 antigen.

question_text: Tyndall phenomenon is used in the visualization of
explanation:
An aqueous flare is an optical phenomenon based on light scattering within the anterior chamber of the eye. This phenomenon occurs when an inflamed eye is viewed at right angles to a beam of light shined obliquely into the anterior chamber.

The fluid within the anterior chamber of the eye is called the aqueous humor. It is normally transparent and lets through all the light from the front of the eye, so it can pass through the lens to fall on the retina.

However, when there are proteins present inside the fluid, the light may reflect in multiple directions, leading to the scattering of light. This is called the tyndall effect, and is due to the presence of turbidity in the aqueoushumor.

Picture showing cells and flare

question_text: A 32-year-old patient presents with blurred vision, photophobia, and mild ocular pain. Examination reveals aqueous flare and keratic precipitates in the anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis) involves inflammation of the iris and ciliary body.

Key features include:

  • Granulomatous or non-granulomatous inflammation
  • Iris nodules
  • Large mutton-fat keratic precipitates (KPs)on the corneal endothelium
  • Anterior chamber cells and flare
  • Posterior synechiae formation

Other Types of Uveitis:

  • Intermediate uveitis
    • Involves the vitreous
    • Findings: vitreous cells, snowball opacities, snowbanking
    • Usually spares the anterior chamber initially(option A ruled out)
  • Posterior uveitis :
    • Involves the choroid and retina
    • Findings: choroidal/retinal granulomas, cystoid macular oedema, periphlebitis ("candle-wax" appearance)
    • Can also present as peripheral multifocal chorioretinitis (small punched-out atrophic spots, suggestive of sarcoidosis) (option B ruled out)
  • Toxoplasma uveitis :
  • Caused by Toxoplasma gondii; cats are definitive hosts
  • Primarily posterior uveitis with focal retinochoroiditis
  • May secondarily involve the anterior chamber, but the initial presentation is posterior (Option C ruled out)

question_text: A 26-year-old patient presents with blurred vision, photophobia, redness, pain in the left eye, along with joint pain. On ocular examination, keratic precipitates and aqueous cells are noted. Which major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is most likely associated with this condition?

The combination of blurred vision, photophobia, eye redness and pain, along with the presence of keratic precipitates, is indicative of anterior uveitis. When anterior uveitis is accompanied by joint pain, it strongly suggests a systemic association such as arthritis-related uveitis.

This condition commonly affects young males and is frequently linked to HLA-B27 positivity. In fact, approximately 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis-a type of inflammatory arthritis-are positive for the HLA-B27 antigen, highlighting a strong genetic association.

Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) / Marie Strumpell Disease

HLA-B47 (Option C): It is linked to congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This condition is marked by symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, arrhythmias, and hypotension.

question_text: What medication is appropriate for a patient with acute anterior uveitis who is experiencing photophobia and blurred vision?
explanation:
Explanation:

Treatment of Anterior Uveitis:

Topical Steroids (First-line therapy):

  • Prednisolone: Commonly prescribed to reduce intraocular inflammation.
  • Loteprednol: A milder steroid option with a lower risk of raising intraocular pressure.

Topical Cycloplegics:

These medications help by:

  • Relaxing the ciliary muscles, which reduces pain
  • Preventing and breaking posterior synechiae (adhesions between the iris and lens)
  • Improving blood flow, aiding in the healing process
  • Example: Atropine

Non-Steroidal Options:

  • Voclosporin: A non-steroidal agent included in the Luminate program, used in selected cases of uveitis.

For Chronic or Vision-Threatening Uveitis:

Biologic and Immunomodulatory Therapies:

  • Adalimumab: A TNF-alpha inhibitor used in severe or chronic uveitis
  • Infliximab: Another TNF-alpha blocker for resistant cases
  • Interferon Alpha: Modulates immune response in severe uveitis

Explanation for other options:

Moxifloxacin (Option A): An antibiotic, mainly used to treat bacterial eye infections, not indicated for non-infectious anterior uveitis.

Acetazolamide (Option C): A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used to lower intraocular pressure in conditions like glaucoma, not for uveitis treatment.

Methotrexate (Option D): An immunosuppressant, typically reserved for chronic or refractory uveitis, not the initial treatment for acute anterior uveitis.

question_text: Snowbanking is typically seen in
explanation:
Snowbanking is seen in intermediate uveitis/pars planitis.

Intermedate uveitis(IU):

IU classically affects younger patients, aged 15 to 40 years. Presentation is typically insidious and bilateral but asymmetrical in both eyes.

Symptoms include:

  • Painless floaters
  • Decreased/blurred vision
  • Pain, photophobia and red eye are rare symptoms

Signs include:

  • Snowballs are whitish focal collections of inflammatory cells and exudate, usually most numerous in the inferior vitreous.
  • Snowbanking is characterized by a grey-white fibrovascular and/or exudative plaque, most frequently found inferiorly. It can often be seen only with indirect ophthalmoscopy and scleral depression.
  • Visual acuity is variably affected depending on inflammatory activity and complications.
  • Mild to moderate anterior segment inflammation may occur in 28-50% of patients, characterized by few cells and scattered keratic precipitates in the anterior segment. However, there may be more severe findings of anterior uveitis such as posterior synechia, particularly involving the inferior iris, and especially in IU associated with multiple sclerosis(MS) and in children.
  • Vitreous cells with anterior predominance are a universal finding.
  • Vitreous condensation and haze may occur in severe cases.
  • Peripheral periphlebitis is a common finding(16-36%), particularly in patients with MS.
  • Younger patients may present with vitreous hemorrhage.

Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 423, 459, 487.

question_text: A 54 year old patient has been on treatment of fortified anti-microbials for corneal ulceration for a week. On follow-up visit, slit lamp imaging is as depicted. Iris tissue is seen plugging the perforation and anterior chamber appears formed. What is the next step of management?
option_a: Observation, decrease IOP bandage and close monitoring
explanation:
Patient has developed spontaneous corneal perforation.

Usually, the perforation takes place opposite to some part of the iris which is drawn into the aperture when the aqueous escapes. If the perforation is small, the iris becomes gummed down to the opening and the adhesion organizes to form a layer of scar tissue over the adherent iris which is referred to as a ‘pseudocornea’ and an anterior synechia is formed. The blocking of the perforation with the iris allows the anterior chamber to be reformed as fresh aqueous is rapidly secreted. If the perforation is large, a portion of the iris is carried not only into the opening but also through it, causing a prolapse of the iris. The colour of the iris soon becomes obscured by the deposition of grey or yellow exudate upon the surface, but eventually the iris stroma becomes thinned and the black pigmentary epithelium becomes visible. If a small perforation is over the iris, adhesion to the cornea usually occurs, followed by formation of a pseudocornea by laying down of a mesh of fibrin and collagen, and the defect heals to form an adherent leucoma. This may become detached when the anterior chamber reforms or may remain as a fine adhesion, in which case no special treatment is required. If pseudo-cornea adhesion is stable and anterior chamber remains formed, observation with close monitoring can be done. If anterior chamber becomes flat, more drastic measures such as sealing with tissue glue or keratoplasty maybe required depending on size of the perforation.

Evisceration should be carried out only in cases of painful blind eye.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 12 – Diseases of Cornea.

question_text:
A 34-year-old male individual presented with redness in both eyes for the past 10 weeks. It was associated with mild dull aching pain and slight blurring of vision in both eyes. There was a history of weight loss of approximately 6 kg along with intermittent episodes of dry cough over the past 1 year. There was no history of fever/rash/anorexia/joint pains or haemoptysis.
On examination, distant visual acuity in both eyes was 6/9. There was a mild circumcorneal ciliary congestion in both eyes. Granulomatous keratic precipitates (KPs), cells and flare were present. The intraocular pressure was 26 mm and 28 mm of Hg in the right and the left eye respectively. The routine haemogram, blood sugar and urine analysis were normal. Mantoux test was negative with an induration of 4 mm after 72 h. The chest radiograph is shown here. Serum angiotensin converting enzyme(ACE) level was raised to 108 U/L(normal range being 8.00-65.00 U/L). Serum calcium level was normal. Pulmonary function tests were normal. What is your diagnosis
explanation:
Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown etiology with variable clinical manifestations in multiple organs, including the lungs, skin, lymph nodes, spleen and eyes. After the lungs, the eyes are the second most commonly involved organ in sarcoidosis and ocular involvement has been reported in about 20-50% of patients.

Ocular sarcoidosis most commonly manifests as a granulomatous bilateral anterior uveitis, which accounts for nearly two-thirds of all cases. About 14-28% of patients with ocular sarcoidosis show posterior segment lesions, such as vitritis, periphlebitis, chorioretinitis and optic nerve granuloma. These findings in the question(uveitis, weight loss, hilar lymphadenopathy, negative montoux, high ACE levels) typically lead to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

Reference: A.K. Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 438.

question_text: Among the given options, which specific sign is considered pathognomonic for acute anterior uveitis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Anterior Uveitis:

Definition:

It is the most common form of uveitis, affecting the anterior part of the eye.

Clinical Features:

  • Eye pain
  • Redness
  • Photophobia (sensitivity to light)
  • Blepharospasm (involuntary eyelid closure)
  • Serous discharge
  • Blurred and decreased vision

Examination Findings:

Keratic Precipitates (KPs):

  • Non-granulomatous: Fine, grayish deposits mainly made up of lymphocytes
  • Granulomatous: Larger, greasy-appearing deposits called "mutton-fat KPs,"consisting of macrophages
  • Location: Usually found on the lower corneal endothelium within Arlt's triangle, an area influenced by convection currents in the aqueous humor

Other Signs:

  • Aqueous Cells: Signify active inflammation
  • Aqueous Flare: Cloudiness in the anterior chamber caused by protein leakage from inflamed vessels
  • Muddy Iris: Iris swelling due to protein leakage
  • Miosis: Pupil constriction caused by toxins released from inflamed tissue
  • Iris Nodules:
    • Koeppe's Nodules: At the pupillary margin; seen in both granulomatous and non-granulomatous uveitis
    • Busacca Nodules: Located on the iris surface; typical of granulomatous uveitis

Complications:

  • Posterior Synechiae: Iris sticking to the lens, potentially causing a festooned (scalloped) pupil
  • Seclusio Pupil / Ring Synechiae: Adhesions all around the pupillary border, which can lead to iris bombe and angle-closure glaucoma
  • Occlusio Pupil: Complete coverage of the lens by synechiae
  • Cyclitic Membrane
  • Rubeosis Iridis: New abnormal blood vessel growth on the iris

Explanation for other options:

Aqueous Flare (Option A): Indicates protein and inflammatory cells in the aqueous humor and is commonly seen in anterior uveitis, but it is not pathognomonic.

Festooned Pupil (Option C): Seen with posterior synechiae in chronic uveitis.

Busacca Nodules (Option D): Larger granulomatous nodules, typically found in chronic anterior uveitis linked with diseases like sarcoidosis or tuberculosis.

question_text: A middle aged female came to your OPD with breathlessness, joint pain and blurred vision. On examination granulomatous uveitis was seen. What is the most probable diagnosis
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's systemic presentation (breathlessness/pulmonary involvement, joint pain/arthritis, and blurred vision/uveitis) coupled with granulomatous uveitis is strongly suggestive of Ocular Sarcoidosis.

  • Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory disease that commonly affects the lungs (causing breathlessness) and joints (causing arthritis).
  • Granulomatous uveitis (often bilateral anterior, intermediate, or panuveitis) is the most common ocular manifestation. These features are suggestive of ocular sarcoidosis The most common ocular manifestation overall is uveitis, reported in 30-70% of cases. Sarcoidosis can present with anterior, intermediate, posterior or panuveitis and should be on the differential for any patient with uveitis. The most common type is bilateral anterior uveitis.

Explanation for the other options:

  • A. HLA B 27 uveitis is typically acute, recurrent, and non-granulomatous; it is also less likely to cause significant breathlessness (unless associated with severe Psoriatic Arthritis or Enteropathic Arthritis).
  • B. Ocular leprosy primarily presents with chronic non-granulomatous uveitis and corneal nerve thickening, rarely a complex systemic presentation involving the lungs and joints.
  • C. Syphilitic uveitis causes panuveitis/posterior uveitis, but the systemic presentation is less specific for the breathlessness/arthritis triad.

Key Takeaways:

The combination of granulomatous uveitis with pulmonary (breathlessness) and arthritic symptoms in a middle-aged adult is highly characteristic of Sarcoidosis.

question_text: What will be observed in a patient diagnosed with sympathetic ophthalmitis, and a history of penetrating eye injury?
explanation:
Explanation

  • Sympathetic ophthalmitis is a rare but serious complication that develops after penetrating trauma or surgery to one eye.
  • It manifests as bilateral granulomatous panuveitis, meaning both the anterior and posterior uveal structures are inflamed.
  • The mechanism involves a T-cell-mediated autoimmune response against melanocyte-associated antigens such as tyrosinase peptides.
  • The risk is greatest when the ciliary body is injured.

Sympathetic Ophthalmitis (SO)

Definition

  • Bilateral granulomatous inflammation of the uveal tract occurring after trauma or surgery to one eye.

Etiology & Pathogenesis

  • Trauma to one eye ("exciting eye") is followed weeks to months later by inflammation in the opposite, undamaged eye ("sympathizing eye".
  • Autoimmune hypersensitivity reaction against retinal S-antigen.

Histopathology

  • Dense lymphocytic infiltration of the choroid.
  • Granulomatous foci with epithelioid cells containing melanin.
  • Dalen-Fuchs nodules: granulomas between Bruch's membrane and the RPE (also seen in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome).

Clinical Features

  • Exciting eye: persistent redness and irritation after trauma.
  • Sympathizing eye: blurred vision, photophobia, and loss of accommodation (difficulty with near vision is often the first symptom).
  • Anterior granulomatous uveitis in both eyes.
  • Fundus findings: exudative retinal detachment, vasculitis, optic disc swelling, Dalen-Fuchs nodules.
  • Chronic cases: sunset glow fundus due to diffuse chorioretinal depigmentation.

Investigations

  • Fundus exam: nodules, vasculitis, retinal detachment.
  • B-scan: choroidal thickening, retinal detachment.
  • Imaging used to exclude mimickers such as VKH.

Treatment

  • Preventive: Enucleation of a severely damaged eye within 10-14 days can reduce risk.
  • Medical: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone followed by oral taper).
  • Adjunct: Topical steroids and cycloplegics.
  • Immunosuppressive agents may be required in refractory cases.

Causes of Panuveitis:

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Acute anterior uveitis (Option A): Inflammation limited to the anterior uvea can occur, but sympathetic ophthalmitis characteristically involves the entire uveal tract (panuveitis), not just the anterior chamber.

Pars planitis (Option B): A form of intermediate uveitis affecting the pars plana, usually idiopathic or linked to autoimmune disease, not trauma-induced or typical of sympathetic ophthalmia.

Chronic anterior uveitis (Option D): While chronic anterior inflammation may persist, sympathetic ophthalmitis typically involves both anterior and posterior segments, making panuveitis the hallmark.

Key Takeaway:

Sympathetic ophthalmitis is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis triggered by trauma or surgery to one eye, mediated by autoimmune T-cell reactivity against uveal antigens. Prompt recognition and aggressive corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy are vital to preserve vision.

question_text: Which of the following is true about sympathetic ophthalmitis?
explanation:
Sympathetic ophthalmitis is a serious bilateral granulomatous(non-suppurative) panuveitis which follows a penetrating ocular trauma.

The injured eye is called exciting eye and the fellow eye which also develops uveitis is called sympathizing eye.

Very rarely, sympathetic ophthalmitis can also occur following an intraocular surgery.

Pathology:

  • The primary inflammatory mediators are thought to be T cells(initial wave of infiltrative cells is composed of CD4+ helper T cells and a later wave of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) that invade the uveal tract.
  • The inflammation is usually granulomatous and the choroid is diffusely thickened with lymphocytes, nests of epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells. The epithelioid cells and giant cells often contain melanin pigment.
  • The inflammatory process does not usually involve the choriocapillaris(in contrast to Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome) or the retina.
  • Dalen-Fuchs nodules, which are clusters of epithelioid cells containing pigment, lying between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane, are also seen.
  • Anteriorly, the iris can appear thickened with nodular infiltrations.

Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 439.

question_text: A 20-year-old nurse in an ophthalmology clinic complains of right-sided brow ache. Examination of both eyes is normal except for the presence of a 1.5 mm, nonreactive right pupil. The pupil does not dilate in darkness. The left pupil is 4 mm and briskly reactive. She has no ptosis and normal ocular motility. The anterior chamber has no cell and flare. What is the most likely etiology?
option_a: Exposure to a cholinergic(pilocarpine like) substance in the right eye
option_b: Exposure to an anticholinergic(atropine like substance) in the right eye
explanation:
• A cholinergic exposure will produce a pupil that is miotic and nonreactive to light or near.
  • Atropine or any anticholinergic substance will produce a mydriatic pupil, not a miotic pupil.
  • The Horner syndrome can produce a small pupil, but this pupil will still respond to light and near stimuli.
  • Uveitis can produce a small and poorly reactive pupil, but the absence of cell and flare make this less likely.

Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 222/424.

question_text: A patient presents with the following finding .What is the most likely complication associated with it ?
explanation:
Exposure keratopathy (EK) is damage to the cornea that occurs primarily from prolonged exposure of the ocular surface to the outside environment. EK can lead to ulceration, microbial keratitis, and permanent vision loss from scarring.

Under normal circumstances, the eyelids and tear film protect the cornea, an avascular, nonkeratinized epithelium, from trauma, desiccation, and microbial attack. The tear film, a composite fluid of three layers, has several important roles: it nourishes and lubricates the cornea, aids in crisp visual acuity, and protects the cornea from bacterial invasion (Figure 1). Several factors help maintain an adequate distribution of the tear film; these include an intact blink reflex, normal blink rate, and complete eyelid closure during sleep and blinking. Disruption to this system may lead to an epithelial defect. The corneal epithelium serves as a barrier to the outside world through the use of tight junctions and damage to the integrity of this structure can facilitate penetration of microbes and external debris.

Risk Factors

Patients at risk for EK include those who suffer from conditions that interfere with the ability to protect the cornea such asincomplete eyelid closure, inadequate blink reflex, inadequate blink rate and/or decreased protective lubrication of the cornea. A summary of risk factors and conditions is listed below.

Lagophthalmos

Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids completely. Because of this, a portion of the eye remains open during a blink and during sleep, and is subject to damage from exposure. The etiologies of lagophthalmos can be divided into the following subcategories:

Facial nerve dysfunction (paralytic lagophthalmos)

Eyelid dysfunction

Excessive scar tissue or excessive eyelid removal during surgery (cicatricial lagophthalmos)

Physiologic lagophthalmos (as in the case of nocturnal lagophthalmos).

Medication effect (particularly sedatives or neuromuscular blockers)

Paralytic lagophthalmos is most commonly due to facial nerve dysfunction. The facial nerve (CN VII) controls most of the eyelid muscles, and facial nerve dysfunction will therefore lead to weakened eyelid closure (Figure 2). It can be damaged by trauma, cerebrovascular accidents, Bell’s palsy, tumors, infections, immune-mediated causes, and congenital cranial dysinnervation syndromes. Trauma, can be secondary to fractures to the skull base or mandible, or from surgery (particularly neurosurgery). Additionally, the facial nerve is supplied by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and as such may be susceptible to cerebrovascular accidents. Bell’s palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a weakness of facial muscles on one side of the face. It holds its own host of possible causes, most notably, reactivation of herpes simplex virus. Other infectious causes of Bell’s palsy include Lyme disease, varicella, mumps, poliomyelitis, Guillaine-Barré syndrome, leprosy, diphtheria, and botulism. Tumors that have the potential to cause facial nerve dysfunction include acoustic neuromas in the cerebellopontine angle as well as metastases. Lastly, cranial dysinnervation syndromes, such as Mobius’ syndrome and congenital facial palsy, are characterized by facial nerve dysfunction and subsequent lagophthalmos.

Proptosis, a term commonly interchanged with exophthalmos, is anterior displacement of the eyeball with respect to the orbit. This protrusion of the eyeball may be so great as to disrupt normal eyelid closure. Conditions that are associated with proptosis include craniosynostosis syndromes, thyroid disease, orbital tumors and Cushing’s syndrome. Patients with pulsatile exophthalmos syndromes may also present with EK; such patients may include those with aortic regurgitation, neurofibromatosis 1, carotid-cavernous sinus fistulae, arachnoid cysts, and trauma.

Thyroid eye disease warrants special mention as it is one of the leading causes of EK (Figure 3). Thyroid eye disease can cause proptosis of the orbit, eyelid retraction, and chemosis. Proptosis occurs secondary to increased volume behind the orbit due to cellular proliferation, inflammation, and accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the eye muscles and retroorbital adipose and connective tissues. Additionally, patients with thyroid disease may have eyelid retraction as well as periorbital edema secondary to decreased venous drainage from the congested orbital space. Both of these factors contribute to incomplete eyelid closure and increase the risk for EK. Additionally, patients with thyroid dysfunction may suffer from corneal nerve dysfunction and subsequent malfunctioning of the blink reflex, further increasing the risk of EK. Grave’s disease is an autoimmune disease that results in the overproduction of thyroid hormones (hyperthyroidism). Although thyroid eye disease is traditionally associated with Graves’ disease, it is also occasionally seen in euthyroid patients and in patients with hypothyroid chronic autoimmune thyroiditis.

Patients with either neurologic or neurotrophic diseases may have an impaired blink reflex that could predispose them to EK (Figure 4). Examples of neurologic disease include Parkinson disease or neuromuscular disease. EK results from decreased blink rate and blink force.

Neurotrophic diseases are the result of decreased corneal sensation. They are characterized by corneal nerve dysfunction, which interferes with the normal blink reflex that is needed to lubricate the eye and protect it from the external environment. Neurotrophic disease can be either acquired or hereditary and infectious or non-infectious. Non-infectious non-hereditary forms of neurotrophic keratitis can be secondary to a pathological change, due to autoimmune disease, iatrogenic, substance - induced, or as part of a polyneuropathy syndrome. Examples of decreased corneal nerve function secondary to the effect of ophthalmic pathological changes can be seen in keratoconus, bullous keratopathy, and atopic keratoconjuctivitis. Autoimmune causes of decreased corneal nerve function include Graves’ disease and Sjogren’s syndrome. Iatrogenic corneal nerve dysfunction may occur in refractive vision corrective procedures. Intranasal cocaine abuse may also impair corneal nerve sensitivity and may predispose to EK. Lastly, systemic polyneuropathies may lead to impaired blink reflex secondary to decreased corneal nerve sensitivity and include peripheral diabetic neuropathy, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, vitamin B12 deficiency, and alcoholism.

Hereditary forms of sensory and autonomic neuropathies that have the potential to compromise corneal nerve integrity include Riley-Day syndrome, congenital aniridia, ocular-auriculo-vertebral dysplasia, and multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A and 2B. Lastly, infectious agents that can affect the corneal nerves include herpesviridae (herpes-simplex virus type 1 and varicella-zoster virus, the latter of which can present as Ramsay-Hunt syndrome), Mycobacterium leprae, Acanthamoeba, and fungi.

Lid malposition can prevent adequate closure of the eyelids, leading to EK. Causes of lid malposition include cicatricial retraction, as previously mentioned, ectropion, entropion, and eyelid coloboma.

Ectropion is an outward rotation of the eyelid margin, whereas entropion is an inward rotation of the eyelid margin. Ectropion can be either congenital, involutional, paralytic, cicatricial, or mechanical. Congenital ectropion of the upper lid may be associated with Down syndrome, whereas congenital ectropion of lower lid may be associated with blepharophimosis syndrome. Involutional lower lid ectropion may be caused by disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, laxity of the medial and lateral canthal tendons, and atrophy or degeneration of the orbicularis oculi. This can occur as part of the natural aging process. Paralytic ectropion may be caused by facial nerve palsy leading to laxity of the orbicularis oculi (Figure 5). Cicatricial ectropion can be caused by shortening of the anterior lamella or skin of the orbicularis oculi muscle from actinic skin changes, resection of skin lesions, trauma, burns, toxic reactions to topical eye medications, skin diseases, and aggressive blepharoplasty. A rare cause of cicatricial ectropion is cutaneous anthrax infection, whereby the Bacillus anthracis organisms proliferate at the site of inoculation and form a papule that progresses to form a vesicle, pustule, and ultimately a necrotic black ulcer. When the eyelid is the primary site of entry, progressive lid edema may lead to cicatricial ectropion. Lastly, mechanical pulling of the eyelid may cause ectropion such as in the setting of a tumor.

The causes of entropion may be congenital, acute spastic, involutional or cicatricial. Congenital entropion can occur in the setting of retractor dysgenesis and shortened posterior lamella. Acute spastic entropion may be caused by ocular inflammation or irritation as can be seen with trichiasis. Involutional entropion is associated with medial and lateral canthal laxity or dehiscence, disinsertion or stretching of the lower lid retractor complex, override of the preseptal orbicularis, and extension of orbital fat anterior to the orbital rim. Lastly, cicatricial entropion may be caused by shortening of the posterior lamella from inflammation which may be caused by trachoma, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, herpes zoster, chemical injuries, and toxic reactions to certain topical medications.

Eyelid coloboma is another cause of eyelid malposition that may lead to EK. Eyelid coloboma may be isolated or as part of a syndrome. Isolated eyelid colobomas may present with corneopalpebral adhesions and may be complete, incomplete, or of the abortive type which has variable size and a diverse range of corneopalpebral adhesions. Syndromic variants of eyelid coloboma include Fraser syndrome, Goldenhar syndrome, CHARGE syndrome (coloboma of the eye, heart defects, atresia of the nasal choanae, retardation of growth and/or development, genital and/or urinary abnormalities, ear abnormalities and deafness), or several other more rare associated syndromes.

question_text: A patient presents with a sudden loss of vision and no fundus glow, with no history of trauma. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vitreous haemorrhage occurs when blood accumulates within the vitreous cavity, obstructing the view of the retina and causing sudden visual loss. A hallmark sign is the absence of fundus glow during ophthalmoscopic examination.

Etiology:

  • In adults, the most common cause is proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). In PDR, fibrovascular tissue grows on the retinal surface or attaches to the posterior vitreous, creating traction that can rupture retinal vessels and lead to vitreous bleeding.
  • Other causes include retinal tears, retinal vein occlusion, and trauma (though absent in this scenario).

Clinical features:

  • Sudden decrease in visual acuity
  • Floaters or shadows in the visual field
  • The fundus may be obscured due to blood in the vitreous

Explanation for Other Options:

Acute anterior uveitis (option B): It can cause sudden visual loss along with pain, photophobia, and redness, but the fundus glow is usually preserved.

Optic neuritis (option C): Presents with painful loss of vision and often a relative afferent pupillary defect, but the fundus is typically visible unless there is papilledema.

Acute congestive glaucoma (option D): Causes sudden, painful vision loss with halos, corneal oedema, and a mid-dilated pupil, but the fundus can usually still be seen once corneal oedema clears, and the classic 'no fundus glow' is absent.

question_text: Identify the block:
explanation:
The nasociliary nerve is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1) (which is in turn a branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V)). It is intermediate in size between the other two branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the frontal nerve and lacrimal nerve.

Structure

Course

The nasociliary nerve enters the orbit via the superior orbital fissure,[citation needed] through the common tendinous ring, and between the two heads of the lateral rectus muscle and between the superior and inferior rami of the oculomotor nerve.[citation needed] It passes across the optic nerve (CN II) along with the ophthalmic artery. It then runs obliquely beneath (inferior to) the superior rectus muscle and superior oblique muscle to the medial wall of the orbital cavity whereupon it emits the posterior ethmoidal nerve, and the anterior ethmoidal nerve.

Branches

Branches of the nasociliary nerve include:

posterior ethmoidal nerve

anterior ethmoidal nerve

long ciliary nerves

infratrochlear nerve

communicating branch to ciliary ganglion

Function

The branches of the nasociliary nerve provide sensory innervation to structures surrounding the eye such as the cornea, eyelids, conjunctiva, ethmoid air cells and mucosa of the nasal cavity

Incorrect Options:

Option B. Anterior Ethmoidal
The anterior ethmoidal nerve is a branch of the nasociliary nerve and provides sensory innervation to the anterior part of the nasal cavity and the skin of the tip of the nose (external nasal nerve). It does not supply the entire region anesthetized in a nasociliary nerve block.

Option C. Sphenopalatine
The sphenopalatine ganglion contains parasympathetic fibers and is primarily involved in lacrimation and nasal secretion. A block at this site is used for treating conditions like cluster headaches and trigeminal neuralgia, not for ocular anesthesia.

Option D. Greater Palatine
The greater palatine nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) and provides sensory innervation to the hard palate and posterior part of the nasal cavity. It is not involved in orbital or anterior nasal cavity innervation.

Key Takeaway:

The nasociliary nerve (CN V1) supplies sensory innervation to the eye, nasal mucosa, and ethmoid air cells.

Nasociliary nerve block is used for ocular procedures and anesthesia.

Other nerves like anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, and greater palatine have distinct sensory distributions and are not targeted in this block.

question_text: What symptoms and signs would a patient exhibit if a tumor in the anterior pituitary gland compresses the optic chiasma?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bitemporal hemianopia typically results from tumors near the sella turcica, pressure from a suprasellar aneurysm, or chronic arachnoiditis, which compress the optic chiasma and damage the fibers from the nasal halves of each retina. Therefore, a tumor in the anterior pituitary pressing on the optic chiasma usually presents as bitemporal hemianopia.

Pituitary adenoma:

  • The most common visual defect caused by a pituitary adenoma is bitemporal hemianopia, due to compression of the crossing binasal fibers at the optic chiasma.
  • It is the most frequent suprasellar mass in adults.

Classification:

  • Microadenomas: less than 10 mm; often incidental or cause endocrine symptoms.
  • Macroadenomas: greater than 10 mm; may cause visual field defects due to mass effect.

Common types:

  • Prolactinomas: 30% present with amenorrhea and galactorrhea.
  • Non-functioning adenomas: 20%; do not secrete hormones.
  • Growth hormone-secreting adenomas: 15%; cause acromegaly.
  • ACTH-secreting adenomas: 10%; lead to Cushing's disease.

Clinical features:

  • Visual defects: Compression of the optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Endocrine symptoms: Amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and other hormonal imbalances.

Diagnosis:

  • MRI is the primary imaging modality.
  • Serum prolactin and thyroid function tests.
  • Visual field testing.

Treatment:

  • Medical management:
    • Prolactinomas: Dopamine agonists (e.g., bromocriptine, cabergoline).
    • GH-secreting tumors: Somatostatin analogues (e.g., octreotide).
  • Surgical management:
    • Transsphenoidal approach is preferred.
    • Craniotomy may be needed for large tumors.
    • Sublabial approach used for acute visual deterioration, GH-secreting tumors, Cushing's disease, or large non-functioning adenomas.

Complications:

  • Pituitary apoplexy: Sudden hemorrhage or infarction presenting with headache, visual loss, and ophthalmoplegia.
  • Postoperative risks include CSF leaks, pituitary insufficiency, and diabetes insipidus.

Explanation for other options:

Homonymous hemianopia (Option A): Caused by post-chiasmal lesions such as optic tract, optic radiations, or visual cortex damage.

Inferior quadrantanopia (Option B): Results from lesions in the anterior parietal lobe fibers of the optic radiations.

Superior quadrantanopia (Option D): Caused by lesions in the temporal lobe fibers of the optic radiations.

question_text: Pseudouveitis is seen in
explanation:
Explanation:

A necrotizing malignant melanoma may present with masquerade syndrome, in which tumor presents with inflammatory signs which is mistaken to be a case of endogenous uveitis, and thus, pseudouveitis. Other causes include:

  • Acute leukemia
  • Juvenile xanthogranuloma
  • Lymphoma
  • Anterior segment ischemia

Explanation for the other options:

  • A. Toxoplasmosis causes true infectious uveitis/retinochoroiditis.
  • C. Retinoblastoma (RB) is a common cause of pseudouveitis/masquerade syndrome in children, while Malignant Melanoma is a cause in adults (often presenting with inflammatory signs due to tumor necrosis).
  • D. Sarcoidosis causes true non-infectious granulomatous uveitis.

Key Takeaways:

Pseudouveitis (or Masquerade Syndrome) occurs when a non-inflammatory process (like Malignant Melanoma or Retinoblastoma) mimics true uveitis due to the release of inflammatory mediators or cellular debris.

question_text: In the microscopic structure of retina, the synaptic layer formed by the axons of rods and cones with the dendrites of bipolar neurons and processes of horizontal cells is known as:
explanation:
Explanation:

The retina is composed of a variety of epithelial, neural and glial cell types.

  • Outer plexiform layer: formed by synapses between axons of rods/cones and dendrites of bipolar neurons and horizontal cells.
  • Outer nuclear layer (Option A): Contains cell bodies of rods and cones, not synaptic connections
  • Inner nuclear layer (Option C): Contains cell bodies of bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cells, not synaptic connections.
  • Inner plexiform layer (Option D): Composed of synapses between axons of bipolar cells and dendrites of ganglionic neurons.

Key Takeaways:

  • The outer plexiform layer is crucial for synaptic interactions in the retina, linking photoreceptor outputs to bipolar and horizontal cells.
  • Understanding retinal layers aids in comprehending visual signal processing and the organization of the retina.

question_text: A young patient presents to the ophthalmic outpatient department with gradual blurring of vision in the left eye. Slit lamp examination reveals fine stellate keratic precipitates and aqueous flare and a typical complicated posterior subcapsular cataract. No posterior synechiae were observed. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis, is a chronic non-granulomatous condition presenting as low-grade unilateral anterior inflammation. It is most commonly unilateral.

Patients with FHI are often asymptomatic for many years prior to presentation as, unlike with other anterior uveitides, they typically will have no pain, redness or photophobia.

Signs include:

  • Iris - Heterochromia and atrophy
  • Iris rubeosis
  • Posterior synechiae are absent
  • Stellate, grey - white keratic precipitates. Located diffusely over the entire corneal endothelium.
  • Anterior chamber - faint flare and mild cellular activity
  • Russell bodies - Tiny crystals may be present on the iris surface. These are aggregations of spherical immunoglobulin.
  • Koeppe nodules can be seen - may initially lead to a misdiagnosis of granulomatous uveitis.
  • Amsler sign - Prominent iris and angle vessels that bleed after paracentesis

Complications:

  • Cataract is extremely common - a posterior subcapsular morphology is seen initially
  • Glaucoma is typically a later manifestation

Treatment:

  • Long-term monitoring is indicated to detect glaucoma and other complications. The complications are treated accordingly.
  • Topical steroids may be used short-term for moderate severe exacerbations, but are generally not thought to be helpful in the management of chronic low-grade inflammation.

Reference: Parson, 22nd Edition, Pg no. 238-246.

question_text: Jensen's choroiditis is
explanation:
Choroiditis is usually classified according to the number and location of the areas involved.

Disseminated or diffuse choroiditis:

  • It is diagnosed when small areas of inflammation are scattered over a greater part of the fundus behind the equator.

Multifocal choroiditis:

  • It has fewer and more discrete foci.
  • It is frequently symptomless and discovered only on routine examination.

Central choroiditis:

  • This affects the posterior pole or macular region.
  • It may occur as part of disseminated choroiditis or can occur alone.

Juxtapapillary choroiditis (of Jensen):

  • Usually oval in shape, this type occurs in young persons as an exudation close to and about the same size as the disc.
  • There is generally a sector-shaped defect in the field of vision.
  • The inflammation slowly subsides, leaving a patch of atrophy, but recurrence may take place.

Reference: Kanski, 7th Edition, Pg no. 443.

question_text: Which of the following structures is not a part of the posterior segment of the eye?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Inside the eye, the globe is broadly divided into the anterior segment and posterior segment by the lens.
  • The posterior segment, i.e. the part of the eye that lies behind the lens, is bounded internally by the ciliary body anteriorly and retina posteriorly.
  • Structures present in the posterior segment include the retina, choroid, and the optic disc, and the cavity is filled with a transparent gel-like substance called the vitreous humour.

question_text: Which of the following process is not involved in aqueous formation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Aqueous humour is essentially an ultrafiltrate of plasma. Its formation occurs through a multi-step process:

  • Ultrafiltration (option D): Plasma is filtered from the capillaries of the ciliary stroma into the ciliary body.
  • Transfer across epithelium: This plasma filtrate moves from the ciliary stroma into the posterior chamber, crossing the ciliary epithelium.
  • Diffusion (option A) and active secretion (option B): During this transfer, the aqueous humour formation involves diffusion of solutes and active secretion of ions, which helps in drawing water into the aqueous compartment.

Filtration is not directly involved in aqueous humour formation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Aqueous humour is essentially an ultrafiltrate of plasma
  • Filtration is not directly involved in aqueous humour formation.

question_text: Cataract with posterior lenticonus is seen in
explanation:
Lowe's or oculocerebrorenal syndrome is a severe X-linked disorder associated with posterior lenticonus.

Lowe Syndrome should be suspected in a newborn male patient with congenital cataracts, central hypotonia, and central nervous system delay. Family history may be positive for male relatives with similar findings.

Leukocoria, miosis, microphthalmos and a shallow anterior chamber has been noted in neonates. The cataractous lenses may be small and abnormally formed. Glaucoma is present in more than half of affected males with onset by the age of 6 years and may be difficult to control. Nystagmus can be seen too. Conjunctival and corneal keloids are found in about one-fourth of patients.

Adult female carriers characteristically have peripheral cortical opacities, appearing in a radial configuration. These 'snowflake' opacities seldom cause visual symptoms.

Mental retardation, hypotonia, short stature, and developmental delays are common. Seizures and behavior problems are seen in older children. The renal defect secondary to defective phosphatidylinositol 4, 5-biphosphate 5- phosphatase results in a Fanconi-type aminoaciduria beginning late in the first year of life. The phosphaturia leads to hypophosphatemia and eventually renal rickets

The mutation causing this X-linked disorder is in the OCRL gene located at Xq26.1

Reference: Yanoff and Duker 4th edition 415/416

question_text: Extra layer of cilia posterior to grey line
explanation:
Distichiasis is a rare disorder defined as the abnormal growth of lashes from the orifices of the meibomian glands on the posterior lamella of the tarsal plate.

Incorrect Options:

A. Tylosis
Tylosis refers to the thickening or hyperkeratosis of the skin, commonly on the palms and soles, and is not associated with the growth of eyelashes.

B. Madarosis
Madarosis refers to the loss of eyelashes or eyebrows, rather than the growth of an extra layer of lashes. It can occur due to various causes, including systemic diseases and trauma.

D.Trichiasis
Trichiasis is a condition where the eyelashes grow inwards, towards the eyeball, which can cause irritation or injury to the cornea. It involves misdirected eyelashes rather than an extra layer of lashes.

Key Takeaway: Distichiasis involves the abnormal growth of eyelashes from the meibomian gland orifices on the posterior lamella of the tarsal plate, and it can lead to irritation and discomfort due to the abnormal location of the lashes.

question_text: What is the most common eye manifestation of allergy to tubercular bacilli?
explanation:
The most common eye manifestation of allergy to tubercular bacilli is chronic granulomatous uveitis. Koeppe nodules(small nodules seen at the pupillary margin of the iris) are a sign of it.

The nodules are composed of epithelioid cells and giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes.

Bussacca nodules are present at base of iris. more significant for granulomatous uveitis.

question_text: This procedure is done for which pathology

Enucleation with along optic nerve stump

DESPITE MAJOR advances in chemoreduction and local treatment of retinoblastoma, enucleation remains an important option for patients with extensive tumor. Enucleation in cases of intraocular malignant neoplasm can be lifesaving. One of the basic principles of enucleation for intraocular malignant neoplasms is to obtain a long segment of optic nerve in an effort to remove all of the tumor at the time of the enucleation. This is particularly important in eyes with retinoblastoma, because the tumor most commonly spreads via extension into the optic nerve.

Survival decreases if viable tumor cells are present at the surgical margin of the optic nerve in patients who have undergone enucleation for retinoblastoma.

Longer optic nerve specimens were obtained with the use of long, mildly curved scissors with a temporal approach.

question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with progressive clumsiness over 6 months. On examination, there is leukocoria with absence of the red reflex in the left eye. Ophthalmic imaging reveals an intraocular mass, and the eye is subsequently enucleated. Histopathology is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is the classic sign of retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular malignancy in children.

  • Age of Presentation: Usually before 3 years, with non-familial cases diagnosed by 1 year.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Leukocoria (most common presenting sign)
    • Strabismus (misaligned eyes) due to loss of vision
    • Proptosis in advanced cases
    • Orbital invasion and metastasis in late stages.
  • Histopathology:
    • Small round blue cells are characteristic of primitive neuroectodermal tumours.
    • Anastomosing areas of necrosis
    • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (well-differentiated tumours)
  • Molecular Pathogenesis:
    • RB1 gene mutation on chromosome 13q14, leading to loss of cell cycle control.
    • Loss of both alleles of RB1 leads to uncontrolled retinal cell proliferation.
  • Treatment: Enucleation for large tumors, chemotherapy, focal therapies (laser, cryotherapy) for smaller lesions.
  • Prognosis: Excellent if detected early butpoor with orbital extension or metastasis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Wilms Tumor (Option A):

  • Pediatric renal tumor presenting with abdominal mass, hematuria, hypertension
  • Histology: triphasic pattern - blastemal, stromal, epithelial
  • Not associated with RB1 mutation or intraocular mass

Ependymoma (Option C):

  • Arises in fourth ventricle or spinal cord, leading to hydrocephalus
  • Histology: perivascular pseudorosettes and true ependymal rosettes
  • Not intraocular; CNS tumor
  • Neuroblastoma (Option D):
    • Neural crest tumor, often in adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain
    • Clinical signs: abdominal mass, periorbital ecchymoses ("raccoon eyes"), opsoclonus-myoclonus
    • Histology: Homer-Wright rosettes
    • Immunohistochemistry: chromogranin, synaptophysin, NSE positive

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with a lesion in the right eye. Histopathology reveals Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of a retinal lesion in a young child and the presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathology is highly indicative of Retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular tumour in children, caused by inactivation of both alleles of the RB1 gene.

Retinoblastoma:

Explanation for Other Options:

Optic nerve glioma (Option B): A benign tumour from optic nerve glial cells, often associated with NF1, presenting with vision loss or proptosis; does not form Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C): A malignant soft tissue tumour from skeletal muscle precursors; may involve the orbit in children but lacks rosette formation.

Ocular melanoma (Option D): A malignant tumour of melanocytes in the uveal tract, typically in adults, causing visual changes or dark spots; does not display Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

Key takeaway:

Knudson's Two-Hit Hypothesis:

This hypothesis explains the development of retinoblastoma. According to this model:

  • In heritable retinoblastoma, the child inherits a germline mutation in one allele of the RB1 gene (the first hit). A subsequent somatic mutation in the other allele in the retinal cells (the second hit) leads to tumour formation.
  • In sporadic cases, both alleles of the RB1 gene are inactivated by somatic mutations (both hits occurring postnatally).

question_text: H/o male child presenting with Flexner Wintersteiner rosettes, his eye examination shows white reflex given. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes along with white reflex (leukocoria) strongly suggests retinoblastoma, the most common malignant intraocular tumor in children.

Incorrect choices explanation:

Choice A: Medulloblastoma

  • Medulloblastoma is a cerebellar tumor and does not cause leukocoria.
  • Homer-Wright rosettes, not Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, are seen in medulloblastoma.

Choice C: Rhabdomyosarcoma

  • Rhabdomyosarcoma can affect the orbit, but it does not produce leukocoria or Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.
  • Presents with a rapidly growing orbital mass, not a white reflex.

Choice D: Coat's Disease

  • Coat's disease is a non-malignant retinal disorder that can also cause leukocoria, mimicking retinoblastoma.
  • It involves abnormal retinal vessels with exudative retinal detachment but lacks Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

Key takeaway:

Leukocoria (White Reflex in the Eye) → Due to tumor mass in the retina.

Strabismus (Misalignment of the Eyes) → Due to retinal involvement affecting vision.

Flexner-Wintersteiner Rosettes → Histopathological hallmark of retinoblastoma, showing tumor cells arranged in a circular pattern with a central lumen.

Mutation in the RB1 Gene on Chromosome 13 → Inactivates the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor gene.

question_text: All are true regarding simple congenital ptosis except:

explanation:
In congenital ptosis, in downgaze, the ptotic lid is higher than the normal because of poor relaxation of the levator muscle. This is in contrast to acquired ptosis, in which the affected lid is either level with or lower than the normal lid on downgaze.

Simple congenital ptosis:

Congenital ptosis probably results from a failure of neuronal migration or development with muscular sequelae secondary to this. A minority of patients have a family history.

Signs:

  • Unilateral or bilateral ptosis of variable severity.
  • Absent upper lid crease and poor levator function.
  • In downgaze the ptotic lid is higher than the normal because of poor relaxation of the levator muscle. This is in contrast to acquired ptosis, in which the affected lid is either level with or lower than the normal lid on downgaze.
  • Following surgical correction the lid lag in downgaze may worsen.

Associations:

  • Superior rectus weakness may be present because of its close embryological association with the levator.
  • Refractive errors are common and more frequently responsible for amblyopia than the ptosis itself.

question_text: A 25-year-old man is seen in your office 2 months after blunt trauma to the right orbit. The examination is normal except for blepharoptosis on the right side. Levator function is normal on both sides, and the patient states the eyelid positions were equal on both sides prior to the injury. There is no enophthalmos, and the patient does not complain of diplopia. What is the best next step in managing this patient?
option_a: Surgical exploration and repair of the levator aponeurosis
option_b: Close observation with no plan for surgical correction until 3 to 6 months after initial injury
option_c: Computed tomography (CT) scan to rule out an orbital fracture
option_d: A Tensilon test to rule out new onset Myasthenia Gravis
explanation:
• Blunt trauma to the orbit commonly results in edema and ecchymosis to the periorbital soft tissue. These latter processes may result in stretching, dehiscence, or disinsertion of the levator aponeurosis.
  • It is difficult to correlate the degree of injury to the levator aponeurosis with the severity of blunt injury.
  • Younger patients tend to have enough elasticity in the tissue to allow significant if not complete resolution of the blepharoptosis.
  • However, for all patients, blepharoptosis from blunt injury should be allowed the opportunity to spontaneously resolve without early surgical intervention.
  • Patients should be examined monthly for changes in the eyelid position. If no improvement in eyelid position occurs by 6 months after the injury, it is unlikely that any improvement will occur in the future.
  • In this case, surgical correction may be planned. However, if improvement is noted on a month-to-month basis, then surgery should be delayed until improvement reaches a plateau or all blepharoptosis resolves.
  • A CT scan is helpful in evaluating injury to adjacent bones. There is no evidence of injury to orbital bones based on the exam (i.e., no diplopia or enophthalmos).
  • Given the history of blunt trauma, it is unlikely that a Tensilon test is warranted. Myasthenia gravis should be considered in the diagnosis of adult blepharoptosis in the absence of other predisposing factors.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/865

question_text: Which of the following are the surgical interventions done for BPES?
explanation:
The management of BPES(Blepharophimosis, ptosis, epicanthus inversus syndrome) should address the eyelid malformations, any related visual impairment and primary ovarian insufficiency if present.

Prompt surgical correction of the eyelid malformations can help prevent visual impairment from amblyopia, but later surgeries allow for more precise ptosis correction. For this reason, the exact timing of eyelid surgery is controversial.

Once amblyopia has been ruled out, management of the eyelid malformations typically involves correcting the epicanthus inversus and telecanthus at three to five years of age, followed by ptosis correction one year later.

  • Medial canthoplasty is typically done to target the epicanthus inversus and telecanthus.
  • Lateral canthoplasty can widen the horizontal palpebral fissure and help correct the blepharophimosis.
  • Frontalis sling surgery for correction of ptosis as the levator function is typically poor.

question_text: A 25 year old man presents two months after sustaining blunt trauma to his right orbit. His ophthalmological examination is normal except for right-sided ptosis. Levator function is intact bilaterally, and he reports that his eyelids were symmetric before the injury. There is no enophthalmos or diplopia. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_a: Surgical exploration and repair of the levator aponeurosis
option_b: Close observation with no surgical correction for 3-6 months
option_c: CT scan to rule out an orbital fracture
option_d: Tensilon test to rule out myasthenia gravis
explanation:
Explanation

Post-traumatic ptosis should be observed for at least 3-6 months before considering any surgical intervention.

  • Blunt orbital trauma frequently causes swelling and soft-tissue injury that may stretch or partially detach the levator aponeurosis. In young patients, these changes often improve on their own because of good tissue healing and elasticity.
  • The absence of enophthalmos and diplopia indicates that an orbital fracture is unlikely. Since the ptosis clearly followed trauma, myasthenia gravis testing is also unnecessary.
  • Surgical exploration and repair of the levator aponeurosis (option A): Early surgical intervention is not appropriate because traumatic ptosis often improves on its own as swelling and soft-tissue injury resolve. Surgery should only be considered if the ptosis persists beyond 6 months with no signs of improvement.
  • CT scan to rule out an orbital fracture (option C): A CT scan is useful when orbital fractures are suspected, typically presenting with diplopia, enophthalmos, or restricted extraocular movements.
  • Tensilon test to rule out myasthenia gravis (option D):The Tensilon test is used when ptosis is unexplained or suggests a neuromuscular cause.

question_text: Which is the most common ocular finding in myasthenia gravis?
explanation:
Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular disorder that often presents with ocular symptoms, and the most common ocular finding in MG is ptosis (drooping of the eyelids). This occurs due to weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, which is responsible for lifting the eyelid. Ptosis can start as unilateral and may shift between eyes, eventually becoming bilateral.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • B. Lagophthalmos: This refers to the inability to close the eyelids completely, which can occur in various conditions, including facial nerve paralysis, but it is not the most common finding in MG.
  • C. Proptosis: Proptosis (bulging of the eyeball) is typically seen in Graves' disease, not in myasthenia gravis.
  • D. Enophthalmos: This refers to the sunken appearance of the eyeball, which is not a feature of MG.

Key Takeaway:

Ptosis is the most common ocular finding in myasthenia gravis, typically resulting from weakness of the levator muscle and may present with shifting unilateral involvement progressing to bilateral ptosis.

question_text: A child's ptosis was found to decrease on chewing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking ptosis is a congenital ptosis associated with synkinetic movements of the upper lid on masticating movements of the jaw. Hence when jaw is moved to opposite side/chewing the ptosis improves as LPS also contracts.

This synkinetic movement results from a congenital aberrant connection between motor branches of the trigeminal nerve controlling muscles of mastication and superior division of the oculomotor nerve controlling the levator palpebrae superioris. Although most cases of Marcus Gunn phenomena(MGP) are said to be congenital, acquired forms of this condition are also known to exist.

Marcus Gunn phenomena may develop after eye surgery, syphilis, trauma, pontine tumors, etc. Spontaneous remission of the acquired form may occur, whereas the congenital form typically persists with little to no improvement over life.

question_text: A 58-year-old male smoker presents with a gradual loss of vision in his right eye over the past six months. He describes it as central blurring, making it difficult to read or recognize faces. On fundoscopy, you observe drusen deposits in the macula, along with geographic atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) causes gradual central vision loss, often described as blurring of central vision that affects activities like reading or recognizing faces.
  • Drusen deposits and geographic atrophy in the macula are classic findings.
  • Smoking is a significant risk factor, particularly in older adults.
  • Dry AMD progresses slowly compared to the wet form, and central vision loss is often the main symptom.

Why not others:

  • A) Diabetic retinopathy: Typically shows microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and affects both central and peripheral vision. Drusen deposits and geographic atrophy are not seen in diabetic retinopathy.
  • B) Retinitis pigmentosa: A genetic disorder causing peripheral vision loss ("tunnel vision") and affects night vision. Bone-spicule pigmentation is seen on fundoscopy, unlike the drusen deposits of AMD.
  • D) Retinal artery occlusion: Causes sudden, painless vision loss with a characteristic cherry-red spot on fundoscopy. The gradual loss of vision and drusen deposits are not consistent with this diagnosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Dry AMD presents with gradual central vision loss, drusen deposits, and geographic atrophy.
  • Other options (diabetic retinopathy, retinitis pigmentosa, retinal artery occlusion) do not match the combination of gradual central blurring and fundoscopic findings seen in AMD.

Indications Q – Intraocular malignacy, endophthalmitis, panophthalmitis, traumatic painful blind eye, sympathetic ophthalmitis

Advantages of evisceration over enucleation

  • Shorter operative time
  • Less complex
  • Less disruption of orbital tissues
  • Improved motility

Exenteration - surgical removal of the entire globe and its surrounding structures including muscles, fat, nerves, and eyelids. This is the most radical procedure

Indications - Orbital malignacies like Squamous Cell Carcinoma, sebaceous cell carcinoma, mucormycosis, adenoid cystic carcinoma of lacrimal gland.

question_text: A child presents with this eyelid margin condition and fall of eyelashes also. what is your diagnosis
explanation:
Blepharitis is an inflammation of the eyelids in which they become red, irritated and itchy with dandruff-like scales that form on the eyelashes. It is a common eye disorder caused by either bacteria or a skin condition, such as dandruff of the scalp or rosacea.

Blepharitis is classified into two types.

  1. Anterior blepharitis: Anterior blepharitis occurs at the outside front edge of the eyelid where the eyelashes attach.
  2. Posterior blepharitis: Posterior blepharitis affects the inner edge of the eyelid that touches the eyeball.

The different types and symptoms are as follows:

  • Staphylococcal blepharitis patients frequently exhibit mildly sticking eyelids, thickened lid margins and missing and misdirected eyelashes.
  • Seborrheic blepharitis patients have greasy flakes or scales around the base of eyelashes and a mild redness of the eyelids.
  • Ulcerative blepharitis patients have matted, hard crusts around the eyelashes. Removing the crusts leaves small sores that ooze and bleed. These patients may also experience eyelash loss, distortion of the front edges of the eyelids and chronic tearing. In severe cases, the cornea(the transparent front covering of the eyeball) becomes inflamed.
  • Meibomian blepharitis patients have a blockage of the oil glands in the eyelids, poor quality of tears and redness of the lining of the eyelids.

Reference: Kanski 8/e, Pg. 32.

question_text: Recurrent chalazion in upper lid in an old woman suggest
explanation:
Chalazion and sebaceous carcinoma of the eyelid are diseases that originate predominantly from meibomian glands. Chalazion is a relatively common condition characterized by lipogranulomatous inflammation of meibomian glands in the eyelid. It often arises secondarily to noninfectious obstruction of a meibomian gland duct. Histopathologically, chalazion manifests as a lipogranulomatous reaction to liberated lipid granules contained within a connective tissue pseudocapsule.

On the other hand, sebaceous carcinoma is a relatively uncommon malignant neoplasm that most often arises in the meibomian glands of the eyelid. It results from the malignant proliferation of sebaceous cells that manifest a vacuolated cytoplasm due to the presence of lipid. Sebaceous carcinoma mostly affects older adults.

Reference: Kanski 7/e, Pg. 5.

question_text: Which of the following signs is found in blepharochalasis syndrome?
explanation:
• Blepharochalasis is an uncommon condition characterized by recurrent episodes of painless, non-pitting oedema of both upper lids which usually resolves spontaneously after a few days.
  • Presentation is usually around puberty, episodes becoming less frequent with time.
  • Eyelid skin becomes stretched and atrophic, characteristically said to resemble wrinkled cigarette paper; severe cases may give rise to stretching of the canthal tendons and levator aponeurosis resulting in ptosis, and lacrimal gland prolapse may occur.
  • A hypertrophic form with orbital fat herniation and an atrophic form with absorption of orbital fat have been described.
  • The differential diagnosis includes similarly episodic conditions, particularly drug-induced urticaria and angioedema.
  • Treatment involves blepharoplasty for redundant upper lid skin, and correction of ptosis.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/55

question_text: In a patient presenting with recurrent chalazion, which cancer should be suspected?
explanation:
Explanation:

Sebaceous cell carcinoma is a rare but highly aggressive malignancy that originates from sebaceous glands, particularly the meibomian glands of the eyelids. Because it can mimic benign conditions, such as recurrent chalazion or chronic blepharitis, it is often diagnosed late. A recurrent chalazion in an older patient should therefore raise suspicion for sebaceous carcinoma.

  • Common site: eyelids (meibomian glands, Zeis glands).
  • May present as a nodular mass or diffuse thickening of the eyelid margin.
  • Can spread locally and metastasize.

Explanation of Other Options:

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Option B): Although squamous carcinoma can involve the eyelid, it generally presents with an ulcerative, scaly lesion or a rapidly enlarging mass. It does not typically mimic a recurrent chalazion.

Basal Cell Carcinoma (Option C): Basal cell carcinoma is the most common eyelid malignancy, but it usually appears as a pearly, rolled-margin nodule with central ulceration. It rarely presents as recurrent chalazion and has a more indolent, locally invasive course.

Kaposi's Sarcoma (Option D): Kaposi's sarcoma affects vascular tissues, often seen in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS). It manifests as reddish-purple vascular lesions, not recurrent chalazions.

Reference: Chalazion - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

  • In adults, the canaliculi are 10 mm long (8 mm horizontal, 2 mm vertical), the nasolacrimal sac is 10 mm and the duct is 12 to 15 mm in length.

question_text: Where is the location of the canaliculi that open into the lacrimal sac in relation to the orbit's wall?
explanation:
Explanation:

The canaliculi are fine ducts that begin at the puncta (tiny openings on the medial aspect of the upper and lower eyelids). These ducts carry tears medially and open into the lacrimal sac, which lies in the lacrimal fossa of the orbit.

  • The lacrimal sac is located in the medial canthal region, within a depression formed by the frontal process of the maxilla and the lacrimal bone.
  • Thus, the canaliculi open into the lacrimal sac, which is situated along the medial wall of the orbit.

Explanation of Other Options:

Lateral wall (Option A): The lateral orbital wall (formed mainly by the zygomatic and sphenoid bones) is on the outer side of the eye and has no role in tear drainage.

Superior wall (Option C): Also called the orbital roof (formed by the frontal bone), it separates the orbit from the anterior cranial fossa and does not contain the lacrimal drainage system.

Inferior wall (Option D): The orbital floor (formed mainly by the maxilla) separates the orbit from the maxillary sinus and is unrelated to the canaliculi.

question_text: When passing a probe down the canalicular portion of the lacrimal excretory system, at what length does the tip of the cannula enter the lacrimal sac?
explanation:
The canalicular system is 8-12 mm in length. Usually the canaliculi combine to form a common canaliculus.

The lacrimal drainage system consists of the following structures:

  • The puncta are located at the posterior edge of the lid margin, at the junction of the lash-bearing lateral five-sixths (pars ciliaris) and the medial non-ciliated one-sixth (pars lacrimalis). Normally they face slightly posteriorly and can be inspected by everting the medial aspect of the lids. Treatment of watering caused by punctal stenosis or malposition is relatively straightforward.
  • The canaliculi pass vertically from the lid margin for about 2 mm (ampullae). They then turn medially and run horizontally for about 8 mm to reach the lacrimal sac. The superior and inferior canaliculi usually (>90%) unite to form the common canaliculus, which opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac. Uncommonly, each canaliculus opens separately into the sac. A small flap of mucosa (Rosenmüller valve) overhangs the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac (the internal punctum) and prevents reflux of tears into the canaliculi. Treatment of canalicular obstruction may be complex.
  • The lacrimal sac is 10–12 mm long and lies in the lacrimal fossa between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests. The lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla separate the lacrimal sac from the middle meatus of the nasal cavity. In a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) an anastomosis is created between the sac and the nasal mucosa to bypass an obstruction in the nasolacrimal duct.
  • The nasolacrimal duct is 12–18 mm long and is the inferior continuation of the lacrimal sac. It descends and angles slightly laterally and posteriorly to open into the inferior nasal meatus, lateral to and below the inferior turbinate. The opening of the duct is partially covered by a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner).

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/64
