question_text: What is the most common ocular manifestation in rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
The most common eye-related symptom of rheumatoid arthritis is dryness.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease that classically presents with symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis, joint stiffness, fever, weight loss, and malaise.

Dry eye syndrome, also known as keratoconjunctivitis sicca, is the most common ocular manifestation of RA. It can occur as a result of meibomian gland, lacrimal gland, accessory lacrimal gland, or goblet cell dysfunction.

Characteristics - Symptoms of dry eye syndrome include foreign body sensation, burning, decreased visual acuity, photophobia, and pruritus.

Diagnostic signs include -

  • Less than 5 mm of tear extension on Schirmer's test
  • Tear break-up time of 5 seconds or less
  • Decreased lacrimal lake, and staining with fluorescein, rose bengal, or lissamine green.
  • Up to 25% of patients with RA meet criteria for secondary Sjogren syndrome, which is less commonly associated with xerostomia than is primary Sjogren syndrome.

Other considerations -

  • The normal tear film has antimicrobial properties and contains immunomodulatory factors such as collagenase inhibitors (e.g., alpha-2 macroglobulin).
  • Patients with dry eye syndrome are deficient in these protective mechanisms and have increased proteolytic enzymes such as plasminogen activator in the tear film.
  • Consequentially, dry eye syndrome can lead to superficial punctate keratitis, filamentary keratitis, corneal ulcer, and ultimately, corneal melt.
  • Accordingly, RA is a relative contraindication against refractive surgery, especially LASIK, due to its potential to exacerbate dry eye syndrome.

Treatment -

Lubricating drops and ointments, topical cyclosporine, and oral pilocarpine.

The recent approval of lifitegrast has added a new medication to our armamentarium of topical treatments. In-office procedures include punctal occlusion, use of amniotic membrane, and tarsorrhaphy.

Reference: Parson 20/e, p.460

question_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland moves the eyeball
explanation:
Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common tumor of the lacrimal gland. It is a benign mixed tumour.

  • Clinically it presents as a slowly progressive painless swelling in the upper - outer quadrant of the orbit displacing the eyeball downwards and inwards e in the opposite quadrant
  • It is locally invasive and infiltrate its own pseudocapsule to involve the adjacent periosteum.
  • Histologically, it is characterized by the presence of pleomorphic myxomatous tissue, just like benign mixed tumour of salivary gland.
  • Treatment consists of complete surgical removal with the capsule.
  • Recurrences are very common following incomplete removal.

question_text: What is the most common site of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction?
explanation:
Congenital dacryocystitis is the inflammation of the lacrimal sac in a newborn, most commonly due to delayed/incomplete canalization of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD), most often at the lower end of NLD and near valve of Hasner- occlusion is membranous.

Presents with epiphora, swelling and purulent discharge at inner canthus.

Treatment

  • Massage over lacrimal sac with topical antibiotics -initial treatment of choice for 1 year.
  • Syringing is attempted usually by 9-12 months of age. Most of us do it after 1 year only
  • Probing of NLDshould be undertaken after 12 months of age, as spontaneous resolution is likely to occur by 12 months.
  • Dacryocystorhinostomy after 4 years of age.

Reference: Parson's 21/e p. 464, 466

question_text: Dacryocystorhinostomy involves:
option_a: Opening up the terminal blocked end of the nasolacrimal duct
option_b: Draining the lacrimal sac into the nose via a bypass conduit
option_d: Insertion of drainage tube in the lacrimal sac
explanation:
Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is an operation where by the lacrimal sac is drained into the nose via a bypass conduit.

External DCR -

  • A curvilinear incision as small as 8 mm is made on the side of the nose below the medial canthal tendon, and the dissection is carried down to bone.
  • The periosteum is reflected from the anterior lacrimal crest to reveal the lacrimal sac fossa.
  • The sac is then reflected laterally.
  • The nose is entered by pushing a blunt instrument through the suture line between the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla.
  • Kerrison punches are used to remove bone between the sac fossa and the nose, to create an opening large enough to anastomose the sac and nasal mucosa.
  • Flaps are created in the medial sac wall and in the adjacent nasal mucosa.
  • The posterior flaps and then the anterior flaps of the sac and nasal mucosa are sutured togetherto form a mucosa-lined tunnel across the ostium. The new opening is amade at level of middle meatus
  • Silicone tubes are usually not necessary, but if desired, they can be placed at this time and left in for 6-12 weeks.

Endonasal DCR -

  • When the obstruction is in the lower drainage system and the canaliculi are anatomically normal, an endonasal approach may be attempted as an alternative to an external DCR.
  • The advantage of this procedure is that it avoids any cutaneous incisions.
  • The nasal mucosa is incised, elevated, and removed around the light spot with the use of a scalpel or laser.
  • The thin bone of the lacrimal bone is punctured and enlarged with Kerrison punches.
  • The ostium should not extend behind the posterior lacrimal crest or above the lacrimal sac.
  • The sac mucosa is opened with Vannas scissors, and a portion of the medial wall is excised.
  • Silicone stents must be placed through the system and left for 3-4 months.
  • This approach also allows the surgeon to deal with nasal adhesions, granulation tissue, and hypertrophic turbinates at the same time.

Indications for DCR surgery:

  • Primary acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO)
  • Secondary acquired NLDO, such as due to prior midfacial trauma, chronic nasal or sinus inflammation, nasal surgery, neoplasms, dacryoliths
  • Functional obstruction of outflow, due to lacrimal pump weakness or after facial nerve palsy
  • Congenital NLDO after failed prior probing or intubation
  • History of chronic dacryocystitis

Reference: Parson's 21/e p. 471-474

question_text: Which of the following is a cause of epiphora?
explanation:
Causes of epiphora (overflow of tears at the eyelid margin) include -

Hypersecretion secondary to anterior segment disease such as dry eye ('paradoxical watering') or inflammation.

Defective drainage due to a compromised lacrimal drainage system; this may be caused by:

  • Malposition of the lacrimal puncta.
  • Obstruction at any point along the drainage system, from the punctal region to the valve of Hasner. Ex: Nasolacrimal duct block
  • Lacrimal pump failure, which may occur secondarily to lower lid laxity or weakness of the orbicularis muscle. Ex: Facial nerve palsy

question_text: This test is positive in which ocular pathology
explanation:
This test is regurgitation test : Pressure over the lacrimal sac may reveal a mucocele. The flow of mucoid material from the puncta will confirm the presence of a nasolacrimal duct obstruction. This may be used in adults and children

To avoid false negative results, it is important to apply pressure over the lacrimal sac in the lacrimal fossa in a slightly backward and upward direction. A positive regurgitation test is a confirmatory test for chronic dacryocystitis with NLDO and no further diagnostic testing is usually necessary in these cases

It is also called as Regurgitation on pressure over the lacrimal sac (ROPLAS) with a specificity as high as 99%. 1 This implies that if the ROPLAS test is positive, a nasolacrimal duct obstruction is almost certainly present.

question_text: Which procedure is shown in this picture
explanation:
Probing and irrigation of the lacrimal drainage system should be performed whenever analysis of the lacrimal drainage system is indicated.

In the case of nasolacrimal obstruction–related epiphora, this procedure provides vital insight into the location and severity of obstruction if present. The results not only help identify the cause of a patient’s epiphora but also assist in surgical planning if the results are abnormal.

In the case of trauma to the eyelid or medial face, probing and irrigation can help determine if there is injury to the lacrimal drainage system. In the setting of acute trauma, a visible lacrimal probe inserted in the canaliculus or leakage of irrigation fluid through a traumatized eyelid is an indication of canalicular injury that must be addressed during planned repair of the trauma.

In the case of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction that does not resolve by the age of 12 months, probing of the canaliculi and the nasolacrimal duct is performed with the patient under anesthesia to achieve patency in the system.

question_text: A 60-year-old patient presents with recurrent tearing, discharge, and mild swelling near the inner corner of the eye. The history and clinical findings suggest chronic dacryocystitis. What is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
Explanation:

Chronic dacryocystitis involves long-standing inflammation and infection of the lacrimal sac, usually due to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. Typical symptoms include recurrent epiphora, discharge, and mild swelling at the medial canthus.

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR):

  • Surgical procedure to create a direct drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity.
  • Definitely restores tear drainage, addresses the obstruction, and prevents recurrence.

Explanation of Other Options:

Lacrimal sac massage (Option A): Useful for mild or early nasolacrimal duct obstruction, particularly in infants. It helps express accumulated tears but does not resolve chronic obstruction in adults.

Syringing (Option C): It can help confirm the presence of a blockage and occasionally clear minor obstructions. However, it does not offer a definitive solution for chronic dacryocystitis in adults.

Probing (Option D): Primarily used for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in children. Not suitable for adults with chronic or long-standing obstruction and structural changes.

question_text: Which of the following is not true about the nasolacrimal duct?
option_b: It functions as a mucosa associated lymphoid tissue
option_c: It drains tears into the inferior meatus of the nose
option_d: It is lined by fibres of Horner muscle
explanation:
Upper and lower canaliculi are surrounded by a dense ring of connective tissue and fibres of the Horner muscle and not lacrimal duct ..

Nasolacrimal duct (NLD) / Tear Duct-

  • Carries tears from the lacrimal sac of the eye into the nasal cavity.
  • The duct begins in the eye socket between the maxillary and lacrimal bones, from where it passes downwards and backwards.
  • The opening of the NLD into the inferior nasal meatus of the nasal cavity is partially covered by a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner or plica lacrimalis).
  • This is the reason why excess tears and eye drops flow through the nasolacrimal duct into the nose.
  • Like the lacrimal sac, the duct is lined by stratified columnar epithelium containing mucus-secreting goblet cells, and is surrounded by connective tissue.
  • Serous glands are present in the lamina propria of the ducts
  • NLD is integral to the ocular immune system. It consists of T lymphocytes and CD20, CD45RA rich B lymphocytes. Aggregated follicles are present in nearly one third of the NLD fulfilling the criteria for mucosa associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).

Reference: Khurana Anatomy, 2/e, P. 369

question_text: What is the most common organism implicated in dacryocystitis?
explanation:

question_text: A 55-year-old woman is being evaluated for surgical management of chronic dacryocystitis. Which surgical procedure is considered the treatment of choice in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The preferred treatment for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), a surgical procedure aimed at restoring proper tear drainage.

DCR works by creating a direct communication between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, bypassing the blocked nasolacrimal duct. This effectively resolves the obstruction, allows normal tear outflow, and significantly reduces the risk of recurrence. It is considered the definitive management for long-standing cases of dacryocystitis.


Explanation for other options:

Dacryocystectomy (Option B): This procedure involves the complete removal of the lacrimal sac and is typically reserved for cases of fibrosis or non-functioning sac. It is not the treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis.

Probing (Option C): This is a first-line treatment in infants with congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction. It is not commonly used in adults with chronic dacryocystitis.

Balloon catheter dilation (Option D): This method is used to dilate partially blocked nasolacrimal ducts and may be effective in select cases. However, it is not the primary treatment for chronic dacryocystitis in adults.

question_text: What is the most appropriate treatment for a 55-year-old woman who is experiencing long-term mucopurulent discharge from her left eye and swelling near the inner corner of the eye?
explanation:

Dacryocystitis

  • Infection of the lacrimal sac is usually secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. It may be acute or chronic.
  • Most commonly staphylococcal or streptococcal.

question_text: Which one of the following is not a branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve?
explanation:
• The trigeminal nerve divides into three segments: ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and, mandibular (V3).
  • The ophthalmic nerve is divided into three branches: nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal.
  • The frontal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic (V1) segment, divides into the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves.
  • The maxillary (V2) segment divides into the infraorbital, zygomatic, and superior alveolar nerves.
  • The zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal nerves are branches of the zygomatic nerve (V2).
  • Figure 2-13 shows the three segments of the trigeminal nerve and the various nerve branches.

question_text: Blow out fracture of the orbit, most commonly leads to fracture of
explanation:
The anatomy of the orbital floor predisposes it to fracture.

Most commonly, the inferior orbital wall, or the floor, is likely to collapse, because the bones of the roof and lateral walls are robust. Although the bone forming the medial wall is the thinnest, it is buttressed by the bone separating the ethmoidal air cells.

The inferior orbital neurovascular bundle (comprising the infraorbital nerve and artery) courses within the bony floor of the orbit; the roof of this infraorbital canal is only 0.23mm thick, and the bone of the posterior medial orbital floor averages 0.37 mm thick. By contrast, the bone of the lateral portion of the orbital floor averages 1.25 mm thick, over 5 times the thickness of the bone over the neurovascular bundle. As one might suspect, it is this very thin area of the orbital floor overlying the neurovascular bundle where isolated orbital floor fractures frequently occur.

Reference: 9th/e kanski chapter 22 trauma pg. 894 Orbital floor fracture

question_text: A 15-year-old girl presents with a painless swelling in the right supraorbital region that has been gradually progressing over the past year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:
A dermoid cyst is the most likely diagnosis. This is a congenital choristoma (normal tissue in an abnormal location) that arises from ectodermal tissue trapped along embryonic suture lines. The presentation of a painless, slow-growing, smooth, mobile mass in the uperior temporal (supraorbital) region of the orbit (near the frontozygomatic suture) in a child or young adult is classic for a dermoid cyst.

Explanation of other options:

Lacrimal gland mass (Option A): Usually presents superolateral, may be painful or associated with inflammatory signs, and can be neoplastic or inflammatory. Gradual, painless swelling without other signs is less typical.

Hemangioma (Option C): Typically appears in infancy, is compressible, may blanch, and often regresses spontaneously. Rarely presents as a slowly enlarging lesion in adolescence.

Epidermoid cyst (Option D): Rare in the orbit, usually slow-growing, firm, and not typically localized to suture lines like dermoid cysts.

question_text:
Which of the following nerves are not involved in case of head injury with oculocephalic reflex present?
1. CN III
2. CN IV
3. CN VI
4. CN VII
5. CN VIII
explanation: he oculo-cephalic reflex (OCR) is a reflex eye movement that stabilizes images on the retina during head movement by producing an eye movement in the direction opposite to head movement, thus preserving the image on the center of the visual field. For example, when the head moves to the right, the eyes move to the left, and vice versa. This reflex can be tested by the Rapid head impulse test or Halmagyi-Curthoys-test, in which the head is rapidly moved to the side with force, and is controlled if the eyes succeed to remain looking in the same direction. When the function of the right balance system is reduced, by a disease or by an accident, quick head movement to the right cannot be sensed properly anymore. As a consequence, no compensatory eye movement is generated, and the patient cannot fixate a point in space during this rapid head movement. In comatose patients, once it has been determined that the cervical spine is intact, a test of the vestibulo-ocular reflex can be performed by turning the head to one side. If the brainstem is intact, the eyes will move conjugately away from the direction of turning (as if still looking at the examiner rather than fixed straight ahead). Negative Doll's eyes would stay fixed midorbit, so having negative "doll's eyes" is a sign that a comatose patient's brainstem is not intact. There is one very important contraindication of this examination - trauma of a cervical spine - because we could seriously injured patient. Sometimes a result can be false-positive thanks to influence of some medication (anesthesia).

question_text: 8 ball hyphema is
option_b: Hyphema which occurs during playing pool
option_d: Total hyphema giving black color like in the game of pool
explanation:
Accumulation of red blood cells within the anterior chamber is referred to as a hyphema

Hyphemas can be graded from I-IV in the following manner:

Grade 0: No visible layering, but red blood cells within the anterior chamber (microhyphema)

Grade I: Layered blood occupying less than one third of the anterior chamber

Grade II: Blood filling one third to one half of the anterior chamber

Grade III: Layered blood filling one half to less than total of the anterior chamber

Grade IV: Total filling of the anterior chamber with blood. If the anterior chamber is completely filled with bright red blood it is called a total hyphema. If the anterior chamber is filled with dark red-black blood it is called a blackball or 8-ball hyphema. The black color is suggestive of impaired aqueous circulation and decreased oxygen concentration. This distinction is important because an eight ball hyphema is more likely to cause pupillary block and secondary angle closure


Hyphema treatment depends on the severity of the case. Virtually all patients with it are told to limit their physical activity, wear an eye patch as it heals, and sleep with their heads elevated to help the blood clear out and prevent additional bleeding

Topical corticosteroids (systemic for severe cases) may reduce associated inflammation, although the effect on the risk for rebleeding is debatable.

Indications of removal

  1. IOP of 25 mmhg or more for 5 days with a total hyphema or
  2. IOP of 60 mmHg or more for 2 days are indications for drainage

Former to prevent corneal blood staining and the latter to prevent optic atrophy.

Re bleed most common within 24 hours of primary haemorrhage

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for a 3-year-old boy who has presented with cognitive impairment and difficulty in mobility, along with the provided fundoscopy image?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The combination of cognitive regression, motor difficulties, and a cherry-red spot on fundoscopy is classic for Tay-Sachs disease.
  • This is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of hexosaminidase A, leading to accumulation of GM2 gangliosides in neurons.
  • The disease causes progressive neurodegeneration in early childhood, with rapid decline and early mortality.

Conditions associated with a cherry-red spot

Incorrect Options

Hunter disease (Option B): An X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis presenting with coarse facial features, airway obstruction, hepatosplenomegaly, and cognitive decline, but it does not cause a cherry-red spot.

Hurler syndrome (Option C): Another mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS I), characterized by gargoyle-like facies, corneal clouding, developmental delay, and skeletal abnormalities. A cherry-red spot is not a typical feature.

Gaucher disease (Option D): A glucocerebrosidase deficiency leading to hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bone crises. Ocular cherry-red spots are not a hallmark finding in this condition.

Key Takeaway:

Tay-Sachs disease presents neurodegeneration in infancy, motor delay, cognitive impairment, and the classic cherry-red spot on fundoscopy, making it a key differential in pediatric cases with leukodystrophy-like symptoms.

explanation:

question_text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after being struck in the eye with a baseball. He complains of double vision when looking up and numbness over his cheek and upper lip on the affected side. Which of the following is the most common and characteristic finding associated with an orbital floor "blowout" fracture?
option_c: Rapid improvement of traumatic diplopia over a 24-hour period
explanation:
Explanation:

This clinical scenario is classic for an orbital floor "blowout" fracture. The most common neurologic finding associated with this injury is unilateral midfacial sensory loss (numbness of the cheek, upper lip, and upper gingiva). This occurs because the infraorbital nerve, a branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), runs in a groove along the thin orbital floor. The fracture frequently contuses or entraps this nerve, leading to hypoesthesia in its distribution.

Explanation of Other Options:

Orbital cellulitis (Option A): Infection is a rare complication of an orbital floor fracture, not a common presenting sign.

Immediate enophthalmos (within 24 hours) (Option B): Initially, the eye may be proptotic (pushed forward) due to swelling and hemorrhage. Enophthalmos (sinking of the globe) is a late sign that develops over days to weeks as the edema resolves and orbital fat herniates into the maxillary sinus.

Rapid improvement of traumatic diplopia over a 24-hour period (Option C): The diplopia, especially on upgaze, is caused by entrapment or contusion of the inferior rectus muscle. This is a significant injury that takes weeks to resolve and may require surgical intervention; it does not improve rapidly.

question_text: Most common retrorbital mass in females is
explanation:
Cavernous hemangiomas are the most common vascular lesions of the orbit in adults and account for 5-7% of all orbital tumors. However, debate exists about whether these lesions should actually be considered tumors.

They usually present in middle age (30-50 years of age) and there appears to be a female predilection. Clinical presentation is usually with a slowly growing orbital mass resulting in proptosis. Diplopia and visual field defects (from optic nerve compression) may also occur

They are well circumscribed but seldom encapsulated. Microscopically, they are composed of multiple vascular channels lined by a single layer of flat epithelium and supported by fibrous septa.

if the lesion is found incidentally and no exophthalmos or visual complications are present then conservative management is recommended, with periodic MRI imaging.

In cases where symptoms are present, or growth of the lesion is demonstrated on follow-up imaging, surgical removal is curative.

question_text: A man suffered trauma to the eye from a punch while fighting with another person. What is the most common site of fracture in orbit?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Floor is the weakest wall of orbit due to the presence of Inferior orbital fissure (although medial wall of the orbit is the thinnest wall).
  • Trauma to the orbit can result in fracture of the floor of the orbit known as 'Blowout fracture'

Blow-out fractures of orbit

  • Result from trauma causing backward displacement of the eyeball and an increase in intraorbital pressure, leading to a resultant fracture.
  • Usually due to blunt trauma caused by a large object such as a cricket ball.
  • Since the bones of the lateral wall and the roof are usually able to withstand such trauma, the fracture most frequently involves the floor of the orbit along the thin bone covering the infraorbital canal. Occasionally, the medial orbital wall may also be fractured. (Option A, B, C ruled out).

Clinical Features

  • Periocular signs
  • Periorbital oedema
  • Ecchymosis
  • Subcutaneous emphysema of the eyelids
  • Paresthesia and anesthesia in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve (lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, and upper teeth)
  • Ipsilateral epistaxis (bleeding from maxillary sinus)
  • Proptosis, often due to orbital oedema and hemorrhage
  • Enophthalmos: Due to orbital fat escape, muscle entrapment, and cavity enlargement)
  • Diplopia

Radiological findings:

  • X-ray: Water's view shows 'hanging drop' opacity of the superior maxillary antrum due to herniated orbital contents.
  • CT/MRI: Coronal sections show extent of the fracture and herniation; exhibits the hanging drop or teardrop sign.

Management

General Measures and Medical Treatment:

  • Avoid nose blowing
  • Systemic antibiotics to prevent sinus infection
  • Analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs
  • Cold compresses to decrease swelling
  • Nasal decongestants

Surgical Management:

  • Optimal surgery time: 10-14 days after injury
  • Surgical indications: Persistent diplopia, large herniation, tissue incarceration, enophthalmos >3mm

Orbital Surgeries:

  • Orbitotomy: 4 approaches: anterior, lateral, transfrontal, and temporofrontal
  • Exenteration: Removal of all orbital contents and periorbita through an incision along orbital margins.

question_text: A patient presented with unilateral proptosis which was compressible and increases on bending forward. No thrill or bruit was present. MRI shows a retroorbital mass with enhancement. The likely diagnosis is
explanation:

Orbital varices are usually diagnosed between the ages of 10-30 years

Risk factors for primary orbital varices are not well established. Secondary orbital varices are associated with carotid-cavernous fistula, dural arteriovenous fistula, and intracranial arteriovenous malformation

Most patients will experience unilateral positional proptosis with a head-down position, and intermittent proptosis that is exacerbated by coughing, straining, the Valsalva maneuver, or compression of the jugular veins. This occurs because the orbital venous system is connected to the systemic venous circulation

They can lead to haemorrhage, thrombosis and orbital nerve compression.

question_text: Which of the following is not a typical clinical finding associated with an orbital blowout fracture?
explanation:
Explanation:

Proptosis is not a characteristic feature of a blow-out fracture. In fact, after the initial swelling decreases, patients usually develop enophthalmos because orbital fat and tissues herniate downward through the fractured orbital floor.

  • A blowout fracture involves a break in the orbital floor, often from blunt trauma such as a fist or ball. The inferior rectus muscle may get trapped, producing vertical diplopia and a positive forced-duction test. Damage to the infraorbital nerve results in decreased sensation over the cheek, side of the nose, and upper lip.
  • Tear drop sign (option A): This refers to the appearance on Waters' view X-ray where herniated orbital tissues protrude into the maxillary sinus, creating a "teardrop" shadow, a classic indicator of an orbital floor fracture.
  • Loss of sensation (option C): Occurs due to compression or injury of the infraorbital nerve, resulting in numbness of the lower eyelid, cheek, upper teeth, and the lateral aspect of the nose.
  • Diplopia (option D): Commonly occurs because the inferior rectus muscle becomes entrapped in the fractured floor, restricting upward and downward eye movement and causing double vision.

question_text: Which of the following CT findings is not commonly seen with thyroid-related orbitopathy?

  • The most common cause for unilateral orbital proptosis in an adult is thyroid-related orbitopathy.
  • Even though the clinical finding may indicate a unilateral problem, a CT scan or MRI often show bilateral disease.
  • The CT findings consist of fusiform enlargement of the extraocular muscle, commonly the inferior and medial rectus muscles, with sparing of the tendons.

question_text: Following an orbital blowout fracture, what is the most reliable method to differentiate a restrictive eye movement problem from a paretic problem?
option_c: Motility examination of the cardinal positions of gaze
explanation:
Explanation:

Forced-duction testing is the most accurate clinical method to differentiate a restrictive eye movement problem from a paretic problem.

  • Tests such as alternate prism cover testing, visual field mapping, and routine motility evaluation can detect and measure ocular misalignment, but they cannot determine whether the limitation in movement is caused by mechanical restriction or nerve/muscle paresis.
  • Forced-duction testing is the most accurate clinical method to distinguish these possibilities. It should be performed a few days after the trauma because early swelling or hematoma may falsely suggest restriction. After applying topical anesthesia, the eye is grasped at the limbus and gently moved in the direction of limitation.
  • If the eye moves freely: paresis
  • If movement is resisted: restriction (e.g., muscle entrapment)
  • Alternate prism cover testing (option A): This test helps measure ocular deviation and detect misalignment, but it cannot determine whether the limitation is due to muscle entrapment (restrictive) or muscle weakness (paretic).
  • Goldmann single binocular visual fields (option B): Goldmann perimetry may show diplopia fields or areas of binocular visual disturbance, but it does not differentiate between mechanical restriction and paresis.
  • Motility examination of the cardinal positions of gaze (option C): Observing eye movements is important, but it provides only the pattern of limitation. It does not reliably identify whether the cause is restrictive (e.g., trapped muscle) or paretic (e.g, nerve injury).

question_text: Which of the following is not a common sign of an orbital blowout fracture?
explanation:
• Numbness of the ipsilateral cheek, upper lip, and upper teeth is a classic finding of a blowout fracture.
  • This hypoesthesia is a result of edema or direct injury to the infraorbital nerve as it courses through the infraorbital canal in the vicinity of the fracture site.
  • Restrictive strabismus is present in 40% to 63% of patients with isolated floor fractures. Enophthalmos may be present immediately or may develop later; it can be quantified by using an exophthalmometer.
  • Acute enophthalmos is due to loss of orbital tissue into the maxillary or ethmoid sinus. Late-onset enophthalmos results from atrophy and/or contraction of orbital tissues.
  • Other signs that suggest enophthalmos are a deepening of the superior sulcus or a narrowed palpebral fissure.
  • Tenderness over the zygomaticofrontal suture is not characteristic of an isolated blowout fracture but is a common finding in a zygomaticomaxillary (tripod) fracture.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/864

question_text: What is the preferred management of pediatric optic nerve gliomas confined to orbit?

explanation:
• Optic nerve gliomas that are confined to the orbit can be observed, particularly if vision is good.
  • Radiation is used if the tumor is unresectable because of chiasm or tract involvement and symptoms are progressing.
  • Chemotherapy is effective in progressive chiasmal or hypothalamic gliomas and may avoid complications of radiation.

question_text: A 24-year-old man was involved in an automobile accident in which his face struck the dashboard. He denies any loss of consciousness, but says his vision is blurred in the right eye. Visual acuity is 6/60 OD and 6/6 OS. External examination shows periocular swelling and ecchymosis of the right eye. Motility examination shows moderate restriction to up gaze of the right eye and normal versions of the left eye. Biomicroscopy and dilated fundus examinations are normal. What is the most common location of an orbital blowout fracture?
option_a: The orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve
option_b: The orbital aspect of the zygoma
option_c: The orbital aspect of the maxilla and inferior orbital rim
option_d: The orbital floor lateral to the infraorbital nerve
explanation:
• A blowout fracture is a fracture of the orbital floor while the inferior orbital rim remains intact.
  • The most common location of this type of fracture is the posteromedial orbital floor, which is medial to the infraorbital nerve.
  • The inferior orbital rim and the adjacent anterior portion of the floor are stronger by comparison.
  • The floor is composed primarily of the orbital plate of the maxilla, which is thinnest on the medial side of the infraorbital sulcus.
  • Most of the medial orbital wall consists of the very thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid bone.
  • The lateral orbital wall consists of the zygomatic bone and the greater wing of the sphenoid and is the strongest of the orbital walls; a blowout fracture rarely occurs in this area.

Reference: Kanski 8th edition/864

question_text: A 24-year-old man is evaluated after his face struck the dashboard in a car accident. He reports blurred vision in his right eye but did not lose consciousness. Visual acuity is 6/60 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left. The right eye shows eyelid swelling and bruising. Eye movement testing reveals a limited upward gaze in the right eye, while the left eye moves normally. Slit lamp and fundus examinations are unremarkable. What is the most frequent site of an orbital blowout fracture?
option_a: The orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve
option_b: The orbital aspect of the zygoma
option_c: The orbital aspect of the maxilla and inferior orbital rim
option_d: The orbital floor lateral to the infraorbital nerve
explanation:
Explanation

The orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve is the most frequent site of an orbital blowout fracture.

  • A blowout fracture occurs when the orbital floor breaks while the inferior orbital rim stays intact. The most vulnerable area is the posteromedial orbital floor, located medial to the infraorbital nerve, because this region is the thinnest portion of the floor. It is primarily formed by the orbital plate of the maxilla, which becomes especially delicate near the medial side of the infraorbital sulcus.
  • In contrast, the inferior rim and the lateral orbital wall are much thicker and structurally stronger, making them less likely to fracture in a typical blowout injury. The medial wall (lamina papyracea) is also thin, but blowout fractures characteristically involve the floor rather than the wall. Infraorbital hypoesthesia, Restriction of supraduction, and Enophthalmos are signs of an orbital blowout fracture.
  • The orbital aspect of the zygoma (option B): This is part of the lateral orbital wall, which is the strongest of all the orbital walls. Blowout fractures rarely occur here because significant force is required to break this bone.
  • The orbital aspect of the maxilla and inferior orbital rim (option C): In a true blowout fracture, the inferior orbital rim stays intact while the floor breaks. If the rim is fractured, it is not a pure blowout fracture but rather a more complex orbital fracture pattern.
  • The orbital floor lateral to the infraorbital nerve (option D): The lateral portion of the orbital floor is thicker and stronger than the medial portion. The most common fracture site is medial, where the bone is thinnest, not lateral to the infraorbital nerve.

question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with vertical diplopia, particularly when walking downstairs. She reports tilting her head to one side to reduce the double vision. Which cranial nerve is most likely involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

Trochlear nerve (4th cranial nerve) palsy affects the superior oblique muscle, responsible for downward and inward eye movement. Dysfunction results in vertical diplopia, which is especially noticeable during activities requiring downward gaze, such as descending stairs. Patients often adopt a compensatory head tilt to minimize the diplopia.

Trochlear Nerve (CN IV):

  • Anatomy: Nucleus located in the midbrain near the inferior colliculus. CN IV is unique as it exits dorsally from the brainstem. It is the smallest cranial nerve, but it has the longest intracranial course.
  • Function: Innervates the contralateral superior oblique muscle.
  • Lesion Localization:
    • Nuclear lesion → contralateral superior oblique palsy
    • Cavernous sinus or orbital lesion → ipsilateral superior oblique palsy

Trochlear Nerve Palsy:

  • Congenital: May manifest at any age; children often show abnormal head posture, adults may report intermittent diplopia.
  • Acquired: Most commonly traumatic, presenting with more obvious symptoms.

Clinical Features:

  • Hypertropia
  • Excyclotorsion (outward rotation of the eye)
  • Vertical diplopia, worse on downgaze
  • Depressed chin with face turned to the opposite side
  • Head tilt toward the opposite shoulder

Management:

  • Spontaneous Resolution: Vascular or trauma-related cases may resolve within 3–6 months
  • Compressive Lesions: Surgical intervention required
  • Surgical Options (Knapp approach):
    • Inferior oblique weakening
    • Strengthening superior oblique action

Explanation of Other Options:

3rd nerve (Option A): Involves multiple extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris, causing ptosis and misalignment; vertical diplopia is not isolated.

6th nerve (Option B): Innervates the lateral rectus; palsy produces horizontal diplopia rather than vertical.

7th nerve (Option C): Controls facial muscles; does not affect eye movement or cause diplopia.

question_text: Which part of optic nerve is most likely involved in traumatic optic neuropathy?
explanation:
• When a rotational or shearing force is transmitted to the frontal areas in closed head injuries, damage to the optic nerve can occur.  
  • The blow is typically ipsilateral to the frontal area and usually severe enough to produce a loss of consciousness.
  • The nerve damage is produced by shearing forces that may be induced in the relatively immobile canalicular portion of the nerve by the movement of the brain due to frontal impact.
  • There may be direct damage by disruption of the nerve fibres or indirect damage by disruption of the blood supply.
  • Oedema or haemorrhage can also induce nerve damage by compressing the nerve within the optic canal.
  • In addition, in a fracture of the wall of the optic canal, bone fragments can directly exert pressure on the optic nerve.
  • Rarely, blunt trauma can lead to optic nerve damage in the orbit, producing an optic nerve head avulsion.
  • However, in most cases, traumatic optic neuropathy affects the canalicular part of the nerve and the fundus usually appears normal, with the disc pallor typical of optic atrophy developing after 3–4 weeks.
  • Early onset of pallor implies a substantial disruption of the blood supply to the optic nerve head.
  • In most cases, the visual loss is maximum from the time of impact but can also be delayed by a few hours and progress over the next few days

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: Which of the following conditions is/are associated with development of papilledema?
explanation:
• By definition, papilloedema is disc oedema due to increased intracranial pressure.
  • An intracranial tumour in any position may induce it. In general, those tumours which tend to produce internal hydrocephalus are most likely to cause papilloedema.
  • The site of the tumour is more important than its nature, size or rate of growth.
  • Other intracranial causes include a brain abscess, thrombosis of the cavernous sinus or other intracranial veins, aneurysm, subarachnoid haemorrhage, pseudotumour cerebri andhydrocephalus.
  • Malignant hypertension can also cause papilloedema, usually by raising the intracranial tension, but may produce signs of disc oedema in the absence of raised intracranial pressure as seen in grade IV hypertensive retinopathy.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding papilledema is/are incorrect?

  • The relative amount of swelling may be of localizing significance in these cases but its value has been overestimated. In frontal tumours and middle ear disease, however, the swelling is usually greater on the side of the lesion.
  • The time of onset is a more important indication than the amount of swelling, the localizing value being attached to the side first affected.
  • Thus, the swelling may be actually less on the side first affected owing to subsidence associated with commencing atrophy.
  • Unilateral papilloedema, with or without optic atrophy on the other side, suggests a tumour of the opposite olfactory groove or orbital surface of the frontal lobe or of the pituitary body (the Foster-Kennedy syndrome).

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 50-year-old woman presenting with sudden onset of eye pain and redness? An image of the affected eye is provided for evaluation
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of a 50-year-old woman with sudden onset of eye pain and redness, along with the image showing conjunctival injection and congestion, is strongly suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma:

This is a sudden and severe form of glaucoma caused by blockage of the drainage angle, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure (IOP). It is an ophthalmic emergency.

Clinical Features:

  • Sudden, painful red eye
  • Ciliary flush around the cornea due to dilated ciliary vessels; in chronic cases, caput medusae (prominent episcleral vessels)
  • Cornea: Initially clear but becomes hazy, may show epithelial bullae (bullous keratopathy) or filaments (filamentary keratitis)
  • Headache, nausea, and vomiting may accompany ocular symptoms
  • Anterior chamber: Markedly shallow
  • Iris: Often atrophic
  • Pupil: Mid-dilated and fixed
  • Optic disc: Shows glaucomatous optic atrophy
  • Intraocular pressure (IOP): Significantly elevated; the eyeball feels stony hard

Management of Absolute Glaucoma:

In absolute glaucoma, vision is irreversibly lost, so the primary goal is pain relief and IOP reduction.

  • Retrobulbar alcohol injection:
    • Used for pain relief
    • Administer 1 mL of 2% xylocaine, followed by 1 mL of 80% alcohol after 5–10 minutes
    • Acts by suppressing the ciliary ganglion
  • Cyclodestructive procedures (e.g., cyclocryotherapy or cyclophotocoagulation):
    • Preferred treatment in this scenario
    • Destroys secretory ciliary processes, reducing aqueous humor production and lowering IOP
  • If pain is persistent despite treatment, enucleation or evisceration may be considered.

Explanation for other options:

Acute retrobulbar neuritis (Option A): It is also known as optic neuritis, typically presents with vision loss, eye pain, and decreased color vision. It is not characterized by redness and congestion of the eye, so it is less likely to be the correct diagnosis in this case.

Acute anterior uveitis (Option C): It is also known as iritis, is inflammation of the iris and the anterior chamber of the eye. It commonly presents with symptoms of a red, painful eye with photophobia (sensitivity to light) and decreased vision. The image showing redness and congestion supports this diagnosis. Acute anterior uveitis can be associated with underlying systemic conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis. It is the most likely diagnosis based on the given scenario.

Severe keratoconjunctivitis (Option D): It refers to inflammation of both the cornea and the conjunctiva. While it can cause redness and irritation of the eye, it is not commonly associated with acute onset and severe pain. It is less likely to be the correct diagnosis in this case.

question_text: Identify the test shown in the Image:
explanation:
Cover testing is the gold standard for the objective method for determining the presence, type, and magnitude of ocular misalignment (strabismus). It is typically performed by the ophthalmologist, orthoptist, or ophthalmic technician. Cover testing can be done at both near and distance. When performed at near, an accommodative fixation target is held at a distance of 33 centimeters. At distance, the patient fixates on a target at a distance of 6 meters.

Cover-uncover test

The cover-uncover test is generally performed first. The cover-uncover test is useful to identify a tropia and differentiate it from a phoria. The test is done by using an opaque or translucent occluder to cover one eye. The occluder is held in front of the eye for a few seconds and then removed. When the fixing eye is occluded, the examiner will observe the non-occluded eye move to pick up fixation if a tropia is present. If no tropia is present, the non-occluded eye will remain stationary. To assess for a phoria, or latent deviation, the examiner observes the eye behind the occluder. If a phoria is present, the uncovered eye does not move, however the eye that is behind the occluder will deviate and return to a straight position when the occluder is removed.

Alternate cover test

The alternate cover test is generally performed after the cover-uncover test. The alternate cover test is the most dissociative cover test and measures the total deviation, which includes the tropia plus the phoria. For this test, the examiner occludes one eye and then the other, switching the occluder back and forth between eyes. When performing the alternate cover test, it is important to hold the occluder over each eye for at least a few seconds in order to allow the non-occluded eye enough time to pick up fixation. In general, the faster the eyes are able to recover when the occluder is switched, the better the control of the deviation.

question_text: What is the use of this instrument given in the figure
option_a: To know which muscle is paralysed
option_c: To measure exact amount of squint
explanation:
Maddox rod test: Used to detect and measure heterotropias(tropias) and heterophorias(phorias).

It is a dissociating test or an evaluation where the patient is presented with different objects for each eye to look at such that the images can't be merged. The test uses the principle of diplopic projection.

When the Maddox rod is placed vertically over the right eye, the patient should see a horizontal red line and a white light. When the Maddox rod is placed horizontally over the right eye, the patient should see a vertical red line and a white light. If the eyes are aligned, the red line will go through the white light. If the eyes are not aligned, the red light will be deviated in the opposite direction of the eye relative to the white light. For example, with a right hypertropia, the patient will see the red line deviated below the white light.

Picture of Maddox wing

The Maddox Wing is a hand-held device that is used to measure the degree of heterophoria at near. The device consist of a septum to dissociate the two eyes and a separate slit aperture for each eye.

question_text: Identify the test being done
explanation:
Double Maddox rod test: The double Maddox rod test, based on a red Maddox rod in front of one eye and a clear Maddox rod in front of the other, is used to measure cyclodeviation, typically in patients with superior oblique muscle paresis.

Orient two Maddox rods(one white and one red or two red at 90 degrees, so the striations are vertical, in trial frames. If the lines are horizontal with the rods, there are 0 degrees of torsion. If the lines aren't parallel, there is torsion present. Uncover test: To assess for a phoria or latent deviation, the examiner observes the eye behind the occluder. If a phoria is present, the uncovered eye does not move, however the eye that is behind the occluder will deviate and return to a straight position when the occluder is removed.

Alternate Cover Testing(ACT) determines the total amount of manfiest and latent deviation of the eye. A cover-uncover test is done before moving on to alternate cover testing.

Reference: AAO basics by Kara M. Cavuoto, M.D. 2023.

question_text: What type of tropia is seen in a V-pattern strabismus?
explanation:
• V-pattern strabismus is a pattern in which the eyes are more abducted in downgaze than in upgaze.
  • The etiology is unknown except in cases of extraocular muscle palsies.
  • Multiple theories suggest primary or secondary muscle dysfunction, which can involve inferior oblique muscle overaction, superior oblique muscle underaction, horizontal rectus muscle dysfunction or extorsion of the globe and bony orbit which may lead to a V- or A- pattern.
  • Infantile esotropia usually presents with a V-pattern.
  • Refractive esotropia, intermittent exotropia and sensory exotropia are not commonly V-patterned.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg no. 1221.

question_text: Identify the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Third nerve palsy

the most common ocular manifestations are diplopia and ptosis. In addition, depending on affected section of the third cranial nerve track it can also produce other neurologic manifestations as involuntary movements, hemiplegia, and altered mental status.

Physical examination

Consist on complete ophthalmic exam including visual acuity, ductions and versions, levator function, pupils reaction to light and to accommodation. In addition, general physical and/or neurological evaluation should be consider.

Signs

The presenting signs depend on the affected area of 3rd nerve track. In some cases, the precise site of the lesion is clear, whereas in others, the location of the lesion is speculative. It can present in different ways causing somatic extraocular muscle dysfunction (superior, inferior, and medial recti; inferior oblique; and levator palpebrae superioris) and autonomic (pupillary sphincter and ciliary) muscles.

Symptoms

Symptoms depend on the location of the lesion. The most common ocular complaint is diplopia secondary to somatic extraocular muscle dysfunction, but pain and ptosis can also me present.

Clinical diagnosis

Diagnosis is made by physical examination.

Diagnostic procedures

Acquired oculomotor nerve palsy can be secondary to many etiologies. Nevertheless, neuroimaging is usually done if intracranial pathology is suspected. In a conscious patient presenting with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and mydriasis a compressive etiology, as an intracranial aneurysm, must be ruled out. If an intracranial aneurysm is suspected, a computed tomography angiography (CTA) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI and MRA) should be performed, with a 90% sensitivity in aneurysms of 3mm or greater in diameter, although the gold standard is digital subtraction angiography (DSA).

Laboratory test

If a patient presents with complete oculomotor nerve palsy without pupil involvement it is most likely to be related to an ischemic process, but compression and inflammation should also be considered. Evaluation and management will vary according to patient's systemic illnesses, age, and associated symptoms. Nevertheless, basic workup is recommended. This may include the following: vital signs (e.g. blood pressure), complete blood count (CBC), sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP). Covid-19 testing may also be indicated. Central nervous system imaging (MRI or CT) and angiographic studies (MRA, CTA or catheter angiogram) can be used to rule out acute intracranial pathology, especially if ophthalmoplegia is associated with pain.

Differential diagnosis

Myasthenia Gravis

Thyroid associated orbitopathy

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia

Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia

Orbital pseudotumor

Giant cell arteritis

Management

Acquired oculomotor nerve palsy evaluation depends on signs and symptoms, patient's age and systemic diseases. Management depends on the presented scenarios. In a conscious patient presenting with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and mydriasis a compressive etiology, as an intracranial aneurysm, must be ruled out. On the other hand if a patient presents with complete oculomotor nerve palsy without pupil involvement it is most likely to be related to an ischemic process, but compression and inflammation should also be considered. The majority of complete or incomplete CN III palsies without pupil involvement are secondary to an ischemic process. These patients observe an improvement after the first 4 weeks with full resolution in 12 weeks of the insult. Those patients that are left with a residual deficit can consider prisms or strabismus surgery after 6 months of stability. In these cases the main goal of strabismus surgery is to provide alignment in primary and reading position.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(Option B) Fourth Nerve (Trochlear) Palsy:

Causes vertical diplopia, worsened by looking down (e.g., reading, walking downstairs).

Head tilt to the opposite side of the affected eye compensates for misalignment.

Most commonly congenital or due to trauma.

(Option C) Sixth Nerve (Abducens) Palsy:

Causes horizontal diplopia due to inability to abduct the eye.

Often associated with increased intracranial pressure (ICP), trauma, diabetes, or tumors.

Patients may turn their head toward the affected side to compensate.

(Option D) Medial Rectus (MR) Palsy:

Isolated MR palsy is rare since it is usually affected in CN III palsy.

If present, it could be due to internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) from a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), commonly seen in multiple sclerosis or stroke.

Key Takeaway:

Third nerve palsy is characterized by ptosis, "down and out" eye position, and diplopia. Pupil involvement indicates a compressive lesion (aneurysm until proven otherwise), while pupil-sparing palsy is often ischemic. Prompt neuroimaging is crucial in suspected cases.

question_text: A 10-month-old, full-term, and previously healthy child is brought in for evaluation after his parents noticed the finding in his left eye, as shown in the image. A subsequent CT scan of the orbits demonstrates an intraocular mass with localized calcification. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation :
The diagnosis is retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood. The clinical presentation is classic. The image shows leukocoria ("white pupil"), which is the most common presenting sign of this tumor. This finding, combined with the patient's age (typically diagnosed within the first few years of life) and the presence of intraocular calcification on CT scan, is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma.

Explanation of Other Options:
(A) Organized vitreous hemorrhage: This can cause leukocoria, but it is less common in this age group without a history of trauma, and it typically does not show the distinct, focal calcification seen in retinoblastoma.

(B) Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP): This is a key differential for leukocoria, but the patient's history as a full-term infant makes ROP highly unlikely, as it primarily affects premature infants.

(C) Coats' disease: This is another important cause of unilateral leukocoria, characterized by retinal telangiectasia and exudation. However, it typically presents in slightly older male children, and while it can have calcification, it is less common and dense than the classic intratumoral calcification of retinoblastoma.

question_text: A 3-month-old baby, born preterm at 33 weeks of gestation, is brought by parents with complaints of a white pupillary reflex for 2 weeks. CT revealed calcification of the globe in both eyes. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in a preterm infant, accompanied by globe calcification on CT scan, is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma

  • The most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.
  • Results from the proliferation of neural cells which have failed to evolve normally.
  • Retinoblastoma typically occurs in young children, usually before 5 years of age.
  • Associated with RB gene mutation on chromosome 13q14.

Clinical Presentation

  • Leukocoria: White pupillary reflex is the most common presentation.
  • Strabismus
  • Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma
  • Poor vision
  • May be asymptomatic in 3% cases

Evaluation and Diagnosis

Histopathology

  • Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific): These are composed of an "empty" lumen surrounded by columnar cells
  • Homer-Wright rosettes: These are pseudo-rosettes and consist of cells surrounding a central lumen made up of their processes
  • Undifferentiated tumor cells
  • Areas of necrosis and calcification

Fundus Examination

  • Shows a white, elevated retinal mass, which may have endophytic, exophytic, or mixed growth patterns.

Imaging:

  • CT Scan: Detects calcification in ~90% of cases.
  • MRI: Superior for assessing optic nerve involvement and extraocular extension.
  • Ultrasound: Useful as an initial screening tool.

Staging and treatment of Retinoblastoma

Explanation of other options:

Retinopathy of Prematurity (Option A): While ROP is common in preterm infants, it typically presents with abnormal blood vessel development in the retina. Leukocoria in ROP is usually due to retinal detachment or scarring, not calcification. ROP does not typically show calcifications on CT unless complicated by retinal detachment.

Glaucoma (Option C): Congenital glaucoma may cause enlarged corneas and optic nerve damage, but typically does not present with leukocoria or calcification.

Congenital cataract (Option D): Can cause leukocoria, but is characterized by lens opacity, not intraocular calcification, and would not show calcification on CT.

Key Takeaways:

Important Features of Retinoblastoma:

  • Age of Presentation: Typically presents in infancy or early childhood.
  • Leukocoria: The most common presenting sign, seen as a white pupillary reflex.
  • Fundus Examination: Reveals a white, elevated retinal mass.
  • Histopathology: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes-rosettes with a central lumen-are the most specific feature.

Reference:

  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562319/
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK572080/
  3. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574553/

question_text: A 10-month old, full-term gestation and previously healthy child, presents for further evaluation of leukocoria (white pupil) in his left eye, which was first noted by the child's parents in a recent photograph. A CT scan shows evidence of a mass with localized calcification in the left eye. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Retinoblastoma

  • Most common malignant ocular tumor of childhood
  • Also among the most common pediatric solid tumors
  • Age of diagnosis:
    • Familial/bilateral: usually within the first year of life
    • Sporadic/unilateral: typically between 1-3 years
  • Most common presenting sign: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex)
  • Other presentations:
    • Strabismus (~25% present initially with this)
    • Less common: vitreous hemorrhage, hyphema, glaucoma, proptosis, ocular inflammation, hypopyon
  • Imaging:
    • CT scan showing intraocular calcification strongly supports the diagnosis

ROP (Option B): Occurs in premature infants; history differs.

Coats disease (Option C): May cause leukocoria but typically lacks calcification.

Key Takeaways:

Leukocoria + intraocular calcification on CT → retinoblastoma most likely.

question_text: A 2-year-old child is brought for evaluation due to the rapid, spontaneous onset of the bilateral periorbital findings shown in the image. A systemic workup reveals a primary abdominal malignancy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image displays bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes") and proptosis. This presentation in a young child is a classic and pathognomonic sign of orbital metastasis from neuroblastoma.

Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood, often arising from the adrenal medulla. Orbital metastases cause proptosis from mass effect and ecchymosis due to hemorrhage within the tumor deposits. A workup will typically show elevated urine levels of catecholamine metabolites, such as vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA).

Explanation of Other Options:

(A) Rhabdomyosarcoma: This is the most common primary malignant orbital tumor in children and typically presents with rapid, progressive, unilateral proptosis. Spontaneous ecchymosis is not a characteristic feature.

(B) Retinoblastoma: This is an intraocular tumor. Its most common presentation is leukocoria ("white pupil"). Orbital invasion is a late finding and does not typically present with bilateral spontaneous ecchymosis.

(D) Leukemia: Orbital involvement, often from acute myelogenous leukemia (presenting as a myeloid sarcoma or "chloroma"), can cause proptosis. However, severe bilateral ecchymosis is a much less common finding compared to neuroblastoma.

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents with progressive hearing loss, tinnitus, and unsteadiness. Over the past few months, he has also developed a mild facial weakness. An MRI of the brain reveals a mass at the cerebellopontine angle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Vestibular schwannomas are benign tumors that arise from the Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII).

Key Features:

  • Progressive hearing loss (typically unilateral) is a common initial symptom.
  • Tinnitus (ringing in the ears).
  • Unsteadiness or imbalance due to vestibular involvement.
  • As the tumor grows, it can compress nearby structures like the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), leading to facial weakness.
  • Cerebellopontine angle mass on MRI is a hallmark finding.

Why not others

B. Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of: episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, feeling of fullness in the ear.

C. Bell's palsy is an acute condition involving unilateral facial paralysis due to dysfunction of the facial nerve. It is characterized by sudden onset of facial weakness or paralysis,

  • No hearing loos, tinnitus or unsteadiness.

D. Multiple Sclerosis (MS): It is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS), primarily affecting the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. It is demyelinating disorder causing sensory disturbances and varied neurological deficits.

  • Pt. presents with symptoms like optic neuritis (visual disturbances), weakness, numbness, and balance problems, often with remissions and relapses.
  • While MS can cause unsteadiness and facial weakness, hearing loss and tinnitus are not typical features of MS.

Key Takeaways:

Key features of vestibular schwannoma should be remembered as PUT (progressive hearing loss, unsteadies, tinnitus). It mainly involves th cranial nerve.

Level: May know

Reference: Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 509

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a sudden onset of unilateral right eye pain, loss of vision, and a severe headache. She reports halos around lights and nausea. Her past medical history is unremarkable. On examination, the right eye is red, the pupil is mid-dilated and non-reactive to light, and intraocular pressure is significantly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency marked by sudden, severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision, and halos around lights.
  • Additional symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and headache, often due to rapidly increasing intraocular pressure.
  • Physical exam reveals a red eye, a mid-dilated, non-reactive pupil, and significantly elevated intraocular pressure, which can lead to optic nerve damage and permanent vision loss if untreated.
  • Risk factors include hyperopia (farsightedness), age, female gender, and family history of glaucoma.

Why not others:

  • A) Optic neuritis: Presents with painful vision loss, typically with eye movement pain, but there is no red eye, no elevated intraocular pressure, and the pupil shows an afferent pupillary defect. It is commonly associated with multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating diseases.
  • C) Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO): Characterized by painless vision loss and a "blood and thunder" appearance of the retina on fundus exam. It does not cause eye pain, pupil abnormalities, or elevated intraocular pressure.
  • D) Retinal detachment: Typically presents with painless vision changes, such as floaters, flashes of light, or a "curtain" effect over vision. There is no red eye, no pupil abnormalities, and no elevated intraocular pressure.

Key Takeaways:

  • Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with painful vision loss, halos, and a mid-dilated, non-reactive pupil with elevated intraocular pressure, requiring urgent treatment.
  • Other options (optic neuritis, CRVO, retinal detachment) lack key findings such as eye pain and increased intraocular pressure, making them less likely.

Level: Must know

Reference: Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 445

question_text: Identify the chart in the given picture
explanation:
Diplopia Charting

Diplopia chart is the record of separation of the diplopic or double images in the nine positions of gaze. It can be plotted charted in patients who cooperate and can appreciate the double vision and with incomitant or comitant deviation.

The method

The patient should be comfortable with his head erect and should preferably be still throughout the examination. The test is preferably carried out in a dark room. Red glass is put in front of one of the eyes (red in front of right, R for R, is a convention). It is desirable to use Armstrong goggles since these are shaped to fit the orbital margin and therefore patient would be looking only through the colored medium. The examiner holds the torch (vertical source of light) at around 1/2 m or 1 m (It is important to mention the distance on the chart). This source of light could be horizontal if the complaint is of vertical separation of images

The light is held directly in front of the patient at first.

If the patient sees a single image, the examiner must establish whether it is a fused image, if suppression is present or if one image is obscured, for example by the patient's nose bridge. If there is no double vision in the primary position, the position in which double vision appears and is maximal is to be noted.

If the patient notes a double image, the relative position of these images is noted. The light is now carried to the right and then to the other 8 positions of gaze. In each gaze position the patient must be asked whether the images are parallel or tilted; if the torsion is present colored pencils can be given to an observant patient to show the separation in torsion. Also, in each gaze patient should be asked the amount of separation subjectively and its increase in a particular gaze.

Interpretation of a diplopia chart

To interpret the diplopia chart the most important questions are

The position in which diplopia appears

The position in which the separation of the image is the greatest

In the direction of the action of the paralyzed muscle, the double vision or the separation would be greatest because of the underaction of the muscle and overaction of the antagonist muscle and yoke muscle.

Hess Charting

It aids in the diagnosis of ocular motility defects. It measures the deviation and the amount of underaction and overaction of muscles. It is a repeatable and reliable record of the condition and is, therefore, a good way to show improvement or deterioration of the condition.

Hess Chart (principle)

The principle is the foveal projection. The chart is plotted based on Hering's and Sherrington's law of innervation. The dissociation of two eyes is by the means of colors or mirrors (as in Less screen). Now foster torches are used for projection of the target.

There is an illuminated Hess screen on which each target can be lit up in turn and its position indicated by the patient using a linear green light. Less screen used the principle of the mirror.

Hess Chart (method)

The test is performed with each eye fixating in turn. It is done at 50 cms. The patient wears complimentary red and green glasses. The left eye is tested first followed by right eye. The read glasses are placed on the right eye first (Red for right, R for R)

The chart has electronically operated board

with small red lights. The red lights can be illuminated as needed separately. The foster torch is of green light and is in the patient's hand. The patient is asked to place the green light in each of the points on the red light as illuminated on the chart. Next, the goggles are changed and the left eye has red goggles and the eye to be tested is the right eye.

Hess Chart (recording)

The recording, as mentioned above, is done first with the red glass over the red-eye and repeated with red over the left eye. The eye that has the red glass is the fixing eye. The eye with the green glass is the eye being tested. The required points are joined to form an inner and outer square.

Hess Chart (precautions)

The patient's head must remain straight throughout the procedure/ test. Occasionally, it becomes necessary to hold the head in the correct position. The foveae must have a common visual direction

Hess Chart (indications)

Any patient who complains of double vision should be tested on the Hess chart. Specific indications are

All patients of incomitant strabismus with normal retinal correspondence (NRC).

Patients of esophoria or intermittent Esotropia of divergence weakness type to rule out 6th nerve palsy.

To provide a baseline in conditions likely to develop defective ocular movements like in thyroid-related orbitopathy.

Hess Chart (interpretation)

The interpretation of Hess chart is done on basically three broad parts: Position, Size and Measurement, and Shape

Hess Chart (position)

The basic principle of Hess chart if foveal projection, therefore, the higher field belongs to the higher eye. This is the opposite of diplopia charting where the higher image is of the lower eye. The position of the central dot indicates whether the deviation is in the primary position or not. The position of the central dot is to be seen both fixing the right eye and fixing the left eye.

Hess Chart (size)

The variation in the size of the Hess chart of each eye is due to the Hering's law. The small field belongs to the eye with the primary limitation of movement. Underaction can be seen with the inward movement of the dots and therefore the whole curve. Maximum displacement occurs in the direction of the affected muscle if the patient has presented early before the spread of comitance.

Overaction can be seen by noting the outward displacement of the dots. Maximum displacement occurs in the direction of the main action of the overacting contralateral synergist in the larger field.

Overaction can be seen by noting the outward displacement of the dots. The maximum displacement of the dots occurs in the direction of the main action of the overacting contralateral synergist in the larger field.

If the inward and outward displacement is less marked, secondary underactions and overactions are present as a result of the development of muscle sequel. The outer field should be examined for small underactions and overactions which may not be apparent in the inner field.

A narrow field restricted in opposing directions of movement denotes a mechanical restriction of ocular movement. Equal sized field denote either symmetrical limitation of movement in both eyes or a non-paralytic strabismus

Hess Chart (Shape and measurements)

Each small square on the grid subtends 50 at the working distance of 50 cm, therefore the amount of deviation can be calculated. In the primary position, the amount could be calculated by fixing either eye by the displacement of the pointer from the center dots. The amount of underaction and overaction can be calculated in the various positions and hence the amount of excursions can also be calculated. Cyclotropia can also be measured in degrees by the torsion placement of the chart. A linear pointer can also be used to calculate the same.

Hess Chart (value)

It can be used to assess the progress of the disorder. It helps in finding out whether the underaction in a particular gaze is improving or not. This could help the ophthalmologist in planning the treatment and evaluate the results. However, a Hess chart should not be viewed in isolation; the importance of a good clinical ocular motility examination cannot be understated. Apart from the clinical examination, diplopia charting and binocular visual field testing also help in the better management of the patient.

Incorrect Option Explanations:

Option A: Snellen Chart

  • The Snellen chart is used for visual acuity testing, not for evaluating ocular motility or strabismus.
  • It consists of letters arranged in decreasing sizes to measure central vision at a standard distance (usually 6 meters or 20 feet).

Option B: ETDRS Chart

  • The Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart is used for accurate visual acuity measurement, particularly in research and clinical trials for diabetic retinopathy and low vision.
  • It has a logarithmic progression of letter sizes and is used at a 4-meter testing distance.

Option D: Pelli-Robson Chart

  • The Pelli-Robson chart is designed for testing contrast sensitivity, which is important for detecting conditions like optic neuritis, cataracts, and early glaucoma.
  • It features letters of the same size but varying contrast levels, unlike the Hess Chart, which evaluates eye muscle function.

Key Takeaway:

  • The Hess Chart is specifically used for assessing ocular motility defects by identifying muscle paresis, overactions, and mechanical restrictions.
  • It is different from visual acuity and contrast sensitivity charts, which assess different aspects of vision.
  • Diplopia charting and Hess charting are complementary tools for diagnosing ocular misalignments and nerve palsies.
  • The Hess Chart helps in tracking disease progression and planning treatment for strabismus and other motility disorders.

question_text: Which of the following combinations of cylindrical lenses can be employed for the treatment of astigmatism in the with-the-rule orientation?
explanation:
Explanation:
With-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism means the steepest corneal meridian is vertical (around 90°) and the flattest is horizontal (around 180°). To correct this, a lens must add plus power along the flat meridian (180°) or subtract power (add minus) along the steep meridian (90°). The combination -3.00 DC x 180, +1.00 DC x 90 effectively does this: the -3.00 cylinder at 180° flattens the horizontal plane, and the +1.00 cylinder at 90° adds power to the vertical plane.

Astigmatism is a refractive error caused by an irregular curvature of the cornea or lens, preventing light from focusing to a single point on the retina and resulting in blurred vision. Its correction necessitates the use of cylindrical lenses tailored to the specific axis of the

curvature.

There are two primary classifications based on the orientation of the steepest meridian:

  • With-the-Rule (WTR) Astigmatism: The vertical meridian (approximately 90°) is steeper than the horizontal. This is considered the more common physiological norm, partly due to constant eyelid pressure on the cornea. It is corrected with a minus cylinder lens placed at 180° (Option A and B ruled out) or, equivalently, a plus cylinder lens placed at 90° (Option C ruled out).
  • Against-the-Rule (ATR) Astigmatism: The horizontal meridian (approximately 180°) is steeper than the vertical. This pattern is more frequently observed in older patients. It is corrected with a plus cylinder lens placed at 180° or, equivalently, a minus cylinder lens placed at 90°.

The lens power can be calculated easily with this table:

Explanation of other options:

+5.00 DC x 180, -3.00 DC x 90 (Option A): This adds plus power at 180° (incorrect for WTR) and subtracts power at 90° (correct axis but wrong combination).

+7.00 DC x 180, +5.00 DC x 90 (Option B): This adds plus power on both axes, which does not correct the refractive error difference between meridians.

-4.00 DC x 180, -5.00 DC x 90 (Option C): This subtracts power on both axes, which also

fails to correct the relative difference between the two meridians.

Key Takeaways:

  • WTR astigmatism: Steep meridian ~90°, Flat meridian ~180°.
  • Correction: Minus cylinder axis 180° OR Plus cylinder axis 90°.
