explanation:
Clinical findings of an acquired third nerve palsy depend on the affected area of the oculomotor nerve pathway. It can be divided into a partial or complete palsy. A complete third nerve palsy presents with complete ptosis, with the eye positioned downward and outward with the inability to adduct, infraduct or supraduct, as well as a dilated pupil with sluggish reaction.

A partial third nerve palsy may be more common and can present with variable duction limitation of the affected extraocular muscles and with variable degrees of ptosis and/or pupillary dysfunction.

There are many etiologies for oculomotor palsy including a vasculopathic process, trauma, compression(e.g. aneurysm), infiltrative(e.g. leukemia), toxic(e.g. chemotherapy) etc.

Risk factors may coincide with the potential underlying etiologies listed above and can include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, vasculitis, trauma, infections, tumor, aneurysm.

question_text: Which cranial nerve is responsible for innervating the lateral rectus muscle of the eye?
explanation:
Explanation:

The cranial nerve, which is responsible for innervating the lateral rectus muscle of the eyes, is the 6th nerve.

Overview of Cranial Nerves Related to Eye Movement:

  • Optic nerve (CN II):
    • Purely sensory
    • Transmits visual information from the retina to the brain
  • Oculomotor nerve (CN III) (option C ruled out):
    • Provides motor innervation to most extraocular muscles:
      • Superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique
    • Also innervates the levator palpebrae superioris, ciliary muscle, and sphincter pupillae
  • Trochlear nerve (CN IV) (option D ruled out):
    • Motor innervation to the superior oblique muscle
  • Abducens nerve (CN VI) :
    • Motor innervation to the lateral rectus muscle
    • Responsible for the abduction of the eyeball
  • Trigeminal nerve (CN V):
    • The ophthalmic branch provides sensory innervation to the eye
    • Mediates the afferent limb of the corneal and lacrimation reflexes
  • Facial nerve (CN VII) (option B ruled out):
    • Motor innervation of orbicularis oculi
    • Efferent limb of the corneal and lacrimation reflex
    • Does not control the extraocular muscles

Key takeaway:

  • Sympathetic fibres (via long ciliary nerves):Dilate the pupil (mydriasis)
  • Parasympathetic fibres (via short ciliary nerves):Constrict the pupil (miosis)

question_text: A 30 year old complains of diminishing vision on right halves of both eyes .What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Lesions of optic tract

The optic tract is a continuation of the optic nerve that relays information from the optic chiasm to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), pretectal nuclei, and superior colliculus. The optic tract represents the first stage in the visual pathway in which visual information is transferred in a homonymous nature. Main characteristic feature of lesion involving whole optic tract is homonymous hemianopsia. A lesion in the left optic tract will cause right-sided homonymous hemianopsia, while a lesion in the right optic tract will cause left-sided homonymous hemianopsia.

Causes

The optic tract syndrome is characterized by a contralateral, incongruous homonymous hemianopia, contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and optic atrophy due to retrograde axonal degeneration. Causes of optic tract lesions are also classified into intrinsic and extrinsic forms. Intrinsic lesions include demyelinating diseases and infarction. Such lesions produce optic tract syndrome type II. Extrinsic or compressive lesions are caused by pituitary craniopharyngioma, tumours of optic thalamus. Other causes include syphilitic meningitis, gumma and tubercular meningitis etc.

Signs and symptoms

Visual field-homonymous hemianopia

Wernicke's pupillary reaction- No pupillary reaction when light shown to the blind half of retina, but if light is shown to seeing half, pupil shows reaction.

A lesion in the left optic tract results in right homonymous hemianopia (loss of vision in the right halves of both eyes). The optic tract carries visual information from the contralateral visual field, meaning a lesion in the left optic tract will affect the right visual field of both eyes.

Incorrect Options:

  • (B) Right Occipital Lobe:
    A right occipital lobe lesion can also cause left homonymous hemianopia, but macular sparing is often present due to dual blood supply from the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA). Since macular sparing is not mentioned in the question, this is less likely.
  • (C) Optic Chiasma:
    A lesion at the optic chiasm typically causes bitemporal hemianopia, affecting the peripheral vision of both eyes. The question specifies vision loss in the right halves of both eyes, which rules out this option.
  • (D) Right Optic Nerve:
    A lesion in the right optic nerve causes complete vision loss in the right eye, not in both eyes. Since the patient has vision loss in both eyes, this is incorrect.

Key Takeaway:

  • Homonymous hemianopia (same side field loss in both eyes) = Optic tract or Occipital lobe lesion
  • Right homonymous hemianopia = Left optic tract lesion
  • Left homonymous hemianopia = Right optic tract lesion
  • Bitemporal hemianopia (peripheral vision loss) = Optic chiasm lesion
  • Complete vision loss in one eye = Optic nerve lesion

question_text: Lesion producing incongruous homonymous hemianopia with wernicke's hemianopic pupil?
explanation:
Lesions of optic tract

The optic tract is a continuation of the optic nerve that relays information from the optic chiasm to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), pretectal nuclei, and superior colliculus. The optic tract represents the first stage in the visual pathway in which visual information is transferred in a homonymous nature. Main characteristic feature of lesion involving whole optic tract is homonymous hemianopsia. A lesion in the left optic tract will cause right-sided homonymous hemianopsia, while a lesion in the right optic tract will cause left-sided homonymous hemianopsia.

Causes

The optic tract syndrome is characterized by a contralateral, incongruous homonymous hemianopia, contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), and optic atrophy due to retrograde axonal degeneration.Causes of optic tract lesions are also classified into intrinsic and extrinsic forms. Intrinsic lesions include demyelinating diseases and infarction. Such lesions produce optic tract syndrome type II. Extrinsic or compressive lesions are caused by pituitary craniopharyngioma, tumours of optic thalamus. Other causes include syphilitic meningitis, gumma and tubercular meningitis etc.

Signs and symptoms

Visual field-homonymous hemianopia

Incongruous homonymous hemianopia.

Wernicke's pupillary reaction- No pupillary reaction when light shown to the blind half of retina, but if light is shown to seeing half, pupil shows reaction.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(B) Visual Cortex Lesion - Lesions in the visual cortex (occipital lobe) produce congruous homonymous hemianopiarather than incongruous defects. Since the pupillary light reflex is subcortical, visual cortex lesions do not cause Wernicke’s hemianopic pupil.

(C) Optic Radiations Lesion - Lesions in the optic radiations (parietal or temporal lobes) can cause homonymous hemianopia, but these defects are usually more congruous (i.e., similar in both eyes). Importantly, optic radiation lesions do not cause Wernicke’s pupil because the pupillary light reflex pathway is unaffected.

(D) Optic Nerve Lesion - Optic nerve damage causes monocular vision loss, not homonymous hemianopia. It can lead to an afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), but not Wernicke’s hemianopic pupil, which is specific to optic tract lesions.

Key Takeaways:

  • Optic tract lesions cause incongruous homonymous hemianopia and Wernicke’s hemianopic pupil.
  • Wernicke’s hemianopic pupil occurs when there is no pupillary reaction in the blind half but a normal reaction in the seeing half.
  • Visual cortex and optic radiation lesions do not produce Wernicke’s pupil.
  • Optic nerve lesions cause monocular blindness, not homonymous hemianopia.

question_text: After trauma, A person cannot move eye outword beyond mid point. The nerve injured is ?
explanation: Ans, D. 6th All the extraocular muscles are supplied by 3rd cranial (occulomotor) nerve except for superior oblique and lateral rectus. superior oblique muscle is supplied by 4thcranial (trochlear) nerve, and lateral rectus muscle is supplied by 6th cranial (abducent) nene. Beside these extraocular muscles, occulomotor (3rd) nerve also supplies levator palpebrae superioris, sphinctor pupillae (causes pupillary constriction), and ciliary muscle (causes accommodation).

question_text: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty reacting to bright light. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent, but the near reflex is preserved. Where is the lesion located?
explanation:
Explanation:

Absent light reflex with preserved near reflex (light-near dissociation) localises the lesion to the pretectal area of the midbrain.

  • This is the classic light-near dissociation:
    • Light reflex absent
    • Near reflex preserved
  • Seen in dorsal midbrain (pretectal) lesions, such as:
    • Argyll Robertson pupil (classically in neurosyphilis).
    • Parinaud's (dorsal midbrain) syndrome.

Features of the Argyll Robertson pupil:

  • Accommodation Reflex present (ARP)
  • Light reflex absent
  • Constricted pupil
  • It is an example of light near dissociation
  • Seen in neurosyphilis

Optic nerve (Option A): An optic nerve lesion causes an afferent pupillary defect and usually impairs both light and near responses when the affected eye is used as the stimulus (and is associated with decreased vision). It does not produce isolated loss of the light reflex with a preserved near reflex.

Oculomotor nerve (Option B): A lesion of CN III disrupts the efferent parasympathetic pathway to the sphincter pupillae, producing a dilated, poorly reactive pupil - both light and near constriction are lost on the affected side. Ptosis and palsies of extraocular movement accompany it.

Edinger-Westphal nucleus (Option C): Damage to the Edinger-Westphal (efferent parasympathetic) nucleus prevents pupil constriction for both light and accommodation, so the near reflex would also be lost. Therefore it cannot explain preserved near response

question_text: The movement is lost outward after trauma due to  :
explanation:
The sixth cranial nerve (CN VI, Abducens nerve) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which is responsible for abduction (outward movement) of the eye.

  • Key features of CN VI palsy:
    • Loss of lateral (outward) movement of the affected eye.
    • Diplopia (double vision) in horizontal gaze, especially when looking toward the affected side.
    • Head-turn compensation - The patient may turn their head towards the affected side to minimize diplopia.
    • Common causes include trauma, increased intracranial pressure (ICP), diabetes, hypertension, and brainstem lesions.

Since the question states loss of outward movement after trauma, the most likely nerve affected is CN VI (Abducens nerve), making option (C) the correct answer.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(A) Third Nerve Palsy (Oculomotor Nerve Palsy)

  • CN III controls most extraocular muscles (superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique) and levator palpebrae superioris.
  • A lesion causes ptosis (drooping eyelid), a "down and out" eye position, and pupillary dilation.
  • Outward movement (abduction) is preserved because the lateral rectus (CN VI) is intact.
  • Incorrect answer because outward movement loss is specific to CN VI palsy.

(B) Trochlear Nerve Palsy (Fourth Nerve Palsy)

  • CN IV innervates superior oblique, which helps with intorsion and depression in adduction.
  • A lesion leads to vertical diplopia, worse when looking down (e.g., walking downstairs).
  • Patients compensate by tilting their head to the opposite side.
  • Incorrect answer because trochlear nerve palsy does not cause loss of outward movement.

(D) Facial Nerve Palsy (Seventh Nerve Palsy)

  • CN VII controls facial muscles, not extraocular movements.
  • Causes facial asymmetry, inability to close the eye (Bell’s phenomenon), and loss of forehead wrinkling.
  • Incorrect answer because CN VII does not control eye movements.

Key Takeaways:

  • Abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy causes loss of outward (lateral) eye movement.
  • Common causes include trauma, increased ICP, and vascular diseases.
  • Third nerve palsy causes ptosis and a "down and out" eye.
  • Trochlear nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia and head tilt.
  • Facial nerve palsy affects facial muscles, not eye movements.

question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with altered sensation in his limbs, coordination difficulties, and speech disturbances. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent, but the accommodation reflex remains intact. Which condition is most likely responsible?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neurosyphilis, a tertiary complication of syphilis occurring years after initial infection, affects the central nervous system and can present with a variety of neurological deficits. In this patient, the combination of altered sensation, ataxia, and speech impairment, along with absent pupillary light reaction but preserved accommodation, strongly suggests Argyll Robertson pupils, a classic sign of neurosyphilis.

Neurosyphilis and Argyll Robertson Pupils:

  • Pupillary Light Reflex Absent: The reflex, mediated via the optic (CN II) and oculomotor (CN III) nerves, is lost due to involvement of the optic nerve.
  • Accommodation Reflex Preserved: Pupil constriction during near-focus remains intact because the accommodation pathways are usually spared.
  • Other Neurological Features: Sensory deficits, coordination problems (ataxia), and speech difficulties may also be present.

Spirochetal Uveitis in Syphilis:

  • Organism: Treponema pallidum
  • Anterior Uveitis: Can appear as granulomatous or non-granulomatous iritis, commonly in secondary syphilis. Features include iris roseola (dilated iris vessels forming nodules) and "plastic" iritis in congenital cases or Jarisch-Herxheimer reactions.
  • Posterior Uveitis: May manifest as disseminated, peripheral, or diffuse choroiditis.
  • Treatment: Systemic penicillin

Explanation of Other Options:

Horner's Syndrome (Option B): Results from disruption of the sympathetic pathway, causing ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. It does not produce an absent pupillary light reflex with preserved accommodation.

Papilledema (Option C): Swelling of the optic disc due to raised intracranial pressure may impair vision but does not explain the absent light reflex with intact accommodation, nor the additional neurological deficits.

Optic Neuritis (Option D): Inflammation of the optic nerve can cause vision changes, but typically does not present with the combination of absent pupillary light reflex and preserved accommodation, or the broader neurological symptoms seen in this patient.

Reference:

  1. The immune response in tubercular uveitis and its implications for treatment: From anti-tubercular treatment to host-directed therapies - ScienceDirect ( Clinical perspective of tubercular uveitis: From diagnosis to treatment initiation)

question_text: A 45-year-old male arrived at the emergency ward with sudden vision loss and experiencing painful eye movements. Upon examination, the affected eye shows a relative afferent pupillary defect, a normal optic disc, and a central scotoma. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the given clinical scenario, the patient is having classic presentation of retrobulbar optic neuritis.

Key features include:

  • Sudden monocular vision loss.
  • Pain on eye movement (a highly characteristic symptom).
  • Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD) indicating optic nerve dysfunction.
  • Normal optic disc initially (as the inflammation is behind the globe).
  • Central scotoma (a common visual field defect).
  • Uhthoff's Symptom: A temporary worsening or dimming of vision triggered by an increase in body temperature, often due to exercise or a hot environment. Vision typically returns to baseline after cooling down or resting. This is a classic symptom of optic neuritis or multiple sclerosis.
  • Pulfrich's Phenomenon: A delay in neural signaling from a previously affected eye can cause moving objects to appear on an altered path, leading to a subjective impairment in judging the position of moving objects and distorted depth perception. This can occur following optic neuritis.

Optic neuritis refers to inflammation of the optic nerve, which frequently leads to acute, often unilateral, vision loss. This condition most commonly affects young adults and is strongly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS).

Classification of Optic Neuritis:

  1. Papillitis (Anterior Optic Neuritis)
    • Site: Optic disc (head of the optic nerve).
    • Features:
    • Fundoscopy shows a swollen, hyperemic disc with blurred margins.
    • The physiological cup is obscured.
    • Caused by leakage and capillary permeability.
  2. Retrobulbar Neuritis
    • Site: Optic nerve behind the eyeball.
    • Features:
    • Fundoscopy is normal initially ("the doctor sees nothing").
    • Patient presents with vision loss ("the patient sees nothing"), pain on eye movement, and a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD).
  3. Neuroretinitis
    • Site: Optic disc and the surrounding retina (macular area).
    • Features:
    • Fundoscopy shows disc swelling plus a characteristic "macular star" pattern (lipid exudates radiating from the macula).

Explanation of other options:

Optic nerve glioma (Option A): A slow-growing tumor causing progressive, painless vision loss, typically in children.

Eale's disease (Option C): A vasculitis affecting the peripheral retina, presenting with floaters and vitreous hemorrhages, not painful vision loss or RAPD.

Optic atrophy (Option D): The end-stage result of many optic nerve diseases, characterized by a pale disc and permanent vision loss, but not an acute event with pain.

Key Takeaways:

  • Optic neuritis classic triad: Acute vision loss, pain on movement, RAPD.
  • The disc appears normal in retrobulbar neuritis ("the doctor sees nothing").

question_text: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of loss of vision associated with painful eye movements. On examination, a relative afferent pupillary defect is noted in the affected eye, with visual field testing revealing a central scotoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_d: Central retinal vein occlusion: Painless loss of vision
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical scenario of sudden visual loss associated with relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is suggestive of Optic Neuritis.

Optic neuritis:

  • An inflammation of the optic nerve is known as optic neuritis. The optic nerve may be affected by inflammation in any part of its course, based on the site affected it can be:
    • Papillitis
    • Retrobulbar neuritis
    • Neuroretinitis
  • The most common associated cause is a demyelinating disorder of the nerve as occurs in other tracts of the white matter of the central nervous system (multiple sclerosis).

Clinical features

  • Monocular sudden, progressive and profound visual loss is the hallmark of acute optic neuritis.
  • Dark adaptation may be lowered.
  • Visual obscuration in bright light is a typical symptom of acute optic neuritis.
  • Impairment of color vision is always present in optic neuritis.
  • Presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect or Marcus Gunn pupil is of greater diagnostic significance, indicating a defect in the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex due to a pathological lesion in the optic nerve.
  • Depth perception may be impaired, particularly for the moving object.
  • Visual acuity is usually reduced markedly.
  • Visual field changes
    • The most common field defect in optic neuritis is a relative central or centrocecal scotoma.
  • Contrast sensitivity is impaired.

Treatment:

  • Conservative management:
    • Observation and Monitoring.
    • Only for mild symptoms but not recommended for severe cases or first episodes.
  • High-dose corticosteroids: Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) followed by oral prednisolone taper as established by the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial). Indications:
    • Severe vision loss
    • No history of previous episodes
    • MRI evidence of demyelination

Explanation of other options:

Papilledema (Option A): Fundus examination in papilledema shows enlargement of the blind spot and pain on ocular movements is not a presentation in papilledema.

Eale's disease (Option C): Also known as retinal vasculitis, typically presents with recurrent episodes of retinal hemorrhages, floaters, and vision loss in young males.

Central retinal vein occlusion (Option D): Central retinal vein occlusion presents with sudden onset painless loss of vision.

question_text: Homonymous Hemianopia is not seen in lesion of
explanation:
OPTIC TRACT

  • The optic tract contains the crossed nasal fibers from the opposite side and the uncrossed temporal fibers from the same side.
  • Lesions involving the optic tract result in loss of nasal field of the same side and temporal field of the opposite side or contralateral Homonymous Hemianopia.

OPTIC RADIATION

  • The fibers from the optic tract relay into the lateral geniculate body and then continue into the optic radiation. Hence, lesions involving the optic radiation also result in Homonymous Hemianopia.
  • However the fibers responsible for the superior visual field course initially into the temporal lobe before proceeding posteriorly to reach the occipital lobe(Meyer's Loop). Hence, lesions involving the temporal lobe produce contralateral homonymous field defect involving only the superior field. This is known as Superior Quadrantanopia or Pie in the Sky.
  • The fibers responsible for the inferior visual field course through the parietal lobe and subsequently to the occipital lobe. Hence lesions of the parietal lobe result in contralateral homonymous field defect involving only the inferior field. This is known as Inferior Quadrantanopia or Pie on the Floor.

OCCIPITAL CORTEX

  • The occipital lobe is the final destination for the visual pathway and the axons are arranged along the margins of the calcarine sulcus.
  • The most common lesion affecting the occipital cortex is ischemic injury or infarct due to occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery which forms the major source of blood supply. However, a branch of the middle cerebral artery provides additional perfusion to the area where the central field is represented. Hence, in infarct due to occlusion of posterior cerebral artery(PCA), this small central field is often spared.
  • Occipital cortex lesion(infarct due to PCA occlusion) results in contralateral Homonymous Hemianopia with central sparing.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg: 904-905.

question_text: A mass causing a relative afferent pupillary defect and a homonymous hemianopia would most likely be found in which one of the following?
explanation:
1) Lesions of the optic nerve: These are characterised by marked loss of vision or complete blindness on the affected side associated with abolition of the direct light reflex on the ipsilateral side and consensual on the contralateral side. Near (accommodation) reflex is present. Common causes of optic nerve lesions are: optic atrophy, traumatic avulsion of the optic nerve, indirect optic neuropathy and acute optic neuritis.

2)Sagittal (central) lesions of the chiasma: These are characterised by bitemporal hemianopia and bitemporal hemianopic paralysis of pupillary reflexes. These usually lead to partial descending optic atrophy. Common causes of central chiasmal lesion are: suprasellar aneurysms, tumours of pituitary gland, craniopharyngioma, suprasellar meningioma and glioma of third ventricle, third ventricular dilatation due to obstructive hydrocephalus and chronic chiasmal arachnoiditis.

2.1)Lateral chiasmal lesions: Salient features of such lesions are binasal hemianopia associated with binasal hemianopic paralysis of the pupillary reflexes. These usually lead to partial descending optic atrophy. Common causes of such lesions are distension of third ventricle causing pressure on each side of the chiasma and atheroma of the carotids or posterior communicating arteries.

3)Lesions of optic tract: These are characterised by incongruous homonymous hemianopia associated with contralateral hemianopic pupillary reaction (Wernicke’s reaction). These lesions usually lead to partial descending optic atrophy and may be associated with contralateral third nerve paralysis and ipsilateral hemiplegia. Common causes of optic tract lesions are syphilitic meningitis or gumma, tuberculosis and tumours of optic thalamus and aneurysms of superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral arteries.

4)Lesions of the visual cortex: Congruous homonymous hemianopia (usually sparing the macula, is a feature of occlusion of posterior cerebral artery supplying the anterior part of occipital cortex. Congruous homonymous macular defect occurs in lesions of the tip of the occipital cortex following head injury or gunshot injuries. Pupillary light reflexes are normal and optic atrophy does not occur following visual cortex lesions.

Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 290.

question_text: A 22-year-old woman with acute visual loss in the right eye and pain with eye movement from optic neuritis due to multiple sclerosis is most likely to have which one of the following clinical findings?
option_a: Optic disc edema with macular star
explanation:
Clinical Presentation:

  • A 22-year-old woman with acute visual loss in the right eye and pain with eye movement.
  • The cause of the visual loss is optic neuritis.
  • The patient has multiple sclerosis.

Now, let's justify each option:

  1. Optic disc edema with macular star - Incorrect
    • Optic disc edema with a macular star(neuroretinitis) is not typically associated with multiple sclerosis. It is more commonly seen in conditions like cat-scratch disease.
  2. Uveitis with vitritis - Incorrect
    • Uveitis with vitritis is not typically seen in multiple sclerosis. It suggests intraocular inflammation but is not a common manifestation of multiple sclerosis.
  3. Relative afferent pupillary defect - Correct
    • An inflammatory optic neuropathy, as described in the case of optic neuritis associated with multiple sclerosis, often presents with a relative afferent pupillary defect(RAPD). This is due to the unequal transmission of light signals to the brain from the affected eye.
  4. Anisocoria greater in light - Incorrect
    • Anisocoria(unequal pupil size) greater in light is not a typical finding in optic neuritis or multiple sclerosis. It may be seen in other conditions but is not the primary clinical finding in this case.

In summary, option C is correct because a relative afferent pupillary defect(RAPD) is a common clinical finding in cases of optic neuritis associated with multiple sclerosis. Options A, B and D are incorrect because they do not align with the typical presentation of this condition.

Reference: A.K.Khurana, 5th Edition, Pg: 290.

explanation:
A congruous visual field defect is identical between the two eyes, whereas an incongruous defect differs in appearance between the eyes. For lesions behind the LGN, visual field defects are generally more congruous if the lesion is located more posteriorly along the visual pathway.

The optic tract syndrome is characterized by a contralateral, incongruous homonymous hemianopia, contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect(RAPD) and optic atrophy due to retrograde axonal degeneration.

Causes of optic tract lesions are also classified into intrinsic and extrinsic forms. Intrinsic lesions include demyelinating diseases and infarction. Such lesions produce optic tract syndrome type II.

Extrinsic or compressive lesions are caused by pituitary craniopharyngioma, tumours of optic thalamus. Other causes include syphilitic meningitis, gumma and tubercular meningitis etc.

question_text: What is true about optic neuritis?
option_b: Relative afferent pupillary defect is the first sign
explanation:
Optic neuritis describes any condition that causes inflammation of the optic nerve; it may be associated with demyelinating diseases, or infectious or inflammatory processes.

It is also known as optic papillitis (when the head of the optic nerve is involved), neuroretinitis (when there is a combined involvement of the optic disc and surrounding retina in the macular area) and retrobulbar neuritis (when the posterior part of the nerve is involved). Prelaminar optic neuritis describes involvement of the non-myelinated axons in the retina. It is most often associated with multiple sclerosis, and it may lead to complete or partial loss of vision in one or both eyes. Other causes include:

Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy

Parainfectious optic neuritis (associated with viral infections such as measles, mumps, chickenpox, whooping cough and glandular fever)

Infectious optic neuritis (sinus related or associated with cat-scratch fever, tuberculosis, Lyme disease and cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS patients

Autoimmune causes (sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa, MOG antibody disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis)

Diabetes mellitus

Low phosphorus levels

Hyperkalaemia

Signs and symptoms

Example of how optic neuritis affected one eye of a person with multiple sclerosis

Major symptoms are sudden loss of vision (partial or complete), sudden blurred or "foggy" vision, and pain on movement of the affected eye. Early symptoms that require investigation include symptoms from multiple sclerosis (twitching, lack of coordination, slurred speech, frequent episodes of partial vision loss or blurred vision), episodes of "disturbed/blackened" rather than blurry indicate moderate stage and require immediate medical attention to prevent further loss of vision. Other early symptoms are reduced night vision, photophobia and red eyes. Many patients with optic neuritis may lose some of their color vision in the affected eye (especially red), with colors appearing subtly washed out compared to the other eye. Patients may also experience difficulties judging movement in depth, which can be particular troublesome during driving or sport (Pulfrich effect). Likewise, transient worsening of vision with increase of body temperature (Uhthoff's phenomenon) and glare disability are a frequent complaint. However, several case studies in children have demonstrated the absence of pain in more than half of cases (approximately 60%) in their pediatric study population, with the most common symptom reported simply as "blurriness". Other remarkable differences between the presentation of adult optic neuritis as compared to pediatric cases include more often unilateral optic neuritis in adults, while children much predominantly present with bilateral involvement.

On medical examination the head of the optic nerve can easily be visualized by a slit lamp with a high positive lens or by using direct ophthalmoscopy; however, frequently there is no abnormal appearance of the nerve head in optic neuritis (in cases of retrobulbar optic neuritis), though it may be swollen in some patients (anterior papillitis or more extensive optic neuritis). In many cases, only one eye is affected, and patients may not be aware of the loss of color vision until they are asked to close or cover the healthy eye.

Cause

The optic nerve comprises axons that emerge from the retina of the eye and carry visual information to the primary visual nuclei, most of which is relayed to the occipital cortex of the brain to be processed into vision. Inflammation of the optic nerve causes loss of vision, usually because of the swelling and destruction of the myelin sheath covering the optic nerve.

The most common cause is multiple sclerosis (MS) or ischemic optic neuropathy due to thrombosis or embolism of the vessel that supplies the optic nerve. Up to 50% of patients with MS will develop an episode of optic neuritis, and 20-30% of the time optic neuritis is the presenting sign of MS.[citation needed] The presence of demyelinating white matter lesions on brain MRI at the time of presentation of optic neuritis is the strongest predictor for developing clinically definite MS. Almost half of the patients with optic neuritis have white matter lesions consistent with multiple sclerosis.

Some other common causes of optic neuritis include infection (e.g. a tooth abscess in the upper jaw, syphilis, Lyme disease, herpes zoster), autoimmune disorders (e.g. lupus, neurosarcoidosis, neuromyelitis optica), methanol poisoning, vitamin B12 deficiency, beriberi, dysautonomia (i.e. autonomic nervous system dysfunction), and diabetes, or an injury to the eye. In neuromyelitis optica higher AQP4 autoantibody levels are associated with the occurrence of optic neuritis.

Less common causes are: papilledema, brain tumor or abscess in the occipital region, cerebral trauma or hemorrhage, meningitis, arachnoidal adhesions, sinus thrombosis, liver dysfunction, or late stage kidney disease.

Treatment

In most MS-associated optic neuritis, visual function spontaneously improves over 2-3 months, and there is evidence that corticosteroid treatment does not affect the long term outcome. However, for optic neuritis that is not MS-associated (or atypical optic neuritis) the evidence is less clear and therefore the threshold for treatment with intravenous corticosteroids is lower. Intravenous corticosteroids also reduce the risk of developing MS in the following two years in patients with MRI lesions; but this effect disappears by the third year of follow up.

Paradoxically, oral administration of corticosteroids in this situation may lead to more recurrent attacks than in non-treated patients (though oral steroids are generally prescribed after the intravenous course, to wean the patient off the medication). This effect of corticosteroids seems to be limited to optic neuritis and has not been observed in other diseases treated with corticosteroids.

A Cochrane systematic review studied the effect of corticosteroids for treating people with acute optic neuritis. Specific corticosteroids studied included intravenous and oral methylprednisone, and oral prednisone. The authors conclude that current evidence does not show a benefit of either intravenous or oral corticosteroids for rate of recovery of vision (in terms of visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, or visual fields). There are a number of reasons why this might be the case.

Option A: Multiple Myeloma is the cause

  • Optic neuritis is commonly associated with Multiple Sclerosis (MS), infections, autoimmune diseases (e.g., lupus, sarcoidosis), and vitamin B12 deficiency.
  • Multiple myeloma is NOT a direct cause of optic neuritis.

Option C: Painless

  • One of the hallmark symptoms of optic neuritis is pain, especially during eye movements.
  • Painless vision loss is more common in conditions like ischemic optic neuropathy.

Option D: Oral Steroids is DOC

  • Intravenous (IV) corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) are preferred for treatment.
  • Oral steroids alone may actually increase the risk of recurrent optic neuritis, as shown in the ONTT (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial).
  • Oral steroids may be used after IV therapy for tapering but are not the first-line treatment.

Key Takeaway:

  • RAPD is the earliest clinical sign of optic neuritis
  • Optic neuritis is often associated with MS, NOT multiple myeloma
  • Optic neuritis is painful, NOT painless
  • IV steroids (not oral) are the preferred treatment

question_text: A child with whitish pupillary reflex has undergone enucleation and shows bright round blue cells with Flexner wintersteiner rosettes. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Histology of retinoblastomas

The tumor arises from small round cells with large nuclei, i.e., it is a tumor of a group called small round blue cell tumors.

Microscopic features of a well differentiated tumor include Flexnerwintersteiner rosettes (specific for retinoblastoma), Homer Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes and fleurettes formation

  • Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children, typically presenting with leukocoria (whitish pupillary reflex).
  • Histological hallmark: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (specific for retinoblastoma), Homer Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes.
  • It belongs to the small round blue cell tumors group.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(B) Rhabdomyosarcoma: Another small round blue cell tumor but arises from skeletal muscle and does not show Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

(C) Medulloblastoma: A small round blue cell tumor of the cerebellum that also shows Homer Wright rosettes but does not cause leukocoria.

(D) Astrocytoma: A glial tumor that does not belong to the small round blue cell tumor group and lacks Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

Key Takeaway:

Retinoblastoma should be suspected in a child with leukocoria. Histologically, it is a small round blue cell tumor characterized by Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, which are specific for the diagnosis.

question_text: U/L proptosis with B/L sixth nerve palsy:
explanation:
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a condition where a blood clot forms in the cavernous sinus, a large vein located at the base of the skull. The condition often presents with unilateral proptosis that may later become bilateral. This occurs due to the venous congestion and obstruction in the cavernous sinus. Bilateral sixth nerve palsy is a hallmark sign of CST because the sixth cranial nerve (abducent nerve), which controls the lateral rectus muscles of the eye, passes through the cavernous sinus. The pressure from the thrombosis affects both sides, causing the bilateral palsy of the abducent nerve and resulting in double vision or an inability to move the eyes laterally.

Incorrect Options:

B. Thyroid ophthalmopathy
Thyroid eye disease, or thyroid ophthalmopathy, usually presents with bilateral proptosis but is not typically associated with bilateral sixth nerve palsy. It is caused by the swelling of extraocular muscles and orbital fat behind the eyes, leading to proptosis.

C. Retinoblastoma
Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor of the retina, typically seen in children. It does not commonly present with proptosis or bilateral sixth nerve palsy as primary symptoms. Retinoblastoma usually causes a leukocoria (white pupil reflex) rather than nerve palsies.

D. Orbital pseudotumor
Orbital pseudotumor is an inflammatory condition that affects the orbit, often leading to unilateral proptosis. While it can cause some cranial nerve palsies, including involvement of the sixth nerve, it does not typically result in the bilateral palsy seen in cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Key Takeaway: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a serious condition that can present with unilateral proptosis and bilateral sixth nerve palsy, due to the involvement of the sixth cranial nerve, which passes through the cavernous sinus.

question_text: A son gives history of his father is neglecting left side of body during bath, Which part of brain is involved in a case of Left hemineglect?
explanation:
The parietal lobe is one of the four major lobes of the cerebral cortex in the brain of mammals. The parietal lobe is positioned above the temporal lobe and behind the frontal lobe and central sulcus.

The parietal lobe integrates sensory information among various modalities, including spatial sense and navigation (proprioception), the main sensory receptive area for the sense of touch in the somatosensory cortex which is just posterior to the central sulcus in the postcentral gyrus, and the dorsal stream of the visual system. The major sensory inputs from the skin (touch, temperature, and pain receptors), relay through the thalamus to the parietal lobe.

Several areas of the parietal lobe are important in language processing. The somatosensory cortex can be illustrated as a distorted figure - the cortical homunculus (Latin: "little man") in which the body parts are rendered according to how much of the somatosensory cortex is devoted to them. The superior parietal lobule and inferior parietal lobule are the primary areas of body or spatial awareness. A lesion commonly in the right superior or inferior parietal lobule leads to hemineglect.

Functions of the parietal lobe include:

Two point discrimination - through touch alone without other sensory input (e.g. visual)

Graphesthesia - recognizing writing on skin by touch alone

Touch localization (bilateral simultaneous stimulation)

The parietal lobe plays important roles in integrating sensory information from various parts of the body, knowledge of numbers and their relations, and in the manipulation of objects. Its function also includes processing information relating to the sense of touch. Portions of the parietal lobe are involved with visuospatial processing. Although multisensory in nature, the posterior parietal cortex is often referred to by vision scientists as the dorsal stream of vision (as opposed to the ventral stream in the temporal lobe). This dorsal stream has been called both the "where" stream (as in spatial vision) and the "how" stream (as in vision for action). The posterior parietal cortex (PPC) receives somatosensory and visual input, which then, through motor signals, controls movement of the arm, hand, and eyes.

Various studies in the 1990s found that different regions of the posterior parietal cortex in macaques represent different parts of space.

The lateral intraparietal (LIP) area contains a map of neurons (retinotopically-coded when the eyes are fixed) representing the saliency of spatial locations, and attention to these spatial locations. It can be used by the oculomotor system for targeting eye movements, when appropriate.

The ventral intraparietal (VIP) area receives input from a number of senses (visual, somatosensory, auditory, and vestibular). Neurons with tactile receptive fields represent space in a head-centered reference frame. The cells with visual receptive fields also fire with head-centered reference frames but possibly also with eye-centered coordinates

The medial intraparietal (MIP) area neurons encode the location of a reach target in eye-centered coordinates.

The anterior intraparietal (AIP) area contains neurons responsive to shape, size, and orientation of objects to be grasped as well as for manipulation of the hands themselves, both to viewed and remembered stimuli. The AIP has neurons that are responsible for grasping and manipulating objects through motor and visual inputs. The AIP and ventral premotor together are responsible for visuomotor transformations for actions of the hand.

More recent fMRI studies have shown that humans have similar functional regions in and around the intraparietal sulcus and parietal-occipital junction. The human "parietal eye fields" and "parietal reach region", equivalent to LIP and MIP in the monkey, also appear to be organized in gaze-centered coordinates so that their goal-related activity is "remapped" when the eyes move.

Emerging evidence has linked processing in the inferior parietal lobe to declarative memory. Bilateral damage to this brain region does not cause amnesia however the strength of memory is diminished, details of complex events become harder to retrieve, and subjective confidence in memory is very low. This has been interpreted as reflecting either deficits in internal attention, deficits in subjective memory states, or problems with the computation that allows evidence to accumulate, thus allowing decisions to be made about internal representations.

Clinical significance

Features of parietal lobe lesions are as follows:

Unilateral parietal lobe

Contralateral hemisensory loss

Astereognosis - inability to determine 3-D shape by touch.

Agraphaesthesia - inability to read numbers or letters drawn on hand, with eyes shut.

Contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia

Asymmetry of optokinetic nystagmus (OKN)

Sensory seizures

Dominant hemisphere

Conduction aphasia

Dyslexia - a general term for disorders that can involve difficulty in learning to read or interpret words, letters, and other symbols

Apraxia - inability to perform complex movements in the presence of normal motor, sensory and cerebellar function

Gerstmann syndrome - characterized by acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left-right disorientation

Non-dominant hemisphere

Contralateral hemispatial neglect

Constructional apraxia

Dress apraxia

Anosognosia - lack of awareness of the existence of one's disability

Bilateral hemispheres

Balint's syndrome

Damage to this lobe in the right hemisphere results in the loss of imagery, visualization of spatial relationships and neglect of left-side space and left side of the body. Even drawings may be neglected on the left side. Damage to this lobe in the left hemisphere will result in problems in mathematics, long reading, writing, and understanding symbols. The parietal association cortex enables individuals to read, write, and solve mathematical problems. The sensory inputs from the right side of the body go to the left side of the brain and vice versa.

The syndrome of hemispatial neglect is usually associated with large deficits of attention of the non-dominant hemisphere. Optic ataxia is associated with difficulties reaching toward objects in the visual field opposite to the side of the parietal damage. Some aspects of optic ataxia have been explained in terms of the functional organization described above.

Apraxia is a disorder of motor control which can be referred neither to "elemental" motor deficits nor to general cognitive impairment. The concept of apraxia was shaped by Hugo Liepmann about a hundred years ago.[clarification needed] Apraxia is predominantly a symptom of left brain damage, but some symptoms of apraxia can also occur after right brain damage.

Amorphosynthesis is a loss of perception on one side of the body caused by a lesion in the parietal lobe. Usually, left-sided lesions cause agnosia, a full-body loss of perception, while right-sided lesions cause lack of recognition of the person's left side and extrapersonal space. The term amorphosynthesis was coined by D. Denny-Brown to describe patients he studied in the 1950s.

Can also result in sensory impairment where one of the affected person's senses (sight, hearing, smell, touch, taste and spatial awareness) is no longer normal

Incorrect Option Explanations:

Option A: Pre-motor cortex - The pre-motor cortex is involved in planning and execution of movements but does not primarily contribute to spatial attention or neglect syndromes.

Option B: Right Parietal Lobe - While the right parietal lobe is involved in spatial processing, hemineglect is more specifically associated with damage to the right temporo-parietal junction, rather than the parietal lobe alone.

Option C: Left temporo-parietal lobe - Damage to the left temporo-parietal lobe does not typically cause hemineglect, as the right hemisphere plays a dominant role in spatial awareness.

Key Takeaway:

question_text: A 65-year-old male with a history of Diabetes and hypertension presents to the OPD with complaints of diplopia and squint. On examination secondary deviation is seen to be more than primary deviation. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
B) Incomitant squint

Incomitant squint is a squint in which the angle of deviation differs depending upon the direction of gaze i.e, amount of deviation varies in different directions of gaze. There are many type of incomitant squints (paralytic, restrictive, 'A' & 'V' pattern), however the most common type is Paralytic squint and the word incomitant squint is usually used for paralytic squint. Therefore, I will explain paralytic squint here Paralytic squint is the most common type of squint in adults. Paralytic squint is the strabismus resulting from complete or incomplete paralysis of one or more extraocular muscles. There are many causes like neurogenic (e.g. meningitis, cranial nerve palsy etc.), myogenic (myopathies), or neuromuscular junction lesions.

Symptoms of paralytic squint are :-

i) Diplopia : It is the main symptom. It is most marked in the direction of action of paralysed muscle. For example in left rectus palsy, the maximum diplopia occurs when patient tries to see horizontally on left side and in left superior oblique palsy (causes Dextrodepression) diplopia is maximum when patient tries to look downward and right.

It is worth noting here that in diplopia, if the images are separated horizontally it is probable that either a lateral or a medial recuts is affected; when the images are separated vertically or the image is tilted (torsion) it is likely that one or more of the vertical recti or the tilted (torsion) it is likely that one or more of the vertical recti or the obliques are affected.

ii) Other symptoms : Confusion, nausea & vertigo, ocular deviation,loss of stereopsis.

Signs of paralytic squint are :-

i) Secondary deviation is more than primary deviation:- Primary deviation is the deviation in the affected eye and is away from the action of paralysed muscle. Secondary deviation is the deviation of normal eye seen under cover, when the patient is made to fix with the squinting eye.

ii) Restriction of ocular movements

iii) Compensatory head posture :- Patients with a paralytic squint move their head such that the eyes occupy a position in the orbit where the angle of squint is minimal and this can avoid confusion and diplopia. Head is turned towards the action of paralysed muscle.

When the horizontal recti (medial or lateral) are affected, the characteristic posture is a turn of the face to right or left, e.g. in left lateral rectus palsy the head is turned to the left and in left medial recuts palsy the head is turned to the right. When a vertical rectus (superior or inferior) or an oblique muscle is affected, a tilt of the head to the right or left with depression or elevation of the chin is adopted to reduce both the vertical deviation and rotation, e.g in superior oblique palsy (dextrodepression of left eye is affected) the head is tilted to left so that the left eye can see down and medially.

iv) There is false projection or orientation

v) There is no amblyopia and visual acuity is normal as paralytic squint develops in adults when visual acuity has already develop

Incorrect Options Explanation:

(B) Incomitant Squint - While paralytic squint is a type of incomitant squint, the term incomitant squint is a broader category that includes both paralytic and restrictive squints. The defining feature of incomitant squint is that the angle of deviation varies depending on the direction of gaze, but since paralytic squint is the most common form of incomitant squint in adults, paralytic squint is the best answer.

(C) Restrictive Squint - Restrictive squint occurs due to mechanical restriction of ocular movements, such as in thyroid eye disease, trauma (orbital fractures), or fibrosis of extraocular muscles. Unlike paralytic squint, restrictive squint does not usually show secondary deviation greater than primary deviation.

(D) Pseudo Squint - Pseudo squint refers to a false appearance of strabismus without actual ocular misalignment, commonly seen in infants due to epicanthal folds or wide nasal bridges. It is not associated with diplopia or restricted ocular movements, making it an incorrect choice.

Key Takeaways:

  • Paralytic squint is the most common type of incomitant squint in adults.
  • Secondary deviation is greater than primary deviation, a key distinguishing feature of paralytic squint.
  • Diplopia is maximal in the direction of action of the affected muscle.
  • Diabetes and hypertension are common risk factors due to their association with cranial nerve palsies.
  • Restrictive squint is due to mechanical restriction, while pseudo squint is only a false appearance of strabismus.

question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of oculomotor nerve palsy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Limited abduction (inability to move the eye outward) is a feature of abducens nerve palsy. This movement is controlled by the lateral rectus muscle, which is innervated by the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI).

Extraocular muscles: Innervation and actions

  • All extraocular muscles are supplied by oculomotor nerve (CN III), except the lateral rectus and superior oblique.
  • Superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV), while abducens nerve (CN VI) supplies the lateral rectus.

Oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III)

  • Motor nerve originating from the midbrain, at the oculomotor sulcus on the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle.
  • Course: It emerges from the midbrain and passes through the cavernous sinus to the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.

Components:

  • Oculomotor nucleus (Somatic component, General Somatic Efferents):
    • Superior division: Supplies levator palpebrae superioris and superior rectus
    • Inferior division: Supplies medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique.
  • Edinger-Westphal nucleus (Parasympathetic component, General Visceral Efferents):
    • Supplies sphincter pupillae (pupil constriction) and ciliaris muscle

Features of oculomotor nerve palsy:

  • Ptosis: Results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) muscle. (Option D ruled out)
  • Ocular deviation: In third-nerve palsy, the lateral rectus and superior oblique are spared, and their unopposed action causes the eye to assume a "down and out" position (exotropia). (Option A ruled out)
  • Pupil involvement: In compressive lesions, the pupil becomes fixed and dilated due to sphincter pupillae paralysis, and ciliary muscle paralysis causes loss of accommodation. In ischemic lesions, the pupil is usually spared. (Option B ruled out)
  • Diplopia: Arises from ocular misalignment, but is often masked by ptosis, which prevents the patient from noticing double vision.

Note:

  • The nerve fibers innervating the pupillary muscles are located superficially in the nerve trunk and pial blood vessels supply these fibers.
  • The main trunk of the fibers is supplied by the vasa vasorum.
  • Diabetic and hypertensive microangiopathy will affect the vasa vasorum and thus spare the pupillary fibers.
  • Hence, pupil-sparing 3rd nerve lesions are seen with ischemic lesions such as diabetes, hypertension, or arteriosclerotic disease.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526112/

question_text: A patient 35 year old presented with R hypertropia which increases on right gaze and on tilting head on right shoulder. What is the muscle involved
explanation:
This is based on park 3 step test

Step 1 find out which muscle are paralysed making R eye hypertropic: R SO, R IR and L IO and L SR(so we are now having four muscles)

Step 2 in which gaze hypertropia increase: that is Right gaze here, so select Right sided muscles which take eyes on right side: R IR and L IO

The field of action of an extraocular muscle is the direction in which the muscle's primary action is the greatest. In each of the cardinal positions of gaze, there is always one muscle in each eye which is the prime mover. When measuring a deviation in side gazes for step two of the three-step test, the examiner is attempting to isolate specific muscles which are the prime movers in those gazes.

Here R IR is pure depressor when right eye looks on right side, Also LIO is pure elevator when left eye looks on right side.

Hence either of these 2 muscles are the culprit ones.

So now we are left with two muscles only

Step 3: In which head tilt hypertropia increases: so here it is in Right head tilt: hence the correct one is LIO

During right head tilt as a compensation Right eye undergoes an intortion(done by superiors - SIN pneumonic) → and Superiors are not in the option for right eye so this muscle is eliminated

Similarly for right head tilt left eye undergoes extortion(done by obliques → and here we have an option of L IO, so this muscle is paralysed as this action is not happening and hence hypertropia is increased.

During head tilt to the right, the otolith system sends impulses to the extraocular muscles that assist in torsion, because the eyes need to adjust to the right head tilting by a compensatory rotation to the left around the anteroposterior (Y) axis. On right head tilt, the left eye excyclotorts due to the actions of the left inferior oblique and the left inferior rectus. Likewise, the right eye incyclotorts due to the actions of the right superior oblique and the right superior rectus

If the deviation increases on right head tilt and decreases on left head tilt, then the right superior oblique is implicated as the paretic culprit. The reason for this is because the right superior oblique and right superior rectus muscles work together to incyclotort the right eye in right head tilt. Usually they offset each other in terms of vertical movement, because the superior oblique depresses and the superior rectus elevates. However, in the case of the paretic right superior oblique, the elevating action of the right superior rectus is unopposed and causes an increase in the right hypertropia when the patient tilts his or her head to the right. The deviation is decreased or absent when the head is tilted towards the unaffected eye because the superior oblique muscle is not stimulated in the affected eye, but it is stimulated in the unaffected eye.

question_text: Which muscle serves as the yoke muscle for the right lateral rectus?
explanation:
Explanation:

Yoke muscles are paired extraocular muscles (one from each eye) that act together to produce conjugate (coordinated) eye movements. This concept is explained by Hering's Law of Equal Innervation, which states that equal neural impulses are sent to a pair of yoke muscles during gaze.

  • The right lateral rectus abducts the right eye.
  • Its yoke partner for rightward gaze is the left medial rectus, which adducts the left eye
  • Together, they allow both eyes to move simultaneously to the right (dextroversion).

Sherrington's Law of Reciprocal Innervation complements this by stating that when one muscle contracts, its antagonist relaxes (e.g., when lateral rectus contracts, ipsilateral medial rectus relaxes).

Yoke muscles

  • Yoke muscles are pairs of extraocular muscles, one in each eye, that work together to ensure coordinated eye movements in the same direction.
  • These muscles function according to Hering's Law of Equal Innervation, which ensures that corresponding muscles in both eyes receive equal neural impulses for synchronised movement.
  • Hering's Law of Equal Innervation would mean that the right lateral rectus (yoke muscle) should be balanced with the left medial rectus (vs Sherrington's law: This law about reciprocal innervation states that increased innervation and contraction of a muscle is automatically associated with reciprocal decrease in innervation and contraction of its antagonist).
  • The yoke muscle pairs facilitate various eye movements:


Explanation of Other Options:

Right superior oblique (Option A): Primarily responsible for intorsion, depression, and abduction, but it does not act as a yoke partner for horizontal gaze of the right lateral rectus.

Left lateral rectus (Option C): Abducts the left eye. In rightward gaze, the left eye needs to adduct, not abduct, so it is not the yoke muscle.

Right medial rectus (Option D): Adducts the right eye, which is the opposite action of the right lateral rectus. It is an antagonist, not a yoke partner.

question_text: A person comes with paralysis of all extraocular muscles. What is the most probable site of lesion?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • All extraocular muscles are supplied by the oculomotor nerve except the superior oblique, which is supplied by the trochlear nerve, and the lateral rectus, which is supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI).
  • The oculomotor nerve arises from the upper midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus, the trochlear nerve arises from the lower midbrain, and the abducens nerve arises from the pons at the pontomedullary junction.
  • Therefore, a midbrain lesion can paralyze most extraocular muscles except the lateral rectus, while a lesion affecting the entire brainstem can paralyze all extraocular muscles. Hence, among the given options the midbrain is the most accurate answer.

Explanation of other options:

Upper medulla (Option A): Lesion of upper medulla affects cranial nerves IX and X, causing dysphagia and loss of gag reflex; eye movements remain normal.

Lower medulla (Option B): Lower medulla is associated with the hypoglossal nucleus, which if affected can lead to paralysis of the tongue muscles only.

question_text: A 60-year-old male presents with left eyelid drooping and experiencing double vision. Upon examination, it was observed that the pupil in the affected eye was dilated. The following eye movement examination was conducted. Which nerve is most likely injured in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image is suggestive of paralytic strabismus. The patient presents with a left eye that is deviated down and out in primary gaze, associated with ptosis, diplopia, and impaired elevation and adduction. These findings are characteristic of oculomotor (third cranial nerve) palsy.

Features of third nerve palsy

  • Ptosis: Due to paralysis of the LPS (levator palpebrae superioris) muscle
  • The eyeball is deviated down and outwards (due to actions of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles).
  • The pupil is fixed and dilated (due to paralysis of the sphincter pupillae muscle)
  • Ocular movements are restricted
  • Accommodation is completely lost (due to paralysis of the ciliary muscle)
  • Crossed diplopia is elicited by raising the eyelid.
  • Absence of Both direct and consensual reflexes in the affected eye
  • These compensatory head postures are motor adaptations used to minimise the effects of double vision
    • Horizontal Diplopia: The patient often tilts the head downward
    • Vertical Diplopia: The head is positioned with the chin either raised or lowered
    • Torsional Diplopia: The head is tilted sideways

Explanation of other options:

Optic nerve injury (Option A): Injury to the optic nerve would cause visual disturbances.

Trochlear Nerve injury (Option C): This pertains to a neurological disorder where damage to the fourth cranial nerve, or trochlear nerve, results in vertical diplopia when the patient looks down and inability to DEPRESS the eye completely.

Abducens Nerve injury (Option D): This is a disorder marked by the impairment of the sixth cranial nerve, resulting in lateral gaze palsy.

question_text: What is the diagnosis based on the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis shown in the diagram is Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO).

In INO, the lesion occurs in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). In the example provided, during leftward gaze, the right eye shows impaired adduction while the left eye demonstrates nystagmus during abduction. This indicates a lesion in the right MLF, which disrupts coordinated eye movement during left gaze, whereas rightward gaze remains normal. Typically, INO is characterized by impaired adduction on the side of the lesion and abduction of nystagmus in the contralateral eye

Horizontal eye movements are initiated by the horizontal gaze center, or paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF). The PPRF sends two main outputs:

  • To the ipsilateral sixth cranial nerve nucleus, producing abduction of the same-side eye.
  • The contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus, which relays the signal to the opposite third cranial nerve nucleus, causes adduction of the contralateral eye.

These two pathways from the PPRF coordinate to generate conjugate horizontal eye movements.

Explanations for other Options:

3rd cranial nerve palsy (Option B): Third cranial nerve (oculomotor) palsy causes ptosis, and the eye is typically deviated downwards and outwards, with slight torsion, due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles.

Horizontal gaze palsy (Option C): Horizontal gaze palsy results from a lesion in the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF). This produces an inability to move both eyes toward the side of the lesion, causing ipsilateral horizontal gaze weakness.

Thyroid eye disease (Option D): Thyroid eye disease (Graves orbitopathy) presents with lid retraction, lid lag, and proptosis, reflecting the effects of autoimmune orbital tissue inflammation and fibrosis..

question_text: A patient having a left sided head tilt. In examination there is right sided hypotropia, increase on dextroversion and right head tilt. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
To rule out SO palsy, The three-step test, also known as the Parks-Bielschowsky three-step test or the Parks-Helveston three-step test, is a diagnostic test used to identify which muscle is paretic in the case of an acquired hypertropia. This method uses the cover-uncover test, with or without the Maddox rod to measure the amount of deviation in different head positions. It was first described by Bielschowsky in 1935 and later popularized by Marshall M. Parks. This test is most useful in diagnosing superior oblique palsies in clinical practice.

The three-step test may also be used to diagnose the less common inferior oblique or vertical rectus muscle palsy and can be used in differentiating DVD from other vertical strabismus. It is designed for the diagnosis of a single paretic vertical muscle and is unreliable when there are multiple paretic muscles or in restrictive strabismus. This test may also help in identifying if a superior rectus palsy is true or simulated in a patient with an inhibitional palsy of the contralateral antagonist.

The first step in the three-step test is to determine which eye is hypertropic in primary position.

The second step is to determine whether the hypertropia increases on right or left gaze.

The third step is determination if the hypertropia increases upon left head tilt or right head tilt. For this test, the ophthalmologist or orthoptist uses prisms to quantify the hypertropia in primary position, side gazes, and head tilts. Alternatively, it can be helpful to quantify smaller deviations using prisms and a Maddox rod or red filter

Superior rectus palsy is a disorder associated with dysfunction of the cranial nerve 3rd (oculomotor nerve), which is responsible for causing contraction of the superior rectus muscle's to perform the primary action of elevating the eye, causing the cornea to roll superiorly (i.e., turn upward).

The inability of an eye to turn upward results in convergent strabismus or esotropia of which the primary symptom is diplopia (commonly known as double vision) in which the two images appear side-by-side.

Contraction of superior rectus causes the eye to simultaneously move in several planes; elevation in the transverse plane, adduction in the vertical plane and internal rotation (intorsion) in the anteroposterior plane. These contrasting movements are achieved because the muscle fibers course obliquely; at a 23 degrees angle with the median plane of the eye.

However, when shifting the gaze upwards, the eyeball can elevate without the movements of adduction and internal rotation. That's because superior rectus usually contracts together with the inferior oblique muscle, whose fibers and pull are oriented in a way to oppose the adduction and internal rotation produced by the superior rectus and decrease them to a minimum. Thus, the end result is elevation of the eyeball.

Being connected with the levator palpebrae superioris via check ligament, superior rectus contraction is also associated with the elevation of the upper eyelid.

The inability of an eye to turn upward results in convergent strabismus or esotropia of which the primary symptom is diplopia (commonly known as double vision) in which the two images appear side-by-side.

Incorrect Options:

Option A: Right Superior Oblique (RSO) Palsy: Would cause right hypertropia, not hypotropia.

Option B: Left Superior Oblique (LSO) Palsy: Would cause left hypertropia, not right hypotropia.

Option C: Right Inferior Oblique (RIO) Palsy: Would cause right hypertropia, not hypotropia.

Key Takeaway: Right superior rectus palsy presents with right hypotropia, worsened in right gaze and right head tilt, diagnosed via the three-step test.

question_text: Which pair of yoke muscles is responsible for levodepression?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Right Superior Oblique (RSO) and the Left Inferior Rectus (LIR) coordinate to produce levodepression: downward movement of both eyes during leftward gaze.

  • Right Superior Oblique (RSO): Depresses the right eye when it is abducted (turned outward).
  • Left Inferior Rectus (LIR): Depresses the left eye when it is adducted (turned inward).
    Together, these muscles ensure synchronized downward movement of the eyes toward the left.

Yoke Muscles:

  • Yoke muscles are pairs of extraocular muscles, one in each eye, that act together to move the eyes in the same direction.
  • They function according to Hering's Law of Equal Innervation, which ensures that corresponding muscles in both eyes receive equal neural signals for coordinated movement.
  • Sherrington's Law contrasts this by stating that contraction of a muscle is accompanied by reciprocal relaxation of its antagonist.

Examples of Yoke Muscle Coordination:

  • Horizontal Gaze:
    • Leftward gaze (Levoversion): Left lateral rectus + Right medial rectus
    • Rightward gaze (Dextroversion): Right lateral rectus + Left medial rectus
  • Vertical Gaze:
    • Upward gaze (Elevation): Right and Left superior rectus + Right and Left inferior oblique
    • Downward gaze (Depression): Right and Left inferior rectus + Right and Left superior oblique
  • Convergence: Both medial rectus muscles contract to move the eyes inward for near vision.

Explanation of Other Options:

LSO and RIR (Option A): LSO contributes to depression but not for levodepression; RIR also depresses the eye but does not pair with LSO for leftward downward gaze.

RIO and LIR (Option C): RIO aids in elevation, not depression; although LIR contributes to depression, this pair does not generate levodepression.

LIO and RIR (Option D): LIO helps elevate the eye rather than depress it; RIR contributes to depression but does not pair with LIO for levodepression.

question_text: Which nerve ganglion is involved in pathology of HZO?
explanation:
Pathology of HZO/ VZV:

After an infection with chickenpox in childhood or youth, the virus lies dormant to appear later, particularly in elderly people with depressed cellular immunity, causing the clinical picture of zoster. In zoster ophthalmicus, the chief focus of infection is the Gasserian ganglion from where the virus travels down one or more of the branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve so that its area of distribution is marked out by rows of vesicles or the scars left by them, exactly as in herpes zoster in other parts of the body.

Geniculate Ganglion: Facial Nerve ganglion with sensory + motor component- supply to Orbicularis oculi muscle of eye

Inferior Cervical ganglion: Sympathetic supply to eye

question_text: A patient experiences a sudden, painful loss of vision in one eye. Which anatomical structure is most likely affected?
explanation:
Explanation:

Sudden, painful vision loss in a single eye usually indicates a lesion affecting the optic nerve, most commonly due to optic neuritis. Patients often report pain on eye movement, and the condition is frequently associated with demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis.

Types of Optic Neuritis:

Clinical Features:

  • Monocular, sudden, and progressive visual loss
  • Pain worsened by eye movement
  • Impaired colour vision
  • Visual field defects: central or centrocecal scotoma
  • Reduced contrast sensitivity
  • Uhthoff's phenomenon: transient visual blurring with heat or exercise
  • Pulfrich phenomenon: depth perception changes for moving objects

Explanation for other options:

Optic chiasma (Option B): Lesions here typically produce bitemporal hemianopia by affecting crossing nasal fibres. These do not cause sudden monocular vision loss or pain.

Optic tract (Option C): Damage leads to homonymous hemianopia, affecting the same visual field in both eyes. Painful monocular vision loss is not characteristic of optic tract lesions.

Visual cortex (Option D): Lesions in the visual cortex may result in cortical blindness or homonymous visual field defects. Vision loss is usually bilateral or symmetric, and pain is absent, unlike in optic neuritis.

question_text: By definition, Papilledema is related to which condition?
explanation:
• Papilloedema is defined as oedema of the optic disc or nerve head due to raised intracranial pressure.
  • Since the optic nerve is enclosed up to the lamina cribrosa within the meningeal sheaths common to the brain, and the subarachnoid and subdural spaces around the nerve are freely continuous with those around the brain, any rise in the intracranial pressure becomes equally evident around the nerve.
  • When this occurs, the subarachnoid space sometimes becomes so distended that it is ampulliform just behind the globe.
  • As a result, oedema develops at the optic disc: this is a purely hydrostatic, noninflammatory phenomenon.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding management of traumatic optic neuropathy is/are incorrect?
option_a: CT scan imaging will be required to identify type and level of lesion
option_b: High dose IV Methyl prednisolone therapy is effective in all cases
option_c: Optic nerve sheath decompression is required in all cases
explanation:
• Visual loss is maximum from the time of impact but can also be delayed by a few hours and progress over the next few days.
  • Computed tomography helps diagnose a fracture of the canal with a bone fragment pressing on the nerve and the presence of a haemorrhage in the nerve sheath.
  • If either of these conditions is present, surgical intervention is required.
  • High-dose intravenous corticosteroids (dexamethasone 3–5 mg/kg/day or methylprednisolone 20–30 mg/kg/day) have been reported to be effective in some cases.
  • Visual evolved potentials help in monitoring the response to therapy, particularly when the visual acuity is very poor.
  • Treatment should be instituted within 24–48 hours and if improvement occurs, oral steroid therapy can be started and the drug tapered off over the next 2 weeks.
  • If there is no visual improvement within 1–2 days of this high dose of steroids and particularly if there is worsening, presumably from oedema or haemorrhage within the nerve or canal, optic canal decompression through either a transethmoidal or transfrontal approach should be performed.
  • Another indication for optic canal decompression in such cases is if vision worsens as the steroids are tapered off.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: Optic radiation arises from
explanation:
VISUAL PATHWAY

The visual impulse travels from the rods and cones of the retina via the bipolar cells, ganglion cells and nerve fiber layer to the optic nerve. Beyond the optic nerve lies the optic chiasma.

At the level of the chiasma, the fibers from the nasal part of the retina cross over to the other side whereas the temporal fibers continue on the same side.

Beyond the optic chiasma is the optic tract. Thus, the optic tract contains the temporal fibers from the same side and the nasal fibers which have crossed over from the opposite side.

Beyond the optic tract, the fibers pass through the lateral geniculate body and the optic radiation. The optic radiation thus contains the same fibers as the optic tract.

Finally the fibers reach the occipital lobe of the brain where the primary visual area(area no 17)and the accessory visual areas(18 and 19) are located.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg: 910-911.

question_text: A patient presents with perimetry report showing left sided Centrocecal scotoma and right sided superotemporal quandrantanopia. Likely site of lesion is
explanation:
JUNCTIONAL SCOTOMA OF TRAQUAIR

  • Lesion affecting the proximal part of the optic nerve results in a rare type of visual field defect consisting of ipsilateral central/centrocecal scotoma and contralateral upper temporal hemianopia. This is called junctional scotoma of Traquair.

Lesions in the visual pathway

Lesions in the visual pathway are associated with typical defects of the visual field depending upon the fibers present in that part of the pathway.(Note: Lesions involving the nasal fibers result in temporal field defect. Lesions involving the temporal fibers result in nasal field defect)

  • Optic nerve: Central scotoma, Centrocecal scotoma, Altitudinal scotoma
  • Optic chiasma: Central lesion: Bitemporal hemianopia Peripheral lesion: Binasal hemianopia
  • Optic tract: Incongruous homonymous hemianopia
  • Optic radiation: Congruous homonymous hemianopia
  • Occipital cortex: Congruous homonymous hemianopia with central sparing
  • Lesion in temporal lobe: Superior quadrantanopia or Pie in the sky
  • Lesion in the parietal lobe: Inferior quadrantanopia or Pie on the floor
  • Proximal part of the optic nerve: Junctional scotoma of Traquair

Reference: Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, Pg: 904-905.

question_text: Combined paralysis of 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerve results in
explanation:
Total ophthalmoplegia:

  • In this condition all extraocular muscles including LPS and intraocular muscles, viz., sphincter pupillae, and ciliary muscle are paralysed.
  • It results from combined paralysis of third, fourth and sixth cranial nerves.
  • It is a common feature of orbital apex syndrome and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

External ophthalmoplegia:

  • In this condition, all extraocular muscles are paralysed, sparing the intraocular muscles. It results from lesions at the level of motor nuclei sparing the Edinger-Westphal nucleus.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia:

  • In this condition there is lesion of the medial longitudinal bundle. It is the pathway by which various ocular motor nuclei are linked.
  • Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is characterized by: defective action of medial rectus on the side of lesion, horizontal nystagmus of the opposite eye and defective convergence.
