question_text: Which is the commonest cause of inherited optic atrophy?
explanation:
• Dominant optic neuropathy (kjer autosomal dominant optic atrophy).
  • This is the commonest inherited optic nerve disorder. Insidious visual loss begins between the ages of 5 and 10 years.
  • Visual impairment varies from mild to moderate. Visual acuity may remain 6/6 (20/20) or be as low as 6/60 (20/200); very rarely is it worse.
  • Though bilateral, involvement of the two eyes may be asymmetrical.
  • There is loss of colour perception and a central scotoma.
  • Visual loss may progress for a few years but generally stabilizes after the teens.
  • There are generally no associated neurological abnormalities.
  • The differential diagnosis is from: (i) a compressive lesion, (ii) vitamin deficiency, (iii) drug effect and (iv) toxin-induced neuropathy.
  • A detailed family history should be taken. In case other family members are unaffected or unavailable for examination, a CT or MRI scan should be performed to rule out the possibility of a compressive lesion.

 Recessive optic neuropathy

  • Simple: Isolated optic atrophy of recessive inheritance represents a rare entity described in the older literature where, in most instances, detailed investigations were not done and not well documented clinically.
  • Cases reported were of optic atrophy with consanguineous parentage.
  • Complicated hereditary optic neuropathy: This is a group of disorders with recessive inheritance with several other associated systemic features.
  • These include bilateral optic atrophy with polyneuropathy (e.g. Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease), inborn errors of metabolism or spinocerebellar degenerations with mild mental deficiency (Friedrich and Marie ataxia and Behr syndrome).
  • Also included in this category is Wolfram syndrome, which is characterized by the association of early childhood-onset optic atrophy with diminished vision (usually in the 6/60 [20/200] range) and juvenile diabetes.
  • It is recalled by the mnemonic DIDMOAD (diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and deafness).

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: Which of the following does not cause a Horizontal gaze palsy?

Lesions of MLF result in internuclear ophthalmoplegia, INO (option A). Lesions affecting MLF along with ipsilateral PPRF or abducens nucleus produce one and half syndrome. (option B)

Contralateral frontal eye field lesions or ipsilateral pontine lesions produce horizontal gaze palsy by affecting voluntary conjugate gaze. Option D Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome (Progressive Supranuclear Palsy), however, primarily causes supranuclear ophthalmoplegia where vertical gaze is affected first (especially downgaze) followed later by horizontal gaze and reflex eye movements are preserved. Since it does not produce a primary horizontal gaze palsy, it is the correct answer.(Option C)

question_text: Which of the following anti-tubercular drugs is not implicated in development of toxic optic neuropathy?
explanation:
• Ethambutol is an oral chemotherapeutic agent used in the treatment of tuberculosis and may produce an optic neuritis resulting in reduced visual acuity and colour vision, and, eventually, a central scotoma.
  • Neuritis is reversible when the drug is discontinued but patients should be examined monthly during the early stages of therapy.
  • A dose of 15 mg/kg/day is the upper limit of safety with regard to eye complications.
  • Optic atrophy has also been reported following the use of other antitubercular drugs such as streptomycin and isonicotinic hydrazide (INH).
  • No specific treatment is useful, apart from discontinuation of the drug. Gradual recovery to a variable extent has been known to occur.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy is incorrect?
option_a: Males are more frequently involved than females
option_b: Vision loss is progressive through life
explanation:
Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy

  • This form of retrobulbar neuropathy usually commences at about the 20th year of life.
  • Initially, cyanide intoxication was believed to play a part but a genetic aetiology has now been established.
  • Transmission of the disease is generally through an unaffected female to all offspring, but the disease manifests mostly in males, although females are also affected.
  • Hereditary transmission is by mitochondrial DNA, which resembles the X-chromosomal inheritance pattern in some ways, in that all daughters are carriers and it is transmitted by women to all offspring, but while 50%–70% of sons and 10%–15% of daughters manifest the disease, none of the sons can transmit it.
  • It differs from sex-linked (X-linked) transmission in that affected males do not pass on the trait or carrier state to any of their offspring—sons or daughters.
  • Although it is an inherited disorder, in some cases a positive family history is not elicited.
  • Members of the same family often show identical peculiarities in the progress of the disease.
  • Males are affected 5–10 times more commonly than females and the ratio varies from country to country.
  • It usually occurs in young males 15–30 years of age and sometimes manifests in females in the second or third decade of life.
  • Vision generally fails rapidly at first; the loss is gradual thereafter but remains stationary or slowly improves after 6 months.
  • Visual loss is painless and both the eyes are always involved, although one may precede the other by a period varying from a few days to 18 months.
  • In two-thirds of the cases, there is a central or centrocaecal scotoma, either partial for colours or also for white.
  • The peripheral field is usually normal, but concentric contraction or sector-shaped defects may occur.
  • Total and permanent colour blindness has been known to follow.
  • The central scotoma generally persists, but progressive constriction of the field to complete blindness is rare.
  • The fundus is at first normal or there is slight swelling with blurring of the edges of the disc.
  • Small, telangiectatic blood vessels are seen near the disc which do not leak on fluorescein angiography.
  • In the later stages, after several months, optic atrophy ensues, with pallor confined to the temporal side or involving the whole disc.
  • Apart from headache, the general health is good.
  • Several Leber-specific gene mutations have been identified and if facilities for testing are available, blood samples can be sent for an analysis.
  • No specific treatment is effective and genetic counselling should be offered.

Reference: Parson’s diseases of the Eye-Chap 18 – Diseases of the Optic Nerve

question_text: Papilledema can be seen in which stage of HTN Retinopathy
explanation:
Grading of hypertensive retinopathy:

Keith and Wegner(1939) have classified hypertensive retinopathy changes into following four grades:

  • Grade I: It consists of mild generalized arteriolar attenuation, particularly of small branches, with broadening of the arteriolar light reflex and vein concealment.
  • Grade II: It comprises marked generalized narrowing and focal attenuation of arterioles associated with deflection of veins at arteriovenous crossings (Salu's sign).
  • Grade III: This consists of Grade II changes plus copper-wiring of arterioles, banking of veins distal to arteriovenous crossings (Bonnet sign), tapering of veins on either side of the crossings(Gunn sign) and right-angle deflection of veins(Salu's sign). Flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates are also present.
  • Grade IV: This consists of all changes of Grade III plus silver-wiring of arterioles and papilledema.

Reference: A.K. Khurana, 5th edition, Page no. 258.

question_text: A histologic specimen from an enucleated eye of a child with leukocoria shows the findings in the image below. This structure, along with Homer Wright rosettes and fleurettes, is characteristic of which diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image displays classic Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, which are a specific histopathological finding for retinoblastoma. These structures represent a form of photoreceptor differentiation, consisting of a ring of cuboidal tumor cells surrounding a quiet central lumen.

The presence of these rosettes, along with other differentiating structures like the more primitive Homer Wright rosettes (neuroblastic rosettes with a fibrillary core) and the well-differentiated fleurettes (clusters of cells showing advanced photoreceptor features), confirms the diagnosis of retinoblastoma.

Explanation of Other Options:

Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option B): This tumor shows malignant mesenchymal cells, including characteristic "strap cells" or rhabdomyoblasts which may have cross-striations. It does not form rosettes.

Optic Nerve Glioma (Option C): This is a low-grade astrocytoma. Histology shows spindle-shaped pilocytic astrocytes and characteristic eosinophilic structures called Rosenthal fibers. It does not form rosettes.

Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (Option D): This malignant eyelid tumor shows lobules of pleomorphic cells with foamy, lipid-rich cytoplasm (sebaceous differentiation) and often exhibits comedonecrosis. It does not form rosettes.

explanation:

question_text: A 40-year-old female with gradual bilateral vision decrease, eyelid skin lesions and history of mild electric shock. What is your probable diagnosis for decrease in vision?

explanation:
Explanation:

Atopic dermatitis is associated with shield-shaped anterior subcapsular cataracts (shield cataract). Although posterior subcapsular cataracts are more frequent in atopic dermatitis, shield-shaped cataracts are more specific. Proposed mechanisms: topical/systemic steroids, intense eye rubbing (mechanical), intraocular inflammation, and altered antioxidant defenses (e.g., decreased inducibility of superoxide dismutase).

Traumatic cataract (Option A): Possible with history of significant trauma but context here suggests atopy.

Shield cataract due to electric shock (Option C): Electric shock can cause cataract but presentation/context less consistent.

Radiational cataract (Option D): Associated with ionising radiation exposure.

Key Takeaways:

Shield-shaped anterior subcapsular cataract → classically associated with atopic dermatitis (consider steroid use and eye rubbing).

question_text: Which of the following represents the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults?
explanation:
Explanation:

Malignant choroidal melanoma is the leading primary intraocular malignancy in adults. It arises from the choroid, the eye’s vascular layer, and can lead to vision loss. Typically, it presents as a pigmented mass within the choroid. Early diagnosis and management are essential to reduce the risk of metastasis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Retinoblastoma (Option A): This is the most common intraocular malignancy in children, usually under 5 years of age, and originates from the retina rather than the choroid.

Reticulum cell sarcoma (Option C): Also known as histiocytic lymphoma, this tumor can involve the eye but is far less frequent as a primary intraocular malignancy compared with choroidal melanoma.

Neurofibroma (Option D): A benign tumor originating from Schwann cells of nerve tissue. While it may involve ocular structures in neurofibromatosis, it is not classified as a primary intraocular malignancy.

question_text: Trilateral Retinoblastoma is BL retinoblastoma with
explanation:
• Heritable(hereditary, germline) retinoblastoma accounts for 40%.
  • In heritable retinoblastoma one of the pair of alleles of RB1 is mutated in all the cells in the body.
  • When a further mutagenic event('second hit' according to the 'two-hit' hypothesis proposed by Knudson) affects the second allele, the cell may then undergo malignant transformation.
  • Because of the presence of the mutation in all cells, a large majority of these children develop bilateral and multifocal tumours.
  • Heritable retinoblastoma patients also have a predisposition to non-ocular cancers such as pinealoblastoma ('trilateral retinoblastoma', which occurs in up to 10%, usually before the age of 5), osteosarcomas, soft tissue sarcomas and melanomas; each of these tends to occur in a particular age group.
  • The risk of a second malignancy is about 6% but this increases five-fold if external beam irradiation has been used to treat the original tumour, the second tumour tending to arise within the irradiated field.

question_text: Chemotherapy agents for retinoblastoma:
explanation:
The standard chemotherapy regimen for retinoblastoma consists of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide. These drugs are used in systemic chemotherapy, often in 6 cycles, to shrink tumors before focal treatments like laser therapy or cryotherapy.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  • B. Vinblastine, Etoposide, and Bleomycin: This combination is commonly used for germ cell tumors (e.g., testicular cancer, Hodgkin’s lymphoma) and is not a standard regimen for retinoblastoma.
  • C. Vinblastine, Vincristine, and Etoposide: While vincristine and etoposide are used in retinoblastoma treatment, vinblastine is not a standard choice for this disease.
  • D. Vinblastine, Vincristine, and Cisplatin: Cisplatin is sometimes used as an alternative, but vinblastine is not a mainstay of retinoblastoma treatment.

Key Takeaway:

The most commonly used chemotherapy regimen for retinoblastoma is a combination of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide.

Some of the chemo drugs used to treat retinoblastoma include:

  1. Carboplatin
  2. Cisplatin
  3. Vincristine
  4. Etoposide

question_text: In a three-year-old boy, his parents have noticed a progressive decline in coordination over the last six months. During a physical examination, a growth resembling a cauliflower is observed in the left eye, along with leukocoria and the absence of a red reflex. Microscopic analysis of the sample reveals the presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which gene is associated with this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical findings - leukocoria, cauliflower-like intraocular mass, absent red reflex, and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histology - are classic for retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.

  • Age: Typically presents before 5 years
  • Common features: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), strabismus, painful red eye, poor vision
  • Fundus exam: White, elevated retinal mass (endophytic, exophytic, or mixed)
  • Histopathology: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (specific), Homer-Wright rosettes (pseudo-rosettes), undifferentiated tumor cells, necrosis, calcification
  • Imaging: CT shows calcification (90%), MRI useful for optic nerve/extraocular spread

Genetics: Mutation in RB1 gene on chromosome 13q14 Most specific histopathological feature of retinoblastoma is Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, which are rosettes with a central lumen as shown in the diagram below.

Explanation of Other Options:

ATP7B gene (Option B): This gene is mutated in Wilson's disease, a disorder of copper metabolism causing hepatic and neurological symptoms. It does not cause retinoblastoma.

Rhodopsin gene (Option C): Mutations here are associated with retinitis pigmentosa, a progressive degenerative retinal disease with night blindness and peripheral vision loss. Not linked to retinoblastoma.

FBN1 gene (Option D): This gene is mutated in Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder affecting the heart, skeleton, and eyes (ectopia lentis, myopia). Not related to intraocular tumors.

  • The fissure is located inferiorly on the globe, and the corresponding inferior iris (Fig. 2-10), choroidal, and optic nerve colobomas can be seen with failure of the fissure to close properly.
  • Lid colobomas are different from these colobomas, as they do not occur from failure of the fetal fissures.

question_text: Which nucleus is formed in the first 3 months of gestation?
explanation:
Embryonic nucleus is formed in the first 3 months of gestation.

The crystalline lens of the eye is made up of a lens capsule, lens epithelium and lens fibres.

Lens fibres are protein fibres arranged closely in concentric layers. They are formed throughout life so that the oldest fibres are at the center and the newest fibres are most superficial. Hence, the lens fibres may be divided into -

  • Nucleus: It is the central part of the lens containing the older fibres. It is again subdivided into -
    • Embryonic nucleus → Formed in the first 3 months of gestation.
    • Fetal nucleus → Formed till birth.
    • Infantile nucleus → Formed from birth to puberty.
    • Adult nucleus → Formed after puberty.
  • Cortex: It is the peripheral part containing the new formed fibres.

Reference: Yanoff and Duker Ophthalmology, 4th Edition, Page Number 329-330.

question_text: Most common distant site of metastasis in malignant melanoma
explanation:
Uveal melanoma is a malignant tumor arising from melanocytes in the uveal tract (iris, ciliary body, or choroid). It is the most common primary intraocular tumor in adults with an age-adjusted incidence of 6 per million. The choroid is the most common site involved and gives rise to 90% of uveal melanomas. Melanomas arising within the ciliary body comprise 7% and melanomas of the iris account for 2%

There is a strong tendency for metastasis, particularly to the liver, and prognosis is poor when the tumor has disseminated.

question_text: A 60-year-old male patient presents to the ophthalmology clinic with complaints of visual disturbances. He reports that he is unable to see on the left side from his left eye and the left side from his right eye. However, he notices that his central vision remains intact and unaffected. The patient denies any recent trauma or other significant medical history. What is the most likely visual deficit that the patient is experiencing?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient has loss of the left visual field in both eyes → this is a homonymous hemianopia (same side of visual field lost in both eyes). Preservation of central (macular) vision indicates macular sparing, a pattern classically caused by lesions of the visual cortex (usually in the occipital lobe) supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA).
  • Macular sparing occurs because the macular cortical representation often receives dual blood supply (PCA ± middle cerebral artery territory), protecting central vision despite cortical injury.

Visual Pathway:

  • Temporal fibers carry impulses from the Nasal field, and Nasal fibres carry the Temporal field.


Explanation of Other Options:

Quadrantanopia (Option A ruled out): Quadrantanopia is loss of a single quarter of the visual field (e.g., superior or inferior quadrant), not the entire left half of both eyes. The patient has hemianopia, not a quadrant defect.

Heteronymous hemianopia (Option B ruled out): Heteronymous (bitemporal) hemianopia results from lesion at the optic chiasm and produces loss of the temporal visual fields of both eyes - not the left fields of both eyes. This is therefore inconsistent.

Homonymous hemianopia (Option C ruled out): A plain homonymous hemianopia fits loss of the same side in both eyes, but does not specify macular sparing. Because central vision is preserved in this patient, the more precise diagnosis is homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (cortical lesion), so Option C is incomplete.

question_text: Vortex vein invasion is seen in
explanation:
The vortex veins drain the venous system of the choroid, ciliary body, and iris (see Fig 1-19). Each eye contains 4-7 (or more) veins. One or more veins are usually located in each quadrant and exit 14-25 mm from the limbus, between the rectus muscles. The ampullae of the vortex veins are 8-9 mm from the ora serrata and are visible by indirect ophthalmoscopy.

Uveal melanoma is the most frequent primary intraocular malignancy in adults. It can affect any part of the uveal tract, but choroidal melanoma is predominant, while iris and ciliary body melanomas are less common. vortex vein invasion is seen in uveal melanoma and associated with a choroidal location, large tumour size, spindle cell bias, presence of extracellular matrix loops/networks and genetic markers. A higher proportion of patients with vortex vein invasion progress to develop liver metastasis

Reference: Kanski's Synopsis of Clinical Ophthalmology (Fourth edition) 2023, Page 322

question_text: 4Δ Base Out Test is mainly used for
explanation:
The purpose of this test is to detect a small central suppression scotoma(or foveal suppression)

Instruct the patient to look at a distance target. A 4-BO prism is quickly placed over one eye and the movements of both eyes are observed.

Interpretations

Normal response: Both eyes shift in the direction of the apex of the prism followed by convergence of the eye without prism. A sudden displacement of the image onto the parafovea in the eye with the prism will cause the eye to shift toward the apex of the prism. Due to Hering's law of equal innervation, the fellow eye will shift the same magnitude in the same direction at the same time. The fellow eye will then converge to avoid diplopia.

Foveal suppression scotoma: Failure of the eye with the prism to shift in response to prism placement indicates suppression of ipsilateral eye. Failure of the contralateral eye to converge indicates foveal suppression of the contralateral eye.

Reference: kanski, 8th Edition.

explanation:
MRI is contraindicated in magnetic FB of eye.
